Create src/lib/firebase.ts: import { initializeApp } from 'firebase/app'; import { getMessaging, getToken, onMessage } from 'firebase/messaging'; const firebaseConfig = { // Your Firebase config apiKey: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_FIREBASE_API_KEY, authDomain: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_FIREBASE_AUTH_DOMAIN, projectId: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_FIREBASE_PROJECT_ID, storageBucket: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_FIREBASE_STORAGE_BUCKET, messagingSenderId: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_FIREBASE_MESSAGING_SENDER_ID, appId: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_FIREBASE_APP_ID, }; const app = initializeApp(firebaseConfig); export const messaging = typeof window !== 'undefined' ? getMessaging(app) : null; export const getFCMToken = async (): Promise<string | null> => { if (!messaging) return null; try { const token = await getToken(messaging, { vapidKey: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_FIREBASE_VAPID_KEY, }); return token; } catch (error) { console.error('Error getting FCM token:', error); return null; } }; export const onMessageListener = () => new Promise((resolve) => { if (!messaging) return; onMessage(messaging, (payload) => { resolve(payload); }); });

Create src/hooks/useSocket.ts: import { useEffect, useRef, useState } from 'react'; import { io, Socket } from 'socket.io-client'; interface Notification { id: string; title: string; body: string; data?: any; timestamp: string; } export const useSocket = (serverUrl: string, userId?: string) => { const [socket, setSocket] = useState<Socket | null>(null); const [connected, setConnected] = useState(false); const [notifications, setNotifications] = useState<Notification[]>([]); const socketRef = useRef<Socket | null>(null); useEffect(() => { if (!userId) return; const socketInstance = io(serverUrl); socketRef.current = socketInstance; setSocket(socketInstance); socketInstance.on('connect', () => { setConnected(true); console.log('Connected to server'); }); socketInstance.on('disconnect', () => { setConnected(false); console.log('Disconnected from server'); }); socketInstance.on('authenticated', (data) => { console.log('Authenticated:', data); }); socketInstance.on('notification', (notification: Notification) => { setNotifications((prev) => [notification, ...prev]); // Show browser notification if permission granted if ('Notification' in window && Notification.permission === 'granted') { new Notification(notification.title, { body: notification.body, icon: '/icon-192x192.png', }); } }); return () => { socketInstance.disconnect(); socketRef.current = null; }; }, [serverUrl, userId]); const authenticate = async (fcmToken?: string) => { if (socket && userId) { socket.emit('authenticate', { userId, fcmToken }); } }; const sendNotification = (data: { recipientId: string; title: string; body: string; type: 'realtime' | 'push' | 'both'; data?: any; }) => { if (socket) { socket.emit('sendNotification', data); } }; return { socket, connected, notifications, authenticate, sendNotification, clearNotifications: () => setNotifications([]), }; };

Create src/app/page.tsx: 'use client'; import { useEffect, useState } from 'react'; import { useSocket } from '@/hooks/useSocket'; import { getFCMToken } from '@/lib/firebase'; export default function Home() { const [userId, setUserId] = useState(''); const [fcmToken, setFcmToken] = useState(null); const [recipientId, setRecipientId] = useState(''); const [notificationTitle, setNotificationTitle] = useState(''); const [notificationBody, setNotificationBody] = useState(''); const [notificationType, setNotificationType] = useState<'realtime' | 'push' | 'both'>('both'); const { connected, notifications, authenticate, sendNotification, clearNotifications } = useSocket( process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_BACKEND_URL || 'http://localhost:5000', userId ); useEffect(() => { // Request notification permission if ('Notification' in window && Notification.permission === 'default') { Notification.requestPermission(); } // Get FCM token getFCMToken().then(setFcmToken); }, []); const handleLogin = () => { if (userId.trim()) { authenticate(fcmToken || undefined); } }; const handleSendNotification = () => { if (recipientId && notificationTitle && notificationBody) { sendNotification({ recipientId, title: notificationTitle, body: notificationBody, type: notificationType, }); // Clear form setRecipientId(''); setNotificationTitle(''); setNotificationBody(''); } }; return (

Create test/load-test.js: const io = require('socket.io-client'); const BACKEND_URL = process.env.BACKEND_URL || 'http://localhost:5000'; const NUM_CLIENTS = 100; const TEST_DURATION = 60000; // 1 minute async function runLoadTest() { console.log(`Starting load test with ${NUM_CLIENTS} clients...`); const clients = []; const startTime = Date.now(); // Create clients for (let i = 0; i < NUM_CLIENTS; i++) { const client = io(BACKEND_URL); clients.push(client); client.on('connect', () => { client.emit('authenticate', { userId: `user-${i}` }); }); client.on('notification', (data) => { console.log(`Client ${i} received notification: ${data.title}`); }); } // Send notifications periodically const interval = setInterval(() => { const sender = Math.floor(Math.random() * NUM_CLIENTS); const recipient = Math.floor(Math.random() * NUM_CLIENTS); clients[sender].emit('sendNotification', { recipientId: `user-${recipient}`, title: 'Load Test Notification', body: `Message from user-${sender} to user-${recipient}`, type: 'realtime' }); }, 100); // Stop after test duration setTimeout(() => { clearInterval(interval); clients.forEach(client => client.disconnect()); console.log(`Load test completed in ${Date.now() - startTime}ms`); process.exit(0); }, TEST_DURATION); } runLoadTest();

Create comprehensive test suites: // services/user-service/test/user.service.spec.ts import { Test, TestingModule } from '@nestjs/testing'; import { getRepositoryToken } from '@nestjs/typeorm'; import { Repository } from 'typeorm'; import { ConflictException, NotFoundException } from '@nestjs/common'; import { UserService } from '../src/user/user.service'; import { User } from '../src/user/entities/user.entity'; import { UserRole } from '@ecommerce/types'; describe('UserService', () => { let service: UserService; let repository: Repository<User>; const mockRepository = { findOne: jest.fn(), create: jest.fn(), save: jest.fn(), find: jest.fn(), update: jest.fn(), remove: jest.fn(), }; beforeEach(async () => { const module: TestingModule = await Test.createTestingModule({ providers: [ UserService, { provide: getRepositoryToken(User), useValue: mockRepository, }, ], }).compile(); service = module.get<UserService>(UserService); repository = module.get<Repository<User>>(getRepositoryToken(User)); }); afterEach(() => { jest.clearAllMocks(); }); describe('create', () => { it('should create a new user successfully', async () => { const createUserDto = { email: 'test@example.com', password: 'password123', firstName: 'John', lastName: 'Doe', }; const expectedUser = { id: '1', ...createUserDto, hashedPassword: 'hashedPassword', role: UserRole.CUSTOMER, createdAt: new Date(), updatedAt: new Date(), }; mockRepository.findOne.mockResolvedValue(null); mockRepository.create.mockReturnValue(expectedUser); mockRepository.save.mockResolvedValue(expectedUser); const result = await service.create(createUserDto); expect(result).toEqual(expectedUser); expect(mockRepository.findOne).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ where: { email: createUserDto.email }, }); expect(mockRepository.save).toHaveBeenCalled(); }); it('should throw ConflictException if user already exists', async () => { const createUserDto = { email: 'test@example.com', password: 'password123', firstName: 'John', lastName: 'Doe', }; mockRepository.findOne.mockResolvedValue({ id: '1', email: 'test@example.com' }); await expect(service.create(createUserDto)).rejects.toThrow(ConflictException); }); }); describe('findOne', () => { it('should return user if found', async () => { const userId = '1'; const expectedUser = { id: userId, email: 'test@example.com', firstName: 'John', lastName: 'Doe', role: UserRole.CUSTOMER, }; mockRepository.findOne.mockResolvedValue(expectedUser); const result = await service.findOne(userId); expect(result).toEqual(expectedUser); expect(mockRepository.findOne).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ where: { id: userId }, select: ['id', 'email', 'firstName', 'lastName', 'role', 'createdAt', 'updatedAt'], }); }); it('should throw NotFoundException if user not found', async () => { const userId = '1'; mockRepository.findOne.mockResolvedValue(null); await expect(service.findOne(userId)).rejects.toThrow(NotFoundException); }); }); });

Detail 168 Architecture Execution Continuous Integration PREPARATION (Sprint 0) 5 "Have log retention policy to support trace whole log for every sing request (e.g. Add Guid identifier for logs of each request)" (Backend) Implement a correlation ID (e.g., X-Request-ID) that is passed from the Flutter app on every API call, and log this ID in all backend services. Detail 169 Architecture Execution Continuous Integration DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) 5 "Once an environment is created, it will be never changed.The only way to apply changes is by re-creating the whole environment with scripts and using a pipeline." (Infra/DevOps) Adopt an immutable infrastructure pattern where servers/containers are replaced on change, not updated in-place (e.g., standard for Kubernetes/serverless). Detail 170 Architecture Execution Continuous Monitoring RELEASE 5 "When an issue has raised from infrastructure monitoring systems, there are actions that are automatically triggered that will not require manual intervention in order to fix it (for feasible services)." (Infra) Implement autoscaling (e.g., HPA in Kubernetes) to automatically handle high CPU/memory load. Detail 171 Architecture Execution Continuous Monitoring RELEASE 5 "When an issue has raised from application monitoring systems, there are actions that are automatically triggered that will not require manual intervention in order to fix it." (Infra) Configure alerts (e.g., in Datadog) that can trigger automated rollbacks (e.g., via ArgoCD) if a new deployment shows a critical error spike. Detail 172 Architecture Execution Continuous Monitoring RELEASE 5 "The business monitoring tools are measuring key indicators (conversion rate, number of sold items, average response time, etc). If there is an issue with any of those key indicators the team will get notified." (Business) Set up alerts on the business dashboard (e.g., "Signups dropped 50% in 1 hour") that notify the PO and tech leads. Detail 173 Architecture Execution Continuous Monitoring RELEASE 5 "The team can take actions when business monitoring is showing any problems (for example, contact the business responsible)." Create a process: If a business KPI alert fires, the PO and tech lead immediately huddle to triage (is it a bug, marketing issue, or external factor?). Detail 174 Architecture Execution Continuous Monitoring RELEASE 5 There is flexibility to create new business indicators and dashboards whenever it is necessary. (Business/Data) Ensure the data pipeline to the business dashboard (Looker) is flexible and that the PO/Data Analyst can add new charts without developer intervention. Detail 175 Architecture Management Technical Backlog management DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) 5 "The team's maturity on Architecture Process is known by the entire company, project sponsors and stakeholders;There is a plan to manage, spread and scale knowledge beyond the project boundaries." Share the results of the monthly "Architecture Maturity Review" with the engineering manager and project sponsors. Detail 176 Architecture Validation Architecture Evaluation RELEASE 5 "The PO and stakeholders recognize that the code quality is satisfactory through the metrics and goals that are shared with them." Share the SonarQube "Maintainability" rating and Firebase "Crash-free users" metric with the PO and stakeholders regularly. Detail 177 Architecture Validation Non-functional Requirements Validation DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) 5 The developers are responsible for delivering the security test scripts as part of the story scope. For stories handling sensitive data, the "Definition of Done" should include "Security test cases considered" (e.g., "What if I send a 'null' token?"). Detail 178 Architecture Validation Non-functional Requirements Validation DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) 5 The PO and stakeholders recognize that the security of the application is satisfactory through the metrics and goals that are shared with them. Conduct an external penetration test (pen test) annually. Share the summary report (showing 0 critical vulnerabilities) with the PO. Detail 179 Architecture Validation Non-functional Requirements Validation DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) 5 The developers are responsible for delivering the performance test scripts as part of the story scope. For stories in critical areas (e.g., a new list screen), the "Definition of Done" should include "Performance profiled in debug mode" and a screenshot of the DevTools. Detail 180 Architecture Validation Non-functional Requirements Validation RELEASE 5 "The PO and stakeholders recognize that the performance of the application is satisfactory through the metrics and goals that are shared with them." Share the Firebase Performance Monitoring dashboard (showing App Start Time, Slow Renders) with the PO weekly to build confidence. Detail

Item: 11 | Architecture Definition | Architecture & Coding Guidance | PREPARATION (Sprint 0) | 1 | "The foundation of the application architecture is defined and documented (E.g.
application layers, frameworks, logging mechanism, error handling mechanism, transaction control mechanism)." | Create architecture diagrams (e.g., C4 model) showing Flutter app layers (Data, Domain, Presentation), state management (e.g., BLoC), navigation, and error handling. | | This guide outlines how to define and document the core architectural foundations of your Flutter application during the initial setup phase.
documents.s: Completing Item 11: Define and Document Architecture Foundation

documents.t: A clear architectural foundation ensures consistency, maintainability, and scalability. It provides a blueprint for all developers on how to build and structure different parts of the application.

Define Application Layers: Choose a Layering Strategy: A common and effective approach for Flutter is Clean Architecture or a variation, typically involving: Presentation Layer: Contains Widgets, Screens, and state management logic (e.g., Blocs, ViewModels). Responsible for displaying UI and handling user input. Domain Layer: Contains business logic, Use Cases (interactors), and core business entities/models. This layer should be independent of Flutter and any specific framework. Data Layer: Contains Repository implementations, Data Sources (API clients, local database access), and data transfer objects (DTOs). Responsible for fetching and storing data. Define Dependencies: Establish clear dependency rules (e.g., Presentation depends on Domain, Domain depends on Data interfaces, Data implements Domain interfaces). Presentation should not directly access Data. Select Core Frameworks/Libraries: State Management: Formally choose one primary state management library (e.g., flutter_bloc, riverpod, provider). Document why it was chosen (ADR - Item 128). Navigation: Choose a navigation strategy (e.g., Navigator 2.0 with go_router or auto_route, or basic Navigator 1.0). Dependency Injection: Select a DI/Service Locator package (e.g., get_it, injectable). Networking: Choose an HTTP client library (e.g., dio, http). Local Storage: Select a solution if needed (e.g., shared_preferences, sqflite, hive, isar). Define Core Mechanisms: Logging: Choose a logging library (e.g., logger, logging). Define logging levels (DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR). Specify what should be logged (e.g., BLoC state changes, API requests/responses, errors). Document how logs are collected (e.g., print to console in debug, send to Firebase Crashlytics/Datadog in release). Error Handling: Define standard exception types (e.g., ApiException, NetworkException, DatabaseException). Specify how errors propagate through layers (e.g., Data layer catches specific exceptions and returns a Failure object or throws a domain-specific exception). Document how errors are presented to the user (e.g., snackbars, dialogs, inline messages). Specify how critical errors are reported (e.g., FirebaseCrashlytics.instance.recordError). Transaction Control (if applicable): Primarily relevant for backend/database interactions. Document how atomicity is ensured if multiple operations must succeed or fail together. For mobile, this might relate to offline data synchronization logic. Create Architecture Diagrams: High-Level Overview: Use a simple diagram (like C4 model's System Context or Container diagram) showing the Flutter app interacting with backend APIs and third-party services. Layer Diagram: Create a diagram illustrating the chosen application layers (Presentation, Domain, Data) and the dependency flow between them. Component/Feature Diagram (Example): Show how a specific feature (e.g., Login) is implemented across the layers, including key classes (Widget, Bloc, UseCase, Repository, DataSource). Document Everything: Create a central "Application Architecture" section in your team's wiki (Confluence). Include the diagrams. Describe each layer's responsibility. List the chosen frameworks and libraries with links. Detail the logging, error handling, and other core mechanisms. Provide small code snippets demonstrating the standard implementation patterns (e.g., how to create a Bloc, how to handle an error from a repository). Communicate and Review: Present the architecture document to the entire development team. Ensure everyone understands the principles and patterns. Use this document during onboarding and code reviews to enforce consistency.

Item: 6 | Architecture Definition | Architecture & Coding Guidance | SETUP | 1 | "There is a tools will be used to check code style (lint, ESlint, PHPcs, stylecopaalyzers, etc)." | Configure the CI pipeline to run flutter analyze on every PR. Integrate SonarQube/SonarCloud for static analysis. | | This guide details how to set up and enforce automated code style and static analysis checks for your Flutter project.
documents.s: Completing Item 6: Implement Code Style Tools

documents.t: flutter analyze (Dart Analyzer & Linter): Purpose: Checks for Dart language errors, warnings, and stylistic issues based on rules defined in analysis_options.yaml. This is the primary tool for enforcing Dart/Flutter best practices. Setup: Ensure you have a well-defined analysis_options.yaml file (see Item 3). Developers should run flutter analyze locally or rely on IDE integration (VS Code shows issues automatically). CI Integration: Add a step to your CI pipeline (e.g., GitHub Actions workflow) that runs on every Pull Request: - name: Analyze code run: flutter analyze --fatal-infos --fatal-warnings . The --fatal-infos and --fatal-warnings flags ensure the CI job fails if any issues are found, preventing merging of non-compliant code. dart format (Code Formatter): Purpose: Automatically formats Dart code according to official Dart style guidelines (handling whitespace, indentation, line wrapping, etc.). Ensures visual consistency. Setup: Developers should configure their IDE (VS Code) to "Format on Save" for Dart files. Line length can be configured in analysis_options.yaml (though sticking to the default of 80 is often recommended). CI Integration (Optional but Recommended): Add a step to check formatting in the CI pipeline: - name: Check formatting run: dart format --output=none --set-exit-if-changed . This command checks if any files would be changed by the formatter. If so, it exits with an error code, failing the build and indicating that the developer forgot to format their code before committing. SonarQube / SonarCloud (Static Analysis Platform): Purpose: Provides a more comprehensive analysis beyond basic linting. It tracks code smells, security vulnerabilities, code duplication, complexity (Cyclomatic Complexity), and test coverage over time. Offers dashboards and quality gates. Setup: Choose between self-hosted SonarQube or cloud-based SonarCloud. Configure a SonarQube project for your repository. Generate a sonar-project.properties file in your project root (example below). Generate test coverage reports (lcov.info) using flutter test --coverage. CI Integration: Add steps to your CI pipeline (run after tests): # Example sonar-project.properties sonar.projectKey=your_project_key sonar.projectName=Your Project Name sonar.sources=lib sonar.tests=test sonar.language=dart sonar.coverage.exclusions=**/*.g.dart,**/*.freezed.dart # Exclude generated # Path to the lcov report generated by flutter test --coverage sonar.dart.coverage.reportPath=coverage/lcov.info # Path to the analysis report (optional, can help SonarQube) # sonar.dart.analysis.reportPath=analysis_report.json # Example CI Steps (GitHub Actions) - name: Run tests and generate coverage run: flutter test --coverage # Download and run SonarScanner CLI (or use dedicated actions) - name: SonarCloud Scan uses: SonarSource/sonarcloud-github-action@master env: GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} # Needed to decorate PRs SONAR_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SONAR_TOKEN }} # Set in GitHub secrets # Add with: args: '-Dsonar.verbose=true' for debugging Quality Gates: Configure Quality Gates in SonarQube/SonarCloud (e.g., "Coverage on New Code < 80%", "New Blocker Issues > 0") to fail the CI build if quality degrades.

By implementing these tools, especially flutter analyze and dart format enforced in CI, you establish a strong baseline for code quality and consistency. SonarQube adds deeper insights and tracking over time.

Item: 3 | Architecture Definition | Architecture & Coding Guidance | SETUP | 1 | "Coding (includes Unit Testing) practices, coding conventions are documented, explained and followed." | Define and commit a strict analysis_options.yaml file. Document required state management patterns (e.g., BLoC, Riverpod) and widget naming conventions. | | This guide explains how to establish, document, and enforce coding conventions and practices for your Flutter project, ensuring code consistency and maintainability.

Leverage Static Analysis (analysis_options.yaml): Foundation: Start with the official package:lints/recommended.yaml or package:flutter_lints/flutter.yaml. Strict Rules: Create a project-specific analysis_options.yaml file in the project root. Include the recommended set and add stricter rules: include: package:flutter_lints/flutter.yaml analyzer: errors: # Treat common issues as errors missing_required_param: error parameter_assignments: error # Treat info-level lints as warnings (or errors if desired) avoid_print: warning prefer_const_constructors: warning # Add more specific lints... exclude: - '**/*.g.dart' # Exclude generated files - '**/*.freezed.dart' linter: rules: # Enable additional rules beyond the recommended set # Formatting & Style always_declare_return_types: true prefer_single_quotes: true prefer_final_fields: true # Potential Errors avoid_returning_null_for_void: true # Add many more based on team preference... See [https://dart.dev/tools/linter-rules](https://dart.dev/tools/linter-rules) Commit: Commit this analysis_options.yaml file to your Git repository. CI Enforcement: Configure your CI pipeline to run flutter analyze --fatal-infos --fatal-warnings . to fail the build if any rules are violated. Document Higher-Level Practices: Static analysis covers syntax, but not architecture or patterns. Create a "Coding Conventions" page on your wiki. State Management: Explicitly state the chosen state management solution (e.g., BLoC, Riverpod, Provider). Provide links to official documentation and simple project examples of its usage (e.g., how to create a Bloc, how to provide it, how to consume it in a widget). Forbid other state management patterns unless approved by the architect. Project Structure: Define the expected folder structure (e.g., lib/features/feature_name/data, lib/features/feature_name/domain, lib/features/feature_name/presentation). Naming Conventions: Files: snake_case.dart (e.g., login_screen.dart, user_repository.dart). Classes/Enums/Typedefs: PascalCase (e.g., LoginBloc, UserState). Variables/Methods: camelCase (e.g., userName, fetchUserData()). Constants: camelCase or UPPER_SNAKE_CASE (be consistent). Widgets: Be specific (e.g., LoginButton, UserProfileCard). Widget Design: Promote composition over inheritance. Encourage splitting large widgets into smaller, reusable ones. Define guidelines for when to use StatelessWidget vs. StatefulWidget. Error Handling: Specify the standard approach (e.g., using Either type, specific Exception classes, logging errors to Firebase Crashlytics). Unit Testing: Mandate unit tests for business logic (Blocs, UseCases, Repositories). Specify the use of mocking libraries (e.g., mocktail, mockito). Provide examples of common test setups. (Covered more in Item 15). Explain and Review: Introduce the conventions during team meetings and onboarding. Enforce conventions during Pull Request reviews. Link back to the wiki page in comments (e.g., "Please rename this variable according to our camelCase convention: [link]"). Iterate: Revisit the conventions periodically (e.g., quarterly) to refine them based on team feedback and new language features or best practices.

Item: 18 | Architecture Definition | Communication & Alignment | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 1 | "All the development policies, rules, conventions and plans are communicated to the team (e.g. SCM policy, Backup/restore plan, coding style convention, NFR metric targets, Unit test implementation process…)" | Hold an onboarding session for all new team members covering the SCM policy, analysis_options.yaml rules, and testing strategy. | | This guide focuses on ensuring that all documented development policies, conventions, and plans are effectively communicated to and understood by the entire development team. Documentation alone is not enough.

Consistency: Ensures everyone follows the same standards, leading to a more predictable and maintainable codebase. Efficiency: Reduces confusion and rework caused by developers not being aware of established practices. Onboarding: Accelerates the integration of new team members. Buy-in: Explaining the why behind policies increases team acceptance and adherence.

Identify Key Documents: Gather links to all the essential policy and guideline documents created in previous steps: SCM Policy / Git Branching Strategy (Item 1, 7, 8) Local Environment Setup Guide (Item 2) Coding Conventions (analysis_options.yaml, wiki page) (Item 3) Special Use-Case Guidance (Item 4) Technical Debt Management Process (Item 5) Unit Testing Guidance (Item 15) NFR Targets (Item 10, 30) Backup/Restore Plans (Item 12, 13) Communication Guidelines (Item 17) Architecture Foundation Document (Item 11) CI/CD Process Overview Establish Communication Mechanisms: Onboarding: Dedicated Session: Schedule a 1-2 hour onboarding session specifically focused on development processes for every new team member. Walkthrough: Actively walk through the key documents (SCM, Coding Conventions, Testing, CI/CD flow). Don't just send links. Explain the rationale behind the rules. Q&A: Allow ample time for questions. Pairing: Assign an onboarding buddy to help the new member navigate the processes during their first sprint. Team Meetings: Initial Rollout: When a new major policy or convention is introduced (e.g., switching state management libraries), dedicate time in a team meeting or a specific workshop to explain it, discuss it, and answer questions. Reminders/Refreshers: Briefly revisit key policies (e.g., testing expectations, tech debt process) during regular team syncs or retrospectives if adherence seems to be slipping. Documentation Hub: Create a central "Development Hub" or "Team Handbook" page on your wiki. This page should contain links to all the individual policy documents. Keep it organized and easy to navigate. Make this the single source of truth that team members are directed to. Code Reviews: Use PR comments as a micro-communication channel. When providing feedback related to a convention, link directly to the relevant section in the documentation. (e.g., "Per our Testing Guide, Blocs should be tested using bloc_test. Please refactor this test.") Chat Channels: Post announcements about significant updates to policies in the main technical chat channel, including a link to the updated document and a summary of changes. Ensure Understanding: Check for Comprehension: During onboarding or team meetings, ask clarifying questions to ensure people understand, rather than just asking "Any questions?". Seek Feedback: Actively solicit feedback on the policies and documentation. Are they clear? Are they practical? Use retrospectives to gather input. Policies should be living documents. Accessibility: Ensure all documentation is easily discoverable and searchable within your team's wiki or repository. Avoid burying important information in scattered documents or chat history. By actively communicating and reinforcing these policies through multiple channels, you significantly increase the likelihood that they will be understood and followed consistently by the team.

Item: 19 | Architecture Definition | Communication & Alignment | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 1 | "All big technical solutions and decisions are being communicated to the client.
If there is any big change in the architecture, the change is also properly communicated to the stakeholders." | Maintain a lightweight "Architecture Decision Record" (ADR) log for major choices (e.g., choice of state management) and review with stakeholders. | | This guide focuses on the process for communicating significant technical solutions, decisions, and architectural changes to relevant stakeholders, including the client or Product Owner.
documents.s: Completing Item 19: Communicate Big Technical Decisions

documents.t: Transparency: Keeps stakeholders informed about the technical direction and potential impacts (cost, timeline, risk, NFRs). Alignment: Ensures technical solutions meet business needs and constraints. Buy-in: Secures support for major technical investments or changes. Risk Management: Surfaces potential concerns or dependencies early. Documentation: Provides a record of why certain decisions were made (useful for future reference).

Not every technical choice needs stakeholder review. Focus on decisions with significant impact, such as: Choice of Core Frameworks: State management, navigation, database. Major Architectural Pattern Changes: Moving from MVC to Clean Architecture, introducing offline support. Significant Third-Party Integrations: Adding a payment gateway, integrating a new major SaaS platform. Major Refactoring Efforts: Rewriting a core module, upgrading Flutter major versions. Decisions with Significant NFR Impact: Choices affecting performance, security, or scalability noticeably. Solutions with High Cost/Timeline Implications. Deviations from Established Standards.

Identify the Need for Communication: When a "big" technical decision point arises (as defined above), the Tech Lead or Architect should flag it for stakeholder communication. Document the Decision (ADR - Architecture Decision Record): Use a lightweight ADR format (Item 128 provides more detail on creating ADRs internally). A simplified version for stakeholders might include: Title: A short, descriptive title (e.g., "Adopt Riverpod for State Management"). Status: Proposed / Accepted / Deprecated. Context: What is the problem or requirement being addressed? (Keep it concise and business-friendly). Options Considered: Briefly list the main alternatives explored (e.g., BLoC, Provider, Riverpod). Decision: Clearly state the chosen solution. Rationale: Explain why this option was chosen. Focus on benefits relevant to stakeholders (e.g., "Faster development for complex features," "Improved testability leading to fewer bugs," "Better performance"). Acknowledge key trade-offs (e.g., "Slightly steeper learning curve for new developers initially"). Consequences/Impact: Outline the expected impact on timeline, cost, NFRs, user experience, or future development. Store ADRs in a shared, accessible location (Confluence, Git repo). Determine the Audience and Communication Method: Audience: Who needs to know? (Product Owner? Client technical contact? Project Manager? Business stakeholders?) Tailor the message to the audience. Method: For awareness/minor impact: An email summary or a brief mention in a regular status meeting might suffice, linking to the ADR. For significant impact/requiring buy-in: Schedule a dedicated meeting. For ongoing visibility: Maintain an up-to-date ADR log. Prepare the Communication: Focus on the "Why" and "Impact": Stakeholders care less about deep technical details and more about how the decision affects the project's goals, timeline, budget, and quality. Use Clear Language: Avoid excessive jargon. Use analogies if helpful. Visualize: Use simple diagrams to illustrate architectural changes if appropriate. Be Honest about Trade-offs: Acknowledge risks or downsides; don't just sell the benefits. Conduct the Communication: Meeting: Present the context, options, decision, rationale, and impact. Allow ample time for questions and discussion. Clearly state if you are seeking approval or just providing information. Email/Async: Provide a concise summary and link to the full ADR for details. Invite questions. Follow Up: Update the ADR status (e.g., to "Accepted") based on the outcome. Document any key discussion points or action items arising from the communication. Communicate Changes: If a previously communicated decision changes significantly, repeat the communication process to inform stakeholders of the revision and the reasons for it. By proactively communicating significant technical decisions, you build trust and ensure better alignment between the technical team and business stakeholders.

Item: 17 | Architecture Definition | Communication & Alignment | SETUP | 1 | Business & Technical communication channels are faciliated and used effectively. | Establish and document primary communication channels (e.g., Google Chat/Slack for technical, separate channel for Biz/Tech alignment). | | This guide outlines how to establish, document, and encourage the effective use of communication channels for both technical and business discussions within your project team.
Clear channels prevent information silos, reduce noise, ensure messages reach the right audience, and facilitate quicker decision-making.

Identify Communication Needs: Technical Team (Devs, QA, Architect): Needs channels for daily syncs, code discussions, PR reviews, CI/CD alerts, technical questions, troubleshooting. Business & Technical Alignment (PO, Architect, Tech Lead, possibly stakeholders): Needs channels for backlog refinement discussions, NFR clarifications, major technical decision reviews, roadmap alignment, demo feedback. Whole Team (including PO, Stakeholders): Needs channels for major announcements, sprint demos, urgent issues. Alerts & Monitoring: Needs automated channels for build failures, deployment notifications, production alerts. Choose Appropriate Tools: Real-time Chat: Slack or Google Chat are standard. Project Management: Jira, Asana, Trello (for ticket-specific comments). Documentation: Confluence, GitHub Wiki, Notion. Video Conferencing: Google Meet, Zoom, Teams. Email: For formal communication, external stakeholders, or less urgent matters. Establish Specific Channels/Groups: Within your Chat Tool (e.g., Slack/Google Chat): #proj-mobile-tech (or similar): For day-to-day technical discussions, questions, pairing requests among Devs and QA. Keep it focused on code/implementation. #proj-mobile-biz-tech (or similar): For discussions involving the Product Owner, Tech Lead, Architect regarding requirements, priorities, and high-level technical implications. #proj-mobile-alerts (or similar): Automated messages only. CI/CD build status, deployment notifications, production monitoring alerts (from Datadog, Firebase Crashlytics). Discourage manual posting here. #proj-mobile-general (or #proj-announce): For wider team announcements, demo links, important process changes. Project Management Tool (Jira): Use comments within specific tickets for questions/clarifications related to that specific piece of work. Documentation Tool (Confluence): Use comments on wiki pages for feedback or questions about that specific document. Define Channel Etiquette and Purpose: Create a "Communication Guidelines" page on your wiki. For each channel/tool, define: Purpose: What kind of communication belongs here? Audience: Who is typically in this channel? Expected Response Time: (e.g., "Real-time chat for quick questions, expect response within hours. Use Jira comments for ticket specifics.") Dos and Don'ts: (e.g., "Do use threads in chat for focused discussions. Don't @channel or @here unless urgent. Do link Jira tickets when discussing specific work.") Meeting Cadence: List recurring meetings (Daily Standup, Refinement, Retrospective, Demo) and their purpose. Facilitate Effective Use: Lead by Example: Tech leads, architects, and POs should use the correct channels and follow the guidelines. Gentle Correction: If discussions stray into the wrong channel, gently guide them back (e.g., "This seems like a detailed technical discussion, let's move it to #proj-mobile-tech?"). Integrate Tools: Set up integrations to automatically post build status, Jira updates, or monitoring alerts to the designated channels. Review Periodically: During retrospectives, ask if communication channels are working effectively or if adjustments are needed. Document and Onboard: Ensure the "Communication Guidelines" page is linked from the main project onboarding document. Explain the channel structure and expectations to new team members. By clearly defining and facilitating these channels, you create a more organized and efficient communication flow for the entire project team.

Item: 2 | Architecture Definition | Architecture & Coding Guidance | SETUP | 1 | All needed softwares and tools (include versions) for the local environment (developer environment) are documented. | Create an "Onboarding" doc listing the specific Flutter SDK version (e.g., via FVM), Dart SDK, VS Code extensions (Dart, Flutter), Android Studio, and Xcode. | | This guide details how to create comprehensive documentation for setting up the local development environment for your Flutter project. A smooth onboarding experience is crucial for new team members.
documents.s: Completing Item 2: Document Local Environment Setup

documents.t: Identify Required Tools and Versions: Flutter SDK: Specify the exact version required. Strongly recommend using FVM (Flutter Version Management) to easily switch and manage Flutter versions. Document how to install FVM (dart pub global activate fvm) and use it (fvm install <version>, fvm use <version>, fvm flutter ...). Dart SDK: This usually comes bundled with Flutter, but mention the expected version for clarity. IDE: Recommend VS Code as the primary IDE. List essential VS Code extensions: Dart, Flutter, bloc, Error Lens, Pubspec Assist. Include recommended settings (e.g., format on save). Platform SDKs: Android: Specify the required Android Studio version, Android SDK Platform versions (e.g., API 33, 34), and Build Tools version. Mention how to install via Android Studio's SDK Manager. iOS/macOS: Specify the required Xcode version (usually the latest stable from the App Store) and CocoaPods (sudo gem install cocoapods). Version Control: Git (mention required version if specific features are needed). Other Tools: List any project-specific tools like code generation helpers (build_runner), environment variable managers (flutter_config), or specific linters not included in the standard Flutter analysis. Create the Documentation: Create a dedicated "Developer Onboarding" or "Local Setup Guide" page on your team's wiki (Confluence) or as a SETUP.md file in the root of your Git repository. Structure the document logically (e.g., Prerequisites, macOS Setup, Windows Setup, IDE Configuration, Running the App). For each tool, provide: The exact name and required version. A link to the official installation guide. Clear, step-by-step installation instructions (especially for tools like FVM or platform SDKs). Use code blocks for commands. Configuration steps specific to your project (e.g., setting up dart-define variables, running initial code generation). Include Project-Specific Steps: How to clone the repository (git clone ...). How to install dependencies (fvm flutter pub get). How to run code generation if applicable (fvm flutter pub run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs). How to configure environment variables (e.g., creating a .env file, using dart-define). Explain the different environments (dev, staging, prod). How to run the app on an emulator/simulator (fvm flutter run). How to run tests (fvm flutter test). Add Troubleshooting Tips: Include common issues and their solutions (e.g., "Error: CocoaPods not found", "Gradle build failed"). Link to flutter doctor -v as a primary diagnostic tool. Maintain the Document: Assign an owner to keep the document up-to-date as tools or project requirements change. Review and validate the setup steps with every new team member during their onboarding.

Item: 1 | Architecture Definition | Architecture & Coding Guidance | SETUP | 1 | The SCM (Source Control Management) policy is defined and documented. | Document the Git branching strategy (e.g., Trunk-Based Development), PR templates, and merge requirements on the team's wiki (e.g., Confluence). | | This guide outlines the steps to define and document your Source Control Management (SCM) policy, specifically using Git for a Flutter project.
documents.s: Completing Item 1: Define and Document SCM Policy

documents.t: Choose a Branching Strategy: Recommendation: Start with Trunk-Based Development (TBD) for simplicity and faster integration, especially for smaller teams. Developers work on short-lived feature branches (feat/MEC-123-login-button) branched directly from main (the trunk). Branches are merged back to main frequently (at least daily). Releases are typically tagged directly on main or cut from main onto a short-lived release/v1.2.0 branch for final testing/hotfixes. Alternative: Gitflow (if required by organizational standards, but often overly complex for mobile apps). Decision: Select one strategy and stick to it. Document the Chosen Strategy: Create a new page on your team's wiki (e.g., Confluence, GitHub Wiki) titled "Git Branching Strategy". Clearly describe the chosen strategy (e.g., TBD). Include diagrams illustrating the branch flow. Define branch naming conventions (e.g., feat/TICKET-brief-description, fix/TICKET-brief-description, release/vX.Y.Z). Specify the lifetime of branches (e.g., "Feature branches should live less than 2 days"). Define Pull Request (PR) Requirements: On the same wiki page (or a linked one), detail the PR process: PR Template: Create a standard PR template (.github/pull_request_template.md or equivalent) that includes sections for: Description of changes. Link to the Jira ticket. Screenshots/Videos (for UI changes). Testing instructions for QA. NFR checklist (Performance, Security considerations). Reviewers: Specify who needs to review (e.g., "At least one other developer", "Tech Lead for complex changes"). CI Checks: List mandatory CI checks that must pass before merging (e.g., flutter analyze, flutter test, build_runner). Configure these as required status checks in GitHub/GitLab. Merge Policy: Define how PRs are merged (e.g., "Use Squash and Merge", "Do not merge if CI fails"). Communicate and Enforce: Share the link to the wiki page with the team. Discuss the policy during onboarding for new members. Configure branch protection rules in GitHub/GitLab to enforce the policy (require PRs, require status checks, require reviews).

Item: 22 | Architecture Definition | Communication & Alignment | SETUP | 1 | The overall Architecture diagram is shared and explained to all project stakeholders. | Pin the high-level architecture diagram (showing Flutter app, BFE, 3rd party services) in the main developer chat channel and review it during kickoff. | | This guide details how to create, share, and explain a high-level architecture diagram to ensure all project stakeholders (technical and non-technical) have a common understanding of the system's main components and interactions.
documents.s: Completing Item 22: Share Overall Architecture Diagram

documents.t: Common Understanding: Provides a visual overview that's easier to grasp than detailed documentation. Context: Helps everyone understand how the Flutter mobile app fits into the larger ecosystem. Scope Definition: Clarifies the boundaries of the system and its key external dependencies. Onboarding: Gives new team members (including non-technical ones) a quick overview of the system landscape.

Define the Scope and Audience: Audience: All project stakeholders - Developers, QA, PO, Project Manager, key business sponsors, potentially external partners. Level of Detail: Keep it high-level. Focus on major components and interactions, not internal implementation details. The C4 Model's System Context Diagram or Container Diagram level is appropriate. Avoid showing individual classes or functions. Identify Key Components: The Flutter Mobile App itself. The primary Backend For Frontend (BFF) or API Gateway the app communicates with. Major backend microservices (if relevant and known to stakeholders). Key third-party services (Authentication provider like Firebase Auth/Auth0, Payment Gateway like Stripe, Analytics like Firebase Analytics, Push Notifications like FCM/APNS, Mapping Service like Google Maps). Databases (represent as a single box, e.g., "Application Database"). External systems the backend might integrate with (e.g., CRM, ERP). Types of Users (e.g., "Mobile User," "Administrator"). Choose a Diagramming Tool: Use a tool that allows easy creation and sharing: Miro / Mural Lucidchart draw.io (diagrams.net) - Free Excalidraw - Simple, hand-drawn feel PlantUML / Mermaid (Code-based, good for version control) Create the Diagram: Layout: Place the mobile app centrally or prominently. Notation: Use simple boxes for components and arrows for interactions. Label boxes clearly. Label arrows with the purpose of the interaction (e.g., "Logs In via," "Fetches data using," "Sends analytics events to"). Example (Conceptual): +----------------+ +-------------------+ +---------------------+ | Mobile User |<----->| Flutter Mobile App|<----->| Backend API Gateway | +----------------+ +-------------------+ +---------------------+ | ^ | ^ | | | | Uses v | v | +--------------+ | +-----------------+ +-------------+ | Firebase | | | Product Service |---| App DB | | Auth |----- +-----------------+ +-------------+ +--------------+ | | | Sends events to v v +--------------+ +-------------------+ | Firebase | | Firebase Analytics| | Analytics | +-------------------+ +--------------+ Keep it Simple: Resist the urge to add too much detail. Aim for clarity over completeness at this level. Share the Diagram: Embed: Embed the diagram directly into the main project overview page on your wiki (Confluence). Pin: Pin a link to the diagram (or the wiki page) in the main project chat channel(s) (#proj-mobile-general, #proj-mobile-tech). Repository: If using a code-based tool like PlantUML, commit the source file (.puml) and the generated image (.png) to your Git repository (e.g., in a /docs/architecture folder). Explain the Diagram: Kickoff Meeting: Present and walk through the diagram during the project kickoff meeting. Explain what each box represents and how they interact. Onboarding: Use the diagram as a central piece during onboarding sessions for all new team members (technical and non-technical). Reference: Refer back to the diagram during discussions about new features or integrations to provide context. Maintain the Diagram: Update the diagram if major components are added, removed, or interactions change significantly. Assign an owner (e.g., Architect) to keep it reasonably current. It doesn't need to reflect every minor change.

Item: 4 | Architecture Definition | Architecture & Coding Guidance | SETUP | 1 | "There are guidance of flows/steps of special development use-cases (e.g. How to run custom tools, how to set environment variables…)" | Document procedures for running code generation (e.g., build_runner), integration tests (e.g., flutter test integration_test), and using dart-define for environment variables. | | This guide covers documenting specific, non-obvious development workflows or tool usages required for your Flutter project.
documents.s: Completing Item 4: Document Special Use-Case Guidance

documents.t: Identify Special Use Cases: Think about tasks developers need to perform beyond basic coding, running, and testing. Common examples include: Code Generation: Using build_runner for packages like freezed, json_serializable, mockito, auto_route, etc. Environment Configuration: Managing different API endpoints, keys, or feature flags for dev, staging, and production builds (often using dart-define or .env files). Integration Testing: Running specific integration test suites (e.g., flutter test integration_test/app_test.dart). Build Flavors/Schemes: Creating different app builds (e.g., a "dev" app alongside the "prod" app on the same device) using Xcode Schemes and Android Flavors. Updating Native Dependencies: Steps needed after adding a Flutter package that includes native code (e.g., pod install, flutter clean). Using Custom Scripts: Any helper scripts in the repository (e.g., for releasing, code generation). Debugging Specific Issues: Steps for debugging tricky platform-specific issues or performance problems. Document Each Use Case Clearly: Create a dedicated section on your wiki (e.g., under "Developer Guides") or add to your SETUP.md / Onboarding document. Use clear headings for each use case. For each use case, provide: What it is: Briefly explain the purpose (e.g., "Generating Model Classes with Freezed"). When to use it: Explain the trigger (e.g., "Run this after modifying any class annotated with @freezed"). How to use it: Provide exact, step-by-step instructions. Use code blocks for commands. Example Documentation Snippets: Running Code Generation: ## Running Code Generation (`build_runner`) We use `build_runner` to generate boilerplate code for models (`freezed`, `json_serializable`) and mocks (`mockito`). **When:** After you modify any file containing annotations like `@freezed`, `@JsonSerializable`, `@GenerateMocks`, etc. **How:** Run the following command in your terminal at the project root: ```bash fvm flutter pub run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs ``` For continuous generation while you code (useful during heavy model changes), use: fvm flutter pub run build_runner watch --delete-conflicting-outputs Using Environment Variables (dart-define): ## Environment Configuration (`dart-define`) We use `dart-define` to inject environment-specific variables (like API endpoints) at build time. **How:** 1. Access variables in Dart code via `String.fromEnvironment('VAR_NAME', defaultValue: '...')`. 2. When running/building, pass the variables: - **Development:** ```bash fvm flutter run --dart-define=API_ENDPOINT=https://dev-api.example.com --dart-define=API_KEY=DEV123 ``` - **Staging (Build):** ```bash fvm flutter build apk --release --dart-define=API_ENDPOINT=https://staging-api.example.com --dart-define=API_KEY=STAGING456 ``` - **Production (Build):** ```bash fvm flutter build ipa --release --dart-define=API_ENDPOINT=https://api.example.com --dart-define=API_KEY=PROD789 ``` 3. **Note:** Refer to the `launch.json` for VS Code launch configurations and CI/CD scripts (`.github/workflows/main.yaml`) for build examples. Keep it Accessible: Ensure these guides are linked prominently from the main project README or onboarding document so developers can find them easily when needed. Update the guides if the tools or processes change.

Item: 34 | Architecture Definition | Technical Refinement & Design | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 1 | The business stories are splitted into small testable-deployable features. | Enforce a "one PR per story" rule. If a story is too big (e.g., > 3 days), break it down further (e.g., "Create UI," "Integrate API"). | | This guide explains the importance and techniques for splitting larger business requirements (Epics, Features) into small, independently testable, and potentially deployable user stories.
documents.s: Completing Item 34: Split Stories into Small Deployable Features

documents.t: Faster Feedback: Smaller stories can be completed, tested, and potentially demonstrated within a sprint (or even a few days), allowing for quicker feedback from the PO and users. Reduced Risk: Smaller changes are less likely to introduce major bugs and are easier to troubleshoot if issues arise. Merging smaller PRs reduces integration complexity. Improved Flow: Enables a steadier flow of work through the development process (code -> review -> test -> done) rather than having large chunks blocked for long periods. Accurate Estimation: Smaller, well-defined stories are generally easier to estimate accurately. Flexibility: Allows the PO to prioritize smaller increments of value more effectively. Enables CI/CD: Small, independent changes are fundamental to effective Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment.

INVEST Criteria: Stories should ideally follow the INVEST acronym: Independent: Can be developed and tested without strong dependencies on other stories within the same sprint. Negotiable: Details can be discussed and refined between the PO and team. Valuable: Delivers tangible value to the end-user or business (even if small). Estimable: Clear enough for the team to estimate the effort. Small: Can realistically be completed (coded, tested, documented) by one or two developers within a short timeframe (e.g., 1-3 days, definitely fits within a single sprint). Testable: Has clear acceptance criteria that can be verified. Rule of Thumb: If a story takes more than ~3 days of development effort, it's likely too big and should be split.

Use these patterns during backlog refinement sessions involving the PO, developers, and QA: Workflow Steps: Split a feature based on the steps a user takes. Large Story: "User can purchase a product." Split Stories: "User can view product details." "User can add a product to the cart." "User can view the shopping cart." "User can proceed to checkout (enter shipping)." "User can enter payment details." "User can confirm the order." Business Rule Variations: Split based on different rules or scenarios. Large Story: "Calculate shipping costs." Split Stories: "Calculate domestic standard shipping." "Calculate domestic express shipping." "Calculate international shipping (Zone 1)." "Apply free shipping rule for orders over $50." Data Variations / Parameters: Split based on different types of data handled. Large Story: "User can search for products." Split Stories: "User can search for products by name." "User can search for products by category." "User can filter search results by price range." Operational Boundaries (CRUD): Split based on Create, Read, Update, Delete operations. Large Story: "Manage user profile." Split Stories: "User can view their profile." "User can edit their profile name and bio." "User can change their profile picture." "User can delete their account (initial request)." Technical Layers (Use Sparingly): Split by technical layer (UI, API integration, data persistence). Caution: This can violate the "Valuable" principle, as a UI-only story might not deliver end-user value on its own. Use this mainly for enabling complex features or if technical dependencies dictate it. Large Story: "Display user's order history." Split Stories (if necessary): "Backend: Create order history API endpoint." (Requires backend team) "Mobile: Build UI for order history screen (using mock data)." "Mobile: Integrate order history screen with API endpoint." Acceptance Criteria: If a story has numerous complex acceptance criteria, consider splitting it so each new story addresses a subset of the criteria.

Refinement Discipline: Make story splitting a primary focus of backlog refinement meetings. The PO explains the need, and the team collaborates on how to split it effectively. Definition of Ready (DoR): Include "Story is small enough (e.g., fits in a sprint, < 3 days effort)" in your DoR. Do not allow overly large stories into sprint planning. "One PR per Story": Enforce the rule that a single user story should generally correspond to a single Pull Request. If a PR becomes massive, it's a sign the story was too big. Vertical Slices: Prioritize splitting stories into end-to-end "vertical slices" that deliver demonstrable value, rather than splitting horizontally by technical layer, whenever possible. By consistently splitting work into small, manageable pieces, teams can improve predictability, reduce risk, and deliver value more frequently.

Item: 36 | Architecture Definition | Technical Refinement & Design | SETUP | 1 | "The technologies utilized in the project are vastly adopted there is no doubt about it's capabilities;
There is no early adoption and betas versions." | Before adding a new major pub.dev package, verify its popularity (likes, pub points), maintenance status, and Flutter version compatibility. Avoid "beta" packages. | | This guide explains how to establish a clear policy for selecting and adopting technologies (primarily third-party libraries/packages) for your Flutter project, emphasizing stability and proven capabilities.
documents.s: Completing Item 36: Define Technology Adoption Policy

documents.t: Reduces Risk: Avoids relying on unstable, unmaintained, or poorly supported libraries that could introduce bugs, security vulnerabilities, or become obsolete. Ensures Stability: Favors mature technologies with proven track records in production environments. Maintainability: Using well-adopted libraries often means better documentation, larger communities for support, and easier onboarding for new developers. Consistency: Prevents the proliferation of multiple libraries solving the same problem, leading to a more cohesive tech stack. Avoids "Shiny Object Syndrome": Provides objective criteria for evaluating new technologies rather than adopting them just because they are new or trendy.

Define Evaluation Criteria for New Dependencies: Establish a checklist or set of questions to ask before adding a new significant pub.dev package or other major technology: Problem Fit: Does this library clearly solve a necessary problem that isn't easily addressed by the core Flutter SDK or existing project dependencies? Popularity & Adoption: How many Pub Points does it have on pub.dev? (Aim for high scores, e.g., > 120). How many Likes does it have? (Indicates community approval). Is it listed as a Flutter Favorite? (Strong positive signal). Maintenance & Support: When was the last update? (Avoid packages not updated in > 6-12 months). Is the repository active (commits, issues, PRs)? Does the author/organization seem responsive to issues? Is it officially supported by a reputable organization (e.g., Google, flutter.dev)? Stability: Is the current version stable (e.g., 1.0.0 or higher)? Avoid pre-release versions (0.x.y, -beta, -alpha, -dev) for critical functionality unless absolutely necessary and thoroughly vetted. Are there many open issues related to bugs or stability? Compatibility: Does it support the target Flutter/Dart SDK versions for your project? Does it support all target platforms (iOS, Android)? Documentation: Is the documentation clear and comprehensive? Are there good examples? License: Is the license compatible with your project/organization's policies (e.g., MIT, BSD, Apache are generally safe)? Avoid restrictive or unclear licenses. Alternatives: Have existing project dependencies or simpler custom solutions been considered? Does this library significantly overlap with functionality already provided by another package we use? Document the Policy: Create a "Technology Adoption Policy" or "Dependency Management" page on your project wiki. List the evaluation criteria above. State the policy clearly: "New major dependencies (especially those impacting core functionality like state management, navigation, networking, persistence) must be evaluated against these criteria. Pre-release/beta versions should generally be avoided for production code." Define the approval process: "Adding minor utility packages requires developer consensus." "Adding significant new dependencies (e.g., replacing the HTTP client, adding a new database) requires discussion and approval from the Tech Lead/Architect, potentially including an ADR (Architecture Decision Record)." Integrate into Workflow: Discussion: Encourage developers to discuss potential new dependencies with the team before adding them to pubspec.yaml. A quick chat message like "Thinking of using package X for feature Y, thoughts?" can save time. Code Review: During PR reviews, specifically check any newly added dependencies in pubspec.yaml. Ask if the adoption policy was followed, especially for significant additions. Question the need if alternatives exist or if the package seems risky based on the criteria. Regular Review of Existing Dependencies: Periodically (e.g., quarterly or semi-annually), review the project's main dependencies using flutter pub outdated. Check if any key packages have become unmaintained or have known critical security vulnerabilities. Plan migrations away from problematic dependencies as technical debt. By establishing and following this policy, you ensure your project is built on a stable and maintainable foundation of well-vetted technologies.

Item: 20 | Architecture Definition | Communication & Alignment | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 2 | "All the team members, including development, infrastructure and business members share the same communication tool (Teams, Google Chat, Slack, etc)." | Ensure all developers, QAs, and POs are in the primary team chat (e.g., Google Chat) and project management tool (e.g., Jira). | | This guide emphasizes the importance of consolidating primary team communication onto a shared, real-time platform.
documents.s: Completing Item 20: Use a Shared Communication Tool

documents.t: Reduces Fragmentation: Prevents conversations from being scattered across email, multiple chat apps, and DMs, making information hard to find. Increases Visibility: Allows team members (including the PO and potentially key stakeholders) to follow relevant discussions and stay informed. Facilitates Collaboration: Makes it easier to quickly ask questions, share code snippets, get feedback, and resolve issues. Creates a Central Hub: Integrations with other tools (Jira, CI/CD, monitoring) can centralize notifications and workflow updates.

Select the Primary Real-Time Communication Tool: Choose One: Standardize on one main tool for synchronous and near-synchronous team chat. Common choices include: Slack Microsoft Teams Google Chat Considerations: Choose based on organizational standards, existing licenses, required integrations, and team preference. Ensure Universal Access: All Core Team Members: Verify that every member of the core development team (Flutter Devs, Backend Devs, QA, UI/UX Designer, Architect, Tech Lead) and the Product Owner has access to and actively uses the chosen tool. Infrastructure/DevOps: Ensure relevant infrastructure or DevOps team members are included, especially for discussions around environments, deployments, and monitoring. Business Stakeholders (Optional but Recommended): Consider inviting key business stakeholders (e.g., Project Manager, Client Contact) to specific, relevant channels (like #proj-mobile-general or #proj-mobile-biz-tech - see Item 17), but perhaps not the day-to-day technical channel. Set Up Appropriate Channels/Groups:

Item: 88 | Architecture Execution | Software Development | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 2 | The Software Architect is not overloaded by only giving support to the team. | Empower senior developers to act as "area architects" (e.g., for "Auth"). Document common patterns so devs don't need to ask the architect for everything. | | This guide focuses on strategies to ensure the Software Architect can focus on strategic architectural tasks, rather than being solely consumed by providing day-to-day support to the development team, becoming a bottleneck.
documents.s: Completing Item 88: Ensure Architect is Not Overloaded

documents.t: Bottleneck: If every minor technical question or PR review requires the architect, it slows down the entire team. Lack of Strategic Focus: An overloaded architect has no time for forward-looking tasks like researching new technologies, planning architectural evolution, defining long-term technical strategy, or mentoring. Single Point of Failure: Over-reliance on one person creates a knowledge silo and a risk if that person is unavailable. Reduced Team Growth: Prevents other team members (especially seniors) from developing their own architectural understanding and leadership skills.

Clear Documentation (Foundation): Architecture Foundation (Item 11): Well-documented layers, patterns, and mechanisms reduce the need for developers to ask basic "how-to" questions. Include clear code examples. Coding Conventions (Item 3): Standardized code style reduces review friction. Decision Records (ADRs - Item 128): Documenting the why behind major decisions allows developers to understand context without asking the architect repeatedly. Common Recipes/Cookbooks: Create wiki pages for common tasks (e.g., "How to add a new API call," "How to create a new Bloc/Screen"). Empower Senior Developers / Tech Leads: Delegate Reviews: Delegate routine PR reviews to senior developers or tech leads. The architect should focus reviews on PRs with significant architectural impact, complex logic, or those touching critical core components. Establish clear guidelines on which PRs require architect review. Area Ownership / "Area Architects": Assign senior developers as primary technical points-of-contact or "owners" for specific features, modules, or domains (e.g., Authentication, Payments, User Profile). They become the first point of contact for questions within that area and take primary responsibility for its technical design (with architect oversight). Mentoring: Encourage senior developers to mentor junior developers on architectural patterns and best practices. Establish Clear Communication Channels: Guide developers to ask questions in appropriate public channels (e.g., #proj-mobile-tech - Item 17) rather than DMing the architect directly. This allows others (like senior devs) to answer and shares knowledge. Encourage developers to attempt research (checking docs, searching codebase) before asking. Architect's Role Definition: Clarify the architect's primary responsibilities: focus on high-level design, cross-cutting concerns, technical roadmap, major decisions, mentoring, and unblocking the team on complex issues, not every routine task. The architect should act more as a consultant and guide, enabling the team rather than dictating every detail. Regular Architecture Syncs/Reviews: Hold regular (e.g., bi-weekly) architecture sync meetings where developers can bring complex technical questions or proposed designs for discussion with the architect and senior team members. This provides a dedicated forum, reducing ad-hoc interruptions. Use these meetings for proactive guidance rather than just reactive support. Time Management for the Architect: The architect should consciously block out time for focused work on strategic tasks, separate from interrupt-driven support. By actively documenting patterns, delegating responsibilities, and fostering knowledge sharing within the team, the architect can be freed up to provide higher-level guidance and strategic direction, ultimately benefiting the project more than being a constant support bottleneck.
documents.s: Strategies to Empower the Team and Free Up the Architect

documents.t: Item: 35 | Architecture Definition | Technical Refinement & Design | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 2 | The technical documentation is being updated during the project development (when affect to existing documents). | As part of the "Definition of Done," require that any PR changing architecture (e.g., state management, API contract) must include updates to the relevant Confluence docs. | | This guide explains how to establish a process for keeping technical documentation current as the codebase evolves during development sprints. Outdated documentation can be misleading and counterproductive.
documents.s: Completing Item 35: Update Technical Documentation During Development

documents.t: Accuracy: Ensures documentation reflects the actual state of the code and architecture. Reliability: Developers can trust the documentation, reducing time wasted on incorrect information. Onboarding: New team members get an accurate picture of the system. Knowledge Sharing: Captures rationale and design decisions as they happen. Reduces "Documentation Debt": Avoids a large, painful effort to update documentation months after changes were made (which often never happens).

Focus on documentation that describes the system's structure, key decisions, and core processes. This includes: Architecture Foundation Document (Item 11: Layers, core patterns) Architecture Diagrams (High-level, Layer, Component) (Item 11, 22) SCM Policy / Branching Model (Item 1) CI/CD Lifecycle Diagram/Description (Item 26) Coding Conventions (Item 3) Testing Guide (Item 15) NFR Documentation (Item 27, 28, 30) ADRs (Architecture Decision Records) (Item 128) Key Third-Party Dependency List (Item 14) Setup/Onboarding Guides (Item 2) Special Use-Case Guides (Item 4)

Integrate Documentation into the Workflow: Definition of Done (DoD): This is the most effective enforcement point. Add a checklist item to your team's DoD for user stories/tasks: [ ] Relevant technical documentation updated (if applicable). Pull Request Template: Include a reminder in your PR template: Have you updated relevant documentation (Architecture, ADRs, READMEs)? [ ] Yes [ ] N/A Identify When Updates Are Needed: During technical refinement or implementation, developers should ask: "Does this change affect any of our documented architecture, patterns, or processes?" Updates are typically needed when changes involve: Introducing a new library/framework for a core concern (e.g., changing state management). Altering the defined application layers or their responsibilities. Changing the SCM branching model or CI/CD pipeline significantly. Modifying a core mechanism (e.g., error handling, logging). Making a new significant architectural decision (requires a new ADR). Changing API contracts that affect documented interactions. Changing the local setup process. Perform Updates Concurrently with Code Changes: Encourage developers to update the documentation within the same feature branch or shortly after the code changes are made, before the PR is merged. Treat documentation updates as part of the task, not a separate chore to be done later. Review Documentation Updates: PR Review: Code reviewers should check if the PR necessitates documentation updates and verify that the corresponding changes have been made (e.g., by checking linked wiki pages or ADRs). Add this check to reviewer guidelines. Link Updates: Encourage developers to link to the updated wiki page or ADR directly from the PR description for easy review. Keep Documentation Accessible and Co-located: Maintain a central documentation hub (wiki, repository docs folder). Link documentation pages together logically. Consider keeping documentation closer to the code where feasible (e.g., using Markdown files in the Git repository, especially for ADRs or component-specific notes). Wiki pages (Confluence) are often better for higher-level architecture overviews. Periodic Review (Less Critical if DoD is Enforced): Optionally, conduct a brief documentation review (e.g., quarterly) to catch any major inconsistencies, but relying on the DoD is more effective for continuous updates. By integrating documentation updates into the regular development workflow via the Definition of Done and PR reviews, you can maintain accurate and valuable technical documentation with less overhead.

Item: 37 | Architecture Definition | Technical Refinement & Design | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 2 | "The technical refinement usually finishes on time (it is usually done before the planning of the upcoming sprint). The ""Heijunka"" concept is being followed accordingly." | Schedule technical refinement/story-pointing meetings *before* the sprint planning meeting to ensure all stories are "Ready." | | This guide explains how to structure your team's process to ensure technical refinement and estimation of user stories are completed before the sprint planning meeting, enabling smoother planning and execution. The reference to "Heijunka" implies leveling the workload and creating a predictable flow.
documents.s: Completing Item 37: Ensure Timely Technical Refinement

documents.t: Reduces Planning Meeting Length: Sprint planning becomes focused on selecting work and confirming capacity, not on understanding or estimating stories for the first time. Improves Estimation Accuracy: Gives the team more time to discuss technical approaches, identify complexities, and ask clarifying questions before committing to estimates. Ensures "Definition of Ready": Allows time to resolve ambiguities, confirm dependencies, or get missing information (e.g., final API specs) before a story is considered ready for the sprint. Smoother Sprint Start: Developers can start working on sprint tasks immediately after planning, as the technical approach is already broadly understood. Predictable Flow (Heijunka): Creates a more level workload by decoupling the deep thinking of refinement from the commitment pressure of planning.

Schedule Dedicated Refinement Meetings: Cadence: Hold refinement meetings regularly, separate from Sprint Planning. Common cadences: Once or twice per week. One longer session mid-sprint dedicated to refining stories for the next sprint. Attendees: Product Owner (to explain the 'What' and 'Why'), Development Team (including QA, to discuss the 'How' and estimate). Goal: To review stories from the top of the backlog, discuss requirements, clarify acceptance criteria, identify technical approaches, break down large stories (Item 34), identify dependencies/risks, and assign estimates (story points or time). Define "Definition of Ready" (DoR): Formalize the criteria a story must meet before it can be considered during Sprint Planning. Include: Clear description and value statement. Well-defined Acceptance Criteria. Dependencies identified (and ideally resolved or planned for). UX/UI designs attached (if applicable). NFR impacts considered (Item 33). Story has been discussed and estimated by the team during a refinement session. (This is the key link). Structure the Refinement Process: Input: PO prepares stories at the top of the backlog before the meeting. During Meeting: PO presents the story and acceptance criteria. Team asks clarifying questions. Team discusses potential technical approaches, complexities, risks. Team decides if the story needs splitting (Item 34). Team collectively estimates the story (e.g., using Planning Poker with story points). Mark the story as "Refined" or "Ready for Planning" (e.g., move to a specific column on the board or add a label). Output: A set of stories at the top of the backlog that meet the DoR and are ready for the upcoming Sprint Planning. Timing Relative to Sprint Planning: Ensure enough refinement happens before Sprint Planning so there's a sufficient buffer of "Ready" stories (e.g., enough for 1.5 to 2 sprints). Example Schedule (2-week sprints): Week 1, Day 3: Refinement Session 1 (focus on stories for Sprint+1). Week 2, Day 2: Refinement Session 2 (refine more stories for Sprint+1, review any carry-over). Week 2, Day 5 (or Week 3, Day 1): Sprint Planning (selects from "Ready" stories). Discipline During Sprint Planning: Stick to "Ready" Work: Only pull stories that meet the DoR (including prior refinement and estimation) into the sprint. Avoid Deep Dives: If major questions or estimation debates arise during Sprint Planning, it's a sign that refinement was insufficient. Briefly address it or (better) push the story back to the backlog for proper refinement. The goal of planning is selection and capacity confirmation, not initial understanding. By separating refinement from planning, you create a more predictable rhythm, improve the quality of sprint commitments, and reduce stress during planning meetings.

Item: 39 | Architecture Definition | Technical Refinement & Design | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 3 | There are not many changes in the architecture definition during the sprint development. | Invest time in technical refinement. Use Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) to "lock in" major decisions *before* the sprint starts. | | This guide focuses on practices aimed at minimizing disruptive architectural changes after a sprint has already started. While some adaptation is normal, frequent major changes indicate issues in planning or refinement.
documents.s: Completing Item 39: Minimize Architecture Changes During Sprints

documents.t: Sprint Goal Focus: Major architectural shifts can derail the team from achieving the committed sprint goal. Predictability: Reduces volatility and allows the team to focus on delivering the planned work. Reduces Rework: Avoids wasted effort on implementing features based on an architecture that subsequently changes. Maintains Velocity: Frequent changes create churn and slow down overall delivery. Team Morale: Constant changes can be frustrating and demotivating for developers.

Defined Architecture Foundation (Item 11): Having a clear baseline architecture makes deviations easier to identify. Thorough Refinement (Item 37): Discussing technical approaches before the sprint helps surface architectural questions early.

Invest in Upfront Technical Design & Refinement: Identify Architectural Impact: During backlog refinement, explicitly ask if implementing a story requires significant architectural changes or introduces new patterns. Spike/PoC: If there's uncertainty about a technical approach or its architectural implications, schedule a "Spike" (a timeboxed investigation task) in a preceding sprint to explore options before committing to the feature story. Technical Design Docs: For complex features with significant architectural impact, create a brief technical design document outlining the proposed approach before the sprint starts. Review this with the team/architect. Use Architecture Decision Records (ADRs): For significant architectural decisions identified before the sprint (e.g., choosing a caching strategy, deciding on a background processing method), document them using ADRs (Item 128). Review and formally "accept" these ADRs before the relevant stories are pulled into a sprint. This helps "lock in" the decision.
