Set up Flutter (using FVM is recommended). jobs: build_and_deploy: runs-on: macos-latest # Required for iOS builds steps: - name: Checkout code uses: actions/checkout@v3 - name: Set up Flutter using FVM # (Steps to install FVM and run 'fvm install'/'fvm use') # Or use a dedicated Flutter action: uses: subosito/flutter-action@v2 with: channel: 'stable' # Or use specific version from .fvmrc - name: Install dependencies run: flutter pub get Build Artifacts: Add steps to build the release artifacts, using --dart-define (Item 69) or appropriate configurations for the Dev/Test environment. # Build Android App Bundle (for Firebase App Dist) - name: Build Android App Bundle (Dev) run: | flutter build appbundle --release \ --dart-define=API_URL=${{ secrets.DEV_API_URL }} \ --dart-define=API_KEY=${{ secrets.DEV_API_KEY }} # Store DEV_API_URL etc. as GitHub Secrets # Build iOS IPA (for Firebase App Dist) # Requires setting up iOS code signing (certificates, profiles) # Often done using Fastlane or Codemagic's built-in handling - name: Build iOS IPA (Dev) # This step is complex - requires code signing setup # Example using Fastlane (after setting up Fastfile): # run: bundle exec fastlane build_dev_ipa # Or manual xcodebuild commands (more complex) run: | flutter build ipa --release --export-options-plist=path/to/ExportOptionsDev.plist \ --dart-define=API_URL=${{ secrets.DEV_API_URL }} \ --dart-define=API_KEY=${{ secrets.DEV_API_KEY }} iOS Signing: This is often the most complex part. You need to securely install your Apple Developer certificates and provisioning profiles on the CI runner. Tools like fastlane match or Codemagic's key management simplify this significantly. Store keys/passwords in CI secrets. Distribute Artifacts: Add steps to upload the generated .aab (or .apk) and .ipa to your chosen distribution service. # Distribute to Firebase App Distribution - name: Upload Android to Firebase App Distribution uses: wzieba/Firebase-Distribution-Github-Action@v1 with: appId: ${{ secrets.FIREBASE_ANDROID_APP_ID }} serviceCredentialsFileContent: ${{ secrets.FIREBASE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON }} groups: testers # Group alias in Firebase file: build/app/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab - name: Upload iOS to Firebase App Distribution uses: wzieba/Firebase-Distribution-Github-Action@v1 with: appId: ${{ secrets.FIREBASE_IOS_APP_ID }} serviceCredentialsFileContent: ${{ secrets.FIREBASE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON }} groups: testers file: build/ios/ipa/YourApp.ipa # Adjust path Store Firebase App IDs and Service Account JSON/Tokens in your CI/CD platform's secrets management. Notifications: Add a final step to notify the team. - name: Notify Slack on Success if: success() # Only run if previous steps succeeded uses: rtCamp/action-slack-notify@v2 env: SLACK_WEBHOOK: ${{ secrets.SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL }} SLACK_MESSAGE: '🚀 New Dev build available on Firebase App Distribution!' # Add more context like commit hash, version, etc. Configure Secrets: Securely store all necessary API keys, service account credentials, code signing passwords, and webhook URLs in your CI/CD platform's secrets management system. Test and Iterate: Trigger the pipeline manually or by pushing to main. Debug any issues with build steps, signing, or distribution uploads. Refine the workflow as needed. Document: Briefly document the automated deployment process, including the trigger, the distribution platform used, and how testers can access new builds, in your project wiki. Automating Dev/Test deployments significantly accelerates the development feedback cycle and improves the reliability of your internal builds.

Item: 45 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Deployment | PREPARATION (Sprint 0) | 2 | "The deployment to the dev, test environments are automated and executed
in a CI/CD server (Jenkins, Azure DevOps, etc)." | Create a CI/CD pipeline (e.g., GitHub Actions, Codemagic) that, on merge to main, automatically builds and deploys the app to Firebase App Distribution. | | This guide explains how to set up an automated pipeline to build and deploy your Flutter app to development or internal testing environments whenever code is merged into the main development branch (e.g., main or develop).
documents.s: Completing Item 45: Automate Dev/Test Environment Deployments

documents.t: Fast Feedback: Provides testers (QA, PO, other devs) with the latest integrated build quickly after changes are merged. Reduces Manual Effort: Eliminates the error-prone and time-consuming process of developers manually building and distributing internal versions. Consistency: Ensures every internal build is created using the same standardized process. Enables Continuous Integration: Represents the "Continuous Delivery" aspect of CI/CD, getting integrated code into a testable state automatically.

CI/CD Server: A platform to run the automated pipeline (e.g., GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Codemagic, Jenkins, Azure DevOps). Trigger: An event that starts the pipeline (e.g., merge/push to main branch). Build Steps: Commands to check out code, set up Flutter, install dependencies, and build the app artifacts (.apk/.aab, .ipa) configured for the Dev/Test environment. Distribution Platform: A service to host and distribute the internal builds to testers (e.g., Firebase App Distribution, TestFlight Internal Testing, Play Store Internal Testing, self-hosted solution). Notification: Alerting the team that a new build is available.

Choose a CI/CD Platform: Select the platform your team will use (e.g., GitHub Actions). Choose a Distribution Platform: Firebase App Distribution is a popular and easy-to-use choice for distributing both Android and iOS builds internally. TestFlight (Internal) and Play Store Internal Testing are platform-specific alternatives. Configure the Trigger: Set up your pipeline configuration file (e.g., .github/workflows/deploy_dev.yaml) to trigger on pushes or merges to your main development branch. GitHub Actions Example: name: Deploy to Dev (Firebase App Distribution) on: push: branches: - main # Or your main integration branch (e.g., develop) Configure Build Steps: Check out the code. Set up Flutter (using FVM is recommended - Item 2). Set up platform-specific requirements (Java for Android, Xcode/certs for iOS on a macOS runner). Install dependencies (fvm flutter pub get). Run analysis and tests (optional but recommended for this pipeline too, although they should also run on PRs). Build the artifacts configured for your Dev/Test environment. Use --dart-define or .env files (Item 44) to inject the correct API endpoints and keys. Build unsigned debug/profile versions or use dedicated development signing keys – do not use production signing keys for these builds. Android Example: fvm flutter build apk --debug --dart-define=API_ENDPOINT=https://dev-api.example.com (APK is often easier for internal distribution than AAB). iOS Example (on macOS runner): fvm flutter build ipa --debug --export-options-plist=path/to/ExportOptionsDev.plist --dart-define=API_ENDPOINT=https://dev-api.example.com (Requires dev signing setup). Configure Deployment Step (Firebase App Distribution Example): Use a dedicated tool or action to upload the built artifact (.apk or .ipa) to Firebase App Distribution. GitHub Actions Example (using firebase app distribution:distribute CLI): # (Assuming previous build steps generated app-debug.apk) - name: Install Firebase CLI run: npm install -g firebase-tools - name: Upload to Firebase App Distribution run: | firebase appdistribution:distribute app-debug.apk \ --app ${{ secrets.FIREBASE_APP_ID_ANDROID }} \ --token ${{ secrets.FIREBASE_CLI_TOKEN }} \ --groups "qa-team,developers" \ --release-notes "Build ${{ github.run_number }} - ${{ github.sha }}" # Repeat for iOS .ipa file if building both Secrets: Store necessary credentials (Firebase App ID, CLI Token/Service Account) securely in your CI/CD platform's secrets management. Testers/Groups: Configure tester groups in Firebase App Distribution and specify which groups should receive the build. Release Notes: Include useful information like the build number and commit hash in the release notes. Add Notifications: Configure your CI/CD pipeline to send a notification (e.g., to Slack/Google Chat - Item 17) upon successful deployment, indicating a new build is available on Firebase App Distribution with a link. Document the Process: Document how the automated deployment works in your CI/CD documentation (Item 26). Provide instructions for testers on how to access builds from the chosen distribution platform (e.g., "Accept the Firebase App Distribution invite," "Install the Firebase App Tester app"). By automating deployments to your internal environments, you accelerate the feedback loop and free up developer time.

Item: 76 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Integration | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 2 | "Complex code (about 500 LOCs) merging is not performed with high frequency (twice per week).
" | Enforce small, well-defined user stories. If a PR has > 500 LOC changes, it should be scrutinized and potentially broken up. | | (Note: The item phrasing "not performed with high frequency" is slightly awkward. The intent is likely to minimize the occurrence of large, complex merges by keeping changes small.) This guide focuses on practices to minimize the size and complexity of code being merged into the main branch (main), reducing integration risks and improving review efficiency.
documents.s: Completing Item 76: Avoid Frequent Large Merges

documents.t: Increased Risk of Conflicts: Merging large branches that have diverged significantly from main is much more likely to result in complex, hard-to-resolve merge conflicts. Higher Bug Potential: Large changesets make it harder to identify the root cause if bugs are introduced after the merge. The "blast radius" of potential issues is larger. Difficult Code Reviews: Reviewing Pull Requests (PRs) with thousands of lines changed across many files is time-consuming, mentally taxing, and less effective. Reviewers are more likely to miss subtle issues. Blocks Integration: A large, complex merge might block other developers from merging their smaller changes while the issues are resolved. Violates CI Principles: Continuous Integration relies on frequent, small integrations, not infrequent, large ones.

The primary strategy is to keep the units of work (and therefore the corresponding branches and PRs) small. Enforce Small User Stories (Item 34): This is the most effective preventative measure. During backlog refinement, rigorously split large features or epics into small, independent user stories that can ideally be completed in 1-3 days. If a story is estimated as large (e.g., > 5 points), mandate that it be split before being considered "Ready" for a sprint. One PR Per Story Rule: Strictly associate one PR with one user story. If a PR starts growing excessively large (e.g., approaching 500-1000 lines of code changed, touching many unrelated files), it's a strong indicator that the original story was too big and should have been split. Frequent Synchronization (Item 74): Encourage developers to frequently rebase their feature branches onto the latest main. This integrates changes incrementally and prevents branches from diverging too far, making the final merge smaller in terms of conflict potential, even if the total lines changed in the feature are significant. Pull Request Size Guidelines & Review: Guideline: Establish a soft guideline for PR size (e.g., "Aim for PRs under 500 lines of change," or "PRs over 1000 lines require discussion with the tech lead"). Use Lines of Code (LOC) changed as a heuristic, not a strict rule, as context matters (e.g., refactoring might change many lines but be low risk). Scrutinize Large PRs: When a large PR is submitted, reviewers should allocate extra time and scrutiny. Consider: Could this have been broken down into smaller, sequential PRs? Does it mix unrelated changes (e.g., a feature implementation plus a large refactor)? Ask the author to split them. Are the changes well-tested? Feature Toggles for Larger Features (Item 9): For features that are inherently large even when split logically, consider merging the underlying code incrementally behind a feature toggle. This allows integrating the code into main frequently in smaller chunks, even if the complete feature isn't enabled for users yet. Refactoring as Separate Tasks: Avoid bundling large-scale refactoring with feature work in the same PR. Schedule refactoring as separate (potentially larger, but focused) tasks/stories, ideally informed by technical debt tracking (Item 5). By focusing on small stories, frequent integration, and mindful PR sizing, the team can maintain a smooth flow of changes into the main branch, minimizing the risks and difficulties associated with large, complex merges.

Item: 74 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Integration | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 2 | "The branches are often synchronized with
its parent branches, at least before starting implementation or tests run." | Encourage developers to rebase (git pull --rebase origin main) their feature branches daily to avoid large merge conflicts. | | This guide explains the importance of frequently synchronizing feature branches with their parent branch (typically main in Trunk-Based Development) and how to encourage this practice.
documents.s: Completing Item 74: Ensure Frequent Branch Synchronization

documents.t: Smaller, Easier Merges: Integrating changes from the parent branch frequently means dealing with smaller sets of conflicts at a time, which are easier and faster to resolve. Waiting longer leads to larger, more complex, and riskier merges. Reduces Integration Risk: Developers build and test their features against a more up-to-date version of the main codebase, catching integration issues earlier in the development cycle. Prevents Divergence: Keeps feature branches from straying too far from the main line of development, reducing rework. Enables Continuous Integration: Frequent synchronization and merging are core principles of CI.

Use git pull --rebase: Encourage developers working on feature branches (e.g., feat/MEC-123) to frequently update their branch with the latest changes from main (or the parent branch). The git pull --rebase origin main command (run while on the feature branch) is generally preferred over git merge main. Fetch: It fetches the latest changes from origin/main. Rebase: It temporarily "unwinds" the commits made on the feature branch, updates the feature branch's base to the latest commit from main, and then re-applies the feature branch commits one by one on top of the new base. Benefits of Rebase: Linear History: Keeps the Git history cleaner and easier to follow, as it avoids "merge bubble" commits just for synchronization. Conflict Resolution Per Commit: Conflicts are resolved commit by commit as they are re-applied, often making them easier to manage than one large merge conflict. Establish a Cadence: Minimum: Developers should synchronize (e.g., git pull --rebase origin main) at least once a day, typically at the start of their workday. Recommended: Synchronize before pushing significant changes or before running tests locally prior to creating a Pull Request. Before PR: Always synchronize and resolve any conflicts immediately before creating a Pull Request to ensure the PR reflects the feature integrated with the latest main. Team Communication and Training: Explain the why behind frequent synchronization (smaller merges, earlier integration). Provide clear guidance on how to do it (specifically git pull --rebase origin main). Offer support or pairing sessions for developers unfamiliar or uncomfortable with rebase. Explain how to handle rebase conflicts (git add ., git rebase --continue) and how to abort if things go wrong (git rebase --abort). Caution: Emphasize that rebase rewrites history. It should generally only be used on local feature branches that haven't been shared or collaborated on directly with others. Once a branch is pushed and others might pull from it, rebasing can cause confusion. However, for typical feature branches in TBD where only one dev works on it before PR, rebasing before push is standard practice. Code Review Check (Optional): Reviewers can check if a PR branch is significantly behind main, suggesting a rebase might be needed before merging, although CI checks often handle the core integration testing. By fostering a habit of frequent synchronization using git pull --rebase, the team minimizes painful merges and integrates code more continuously, reducing risk and improving flow.
documents.s: Recommended Practice: Rebase Before Push (or Daily)

documents.t: Item: 80 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Integration | PREPARATION (Sprint 0) | 2 | "The build artifact is generated from a CI/CD server (Jenkins, Azure DevOps, etc)" | Prohibit local builds for releases. All test and production artifacts *must* come from the CI/CD pipeline. | | (Note: This item is conceptually identical to Item 73, "Automate Build Artifact Generation". Both emphasize that artifacts must be built on a CI/CD server, not locally.) This guide reiterates the critical practice of generating all official build artifacts (.apk, .aab, .ipa) exclusively on a centralized CI/CD server.
documents.s: Completing Item 80: Generate Artifacts on CI Server

documents.t: Consistency & Reproducibility: CI/CD servers provide a controlled, standardized environment, ensuring every artifact is built identically, regardless of which developer committed the code. This eliminates variability from local machine configurations (OS versions, installed tools, Flutter SDK versions). Reliability: Automated processes are less prone to human error than manual build steps performed locally. Security: Centralizes the management of sensitive signing keys and credentials within the secure environment of the CI/CD platform, rather than distributing them across developer machines. Traceability: Creates an auditable trail linking every official build artifact back to a specific code commit and the CI/CD job that produced it. Efficiency: Automates the build process, saving developer time.
documents.s: Why Centralized Artifact Generation is Crucial

documents.t: Strict Policy: Implement and enforce a strict team policy: Release artifacts (for QA, Staging, Production) are never built on developer laptops. All official builds must originate from the designated CI/CD pipeline. CI/CD Pipeline Setup: Configure your CI/CD pipeline (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Codemagic, Jenkins, etc.) with dedicated jobs/workflows to: Checkout the correct source code version (commit/tag). Set up the precise build environment (Flutter SDK version via FVM, dependencies). Inject environment-specific configuration (--dart-define or .env files retrieved from secrets - Item 69). Execute the flutter build appbundle --release or flutter build ipa --release commands. Handle code signing securely using secrets managed by the CI/CD platform (Item 73). Artifact Archiving: Automatically archive the generated .aab/.ipa files, along with any necessary metadata (version info, commit hash, build logs, symbolication files), in a reliable location (CI artifacts, GitHub Releases, Artifactory, etc. - Item 73). Prohibit Local Release Builds: Communication: Clearly communicate the policy and its rationale to the team. Access Control (Signing Keys): Limit access to production signing keys/certificates strictly to the CI/CD environment. Developers should not have easy access to production secrets locally. Process: Ensure the only way to get a build for QA or Production is through the automated pipeline (e.g., via Firebase App Distribution links generated by CI, or builds submitted to TestFlight/Play Console by CI).

Explicitly state the "CI/CD server builds only" policy in your project's README, onboarding guide, and release process documentation. Document how developers or testers can access the official builds generated by the CI/CD server (e.g., links to Firebase App Distribution). This practice is fundamental to reliable, secure, and reproducible builds in a team environment. It moves artifact generation from an error-prone manual task to a controlled automated process.

Item: 75 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Integration | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 2 | The team commits the runable code with a certain frequency (at least once a day). | Promote a culture of small, frequent commits to feature branches. Avoid "mega-commits" at the end of the week. | | This guide explains the importance of making small, frequent commits to local feature branches during development.

Smaller Units of Work: Each commit represents a small, logical step (e.g., "Add login button UI," "Implement email validation," "Refactor user model"). This makes changes easier to understand, review, and debug. Easier Reversion: If a developer goes down the wrong path, it's much easier to reset or revert back to a recent, known-good state if commits are frequent. Reverting a single large commit made at the end of the day is much harder. Reduced Data Loss: Committing locally acts as a safety net against accidental file deletion or corruption on the developer's machine (especially if pushed to a remote feature branch, though pushing isn't required for the commit itself). Clearer Progress: A series of small commits provides a clearer history of how a feature was developed compared to one massive commit. Facilitates Rebasing/Merging: Smaller commits are generally easier to handle during rebasing (Item 74) or merging.

The item mentions committing "runnable code." This doesn't necessarily mean "fully functional and bug-free" at every commit. It generally means: The code compiles successfully (flutter analyze passes, flutter run starts). It doesn't break fundamental parts of the app unrelated to the work in progress. Ideally, any associated unit tests for the changed code pass. It's acceptable to commit code that represents an intermediate step towards completing a feature, as long as it's a coherent, logical unit and doesn't leave the project in a completely broken state.

Promote the Culture: Explain the Benefits: During team meetings or onboarding, explain why small, frequent commits are beneficial (safety net, easier reviews, better history, etc.). Lead by Example: Tech leads and senior developers should demonstrate this practice in their own work. Focus on Logic Units: Encourage developers to commit after completing a small, logical piece of work, even if the entire feature isn't done. Examples: After creating the basic UI structure for a screen. After implementing a validation function and its tests. After integrating a single API call. After refactoring a specific widget or function. Establish a Cadence Guideline: Minimum: Aim to commit at least once a day, preferably more often. Committing several times a day is common and encouraged. Avoid "Mega-Commits": Actively discourage saving up all changes for a single large commit at the end of the day or week. Emphasize Good Commit Messages: While Item 61 focuses on commit messages linking to tickets before merging, good messages are also important for local commits on feature branches. Encourage clear, concise messages describing the change made in that commit (e.g., Feat: Add email input field to login form, Fix: Correct validation logic for passwords, Refactor: Extract UserAvatar widget). Use Feature Branches: This practice assumes developers are working on isolated feature branches (as per common Git workflows like TBD or Gitflow). Frequent commits are made to the local feature branch. Pushing to the remote feature branch can happen less frequently (e.g., once or twice a day) but still benefits from the small commit history. Code Review (Indirect Enforcement): While reviewers primarily see the final state of a feature branch in a PR, a PR composed of many small, logical commits (even if squashed later) is often easier to understand and review than one giant commit. If a PR contains a single massive commit, it might indicate the developer isn't committing frequently during development. By fostering a habit of small, frequent commits, developers create a safer, more manageable, and more understandable development process for themselves and their reviewers.

Item: 86 | Architecture Execution | Software Development | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 2 | There is a flow of continuous development until the story gets deployed to production. | Document and refine the end-to-end "Definition of Done" which includes "merged to main," "deployed to staging," "QA-approved," and "submitted to store." | | This guide focuses on establishing and documenting a clear, continuous flow for developing user stories, from coding through testing and ultimately to production deployment. A well-defined "Definition of Done" (DoD) is central to this.
documents.s: Completing Item 86: Ensure Continuous Development Flow

documents.t: Predictability: Makes the process repeatable and helps estimate delivery timelines. Efficiency: Reduces ambiguity about what steps are needed to complete a story. Quality: Ensures necessary quality checks (code review, testing) are performed at the right stages. Transparency: Makes the status and progress of work visible to the entire team (Dev, QA, PO). Enables Automation: Provides the structure needed for effective CI/CD automation.

Select Story: Developer picks up a story from the sprint backlog that meets the Definition of Ready (DoR - Item 40). Assigns it to themselves in Jira. Status: To Do -> In Progress. Develop on Feature Branch: Create a feature branch from main (e.g., feat/MEC-123-login-button). Implement the feature, following coding standards (Item 3). Write unit and widget tests (Item 15, 97). Commit frequently with clear messages (Item 75). Synchronize frequently with main (Item 74). Local Verification: Developer runs flutter analyze and flutter test locally to ensure core checks pass. Manually tests the feature on an emulator/device. Push and Create Pull Request (PR): Push the feature branch to the remote repository. Create a PR targeting main, using the PR template (Item 8). Jira Status: In Progress -> In Review (or similar). Automated CI Checks: The CI pipeline automatically runs on the PR (Item 88): Analyze, Test, Build Checks, SonarQube Quality Gate, etc. Checks must pass. Code Review: Assigned reviewers (peers, tech lead) review the code for correctness, standards, test quality, and potential issues. Feedback is provided and addressed by the author via commits to the feature branch. Merge PR: Once CI passes and reviewers approve, the PR is merged into main (e.g., using Squash and Merge - Item 8). The feature branch is deleted. Automated CD to Staging: Merging to main triggers the CD pipeline (Item 70, Item 83), which builds a staging version of the app and deploys it to an internal distribution platform (e.g., Firebase App Distribution). QA Verification: QA receives notification (Item 79) that a new build is available. QA installs the build on test devices. QA executes test cases (manual/automated) based on the story's Acceptance Criteria. Jira Status: In Review -> In QA (or similar). PO/Stakeholder Review (Optional): PO or stakeholders might review the feature on the staging build, potentially during a Sprint Review/Demo. Mark as QA Approved: If QA verifies the story meets all ACs and no critical bugs are found, they mark it as approved. Jira Status: In QA -> Done (or Ready for Release). Release to Production (Separate Process): Stories marked as "Done" are candidates for the next production release, which involves tagging, building production artifacts, submitting to stores, and phased rollout (covered by other items).
documents.s: Key Stages in the Flow (Example for a Feature Story)

documents.t: The DoD is a shared checklist that defines all the criteria a user story must meet before it can be considered truly "complete". It formalizes the flow. Collaborate on DoD: The entire team (Dev, QA, PO, Architect) should collaboratively define the DoD. Key DoD Items (Example): ✅ Code implemented and adheres to coding standards. ✅ Unit and Widget tests written and passing (meeting coverage goal - Item 24). ✅ Code committed to feature branch with appropriate messages. ✅ Feature branch synced with main. ✅ Pull Request created using template. ✅ All CI checks (analyze, test, build, quality gate) passing on PR. ✅ Code review(s) completed and feedback addressed. ✅ PR merged to main branch. ✅ Feature deployed to Staging environment via automated CD. ✅ QA testing completed and passed against all Acceptance Criteria. ✅ No new critical or major bugs introduced. ✅ Relevant documentation updated (if applicable - Item 35). ✅ Product Owner reviewed/accepted (if applicable). Document and Visualize: Document the agreed DoD clearly on the team's wiki. Consider visualizing the development flow (the stages above) as a flowchart on the wiki. Configure Jira workflow statuses to reflect the key stages (e.g., To Do, In Progress, In Review, In QA, Done). Apply Consistently: Refer to the DoD during Sprint Planning (to understand the effort involved) and especially during Sprint Reviews/Retrospectives. A story isn't "Done" until all DoD criteria are met. Avoid moving cards prematurely. A well-defined DoD and development flow create a clear path for stories, improve predictability, and ensure quality gates are consistently applied.
documents.s: Defining and Documenting the "Definition of Done" (DoD)

documents.t: Item: 71 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Deployment | PREPARATION (Sprint 0) | 2 | It is possible to deploy database changes by running scripts that will incrementally upgrade the database according to the changes relevant to that deployment. | (Backend-focused) Ensure the backend team uses a migration tool (e.g., Liquibase, Flyway) to manage DB schema changes. | | (Note: This item primarily concerns the backend database that your Flutter app interacts with, not typically local databases within the app unless they require schema migrations.) This guide explains the importance of managing backend database schema and data changes using version-controlled scripts and migration tools.
documents.s: Completing Item 71: Use Scripts for Database Changes

documents.t: Version Control: Database schema changes (like CREATE TABLE, ALTER COLUMN) are tracked in Git alongside the application code that depends on them. Repeatability: Ensures that the database schema can be reliably recreated or updated to any specific version across different environments (Dev, Staging, Prod, local). Consistency: Prevents schema drift between environments, where manual changes lead to inconsistencies. Automation: Allows database migrations to be integrated into the automated deployment pipeline (Item 49). Rollback Capability: Most migration tools support generating or writing scripts to roll back changes if needed (Item 78). Collaboration: Makes it clear to all developers what database changes are pending or have been applied.

Common database migration tools include: Liquibase: Open-source, supports various databases (SQL, NoSQL), uses XML, YAML, JSON, or SQL formats for defining changesets. Tracks applied changes in a dedicated database table. Flyway: Open-source (with paid options), primarily focused on SQL databases, uses plain SQL files for migrations with specific naming conventions (e.g., V1__Create_users_table.sql). Also tracks applied changes in a dedicated table. ORM-Specific Migrations: Frameworks like Django, Ruby on Rails, TypeORM (Node.js), Alembic (Python/SQLAlchemy) often have built-in migration tools.

Choose and Implement a Migration Tool: The backend team selects a migration tool compatible with their database and language/framework (e.g., Liquibase for a Java/Spring backend with PostgreSQL). Integrate the tool into the backend project structure. Version Control Migration Files: Create a dedicated directory in the backend's Git repository (e.g., /src/main/resources/db/changelog for Liquibase, /db/migration for Flyway). All schema changes (DDL like CREATE, ALTER, DROP) and reference data changes (DML like INSERT, UPDATE for lookup tables) must be defined in migration files within this directory. Never apply manual SQL changes directly to databases (except perhaps for emergency hotfixes, which should then be immediately codified in a migration script). Write Incremental Changesets/Migrations: Each distinct database change or set of related changes should be in its own "changeset" (Liquibase) or versioned SQL file (Flyway). Files should be named and ordered chronologically (e.g., Flyway uses V1, V1.1, V2; Liquibase uses id and author attributes within a master log). Example (Flyway - V2__Add_user_email.sql): ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN email VARCHAR(255); UPDATE users SET email = 'default@example.com' WHERE email IS NULL; -- Example data backfill ALTER TABLE users ALTER COLUMN email SET NOT NULL; Example (Liquibase - in db.changelog-master.xml or included file): <changeSet id="2" author="dev_team"> <addColumn tableName="users"> <column name="email" type="VARCHAR(255)"/> </addColumn> <update tableName="users"> <column name="email" value="default@example.com"/> <where>email IS NULL</where> </update> <addNotNullConstraint tableName="users" columnName="email" columnDataType="VARCHAR(255)"/> </changeSet> Integrate into Local Development: Developers should be able to easily run the migrations to update their local development database schema to the latest version (e.g., via a build tool command like mvn liquibase:update or flyway migrate). Integrate into Deployment Pipeline (See Item 49): Add a step in the backend's CI/CD pipeline that automatically runs the database migration tool before deploying the new application code. The tool will check its tracking table and apply only the necessary pending migrations for that environment.

The backend team should document: The chosen migration tool and its basic usage. The location of the migration files in the repository. How developers run migrations locally. Confirmation that migrations run automatically during deployment. The Flutter team needs to be aware that database changes are managed this way, ensuring consistency across environments. Using database migration scripts is a foundational practice for reliable and automated backend deployments, which indirectly benefits the Flutter app by ensuring the API interacts with a consistent database schema.

Item: 78 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Integration | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 2 | It is possible to rollback the database version when needed. | (Backend) Ensure the backend's migration tool (e.g., Liquibase) supports "rollback" commands. | | (Note: This item is closely related to Item 72 but focuses specifically on the database rollback mechanism, often enabled by migration tools.) This guide focuses on ensuring the backend database migration strategy includes the capability to roll back schema or data changes introduced by migrations.
documents.s: Completing Item 78: Ensure Database Rollback Capability

documents.t: Error Correction: If a deployed migration script causes unforeseen issues (data corruption, performance degradation, application errors), rolling it back can be the fastest way to restore the database to a working state. Reduces Deployment Risk: Knowing that problematic schema changes can be undone (to some extent) reduces the risk associated with deploying database migrations. Complements Code Rollback: Allows database schema/data to be reverted in coordination with rolling back the application code that depends on it (though backward-compatible changes often mitigate the need for immediate DB rollback - see below).
documents.s: Why is Database Rollback Capability Important?

documents.t: The possibility and ease of rollback depend heavily on the migration tool and the nature of the changes: Migration Tool Support (e.g., Liquibase, ORM Migrators): Liquibase: Automatic Rollback: For many common operations (createTable, addColumn, addPrimaryKey, etc.), Liquibase can often automatically generate the corresponding rollback SQL (dropTable, dropColumn, dropPrimaryKey). Explicit Rollback: For more complex changes (custom SQL, data transformations, potentially destructive changes), developers can explicitly define the rollback logic within the <rollback> tag inside a <changeSet>. <changeSet id="3" author="dev_team"> <sql> -- Complex forward change SQL UPDATE users SET status = 'ACTIVE' WHERE created_date > '2023-01-01'; </sql> <rollback> -- Explicit SQL to undo the change UPDATE users SET status = 'PENDING' WHERE created_date > '2023-01-01' AND --[[previous status condition]]--; -- NOTE: Rolling back data changes can be very risky! </rollback> </changeSet> Execution: Liquibase provides commands like liquibase rollback <tag>, liquibase rollbackCount <number>, liquibase rollbackToDate <date> to execute the rollback logic stored in the changelog. ORM Migration Tools (Alembic, Django Migrations, etc.): Often generate both an "up" (apply) and a "down" (revert) migration script/function. Commands like alembic downgrade -1 or python manage.py migrate <app> <previous_migration> execute the downgrade logic. Manual Rollback Scripts (e.g., Flyway Free): Flyway's free version focuses on forward migrations. Rollback typically involves writing new, forward migrations that manually undo the changes of a previous one. Example: V2__Add_user_email.sql (Adds an email column). If V2 causes problems, a developer writes V3__Revert_add_user_email.sql which contains ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN email;. This requires careful manual effort and testing of the revert script. Restore from Backup: This is the ultimate fallback, especially if migrations cause data corruption or if the migration tool doesn't support rollback for the specific changes made. Mechanism: Use the database backups created before the migration (Item 12). Drawbacks: Incurs downtime while the restore operation completes. May result in loss of data written after the backup was taken but before the restore began.

Use a Migration Tool Supporting Rollback: Whenever possible, use a tool like Liquibase or an ORM migrator that has built-in support for defining and executing rollbacks. Write Explicit Rollback Logic: Don't rely solely on auto-generated rollbacks. For any non-trivial or potentially destructive change, write and test the explicit rollback/downgrade logic. Prioritize Backward-Compatible Changes: Design schema changes to be additive and backward-compatible whenever feasible. This is often the best strategy, allowing application code rollback without requiring immediate database schema rollback. The database might have extra columns/tables the old code ignores, which can be cleaned up later. Test Rollbacks: Just as forward migrations are tested, rollback scripts/procedures should be tested in non-production environments to ensure they work as expected. Data Changes are Risky: Be extremely cautious when writing rollback logic for data migrations (UPDATE, DELETE). It's often impossible to perfectly restore the previous state. Prefer application-level data correction if possible, or rely on backups. Document the Procedure: The backend team's documentation should clearly state: The chosen migration tool and its rollback capabilities. The command(s) used to perform a rollback. The policy/expectation for writing explicit rollback logic. The process for restoring from backup as a fallback. Ensuring a viable database rollback mechanism (even if it's just restoring from backup for destructive changes) is a key part of a resilient deployment strategy.

Item: 48 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Deployment | PREPARATION (Sprint 0) | 2 | It is possible to rollback the deployment (code and database). | For the app: Document how to promote a previous, "known good" build in App Store Connect / Play Console. For DB: Ensure DB migration scripts have "rollback" scripts. | | This guide covers ensuring and documenting that you can roll back both the application deployment (Flutter app) and any associated database changes if a deployment goes wrong.
documents.s: Completing Item 48: Ensure Deployment Rollback Capability

documents.t: Fast Recovery: Allows quick restoration of service if a critical bug is introduced by a new deployment (reduces MTTR - Mean Time to Recovery, Item 10). Risk Mitigation: Provides a safety net, making deployments less stressful. Confidence: Increases confidence in deploying more frequently.
You need separate but coordinated strategies for the application and the database.

Challenge: As noted in Item 7, you cannot instantly "pull back" an installed app from user devices. Rollback means distributing a previous, stable version through the app stores. Mechanism: Identify Last Known Good (LKG) Version: Keep track of the version string (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH+BUILD) and corresponding Git tag of the last stable production release. Retrieve LKG Artifact: Ensure you have access to the signed production artifacts (.aab, .ipa) for the LKG version (stored in GitHub Releases, Artifactory, etc. - Item 12). Google Play Store (Android): Go to Production release track in Play Console. Create a new release. Upload the LKG .aab file (or select from library). It will likely need a new, higher build number than the faulty version but can have the same semantic version (e.g., faulty was 1.2.1+60, rollback is 1.2.1+61 built from the code of 1.2.0+55). Alternatively, use a patch version increment (e.g., 1.2.2+61). Submit and roll out to 100%. App Store Connect (iOS): You must increment the version number (e.g., if faulty was 1.2.1, the rollback needs to be 1.2.2). Check out the Git tag of the LKG version (e.g., v1.2.0+55). Update the pubspec.yaml version to the new incremented version (e.g., 1.2.2+61). Re-run pod install if needed. Build and archive using the LKG codebase but the new version number. Upload this new build (1.2.2 (61)) to App Store Connect. Submit for expedited review if the issue is critical. Release once approved. Automation: While the store submission often requires manual steps, the process of finding the LKG tag and building the rollback artifact can be automated via CI/CD (e.g., a "Rollback Build" workflow triggered manually with a tag input). See Item 52/59 for single-click ideas. Documentation: Document these platform-specific steps clearly in your release/rollback runbook (Item 7).

Mechanism: Rely on the capabilities of the database migration tool (Liquibase, Flyway - Item 47) used by the backend team. Prerequisites: Rollback Logic: Developers must consistently write the rollback (undo) logic for every database migration script they create. Liquibase Example (XML): Uses <rollback> tags. Flyway Example (SQL): Requires separate U<version>__undo.sql files or specific procedures. SQL Example (Manual Tagging): --changeset author:yourname id:20251025_add_last_login ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN last_login TIMESTAMP; --rollback ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN last_login; Tool Support: The chosen migration tool must support a rollback command. Execution: If a deployment fails due to a database migration error or introduces bad data related to schema changes, the backend team runs the migration tool's rollback command (e.g., liquibase rollbackCount 1, flyway undo). This command executes the predefined rollback logic for the most recently applied migration(s). Coordination: Database rollbacks must often be coordinated with application rollbacks if the application code depends on the faulty schema changes. Testing: Crucially, test rollback scripts in a non-production environment periodically to ensure they work as expected. Untested rollback logic is unreliable. Limitations: Rollbacks involving destructive changes (dropping tables/columns) can cause data loss if not carefully managed. Some complex migrations might be difficult or impossible to roll back automatically and may require manual intervention or restoring from a backup (Item 12). Documentation: The backend team's documentation should cover how to execute a database rollback using their chosen tool.

Detection: Identify a critical issue post-deployment via monitoring or user reports. Decision: Quickly decide if a rollback is necessary (vs. rolling forward with a hotfix). Execution: Initiate the application rollback process (build/upload LKG version via stores). If necessary, coordinate with the backend team to execute the database rollback. Verification: Monitor the system closely after the rollback to ensure stability is restored. Documenting this entire coordinated process (App + DB) in a rollback runbook is essential.

Item: 72 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Deployment | PREPARATION (Sprint 0) | 2 | It is possible to rollback the deployment (code and database). | For the app: Document how to promote a previous, "known good" build in App Store Connect / Play Console. For DB: Ensure DB migration scripts have "rollback" scripts. | | This guide covers ensuring and documenting the capability to roll back both the application code deployment and associated database changes for your Flutter app and its backend.
documents.s: Completing Item 72: Ensure Deployment Rollback Capability

documents.t: Error Recovery: Provides a mechanism to quickly revert to a known stable state if a new deployment introduces critical issues. Reduces Downtime: Minimizes the time users are affected by deployment failures. Increases Deployment Confidence: Knowing you can roll back makes the team more confident in deploying frequently.

Application Code Rollback (Flutter App): Challenge: Mobile apps installed on user devices cannot be instantly rolled back like web apps. Rollback involves distributing a previous version through the app stores. Mechanism: Promote a previous, known-good build version in the Google Play Console and App Store Connect. Prerequisites: Artifact Storage: Previous release artifacts (.aab, .ipa) must be stored and accessible (Item 12). Version Tracking: Clear mapping between app versions (e.g., 1.2.0+15) and the corresponding Git commit/tag. Procedure: (Covered in detail in Item 7 - Rollback Strategy) Android: Halt staged rollout if applicable. Create a new release in Play Console using the previous stable AAB, roll out to 100%. iOS: Submit a new version (e.g., 1.2.1) using the codebase of the previous stable version (1.2.0), potentially requesting an expedited review. Documentation: The procedure for promoting a previous version in both stores should be clearly documented in the SCM/Release Plan. Backend Application Code Rollback: Mechanism: Depends on the backend deployment strategy. Common methods: Re-deploy Previous Artifact: If using immutable artifacts (e.g., Docker images), re-deploy the container image tag corresponding to the previous stable version. CI/CD pipelines should support triggering a deployment with a specific version/tag. Blue-Green Deployment: Switch traffic back to the "blue" environment running the previous stable version. Canary Release: Reduce traffic to the "canary" (new) version to 0% and shift 100% back to the stable version. Git Revert: Revert the merge commit in Git (Item 7) and let the standard CI/CD pipeline deploy the reverted code. (Slower, involves a new build/deploy cycle). Documentation: The backend team's deployment documentation should clearly outline their specific rollback procedure(s). Database Changes Rollback: Challenge: Rolling back database schema changes, especially destructive ones (DROP COLUMN, DROP TABLE) or complex data transformations, can be difficult and risky. Rolling back data changes is even harder. Mechanism (using Migration Tools - Item 71): Liquibase: Supports defining explicit <rollback> logic within changesets (e.g., dropping a table added in the forward migration). Can automatically generate rollback for some simpler changes (like createTable -> dropTable). liquibase rollback commands can undo changesets. Flyway: Does not directly support automated rollbacks in the free version. Rollbacks typically involve writing new migration scripts (e.g., V3__Revert_add_user_email.sql) that manually undo the changes from a previous script (V2__Add_user_email.sql). The paid version offers undo functionality. ORM Tools: Often provide commands to revert to previous migration versions. Best Practices: Favor Backward-Compatible Changes: Design schema changes to be additive and backward-compatible where possible (e.g., add new nullable columns instead of renaming/dropping old ones immediately). This often allows rolling back the application code without needing to roll back the database schema instantly. The old code simply ignores the new columns. Defer destructive schema changes until the new code is stable. Write Explicit Rollback Scripts: For any non-trivial change, manually write and test the corresponding rollback script/logic. Backup Before Migration: Ensure a database backup is taken just before applying migrations in production (often handled by automated cloud backups - Item 12). Full restore from backup is the ultimate fallback, but involves downtime. Documentation: The backend team's documentation should state: If their migration tool supports rollback commands. The policy on writing explicit rollback scripts. The procedure for executing a database rollback (if supported) or restoring from backup.

Verify Capabilities: Ensure the mechanisms described above are actually in place for the Flutter app (artifact storage), backend code (CI/CD supports deploying old versions), and database (migration tool supports rollback, or policy mandates compatible changes/backups). Document Procedures: Update the main SCM/Release Process document. Add a section detailing the Flutter App Rollback steps via the app stores. Add a section describing (or linking to the backend docs for) the Backend Code Rollback procedure. Add a section describing (or linking to the backend docs for) the Database Rollback strategy (tool support, backward compatibility, backups). Test Rollbacks (Non-Production): Periodically practice rolling back a deployment in a staging environment to ensure the process works and is well-understood. Having a well-defined and tested rollback capability for all components is essential for managing risk in a continuous deployment environment.

Item: 44 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Deployment | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 2 | "The configuration that is specific for each environment, such as API endpoints and configuration for database connection are configured externally to the deployment package as environment variables." | Use dart-defineor.envfiles (e.g., viaflutter_config) to inject environment-specific variables (API endpoints, keys) at build time. Do not hardcode them. | | This guide explains how to manage environment-specific configurations (like API endpoints, API keys, feature flags) externally, rather than hardcoding them directly into your Flutter application code. This is crucial for building artifacts that can target different environments (Dev, Staging, Prod).

Avoid Hardcoding: Prevents sensitive information (API keys) or environment details (URLs) from being committed to version control. Environment Flexibility: Allows the same codebase to be built to target different backend environments or use different keys without code changes. Consistency: Ensures a standard way of managing configuration across the app. Security: Keeps secrets out of the codebase.

Using --dart-define (Recommended for CI/CD): Concept: Pass key-value pairs during the flutter run or flutter build command. These values are accessible in Dart code via String.fromEnvironment, int.fromEnvironment, bool.fromEnvironment. Implementation: Build Command: # Development Run flutter run \ --dart-define=API_ENDPOINT=[https://dev-api.example.com](https://dev-api.example.com) \ --dart-define=API_KEY=DEV123 \ --dart-define=FEATURE_X_ENABLED=true # Production Build flutter build appbundle --release \ --dart-define=API_ENDPOINT=[https://api.example.com](https://api.example.com) \ --dart-define=API_KEY=PROD789 \ --dart-define=FEATURE_X_ENABLED=true Accessing in Dart: const String apiEndpoint = String.fromEnvironment( 'API_ENDPOINT', // Provide a sensible default for local runs if no define is passed defaultValue: '[https://default-api.example.com](https://default-api.example.com)', ); const String apiKey = String.fromEnvironment('API_KEY'); // No default = compile error if not defined const bool isFeatureXEnabled = bool.fromEnvironment( 'FEATURE_X_ENABLED', defaultValue: false, ); // Use these constants in your code (e.g., in your Dio client setup) Dio dio = Dio(BaseOptions(baseUrl: apiEndpoint)); dio.options.headers['Authorization'] = 'Bearer $apiKey'; Pros: Built into Flutter, simple for CI/CD environments where variables are easily passed on the command line, avoids extra files. Cons: Can make local flutter run commands verbose if there are many variables. Defaults need careful management. Values are compiled into the app. Using .env Files (Good for Local Development & CI/CD): Concept: Store configuration variables in .env files (e.g., .env.dev, .env.prod). Use a package like flutter_dotenv or flutter_config to load these values at runtime (or compile time, depending on the package). Implementation (flutter_dotenv example - loads at runtime): Add flutter_dotenv to pubspec.yaml. Create .env files (e.g., .env.dev, .env.prod) and add them to .gitignore. # .env.dev API_ENDPOINT=[https://dev-api.example.com](https://dev-api.example.com) API_KEY=DEV123 # .env.prod API_ENDPOINT=[https://api.example.com](https://api.example.com) API_KEY=PROD789 Load the appropriate file in your main.dart before runApp: import 'package:flutter_dotenv/flutter_dotenv.dart'; Future<void> main() async { WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized(); // Needed before async // Determine which .env file to load (e.g., based on --dart-define) const env = String.fromEnvironment('ENV', defaultValue: 'dev'); await dotenv.load(fileName: ".env.$env"); runApp(MyApp()); } Access variables: import 'package:flutter_dotenv/flutter_dotenv.dart'; String apiEndpoint = dotenv.env['API_ENDPOINT'] ?? 'default_fallback'; String apiKey = dotenv.env['API_KEY']!; // Use ! if you are sure it exists Implementation (flutter_config example - loads at compile time): Add flutter_config to pubspec.yaml. Create .env files as above (add to .gitignore). Setup native platform integration (follow package instructions). Configure build command/CI to select the .env file (e.g., using flutter build --dart-define=ENV_FILE=.env.prod). Access variables (values are compiled in): import 'package:flutter_config/flutter_config.dart'; String apiEndpoint = FlutterConfig.get('API_ENDPOINT'); Pros: Keeps local run commands clean, separates config clearly, standard .env format. flutter_config compiles values in (like dart-define). Cons: Requires an extra package. flutter_dotenv loads values at runtime (slightly less secure, minor startup cost). Requires careful .gitignore management. Need a mechanism (like dart-define) to choose which .env file to load/compile.
documents.s: Methods for Externalizing Configuration in Flutter

documents.t: Choose a Method: Select either --dart-define or an .env package based on team preference and workflow. Using dart-define is often simpler for CI/CD, while .env files can be cleaner for local development. You can combine them (e.g., use dart-define to specify which .env file flutter_dotenv should load). Identify Configuration Variables: List all values that change between environments (API URLs, keys, analytics IDs, feature flags, logging levels). Refactor Code: Remove hardcoded values and replace them with access to the chosen configuration mechanism (e.g., String.fromEnvironment or dotenv.env[]). Create Configuration Files/Variables: If using .env, create the .env.dev, .env.staging, .env.prod files and add them to .gitignore. Store secrets securely (e.g., CI/CD secrets, secrets manager) and inject them into the .env file during the CI/CD build process, not in Git. If using dart-define, ensure your CI/CD pipeline passes the correct defines for each environment build. Store secrets in CI/CD secrets. Configure Build/Run Commands: Update launch.json (for VS Code local runs) and CI/CD scripts (flutter build commands) to pass the correct --dart-define flags or select the correct .env file. Document the Process: On your project wiki, document: The chosen configuration method. Where environment variables are defined (e.g., "See .env.dev (gitignored), values sourced from CI secrets"). How to access variables in Dart code. How to run/build the app for different environments (provide example commands). By externalizing configuration, you create a more flexible, secure, and maintainable application build process.

Item: 69 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Deployment | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 2 | "The configuration that is specific for each environment, such as API endpoints and configuration for database connection are configured externally to the deployment package as environment variables." | Use dart-defineor.envfiles (e.g., viaflutter_config) to inject environment-specific variables (API endpoints, keys) at build time. Do not hardcode them. | | This guide explains how to manage environment-specific configurations (like API endpoints or keys) externally, rather than hardcoding them into your Flutter application source code.

Security: Avoids committing sensitive information (API keys, secrets) directly into the version control system. Flexibility: Allows building the same codebase for different environments (Dev, Staging, Prod) just by changing the configuration provided at build time. Supports the "Build once, deploy anywhere" principle (adapted for mobile). Maintainability: Centralizes configuration, making it easier to update endpoints or keys without changing the application code.

Choose one primary method: Using --dart-define (Recommended for Simplicity): Concept: Pass key-value pairs directly to the flutter run or flutter build command. These values are available at runtime using String.fromEnvironment, int.fromEnvironment, etc. Implementation: Access variables in Dart code: // lib/config.dart abstract class AppConfig { static const apiUrl = String.fromEnvironment( 'API_URL', defaultValue: '[https://default-api.example.com](https://default-api.example.com)', // Default for local run maybe? ); static const apiKey = String.fromEnvironment('API_KEY'); // No default = compile error if missing } // Usage: // http.get(Uri.parse('${AppConfig.apiUrl}/users')); Pass variables during build/run: # Development Run flutter run \ --dart-define=API_URL=[https://dev-api.example.com](https://dev-api.example.com) \ --dart-define=API_KEY=DEV_SECRET_KEY # Production Build (Android) flutter build appbundle --release \ --dart-define=API_URL=[https://prod-api.example.com](https://prod-api.example.com) \ --dart-define=API_KEY=PROD_SECRET_KEY # Production Build (iOS) flutter build ipa --release \ --dart-define=API_URL=[https://prod-api.example.com](https://prod-api.example.com) \ --dart-define=API_KEY=PROD_SECRET_KEY Managing Values: Store the actual --dart-define flags needed for each environment in: CI/CD pipeline scripts (e.g., .github/workflows/main.yaml). VS Code launch.json for local debugging configurations. Shell scripts (build_dev.sh, build_prod.sh). Secrets: For sensitive values like API keys, retrieve them from secure environment variables or secret management systems within your CI/CD pipeline before passing them via --dart-define. Do not commit secrets directly into CI scripts. Pros: Built into Flutter, simple for a few variables, type-safe access using fromEnvironment. Cons: Command line can get long with many variables, managing the flags themselves needs structure (scripts, launch.json). Using .env Files (e.g., with flutter_dotenv or similar): Concept: Store configuration key-value pairs in .env files (e.g., .env.dev, .env.prod). Load the appropriate file at runtime or use build-time code generation. Implementation (flutter_dotenv example - runtime loading): Add flutter_dotenv to pubspec.yaml. Create .env files (e.g., .env.dev, .env.prod): # .env.dev API_URL=[https://dev-api.example.com](https://dev-api.example.com) API_KEY=DEV_SECRET_KEY Add .env* files to .gitignore! Never commit files with secrets. Store templates or non-sensitive defaults if needed. Load the environment file in main.dart: import 'package:flutter_dotenv/flutter_dotenv.dart'; Future<void> main() async { // Load the environment file before running the app // Choose file based on build flavor or dart-define flag const env = String.fromEnvironment('ENV', defaultValue: 'dev'); // Use dart-define to switch env await dotenv.load(fileName: ".env.$env"); runApp(MyApp()); } Access variables: // lib/config.dart import 'package:flutter_dotenv/flutter_dotenv.dart'; abstract class AppConfig { static final String apiUrl = dotenv.env['API_URL'] ?? 'fallback_url'; static final String apiKey = dotenv.env['API_KEY'] ?? ''; // Handle missing keys } Managing Files: Securely manage the .env files outside of Git (e.g., using a secrets manager, injecting them in CI/CD). Pros: Cleaner than long command lines, familiar pattern for many developers. Cons: Runtime loading (flutter_dotenv) adds a small startup cost and variables are typically strings (requiring manual parsing/validation). Build-time generation packages might add complexity. Requires careful .gitignore management.

In your project's README or setup guide (Item 2), document the chosen method (--dart-define or .env files). Explain how to configure the variables for local development (e.g., "Set up your launch.json like this..." or "Create a .env.dev file with these keys..."). Clearly state which files (if any, like .env files) should be added to .gitignore. Link to where CI/CD environment variables or secrets are managed. By externalizing configuration, you create more secure, flexible, and maintainable builds for different environments.

Item: 87 | Architecture Execution | Software Development | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 2 | "The foundation of the application architecture is being followed by the Development team as it was originally described in the documentation
(application layers, frameworks, logging mechanism, error handling mechanism, transaction control mechanism)." | Enforce architecture adherence through mandatory PR reviews by the tech lead or architect. Use analysis_options.yaml to ban forbidden import patterns. | | This guide focuses on ensuring that the development team consistently adheres to the foundational architectural patterns, principles, and mechanisms documented for the Flutter project (as defined in Item 11).
documents.s: Completing Item 87: Follow Documented Architecture Foundation

documents.t: Consistency: A consistent architecture makes the codebase easier to understand, navigate, and maintain for everyone on the team. Maintainability: Following established patterns reduces complexity and makes future modifications or bug fixes less risky and time-consuming. Scalability: A well-defined architecture provides a framework for adding new features without degrading the overall structure. Testability: Architectural patterns like Clean Architecture often promote separation of concerns, making components easier to unit test in isolation. Prevents Architectural Drift: Avoids the gradual degradation of the architecture ("Big Ball of Mud") that can happen if developers introduce ad-hoc solutions or violate established patterns.

Adherence relies on a combination of automated checks, manual reviews, and team culture. Clear Documentation (Prerequisite - Item 11): The architectural foundation (layers, chosen frameworks like Bloc/Riverpod, error handling, logging, navigation) must be clearly documented and easily accessible. Include diagrams and concise code examples illustrating the correct way to implement common patterns (e.g., creating a Bloc, making a repository call, handling errors). Mandatory Pull Request (PR) Reviews: This is the primary mechanism for enforcing architectural adherence. Reviewers: Assign PR reviews to team members who have a strong understanding of the architecture (Tech Lead, Architect, Senior Developers). Review Focus: Reviewers should explicitly check: Layering: Does the code respect the defined layer boundaries (e.g., no direct API calls from Widgets, UI logic kept out of the Domain layer)? Framework Usage: Is the chosen state management library (Bloc, Riverpod) being used correctly according to documented patterns? Are new Blocs/Providers structured properly? Error Handling: Are errors handled according to the defined strategy? Are potential exceptions caught appropriately? Logging: Is logging implemented consistently where required? Dependency Injection: Are dependencies being correctly injected/provided, not manually instantiated where inappropriate? Code Structure: Does the new code fit logically within the established project structure? Provide Feedback: Reviewers should provide constructive feedback when deviations are found, linking back to the architecture documentation. Approval should be withheld until significant architectural violations are addressed. Static Analysis (analysis_options.yaml): While primarily for style and potential errors, static analysis can sometimes help enforce architectural rules: Banning Imports: Use analyzer: errors: invalid_dependency in analysis_options.yaml to define rules that prevent code in one layer (e.g., presentation) from directly importing code from another layer it shouldn't depend on (e.g., data/datasources). This requires careful configuration based on your project structure. # Example (conceptual - syntax needs verification) analyzer: errors: invalid_dependency: error # Treat violations as errors plugins: # Potentially use custom lint rules if needed for complex checks # ... other analyzer settings ... # Configuration for invalid_dependency might go here or via specific lint rules # depending on lint packages used. Research required. Code Snippets and Templates: Provide IDE code snippets (e.g., for VS Code) or templates for creating common architectural components (e.g., a new Bloc/Event/State structure, a new UseCase class) according to the standard pattern. This makes it easier for developers to "do the right thing." Pair Programming and Mentoring: Encourage pair programming, especially when working in complex areas or for developers new to the architecture. Senior developers should mentor junior developers on applying the architectural patterns correctly. Team Communication: Regularly discuss architectural patterns and best practices in team meetings or specific sessions. If a pattern proves problematic or needs refinement, discuss it openly and update the documentation/ADRs accordingly. Don't let unspoken deviations become the norm. Refactoring: Allocate time (e.g., via tech debt tickets - Item 5) to refactor code that deviates significantly from the established architecture. Consistent adherence requires clear documentation, diligent reviews, and a team culture that values architectural integrity. Automated checks like banned imports can provide a valuable safety net.

Item: 47 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Deployment | PREPARATION (Sprint 0) | 2 | It is possible to deploy database changes by running scripts that will incrementally upgrade the database according to the changes relevant to that deployment. | (Backend-focused) Ensure the backend team uses a migration tool (e.g., Liquibase, Flyway) to manage DB schema changes. | | (Note: This item primarily concerns the backend database supporting your Flutter app, not typically the app itself unless it uses a complex local database like sqflite with evolving schemas). This guide explains the importance of using tools and versioned scripts to manage backend database schema changes incrementally and reliably.
documents.s: Completing Item 47: Use Incremental DB Deployment Scripts

documents.t: Reliability & Repeatability: Ensures database schema changes are applied consistently across all environments (Dev, Staging, Prod). Manual changes are error-prone. Version Control: Database schema structure is versioned alongside the application code that depends on it (usually in the backend repository). Auditing: Provides a clear history of all changes made to the database schema. Automation: Enables database migrations to be integrated directly into the automated deployment pipeline (Item 49). Rollback Capability: Most migration tools support generating rollback scripts, making it easier to undo changes if necessary (Item 48). Collaboration: Allows multiple developers to work on database changes concurrently with less risk of conflict.

Database migration tools work by: Tracking Applied Changes: They maintain a special table in the target database (e.g., DATABASECHANGELOG for Liquibase) that records which migration scripts have already been executed. Executing New Scripts: When the tool runs, it compares the list of available migration scripts (in the codebase) against the tracking table. It then executes only the scripts that have not yet been applied, in the correct order.

Choose a Migration Tool: Select a tool compatible with your backend language/framework and database type. Common choices: Liquibase: Java-based, supports many databases (SQL & NoSQL), flexible formats (XML, YAML, SQL, JSON). Flyway: Java-based, primarily SQL-focused, convention-over-configuration approach. Alembic: Python/SQLAlchemy specific. TypeORM Migrations: TypeScript/Node.js specific (for TypeORM). Knex Migrations: JavaScript/Node.js specific (for Knex.js). Rails Migrations: Ruby on Rails specific. (Many frameworks have built-in migration tools). Integrate the Tool into the Backend Project: Add the tool's library/plugin to the backend project's build system (e.g., Maven, Gradle, npm). Configure connection details for the tool to access the database. Establish Scripting Conventions: Location: Store migration scripts in a dedicated directory within the backend's source code repository (e.g., src/main/resources/db/changelog for Liquibase). Naming: Use a consistent naming convention that enforces order (e.g., YYYYMMDDHHMMSS_description.sql, v1.0.1__add_user_email.sql). The tool usually relies on this naming for execution order. Format: Choose a format (SQL, XML, YAML) and stick to it. Pure SQL is often simplest. Granularity: Each script should represent a single, atomic change (e.g., add a column, create an index, insert reference data). Avoid large, multi-purpose scripts. Write Migration Scripts: When a code change requires a database schema change: Create a new migration script (e.g., 20251025210000_add_last_login_to_users.sql). Write the SQL (or XML/YAML) to apply the change (e.g., ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN last_login TIMESTAMP;). (Recommended) Also write the corresponding rollback logic within the same script or a separate one, if the tool supports it (e.g., ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN last_login;). Version Control: Commit the migration scripts to the backend's Git repository along with the application code that depends on them. Automate Execution (See Item 49): Integrate the migration tool command (e.g., liquibase update, flyway migrate) into the backend's deployment pipeline, ensuring it runs before the new application code is deployed. Document the Process: Document the chosen tool, script location, naming conventions, and how to create new migrations in the backend team's development guide. (For Flutter apps using local databases like sqflite): While full migration tools are less common, sqflite provides onUpgrade callbacks during database opening. You need to manually write version-based ALTER TABLE statements within these callbacks and manage the database version number yourself. Ensure these upgrade scripts are well-tested. By adopting an incremental script-based approach using dedicated tools, backend teams can manage database evolution reliably and safely across environments.

Item: 84 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Monitoring | RELEASE | 2 | "The monitoring tools are measuring CPU usage, Disk space, Response time, memory, etc. If there is an issue with any of those infrastructure metrics the team will get notified." | (Infra) Create a "Production Infrastructure" dashboard in Datadog/GCP. Set up alerts for "disk > 90%" and "CPU > 85%." | | (Note: This item primarily concerns the monitoring of the backend infrastructure supporting your Flutter app, typically managed by an Infrastructure or Backend team.) This guide explains the importance of monitoring key infrastructure metrics for your production backend systems and setting up alerts for potential issues.

Proactive Issue Detection: Identifies resource exhaustion (CPU, memory, disk) or performance degradation before it causes a major outage or significantly impacts users. Performance Analysis: Helps correlate infrastructure performance (e.g., high CPU, slow disk I/O) with application-level issues (e.g., slow API response times). Capacity Planning: Provides data to understand resource utilization trends, informing decisions about scaling infrastructure up or down. Troubleshooting: Essential data source when diagnosing outages or performance problems.

For the servers, containers (e.g., Kubernetes pods), databases, and load balancers supporting your backend API: CPU Usage: Percentage of CPU utilized. High sustained CPU (>80-90%) often indicates overload or inefficient code. Memory Usage: Percentage or absolute amount of RAM used. Consistently high memory usage might indicate memory leaks or insufficient resources. Watch for OutOfMemory (OOM) events. Disk Space: Percentage of disk utilized (especially for database storage, logs, or temporary files). Running out of disk space is a common cause of critical failures. Disk I/O: Read/Write operations per second (IOPS) and throughput (MB/s). Slow disk I/O can bottleneck database performance. Monitor disk latency. Network I/O: Bytes sent/received per second. Helps identify network bottlenecks or unexpected traffic patterns. Monitor network latency and packet loss. Database Connections: Number of active database connections. Reaching connection limits can prevent the application from accessing the database. Load Balancer Metrics: Request count, latency (target response time), number of healthy/unhealthy hosts, HTTP error codes (5xx). Container Metrics (Kubernetes): Pod restarts, container CPU/Memory limits vs. usage, readiness/liveness probe failures.
documents.s: Key Infrastructure Metrics to Monitor (Backend Focus)

documents.t: Choose a Monitoring Tool: Cloud Provider Tools: AWS CloudWatch, Google Cloud Monitoring (Stackdriver), Azure Monitor. Often the easiest starting point if your infrastructure is cloud-based. Third-Party Platforms: Datadog, Dynatrace, New Relic, Grafana (often paired with Prometheus for data collection). Offer more advanced features, dashboards, and integrations. Install Monitoring Agents: Deploy monitoring agents (provided by the tool) onto your servers or configure integrations for managed services (databases, load balancers, Kubernetes). These agents collect metrics and send them to the monitoring platform. Configure Metric Collection: Ensure the agents or integrations are configured to collect the key metrics listed above at an appropriate frequency (e.g., every 1-5 minutes). Create Dashboards: Build dashboards within your monitoring tool to visualize the key metrics for your production environment. Group related metrics (e.g., a dashboard for database metrics, another for API server metrics). Use time-series graphs to show trends. Make dashboards accessible to the relevant team members (Backend, DevOps, potentially Flutter team for context). [Image of a server monitoring dashboard] Set Up Alerts: This is crucial for proactive detection. Define alert rules based on thresholds for critical metrics. Essential Alerts: High CPU Usage: e.g., CPU > 90% sustained for 10 minutes. High Memory Usage: e.g., Memory > 90% sustained for 10 minutes (or specific OOM alerts). Low Disk Space: e.g., Disk Usage > 85% or > 90%. Act on this early! High Disk Latency: e.g., Average disk read/write latency > 100ms for 5 minutes. Database Connection Limit Reached: Alert if active connections approach the configured maximum. Load Balancer Unhealthy Hosts: Alert if the number of healthy hosts behind a load balancer drops below a threshold. High Load Balancer 5xx Errors: Alert if the rate of server-side errors (5xx) exceeds a baseline (e.g., > 1% of requests). Container Restarts (Kubernetes): Alert on frequent pod restarts. Notification Channels: Configure alerts to notify the appropriate team via: PagerDuty / Opsgenie (for critical, on-call issues). Dedicated chat channel (e.g., #alerts-prod - Item 17). Email. Tune Alerts: Adjust thresholds based on observed behavior to reduce false positives (noise) while still catching real issues promptly. Document: Document the monitoring tool used. Link to the key production dashboards. Outline the critical alerts configured and the expected response procedure (runbooks - Item 98). By monitoring these fundamental infrastructure metrics and setting up actionable alerts, you create an early warning system that helps maintain the stability and performance of the backend systems your Flutter app depends on.

Item: 145 | Architecture Validation | Architecture Evaluation | PREPARATION (Sprint 0) | 2 | The code quality is measured through static code analysis tools. | Configure flutter analyzewith strict rules inanalysis_options.yaml and run it on every PR. | | This guide covers the fundamental practice of using static analysis tools to automatically measure and check the quality of your Flutter codebase. This is a foundational step for maintaining code health.
documents.s: Completing Item 145: Measure Code Quality with Static Analysis

documents.t: Early Bug Detection: Catches potential errors (like null pointer issues, type mismatches, unused variables) before runtime. Enforce Coding Standards: Automatically checks adherence to formatting rules, naming conventions, and language best practices defined by the team (Item 3). Identify Code Smells: Flags potential maintainability issues like overly complex methods, duplicated code (basic level), or violations of good design principles. Improve Consistency: Ensures all code contributed by different team members adheres to the same baseline rules, making the codebase more uniform and easier to read. Automated Feedback: Provides immediate, objective feedback to developers as they code (via IDE integration) or when they submit code (via CI checks). Reduces reliance on manual review for basic issues. Foundation for Other Metrics: Provides the raw data (lint issues, complexity) often used by higher-level tools like SonarQube (Item 6).
The primary tool for static analysis in Dart and Flutter is the Dart Analyzer, configured via the analysis_options.yaml file.

Configure analysis_options.yaml: Location: This file must exist at the root of your Flutter project. Base Configuration: Start by including a standard set of recommended rules: # Include either flutter_lints (recommended for Flutter projects) include: package:flutter_lints/flutter.yaml # Or the stricter core Dart lints # include: package:lints/recommended.yaml Customize Rules (Item 3): Enable Stricter Rules: Browse the full list of Dart Linter Rules (https://dart.dev/tools/linter-rules) and enable additional rules that promote better code quality and consistency for your team. Add them under the linter: rules: section.
