Examples: linter: rules: # - always_declare_return_types # Example: Enforce return types # - avoid_redundant_argument_values # Example: Clean up code # - prefer_final_locals # Example: Promote immutability # - require_trailing_commas # Example: Improve formatting consistency # ... add many more based on team agreement Adjust Severity: You can change the default severity of rules (e.g., treat certain warnings as errors) under the analyzer: errors: section. analyzer: errors: # Treat missing required parameters as errors missing_required_param: error # Treat avoid_print as a warning (instead of info) avoid_print: warning Exclude Files: Exclude generated files from analysis, as you typically don't control their content. analyzer: exclude: - '**/*.g.dart' - '**/*.freezed.dart' - 'lib/generated_plugin_registrant.dart' Commit the File: Add and commit analysis_options.yaml to your Git repository. Integrate with IDE (VS Code / Android Studio): The Dart/Flutter extensions for VS Code and Android Studio automatically use the analysis_options.yaml file. Issues (errors, warnings, lints) will be highlighted directly in the code editor, providing immediate feedback to developers. Encourage developers to address these issues as they code. Integrate with CI Pipeline (Crucial Enforcement): Add a step to your CI workflow (GitHub Actions, Codemagic, etc.) that runs on every Pull Request. Use the command flutter analyze with flags to fail the build if issues are present. - name: Analyze code # Fails the job if any diagnostic message is produced. # Adjust --fatal-infos / --fatal-warnings based on how strictly # you configure severities in analysis_options.yaml run: flutter analyze --fatal-infos --fatal-warnings . Make this a required status check in your branch protection rules (Item 8). This prevents merging code that doesn't pass static analysis checks. Communicate and Document: Ensure the team understands the purpose of analysis_options.yaml and the importance of adhering to the defined rules. Document any particularly important or non-obvious custom rules in your Coding Conventions guide (Item 3). By setting up and enforcing static analysis via flutter analyze and a well-configured analysis_options.yaml, you establish an essential automated baseline for code quality in your Flutter project. This is often the first and most impactful step in automated quality measurement. ✅

Item: 83 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Integration | PREPARATION (Sprint 0) | 2 | "A merge commit to (a) specified, main, or default branche(s) will trigger the build and the unit tests will run during the build." | Configure the main CI workflow to trigger on pushevents to themainbranch. The first steps must beflutter analyzeandflutter test. | | This guide explains how to configure your Continuous Integration (CI) pipeline to automatically trigger a build and run essential checks (like analysis and unit tests) whenever code is merged into your main integration branch (typically main).
documents.s: Completing Item 83: Ensure Merge Triggers Build and Test

documents.t: Integration Verification: Confirms that the newly merged code integrates correctly with the main codebase and doesn't break anything fundamental. Fast Feedback on Broken Mainline: Immediately alerts the team if the main branch becomes unstable (fails tests or compilation). A broken main branch blocks everyone. Foundation for CD: The successful completion of this build often serves as the trigger for Continuous Deployment (CD) to a development or staging environment (Item 70). "Golden" Branch: Ensures the main branch always represents a stable, tested state of the application (at least passing core checks).
documents.s: Why Trigger Builds on Merge to Main?

documents.t: Identify the Main Integration Branch: Typically, this is the main branch (previously often master). If using Gitflow, this might be the develop branch. For this guide, we'll assume main. Configure the CI Workflow Trigger: In your pipeline-as-code file (e.g., .github/workflows/main.yaml, .gitlab-ci.yml), define a trigger that executes the workflow on push events specifically targeting the main branch. GitHub Actions Example: name: Main Branch CI & Dev Deploy on: push: branches: - main # Trigger ONLY on pushes/merges to the main branch # Optional: Keep pull_request trigger for PR checks in the same file # pull_request: # branches: # - main GitLab CI Example: workflow: rules: - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main" # Trigger for main branch - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event" # Trigger for MRs Ensure this trigger is distinct from or correctly combined with your Pull Request trigger (Item 88). You want checks on both PRs before merge and on the main branch after merge. Define Core Build and Test Steps: Within the job(s) triggered by the push to main, include the essential steps to verify integration: Checkout Code: Get the latest code from main. Setup Environment: Install Flutter (FVM), other dependencies. Install Dependencies: flutter pub get. Static Analysis: flutter analyze --fatal-infos --fatal-warnings . (Item 6). This must fail the job if issues exist. Unit & Widget Tests: flutter test. This must fail the job if any tests fail. (Optional but Recommended) Build Check: Compile the app in at least debug mode for both platforms to catch compilation errors (flutter build apk --debug, flutter build ios --debug --no-codesign). Release builds (flutter build appbundle/ipa --release) might happen here or in a subsequent deployment job. (Optional) Code Generation: Run build_runner if necessary. Ensure Failure Stops the Pipeline: Verify that your CI/CD platform is configured so that if any of the core steps (analyze, test, build) fail, the entire job (and potentially subsequent dependent jobs like deployment) fails and is clearly marked as such. Notifications on Failure (Item 79): Configure immediate notifications (Slack, Google Chat) specifically for failures on the main branch build. This requires urgent attention from the team. Branch Protection (Reinforcement): While not strictly part of the trigger, remember that branch protection rules (Item 8) requiring status checks before merging help ensure that code landing on main has already passed these checks in the PR context, making the post-merge build less likely to fail unexpectedly. The post-merge build acts as a final safeguard. By automatically running core analysis and tests on every merge to main, you maintain the stability and integrity of your primary codebase and enable reliable downstream processes like Continuous Deployment.

Item: 29 | Architecture Definition | Non-functional requirements | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 2 | The Non-functional requirements are approved by the stackholders/business side. | Hold a dedicated review meeting with the Product Owner to get formal sign-off on the NFRs, especially performance and security targets. | | (Note: The item phase is listed as DEVELOPMENT, but approval often happens closer to SETUP after NFRs are defined. The action applies regardless of phase timing). This guide explains the process of formally reviewing and obtaining approval or acknowledgment for the defined Non-Functional Requirements (NFRs) from key stakeholders, particularly the Product Owner (PO) or business representatives.

Shared Understanding & Expectations: Ensures stakeholders understand the quality targets (and their implications) that the team is working towards. Prioritization Alignment: Confirms that the defined NFRs (and the effort required to meet them) align with business priorities. Stakeholders might prioritize speed-to-market over hitting a stringent performance target initially, or vice-versa. Trade-off Acknowledgement: Makes the trade-offs explicit (e.g., achieving higher performance might require more development time or infrastructure cost). Approval implies acceptance of these trade-offs. Basis for Acceptance: Provides objective criteria (the NFR targets) that can contribute to the acceptance of the final product. Accountability: Creates shared accountability for achieving the desired quality attributes.

Prepare for the Review: Finalize NFR Document: Ensure the NFR spreadsheet or document (from Item 28) is populated with specific, measurable targets. Identify Key Stakeholders: Determine who needs to approve or be formally aware of the NFRs. This is almost always the Product Owner. It might also include: Project Sponsor Key Business Users/Representatives Client Contact (if applicable) Compliance Officer (if regulatory NFRs exist) Create a Summary/Presentation (Optional): For non-technical stakeholders, consider creating a brief summary highlighting the most critical NFRs (especially those related to user experience like performance/reliability, and critical business needs like security/compliance) and explaining their importance in business terms. Schedule a Dedicated Review Meeting: Invite the identified key stakeholders (especially the PO). Include the Tech Lead and/or Architect. Set a clear agenda: "Review and Approve Non-Functional Requirements for Project X". Allocate sufficient time (e.g., 60 minutes). Conduct the Review Meeting: Explain NFRs: Briefly explain what NFRs are and why they are important for the project's success. Walk Through Key NFRs: Present the NFR document/spreadsheet or the summary. Focus on the most impactful categories (Performance, Reliability, Security, key Usability aspects). Explain Targets and Measurement: Clearly state the target for each key NFR and how it will be measured (e.g., "We're aiming for app startup under 2 seconds, measured by Firebase"). Discuss Rationale and Trade-offs: Explain why specific targets were chosen (e.g., "Industry standard," "User expectation," "Security best practice"). Crucially, discuss the implications: "Meeting this strict security requirement means we need to implement X, which adds Y days to the schedule. Is this priority aligned?" Solicit Feedback and Questions: Encourage stakeholders to ask questions and express concerns. Be prepared to adjust targets if strong justifications are provided, but defend targets necessary for technical stability or core requirements. Seek Formal Agreement/Sign-off: At the end of the meeting, explicitly ask for approval or formal acknowledgment from the primary stakeholder (PO). "Based on this discussion, do you approve these NFR targets as the quality goals we will work towards?" Document the Approval: Meeting Minutes: Record the meeting minutes, clearly stating that the NFRs were reviewed and approved (or noting any specific exceptions or action items for revision). Update NFR Document: Add a note or status field to the NFR document/spreadsheet indicating the approval date and approver (e.g., "Approved by [PO Name] on [Date]"). Email Confirmation (Optional): Send a follow-up email summarizing the approved NFRs and thanking the stakeholders. Handle Disagreements or Changes: If stakeholders push back strongly on certain targets (e.g., deeming a performance target too costly to achieve), document the disagreement and the accepted (potentially lower) target or the decision to defer the NFR. This manages expectations. If NFRs need to change later in the project due to new information or shifting priorities, repeat the review and approval process for the changes. Formal approval ensures that the quality goals are not just a technical exercise but are aligned with and supported by the business.

Item: 82 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Integration | PREPARATION (Sprint 0) | 2 | The build script steps are controlled using pipeline style or equivalent. | Use a YAML-based pipeline-as-code file (e.g., .github/workflows/main.yaml, codemagic.yaml) checked into Git. | | This guide explains the practice of defining your CI/CD build and deployment pipeline steps as code, typically using a YAML file stored in your project's Git repository.

Instead of configuring build steps through a graphical user interface (GUI) on the CI/CD server (like traditional Jenkins freestyle jobs), you define the entire pipeline – stages, steps, commands, environment variables, triggers – in a text file (usually YAML) that lives alongside your application code in version control. Examples: GitHub Actions: .github/workflows/your_workflow.yaml GitLab CI: .gitlab-ci.yml Bitbucket Pipelines: bitbucket-pipelines.yml Codemagic: codemagic.yaml Jenkins: Jenkinsfile (using Groovy syntax) Azure DevOps: azure-pipelines.yml

Version Control: Your pipeline definition is versioned in Git. You can track changes, revert to previous versions, and use branching/PRs to propose and review pipeline modifications. Reproducibility: The pipeline definition is part of the repository, ensuring that anyone checking out the code can see exactly how it's built and deployed. It makes setting up new CI/CD environments easier. Transparency & Collaboration: The entire team can see and understand the build/deployment process defined in the YAML file. Changes can be reviewed via Pull Requests like any other code change. Consistency: Ensures the pipeline runs the same way every time, regardless of who triggers it or minor server configuration changes (as the definition is in the repo). Code Reuse: Allows templating, sharing steps/jobs across pipelines, or using pre-built actions/orbs/templates provided by the CI/CD platform or community. Disaster Recovery: If the CI/CD server needs to be rebuilt, the pipeline definition is safely stored in Git and can be easily re-applied.

Choose a CI/CD Platform that Supports Pipeline-as-Code: Most modern platforms do (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Codemagic, Azure DevOps, Jenkins Pipeline). Avoid platforms that only offer GUI configuration. Create the Pipeline Definition File: Follow the specific syntax and structure required by your chosen platform. Place the file in the expected location in your project's root directory (e.g., .github/workflows/main.yaml). Define Pipeline Structure: Triggers: Specify when the pipeline should run (e.g., on: [push, pull_request]). Jobs: Define major stages of work (e.g., analyze_and_test, build_android, build_ios, deploy_dev). Specify the runner environment (runs-on: macos-latest). Steps: Within each job, list the sequential commands or actions to execute (e.g., actions/checkout@v3, run: flutter analyze, uses: subosito/flutter-action@v2). Environment Variables & Secrets: Define how configuration and secrets are passed to steps (use the platform's secret management). Caching & Artifacts: Define caching rules and how artifacts are generated and stored (Item 81, Item 73). Dependencies & Parallelism: Define dependencies between jobs (e.g., deploy only if build succeeds) and configure jobs to run in parallel where possible. Commit the File to Git: Add the pipeline definition file (e.g., main.yaml) to Git and push it to your repository. Configure CI/CD Platform: Connect your Git repository to the CI/CD platform. The platform should automatically detect the pipeline file (e.g., .github/workflows/main.yaml) and start running workflows based on the defined triggers. Iterate and Maintain: Treat the pipeline YAML file like any other code. Make changes via feature branches and Pull Requests. Review pipeline changes carefully. Keep the pipeline definition clean, well-commented, and broken down into logical jobs/steps. By defining your CI/CD process as code alongside your application source, you create a more robust, transparent, and maintainable build and deployment system.

Item: 8 | Architecture Definition | Architecture & Coding Guidance | SETUP | 2 | The details about how/when the PR (Pull requests) are created and what are the protected branches is included in the SCM (Source Control Management) plan. | Update the SCM policy to define PR templates, required reviewers, and protected branches (e.g., main, release/*). | | This guide details how to define and document your Pull Request (PR) process and configure protected branches within your Git repository host (e.g., GitHub, GitLab). This should be part of your main SCM Policy document (Item 1).
documents.s: Completing Item 8: Detail PR Process and Protected Branches

documents.t: PR Process: Ensures code changes are reviewed for quality, correctness, and adherence to standards before integration. Protected Branches: Prevents direct pushes or accidental deletion of critical branches (main, release), enforcing the defined PR process.
documents.s: Why Define PR Process and Protect Branches?

documents.t: Define the PR Creation Process: Update your SCM Policy document (from Item 1) with a section like ## Pull Request Process. When to Create: "A PR should be created when a feature, bug fix, or chore is complete on its feature branch (e.g., feat/MEC-123-add-button) and ready for review and integration into main." Target Branch: "All feature/fix branches should target main for their PRs." (Adjust if using Gitflow, e.g., target develop). PR Size: "PRs should be small and focused, ideally representing a single piece of work (one Jira ticket). Large PRs (>500 lines changed) should be discussed with the tech lead before creation." Draft PRs: Encourage using "Draft" or "WIP" PRs early to get feedback before the code is fully complete. Define PR Template: As mentioned in Item 1, create a formal PR template file in your repository (e.g., .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md). Reiterate the required sections in your SCM documentation: Clear Title (e.g., [MEC-123] Feat: Add user login button). Link to relevant Jira ticket(s). Summary of changes made. Testing steps for QA/reviewers. Screenshots/videos for UI changes. Checklist for self-review (e.g., "Tests added/updated?", "Documentation updated?", "Conforms to coding standards?"). Define the Review Process: Assigning Reviewers: "The PR author should request reviews from at least one other developer. For significant architectural changes, the Tech Lead must also review." Use GitHub/GitLab's reviewer request feature. Reviewer Responsibilities: "Reviewers should check for correctness, adherence to coding standards, test coverage, potential bugs, and clarity. Provide constructive feedback." Approval: "At least one approving review is required before merging." Addressing Feedback: "The PR author must address all comments/requested changes before the PR can be approved and merged." Define Merge Process: Who Merges: "PRs should generally be merged by the author after receiving approval and ensuring CI checks have passed." (Or specify if only Tech Leads can merge). Merge Strategy: "Use Squash and Merge to keep the main branch history clean and linear." (Or specify 'Merge Commit' or 'Rebase and Merge' if preferred). Deleting Branches: "Feature branches should be automatically deleted after their PR is merged." (Configure this in the repository settings). Define and Configure Protected Branches: Identify Branches: The most critical branches to protect are: main (or master) release/* (if using release branches) develop (if using Gitflow) Configure Protection Rules (GitHub/GitLab): Navigate to your repository settings > Branches > Branch protection rules. For main (and other key branches): ✅ Require a pull request before merging: Disallow direct pushes. ✅ Require approvals: Set the number of required approvals (e.g., 1). Optionally, dismiss stale approvals when new commits are pushed. ✅ Require status checks to pass before merging: Select all mandatory CI checks (lint, test, build, format check, SonarQube). Optionally, require branches to be up to date before merging. ✅ Do not allow bypassing the above settings (Enforce for administrators). (Optional) Restrict who can push to matching branches (usually empty if direct pushes are disallowed). (Optional) Prevent force pushes. (Optional) Prevent deletions. Document: Briefly list the protected branches and the key protection rules enforced in your SCM policy document. Communicate: Ensure the entire team understands the PR process and why branches are protected.

Item: 13 | Architecture Definition | Architecture & Coding Guidance | PREPARATION (Sprint 0) | 2 | "The backup/restore strategy for pre-production environments (database, files, etc) is defined and documented." | Document the backup/restore process for the staging database. Ensure dev/staging environments can be easily rebuilt from SCM. | | This guide focuses on defining and documenting the backup and restore strategy for your pre-production environments (e.g., Staging, QA, UAT). These environments are typically less critical than production but still require a recovery plan.
documents.s: Completing Item 13: Define Pre-Production Backup/Restore Strategy

documents.t: While less critical than production, losing a staging environment (especially its data) can disrupt testing, delay releases, and require significant effort to rebuild. A defined strategy mitigates this risk.

Lower Criticality: Data loss might be acceptable or recoverable from other sources. Cost Sensitivity: Backup solutions might be less frequent or have shorter retention to save costs. Rebuild vs. Restore: It might be faster/easier to rebuild the environment from scratch (using IaC and seeding data) than to restore a full backup.

Identify Pre-Production Environments and Assets: List your environments (e.g., Staging, QA). Identify key assets for each: Backend Database: (e.g., Staging PostgreSQL DB). Configuration: Environment variables, secrets (often managed similarly to production but with different values). Test Data: Any specific datasets required for testing. Infrastructure: Kubernetes cluster setup, serverless functions (managed via IaC). Source Code / CI/CD Config: Already covered by Git (same as production). Define Backup Strategy for Each Asset: Backend Database (Example: Staging GCP Cloud SQL): Strategy: Use automated backups but potentially with lower frequency/retention than production. Mechanism: Automated Backups (daily snapshots). PITR might be disabled to save cost unless specifically needed for staging testing scenarios. Frequency: Daily (automated). Retention: Shorter retention (e.g., 7 days). Consider: Is restoring essential, or can the DB be wiped and re-seeded with test data easily? If re-seeding is easy, backups might be less critical. Configuration & Secrets: Strategy: Same as production - IaC and Secrets Management. Mechanism: Use the same IaC scripts (Terraform, etc.) but with staging variable files. Use the same secrets manager but with staging/ prefixed secrets. Backup: Implicit via Git (IaC) and secrets manager redundancy. Test Data: Strategy: Define how essential test data is managed. Mechanism: Option A: Generate test data via scripts (e.g., seeding scripts run after deployment). These scripts should be versioned in Git. Backup = Git. Option B: Sanitize and import a subset of production data periodically. The backup is the script/process used for this. Option C: Rely solely on database backups if the specific state needs preservation. Infrastructure: Strategy: Rebuild from Infrastructure as Code. Mechanism: Use Terraform/CloudFormation/etc., versioned in Git. Backup: Git history. Define Restore Procedures (Focus on Rebuilding): Primary Strategy: Emphasize rebuilding the environment from scratch using IaC and data seeding scripts. Run IaC scripts (terraform apply -var-file=staging.tfvars). Deploy the latest application code via CI/CD pipeline to the new infrastructure. Run data seeding scripts or the prod data import process. Secondary Strategy (if needed): Document how to restore the database from its automated backup via the cloud console/CLI, similar to production but targeting the staging instance. Document the Strategy: Create a "Pre-Production Backup and Restore Strategy" page on your wiki, separate from or linked within the production strategy. Detail the chosen approach for each environment (Staging, QA). Clearly state if the primary recovery method is rebuilding via IaC and seeding. If database backups are used, specify frequency and retention. Include links to IaC repositories and data seeding scripts. Test the Rebuild/Restore Procedure: Periodically (e.g., every 6 months), attempt to completely destroy and rebuild a pre-production environment using only IaC, CI/CD, and data seeding scripts. This validates your automation and ensures you can recover quickly even without traditional backups.

Item: 7 | Architecture Definition | Architecture & Coding Guidance | SETUP | 2 | The rollback strategy is described in the SCM (Source Control Management) plan. | Add a "Rollback" section to the SCM doc, detailing git revert for code and the process for promoting a previous build in App Store Connect / Google Play Console. | | This guide explains how to document your rollback strategy for both code changes (via Git) and deployed mobile application versions. This should be part of your main SCM Policy document (Item 1).
documents.s: Completing Item 7: Describe Rollback Strategy in SCM Plan

documents.t: When a deployment introduces a critical bug, having a clear, documented rollback procedure minimizes downtime and user impact.

Add a "Rollback Strategy" Section to SCM Document: Navigate to the wiki page where you documented your Git Branching Strategy (created in Item 1). Add a new H2 or H3 heading: ## Rollback Strategy. Document Code Rollback (Git): Method: The primary method for rolling back code changes (before they reach production users, or for hotfixes) is git revert. Explanation: Explain that git revert <commit-hash> creates a new commit that undoes the changes introduced by the specified commit. Emphasize that revert is preferred over reset --hard on shared branches (main, release/*) because revert preserves project history and is non-destructive. Detail the process: Identify the problematic commit hash(es) on the affected branch (e.g., main). Checkout the branch locally (git checkout main, git pull origin main). Run git revert <commit-hash>. Resolve any merge conflicts if they occur. Push the new revert commit (git push origin main). This will trigger the CI/CD pipeline to deploy the reverted version. Hotfixes: Briefly mention that for critical production bugs, a hotfix/TICKET-description branch might be created from the main or relevant release/* tag, fixed, merged back to main (and potentially develop if using Gitflow), and deployed. A revert might still be used as a temporary immediate measure while the hotfix is prepared. Document Deployed App Rollback (App Stores): Key Difference: Unlike web apps, mobile apps installed on user devices cannot be instantly rolled back via code changes alone. The rollback involves instructing the App Store (Apple) and Google Play Store to distribute a previous, stable version. Google Play Store (Android): Explain the use of Staged Rollouts. If a bug is detected during a percentage rollout (e.g., at 10%), you can Halt the rollout. If the buggy version reached 100%, explain the process: Find the previously known good version number and build number (e.g., 1.2.0+15). In the Google Play Console, go to Release > Production. Click Create new release. Upload the AAB file for the previous stable version (you must keep these artifacts accessible, e.g., in CI/CD artifacts or an artifact repository). Or, select it from the App Bundle library if available. Review the release and roll it out to 100%. Users will eventually auto-update to this "older" version. App Store Connect (iOS): Explain that iOS rollbacks are less direct. You cannot easily "halt" a phased release once started. The primary method is to submit a new, stable version: Find the previously known good version number and build number (e.g., 1.2.0 (15)). Increment the version number (e.g., 1.2.1). Re-archive and upload the build corresponding to the previous stable codebase (using the correct Git tag/commit) but with the new version number (1.2.1). Submit this build for expedited review if the bug is critical. Once approved, release it. Users will update from the buggy version (e.g., 1.2.0) to the "new" stable version (1.2.1). Artifact Storage: Mention where previous release artifacts (.aab, .ipa) are stored and can be retrieved for rollback purposes (e.g., "Release artifacts are stored in GitHub Releases for 90 days"). Review and Communicate: Ensure the team understands both the code (git revert) and app store rollback procedures. Practice the app store procedures (uploading an older build) in a test track if possible.

Item: 15 | Architecture Definition | Architecture & Coding Guidance | PREPARATION (Sprint 0) | 2 | It is clear for all the developers how to implement unit tests for the technology stack used in the project. The process is defined and documented. | Create a wiki page with examples of unit tests (flutter test), widget tests, and state management tests (e.g., bloc_test, mocktail). | | This guide explains how to document clear guidelines and provide examples for writing unit and widget tests in your Flutter project.
documents.s: Completing Item 15: Provide Unit Testing Guidance

documents.t: Clear guidance ensures developers write effective, consistent, and maintainable tests, leading to higher code quality and reduced regressions.

Define Testing Scope and Strategy: Reiterate Goals: Briefly state the team's testing goals (e.g., target code coverage from Item 24, focus on testing business logic). Testing Pyramid: Explain the concept (Unit -> Widget -> Integration -> E2E) and emphasize that this document focuses on Unit and Widget tests, which should form the base of the pyramid. What to Unit Test: Logic in BLoCs/Cubits/Providers, Use Cases, Repositories (with mocked data sources), utility functions, data transformations. Focus on business rules and state changes. What Not to Unit Test: UI rendering details (use Widget tests), framework methods, trivial getters/setters. What to Widget Test: Verify that widgets render correctly based on state, respond to user interactions (taps, text input), and interact correctly with their state management providers (Blocs, etc.). Document Tooling and Libraries: Core Framework: package:flutter_test (comes with Flutter SDK) for both unit and widget tests. Mocking: Mandate the use of a specific mocking library. mocktail is generally preferred over mockito due to its sound null safety and simpler API. Forbid manual mock implementations. State Management Testing: Recommend specific helper libraries: bloc_test: For testing flutter_bloc Blocs and Cubits. provider_test: (If using Provider directly for complex logic). riverpod: (Riverpod has built-in testing support). Matchers: Mention common matchers (expect, findsOneWidget, throwsA, isA<Type>). Create a "Testing Guide" Wiki Page: Structure the page with clear sections (Unit Testing, Widget Testing, Mocking, State Management Testing). Provide Clear Examples: Unit Testing Example (e.g., testing a simple function): // Function to test (e.g., in utils/validators.dart) String? validateEmail(String? email) { if (email == null || email.isEmpty) return 'Email cannot be empty'; if (!email.contains('@')) return 'Invalid email format'; return null; } // Test (in test/utils/validators_test.dart) import 'package:flutter_test/flutter_test.dart'; import 'package:your_app/utils/validators.dart'; void main() { group('validateEmail', () { test('should return error when email is null', () { expect(validateEmail(null), 'Email cannot be empty'); }); test('should return error when email is empty', () { expect(validateEmail(''), 'Email cannot be empty'); }); test('should return error when email format is invalid', () { expect(validateEmail('test.com'), 'Invalid email format'); }); test('should return null when email is valid', () { expect(validateEmail('test@example.com'), isNull); }); }); } Mocking Example (using mocktail): // Interface (e.g., domain/repositories/auth_repository.dart) abstract class AuthRepository { Future<User> login(String email, String password); } // Class using the repository (e.g., domain/use_cases/login_use_case.dart) class LoginUseCase { final AuthRepository authRepository; LoginUseCase(this.authRepository); Future<User> call(String email, String password) async { // Add validation or business logic here if needed return authRepository.login(email, password); } } // Mock (in test/mocks.dart or test/domain/use_cases/login_use_case_test.dart) import 'package:mocktail/mocktail.dart'; import 'package:your_app/domain/repositories/auth_repository.dart'; import 'package:your_app/domain/entities/user.dart'; // Assuming User entity exists class MockAuthRepository extends Mock implements AuthRepository {} // Test (in test/domain/use_cases/login_use_case_test.dart) import 'package:flutter_test/flutter_test.dart'; import 'package:mocktail/mocktail.dart'; import 'package:your_app/domain/use_cases/login_use_case.dart'; // ... import mocks and entities void main() { late MockAuthRepository mockAuthRepository; late LoginUseCase loginUseCase; setUp(() { mockAuthRepository = MockAuthRepository(); loginUseCase = LoginUseCase(mockAuthRepository); }); final tUser = User(id: '1', name: 'Test User', email: 'test@example.com'); final tEmail = 'test@example.com'; final tPassword = 'password123'; test('should call login on the repository and return user on success', () async { // Arrange when(() => mockAuthRepository.login(tEmail, tPassword)) .thenAnswer((_) async => tUser); // Act final result = await loginUseCase(tEmail, tPassword); // Assert expect(result, tUser); verify(() => mockAuthRepository.login(tEmail, tPassword)).called(1); verifyNoMoreInteractions(mockAuthRepository); }); test('should throw exception when repository call fails', () async { // Arrange final tException = Exception('Login failed'); when(() => mockAuthRepository.login(tEmail, tPassword)) .thenThrow(tException); // Act final call = loginUseCase(tEmail, tPassword); // Assert await expectLater(call, throwsA(isA<Exception>())); verify(() => mockAuthRepository.login(tEmail, tPassword)).called(1); verifyNoMoreInteractions(mockAuthRepository); }); } State Management Testing (using bloc_test): // Cubit (e.g., presentation/counter/counter_cubit.dart) import 'package:bloc/bloc.dart'; class CounterCubit extends Cubit<int> { CounterCubit() : super(0); void increment() => emit(state + 1); void decrement() => emit(state - 1); } // Test (in test/presentation/counter/counter_cubit_test.dart) import 'package:bloc_test/bloc_test.dart'; import 'package:flutter_test/flutter_test.dart'; import 'package:your_app/presentation/counter/counter_cubit.dart'; void main() { group('CounterCubit', () { test('initial state is 0', () { expect(CounterCubit().state, 0); }); blocTest<CounterCubit, int>( 'emits [1] when increment is called', build: () => CounterCubit(), act: (cubit) => cubit.increment(), expect: () => [1], ); blocTest<CounterCubit, int>( 'emits [-1] when decrement is called', build: () => CounterCubit(), act: (cubit) => cubit.decrement(), expect: () => [-1], ); }); } Widget Testing Example: // Widget (e.g., presentation/login/widgets/login_button.dart) import 'package:flutter/material.dart'; class LoginButton extends StatelessWidget { final VoidCallback onPressed; const LoginButton({Key? key, required this.onPressed}) : super(key: key); @override Widget build(BuildContext context) { return ElevatedButton( onPressed: onPressed, child: Text('Login'), ); } } // Test (in test/presentation/login/widgets/login_button_test.dart) import 'package:flutter/material.dart'; import 'package:flutter_test/flutter_test.dart'; import 'package:your_app/presentation/login/widgets/login_button.dart'; void main() { testWidgets('LoginButton should display text and be tappable', (WidgetTester tester) async { bool wasPressed = false; // Arrange: Pump the widget await tester.pumpWidget( MaterialApp( // Need MaterialApp for ElevatedButton styles home: Scaffold( body: LoginButton(onPressed: () { wasPressed = true; }), ), ), ); // Assert: Find the widget final buttonFinder = find.widgetWithText(ElevatedButton, 'Login'); expect(buttonFinder, findsOneWidget); // Act: Tap the button await tester.tap(buttonFinder); await tester.pump(); // Allow animations/state changes to settle // Assert: Check if callback was called expect(wasPressed, isTrue); }); } Establish Best Practices: Structure: Place test files adjacent to the source files with _test.dart suffix (e.g., user_repository.dart -> user_repository_test.dart). Use group() to organize tests. Arrange, Act, Assert: Follow this pattern within tests. Readability: Write clear test descriptions (test('should do X when Y happens')). Independence: Tests should be independent and runnable in any order. Use setUp() and tearDown() for common setup/cleanup. Coverage Goal: Remind developers of the target coverage (Item 24). Communicate and Review: Share the testing guide with the team. Review test quality and adherence to guidelines during PR reviews. Conduct pairing sessions if developers are struggling with testing concepts.

Item: 28 | Architecture Definition | Non-functional requirements | SETUP | 2 | All the Non-functional requirements related to the application are being mapped and collected using the Non-functional requirements template spreadsheet <link>. | Create and enforce the use of a standard NFR template, including metric, target, and measurement method (e.g., "App Start Time", "< 2s", "Firebase Performance Monitoring P90"). | | This guide explains how to use a structured template, often a spreadsheet, to refine and document the Non-Functional Requirements (NFRs) collected in the previous step (Item 27). The goal is to move from qualitative statements to more specific, measurable requirements. Note: The item description mentions a specific template spreadsheet via <link>. Since that link isn't available, this guide describes the common elements and purpose of such a template.
documents.s: Completing Item 28: Use NFR Template Spreadsheet

documents.t: Structure: Provides a consistent format for documenting NFRs. Detail: Prompts the team to think through specifics like metrics, targets, and measurement methods. Measurability: Pushes towards defining NFRs in a way that can be objectively verified. Traceability: Can be linked to specific features or architectural components. Clarity: Reduces ambiguity compared to free-form text descriptions.

Obtain or Create the NFR Template: Find Existing Template: Check if your organization has a standard NFR template spreadsheet. If the <link> in the item description pointed to one, use that. Create a Template: If no standard template exists, create a spreadsheet (e.g., Google Sheets, Excel) with columns like: ID: Unique identifier for the NFR (e.g., PERF-01, SEC-01). Category: (e.g., Performance, Reliability, Security - from Item 27). NFR Statement: A concise description of the requirement (e.g., "App should start quickly"). Rationale/Source: Why is this NFR important? (e.g., "User retention," "Compliance requirement"). Metric: How will this NFR be measured? (e.g., "Cold App Startup Time (P90)"). Target: The specific, quantifiable goal (e.g., < 2.0 seconds). Measurement Method/Tool: How and with what tool will the metric be measured? (e.g., "Firebase Performance Monitoring," "Manual test on Galaxy A50," "SonarQube"). Priority: (e.g., Must Have, Should Have, Could Have). Verification: How will compliance be verified? (e.g., "CI Quality Gate," "Release Checklist," "Penetration Test Report"). Scope/Context: Where does this NFR apply? (e.g., "All screens," "Login API endpoint," "iOS only"). Owner: Who is responsible for tracking/ensuring this NFR? (e.g., Tech Lead, QA Lead, Security Team). Status: (e.g., Defined, Implemented, Verified). Populate the Template: Transfer the NFRs collected in Item 27 into the template spreadsheet. Focus on Quantifying: Work through each NFR with the team (Dev, QA, Arch, PO) to fill in the Metric, Target, and Measurement Method columns. This is the core activity bridging Item 27 and Item 30. Initial: "App should start quickly." Refined: Metric: Cold App Startup Time (P90), Target: < 2.0s, Method: Firebase Performance Monitoring. Initial: "App should not crash often." Refined: Metric: Crash-Free User Rate, Target: > 99.9%, Method: Firebase Crashlytics. Initial: "Code should be maintainable." Refined: Metric: Maintainability Rating on New Code, Target: A, Method: SonarQube. Fill in other columns like Priority, Rationale, etc., based on discussions. Review and Refine: Review the populated spreadsheet with the team and PO. Ensure targets are realistic, measurable, and agreed upon. Identify any NFRs that are still too vague or lack a clear measurement method – these require further discussion. Store and Share the Spreadsheet: Store the spreadsheet in a shared location (e.g., Google Drive linked from the project wiki). Ensure the team knows where to find it and understands its purpose. Enforce Use (Ongoing): Refer to this spreadsheet when discussing new features or technical designs ("How will this impact NFR PERF-01?"). Use it as input for defining specific tests (performance tests, security scans). Make updating relevant NFRs part of the process when requirements change. Using a structured template transforms NFRs from a simple list into a actionable set of measurable quality goals for the project.

Item: 77 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Integration | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 2 | "The database scheme is exported and versioned in a source code version control tool (git, svn, etc)." | (Backend) Ensure the backend team versions their database schema (e.g., SQL files, migration scripts) in their Git repository. | | (Note: As with Item 71, this primarily applies to the backend database.) This guide emphasizes the practice of storing the definition of your backend database schema (and changes to it) under version control (Git), just like application code.
documents.s: Completing Item 77: Version Control Database Schema

documents.t: History & Auditing: Provides a complete history of how the database schema has evolved over time. You can see who changed what, when, and potentially why (via commit messages). Reproducibility: Allows you to recreate the exact database schema corresponding to any version of your application code. Essential for testing, debugging older versions, or setting up new environments. Collaboration: Enables multiple developers to work on schema changes concurrently (using branches) and resolve conflicts through standard Git workflows. Consistency: Acts as the single source of truth for the database structure, helping to prevent schema drift between environments. Foundation for Automation: Version-controlled schema definitions (especially migration scripts - Item 71) are essential for automating database deployments.

The specific method depends on whether you are using a database migration tool (recommended) or managing schema definitions directly. Using Migration Tools (Liquibase, Flyway, etc. - Recommended): Mechanism: The migration tool uses definition files (e.g., SQL scripts for Flyway, XML/YAML/SQL for Liquibase) to describe changes to the schema incrementally. Implementation: Create a dedicated directory in the backend's Git repository (e.g., /db/migration, /src/main/resources/db/changelog). Commit all migration files (e.g., V1__Create_tables.sql, V2__Add_email_column.sql, changelog-v1.0.xml) to Git. Changes to the schema are made by adding new migration files to this directory and committing them. Source of Truth: The combination of all migration scripts, applied sequentially by the tool, represents the schema at any given point. Using Schema Definition Files (Less Common for Evolvable Schemas): Mechanism: Store the complete CREATE TABLE, CREATE INDEX, etc., statements for the entire database schema in one or more SQL files. Implementation: Create a directory (e.g., /db/schema). Store the full schema definition (e.g., schema.sql). Commit this file to Git. When the schema changes, edit the definition file directly and commit the changes. Source of Truth: The schema.sql file at a specific Git commit represents the entire schema for that version. Drawbacks: Doesn't easily represent incremental changes, harder to automate updates to existing databases (you need separate ALTER scripts or diffing tools), rollback is not inherently managed. Generally only suitable for simpler schemas or when combined with schema comparison tools. Using ORM Definitions (e.g., Django Models, TypeORM Entities): Mechanism: The schema is often implicitly defined by the code models/entities used by the Object-Relational Mapper. Migration tools associated with the ORM (Item 71) generate the actual SQL migration scripts based on changes detected in these models. Implementation: Commit the model definition files (e.g., models.py, user.entity.ts) to Git. Commit the generated migration scripts (e.g., files in /migrations directory) to Git. Source of Truth: The model files define the desired state, and the generated/committed migration scripts represent the incremental changes needed to reach that state.
documents.s: How to Version Control the Schema

documents.t: Commit Schema Changes with Code: Ideally, commit database schema changes (migration scripts) in the same Git commit as the application code changes that require them. This keeps related changes together. Use a Migration Tool: Strongly recommended for managing schema evolution effectively. Clear Commit Messages: Explain the purpose of the schema change in the commit message. Branching and Review: Treat schema change commits/PRs with the same rigor as application code changes (use feature branches, require code reviews). By version controlling your database schema alongside your application code, you create a more robust, transparent, and manageable development process.

Item: 100 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Monitoring | RELEASE | 3 | "The team can take actions when application monitoring is showing any problems (for example, contact the responsible for fixing it)." | Create a dedicated chat channel (e.g., #alerts-prod) where all Firebase Crashlytics and Datadog alerts are automatically posted. | | This guide focuses on establishing processes and communication channels that enable the development team to become aware of and take appropriate action when application monitoring tools indicate problems.
documents.s: Completing Item 100: Enable Team Actions on App Monitoring Issues

documents.t: Faster Response: Issues identified by monitoring (crashes, performance spikes) can be addressed more quickly if the team responsible for fixing them is notified directly. Reduced MTTR (Mean Time to Recovery): Streamlines the process from detection to resolution. Feedback Loop: Developers see the direct impact of their code in production, reinforcing the importance of quality. Proactive Problem Solving: Allows the team to address issues before they escalate or are widely reported by users.

Configure Automated Alerts: Identify Critical Metrics: Determine which metrics warrant immediate team notification if thresholds are breached (based on NFR targets - Item 30). Examples: Significant increase in crash rate (Firebase Crashlytics Velocity Alerts). New major crash signature appearing. App startup time exceeding target (Firebase Performance Alerts). API error rate spiking (Backend monitoring alerts). Key API endpoint latency exceeding target (Backend monitoring alerts). Set Up Alerts in Tools: Configure alert rules within your monitoring tools (Firebase, Datadog, Sentry, etc.) based on these critical metrics and thresholds. Establish a Centralized Alert Channel: Choose a Channel: Create a dedicated, read-only (for bots/integrations) chat channel (e.g., #proj-mobile-alerts, #alerts-prod-mobile) in your primary communication tool (Slack, Google Chat - Item 20). Integrate Tools: Configure your monitoring tools to send their alerts directly to this channel using webhooks or built-in integrations. Firebase Crashlytics Velocity Alerts -> Slack/Chat. Firebase Performance Alerts -> Slack/Chat. Datadog/Sentry/etc. Alerts -> Slack/Chat. Purpose: This channel serves as the central, immediate notification point for automated alerts. Discourage manual conversation here. Define Triage and Action Process: On-Call / Point Person: Designate who is primarily responsible for monitoring the alert channel and initiating the triage process during working hours (e.g., Tech Lead, rotating developer). Define an on-call rotation for critical out-of-hours alerts if necessary. Triage Steps (Document this): Acknowledge: The on-call person acknowledges the alert in the channel (e.g., using an emoji reaction 👀). Investigate: Briefly investigate the alert using the monitoring tool dashboards (linked from the alert message if possible). Is it a real issue? What's the scope/impact? Is it a known issue? Communicate: Post a summary of the findings in the main technical channel (e.g., #proj-mobile-tech), not the alerts channel. Tag relevant people if needed. Example: "@here Seeing Crashlytics alerts for issue #123 affecting ~5% of users on v1.2.3, seems related to the new profile screen. Creating Jira bug ticket." Create Ticket: Create a high-priority bug ticket in Jira, linking to the alert/monitoring dashboard. Action: Assign the ticket for fixing (might be the on-call person, or assigned based on feature ownership). Escalation: Define steps if the initial investigation can't identify the cause or if the issue is severe (e.g., involve Architect, Backend team, PO). Document the Process: Create a "Production Alert Handling Process" page on your wiki. List the monitoring tools and the types of alerts configured. Specify the #alerts channel. Detail the Triage Steps (Acknowledge, Investigate, Communicate, Ticket, Action). Define the on-call/point person responsibilities and rotation schedule (if any). Outline the escalation path. Review and Refine: Periodically review the alert configuration. Are there too many noisy alerts? Are critical issues being missed? Discuss the effectiveness of the handling process during retrospectives. By setting up automated alerts feeding into a dedicated channel and defining a clear triage process, you empower the team to react swiftly and effectively to production issues identified by monitoring.

Item: 16 | Architecture Definition | Architecture & Coding Guidance | PREPARATION (Sprint 0) | 3 | There is a definition about how to load data for automated testing and this plan meets the project requirements. | Define a strategy to inject mock data for integration/UI tests (e.g., using a mock repository, or tools like Patrol). | | This guide explains how to define and document a strategy for providing consistent and controllable data to your automated integration and end-to-end (E2E) tests in Flutter. Unit tests use mocks directly (Item 15), but higher-level tests often need a more structured approach.
documents.s: Completing Item 16: Define Automated Test Data Loading

documents.t: Consistency: Ensures tests run reliably without being affected by real backend changes or flaky data. Control: Allows you to test specific scenarios (e.g., empty lists, error states, specific user roles) by providing tailored data. Isolation: Prevents tests from polluting real development or staging databases. Speed: Using local mock data is much faster than relying on network calls.
documents.s: Why Define a Data Strategy for Tests?

documents.t: Choose one or a combination of the following strategies based on your testing needs and architecture: Mocking at the Repository Layer (Recommended for Integration Tests): Concept: For integration tests (testing features or flows within the app), replace the real Repository implementations (which talk to APIs/DBs) with mock implementations that return predefined data. Implementation: Use a Dependency Injection (DI) framework like get_it. In your main app setup (main.dart), register the real repositories. In your test setup (test/integration_test/app_test.dart or similar), create mock repository implementations (using mocktail). Before running the app in the test, unregister the real repositories and register the mock ones using your DI container. // Example test setup with get_it and mocktail import 'package:get_it/get_it.dart'; import 'package:mocktail/mocktail.dart'; import 'package:flutter_test/flutter_test.dart'; import 'package:integration_test/integration_test.dart'; // Assuming you have these defined: // import 'package:your_app/main.dart' as app; // Your main entry point // import 'package:your_app/domain/repositories/user_repository.dart'; // import 'package:your_app/domain/entities/user.dart'; // import 'test/mocks.dart'; // Contains MockUserRepository void main() { IntegrationTestWidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized(); late MockUserRepository mockUserRepository; setUpAll(() { // Ensure real dependencies are registered if main does it // app.setupDependencies(); // Or however your app does it // Override with mocks for tests GetIt.instance.allowReassignment = true; // Allow overriding mockUserRepository = MockUserRepository(); GetIt.instance.registerSingleton<UserRepository>(mockUserRepository); }); setUp(() { // Reset mocks before each test if needed reset(mockUserRepository); }); testWidgets('Login screen shows error on failed login', (tester) async { // Arrange: Setup mock response for this specific test when(() => mockUserRepository.login(any(), any())) .thenThrow(Exception('Invalid credentials')); // Act: Start the app app.main(); // Or the relevant function that starts your app await tester.pumpAndSettle(); // Interact with the UI... tap login button etc. await tester.enterText(find.byKey(Key('emailField')), 'wrong@example.com'); await tester.enterText(find.byKey(Key('passwordField')), 'wrong'); await tester.tap(find.byKey(Key('loginButton'))); await tester.pumpAndSettle(); // Assert: Verify mock was called and UI shows error verify(() => mockUserRepository.login('wrong@example.com', 'wrong')).called(1); expect(find.text('Invalid credentials'), findsOneWidget); }); testWidgets('Login screen navigates on successful login', (tester) async { // Arrange: Setup mock success response final tUser = User(id: '1', name: 'Test', email: 'test@example.com'); when(() => mockUserRepository.login(any(), any())) .thenAnswer((_) async => tUser); // Act... // Assert: Verify navigation, perhaps expect find.text('Welcome Test') }); } Pros: Relatively easy to set up with DI, fast execution, good control over data for different scenarios within the app. Cons: Doesn't test the real API contract. Using a Mock Backend Server (Recommended for E2E Tests): Concept: Run a local HTTP server during your E2E tests that intercepts API calls and returns predefined JSON responses. Tools like Maestro or Patrol often integrate well with this. Implementation: Choose a mock server library (e.g., mock_web_server in Dart, or external tools like WireMock, Mockoon). Define expected API requests and their corresponding JSON responses (store these JSON files in your test assets). In your test setup, start the mock server. Configure your app (e.g., via dart-define or DI overrides at the HTTP client level) to point to the mock server's local address (http://localhost:8080) instead of the real API endpoint only during tests. In each test, configure the mock server to expect certain requests and provide specific responses. Pros: Tests the app's networking layer and JSON parsing. Closer to real-world interaction. Cons: More setup required, need to maintain mock JSON responses, slightly slower than repository mocking. Dedicated Test Backend Environment: Concept: Maintain a separate deployment of your actual backend specifically for automated testing. This backend has its own database that can be reset or seeded before test runs. Implementation: Requires significant infrastructure setup (a full, isolated backend environment). Need robust mechanisms to reset the database state before each test run or suite (e.g., API endpoints to clear/seed data, database snapshots). Configure the app (via dart-define) to point to this test environment endpoint during test execution. Pros: Tests against the real backend code and API contract. Highest fidelity. Cons: Slowest execution, complex infrastructure, requires careful state management, can be costly.

Choose your primary strategy (or strategies for different test types - e.g., Repository Mocking for integration, Mock Server for E2E). Create a "Test Data Strategy" section on your "Testing Guide" wiki page (from Item 15). Describe the chosen approach(es): Explain how data is provided (DI overrides, mock server, test backend). Provide Examples: Include code snippets showing how to set up mocks or configure the mock server for a typical test scenario. Location of Test Data: Specify where mock data (e.g., JSON files for the mock server) is stored within the project structure. Tooling: List any specific libraries (mocktail, mock_web_server) or tools used. By defining and documenting this strategy, you ensure your automated tests are reliable and effective.

Item: 53 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Deployment | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 3 | Deployment pipeline contains step/task reflecting actual development flow and release flow. | Structure the CI/CD YAML to mirror the process: Setup->Analyze & Lint->Run Tests->Build App->Deploy to Firebase/Store. | | This guide emphasizes structuring your CI/CD deployment pipelines logically to mirror your team's actual development and release workflow steps.
documents.s: Completing Item 53: Ensure Pipeline Reflects Development Flow

documents.t: Readability & Maintainability: A pipeline structured like the manual process it replaces is easier for developers to understand, troubleshoot, and modify. Clarity: Makes the purpose and sequence of each stage explicit. Troubleshooting: When a pipeline fails, a logical structure helps pinpoint which phase of the process encountered the error (e.g., failure during testing vs. failure during deployment). Onboarding: Helps new team members understand the build and release process by looking at the pipeline definition.

A typical Flutter CI/CD pipeline, whether for PR checks, Dev deployment, or Production release, often follows these logical stages: Setup Environment: Checkout code (specific branch, tag, or PR ref). Set up the build runner environment (e.g., select macOS/Linux, install OS dependencies). Set up Flutter SDK (e.g., using FVM). Set up platform SDKs (Java/Android SDK, Xcode/Gems/CocoaPods). Set up secrets/authentication (e.g., decoding signing keys, logging into cloud services). Install project dependencies (flutter pub get). Validate Code Quality: Run static analysis (flutter analyze). Check code formatting (dart format --set-exit-if-changed). (Optional) Run custom validation scripts. Test: Run Unit & Widget Tests (flutter test --coverage). (Optional/Conditional) Run Integration Tests (can be slow, might run conditionally or in a separate workflow). Static Analysis Platform (Optional but Recommended): Upload coverage reports and analysis results to SonarQube/SonarCloud. Check Quality Gate status. Build Artifact: Run code generation if needed (flutter pub run build_runner build). Build the actual app artifact (.apk, .aab, .ipa). Use --release mode for Staging/Prod builds. Inject environment configuration using --dart-define (Item 44). Include versioning information (--build-name, --build-number) (Item 42). Handle code signing correctly for the target environment/platform. Deploy / Distribute: Upload the artifact to the target platform (Firebase App Distribution, TestFlight, Google Play Console, etc.). Use tools like firebase-tools, fastlane, or specific CI/CD actions. Post-Deployment (Optional): Run smoke tests against the deployed environment. Send notifications (Slack, Google Chat, Email). Create Git tags or releases.

Review Your Current Pipeline(s): Look at your existing CI/CD YAML files (e.g., .github/workflows/*.yaml, codemagic.yaml). Do they follow a logical sequence? Are the steps clearly named? Refactor for Clarity: Use Stages/Jobs: Most CI/CD platforms allow grouping steps into logical stages or jobs (e.g., jobs: in GitHub Actions, stages: in GitLab CI). Use these to represent the major phases (Validate, Test, Build, Deploy). Descriptive Step Names: Give each step a clear name: that explains exactly what it does (e.g., name: Run Unit & Widget Tests, name: Build Android Release App Bundle). Comments: Add comments within the YAML file to explain complex steps or non-obvious configurations. Separate Workflows: Consider separating fundamentally different processes into distinct workflow files (e.g., pr_check.yaml, deploy_dev.yaml, release_production.yaml) instead of having one massive file with complex conditional logic. Link them logically (e.g., deploy_dev triggers on merge after pr_check succeeded). Example Structure (GitHub Actions): name: Build and Deploy App on: # ... trigger ... jobs: # --- Validation Job --- validate: name: Validate Code Quality runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Checkout Code uses: actions/checkout@v3 - name: Setup Flutter (FVM) # ... - name: Install Dependencies run: fvm flutter pub get - name: Check Formatting run: dart format --output=none --set-exit-if-changed . - name: Analyze Code run: fvm flutter analyze --fatal-infos --fatal-warnings . # --- Test Job (Depends on Validation) --- test: name: Run Tests needs: validate # Run after validation passes runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Checkout Code - name: Setup Flutter (FVM) - name: Install Dependencies - name: Run Unit & Widget Tests run: fvm flutter test --coverage - name: Upload Coverage Report (Example) uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3 with: name: coverage-report path: coverage/lcov.info # --- Build Job (Depends on Test) --- build: name: Build App Artifacts needs: test runs-on: macos-latest # Often need macOS for iOS builds # environment: dev # Optional: Scope secrets steps: - name: Checkout Code - name: Setup Flutter (FVM) - name: Setup Java/Android - name: Setup iOS (Certs/Provisioning via Fastlane Match etc.) - name: Install Dependencies - name: Build Android APK (Dev Example) run: fvm flutter build apk --debug --dart-define=... - name: Build iOS IPA (Dev Example) run: fvm flutter build ipa --debug --export-options-plist=... --dart-define=... - name: Upload Build Artifacts (for deployment job) uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3 # ... upload APK and IPA ... # --- Deploy Job (Depends on Build) --- deploy: name: Deploy to Firebase App Dist (Dev) needs: build runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Download Artifacts uses: actions/download-artifact@v3 # ... download APK and IPA ... - name: Install Firebase CLI - name: Deploy Android to Firebase run: firebase appdistribution:distribute ... - name: Deploy iOS to Firebase run: firebase appdistribution:distribute ... - name: Send Slack Notification # ... Documentation: Ensure your CI/CD documentation (Item 26) reflects this logical structure, perhaps even including a simplified flowchart corresponding to the pipeline stages/jobs. By structuring your pipelines logically, you make them more understandable, maintainable, and reflective of your team's actual workflow.

Item: 51 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Deployment | PREPARATION (Sprint 0) | 3 | "The deployment can be executed in a single click for Dev, RC and Stage environments." | Configure the CI/CD pipelines (e.g., GitHub Actions) to be triggerable manually (e.g., workflow_dispatch) with an environment (Dev, Staging) as an input. | | This guide explains how to configure your CI/CD pipelines to allow deployments to non-production environments (like Development, QA, Staging, RC) to be triggered easily, often with a single click or a simple manual action, in addition to any automated triggers.

Flexibility: While automated deployments on merge (Item 45, 46) are great, sometimes you need to deploy a specific branch, commit, or tag to a test environment on demand (e.g., for hotfix testing, testing a feature branch before merging, running performance tests against a specific build). Ease of Use: Simplifies the process for developers or QA to refresh an environment or test a specific version without complex manual steps. Control: Provides a controlled way to trigger deployments outside the normal automated flow.

The exact implementation depends on your CI/CD platform. The key is to have workflows that accept parameters (like branch/tag and target environment) and can be triggered manually. Manual Workflow Triggers (workflow_dispatch in GitHub Actions): Concept: Add a workflow_dispatch event trigger to your existing deployment workflows (or create dedicated manually triggered ones). This adds a "Run workflow" button in the GitHub Actions UI. Implementation (GitHub Actions Example): name: Manual Deploy to Non-Prod on: # Allows manual triggering from the Actions tab workflow_dispatch: inputs: git_ref: description: 'Git branch or tag to deploy (e.g., main, feat/my-feature, v1.2.0-rc1)' required: true default: 'main' environment_target: description: 'Target environment (dev or staging)' required: true type: choice options: - dev - staging default: 'dev' # Optional: Keep automatic trigger too (e.g., on push to main for dev) # push: # branches: [ main ] jobs: build_and_deploy: runs-on: ubuntu-latest # Or macos-latest if needed environment: ${{ github.event.inputs.environment_target }} # Optional: Use GitHub Environments for secrets/rules steps: - name: Checkout specific ref uses: actions/checkout@v3 with: ref: ${{ github.event.inputs.git_ref }} # Checkout the specified branch/tag # ... Setup Flutter/FVM ... - name: Build App (Conditional Config) run: | API_ENDPOINT="" FIREBASE_APP_ID="" if [[ "${{ github.event.inputs.environment_target }}" == "dev" ]]; then API_ENDPOINT="${{ secrets.DEV_API_ENDPOINT }}" # Use GitHub Environment secrets if possible FIREBASE_APP_ID="${{ secrets.FIREBASE_APP_ID_ANDROID_DEV }}" elif [[ "${{ github.event.inputs.environment_target }}" == "staging" ]]; then API_ENDPOINT="${{ secrets.STAGING_API_ENDPOINT }}" FIREBASE_APP_ID="${{ secrets.FIREBASE_APP_ID_ANDROID_STAGING }}" else echo "::error::Invalid environment target" exit 1 fi # Extract version/build number (perhaps combine git hash for non-main builds) VERSION_NAME="1.0.0" # Get from pubspec or input BUILD_NUMBER="${{ github.run_number }}" # Build (e.g., APK for easier distribution) fvm flutter build apk --debug \ --build-name=$VERSION_NAME \ --build-number=$BUILD_NUMBER \ --dart-define=API_ENDPOINT=$API_ENDPOINT - name: Deploy (Conditional Target) # Use conditional steps or logic within the script run: | DISTRIBUTION_GROUP="" if [[ "${{ github.event.inputs.environment_target }}" == "dev" ]]; then DISTRIBUTION_GROUP="developers" elif [[ "${{ github.event.inputs.environment_target }}" == "staging" ]]; then DISTRIBUTION_GROUP="qa-team,uat-testers" fi # Upload to Firebase App Distribution (or other) firebase appdistribution:distribute build/app/outputs/flutter-apk/app-debug.apk \ --app $FIREBASE_APP_ID \ --token ${{ secrets.FIREBASE_CLI_TOKEN }} \ --groups "$DISTRIBUTION_GROUP" \ --release-notes "Manual deploy of ${{ github.event.inputs.git_ref }} to ${{ github.event.inputs.environment_target }}" # ... Notifications ... How it works: This adds a "Run workflow" button on the GitHub Actions page. Users can select the branch/tag and target environment from dropdowns and click to start the deployment. Parameterized Builds (Jenkins, GitLab CI): Most CI/CD platforms allow defining parameters for jobs (e.g., String parameters for GIT_REF, Choice parameters for ENVIRONMENT). Configure the deployment job to accept these parameters. Users can then click "Build with Parameters" (or similar) in the UI, fill in the values, and trigger the job. ChatOps (Advanced): Integrate a chatbot (e.g., Slack bot, Hubot) with your CI/CD API. Define commands like @bot deploy my-app branch:feat/abc env:staging. The bot triggers the parameterized CI/CD job. Requires more setup but offers convenience.

Permissions: Ensure only authorized team members can trigger manual deployments, especially to sensitive environments like Staging. Use CI/CD platform permissions or GitHub Environments protection rules. Clarity: Make the workflow inputs (branch, environment) clear and easy to use. Use choice/dropdown parameters where possible. Configuration Management: The pipeline needs robust logic to select the correct build configurations (API endpoints, keys - Item 44) and deployment targets based on the chosen environment parameter. Use environment variables/secrets scoped to environments. Naming/Versioning: Decide how to handle build numbers for manual deployments from feature branches (e.g., include Git commit hash) to avoid confusion with main branch builds.

Document how to trigger these manual deployments in your CI/CD guide (Item 26). Include screenshots if helpful. Specify who has permission to trigger deployments to each environment. Providing an easy, "single-click" way to deploy specific code versions to non-production environments empowers developers and QA to test effectively without manual build/deploy steps.

Item: 52 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Deployment | PREPARATION (Sprint 0) | 3 | "The rollback can be executed in a single click for Dev, RC and Stage environments" | Create a "Rollback" manual workflow in the CI/CD tool that allows selecting a previous successful build/tag and re-deploying it to Firebase App Distribution. | | This guide explains how to create a mechanism, ideally triggerable via a single click or simple manual action, to roll back non-production environments (Dev, QA, Staging) to a previous known-good state. This is distinct from production rollback (Item 48) and often simpler.

Fast Recovery from Bad Builds: If an automated deployment to Dev/Staging introduces critical bugs blocking testing, quickly revert to the last working version. Testing Specific Previous Versions: Allows QA or developers to easily deploy an older version to investigate regressions or compare behaviour. Simplicity: Provides an easy way for authorized team members (Dev, QA) to restore a stable environment without needing deep CI/CD knowledge or complex manual steps.

The approach involves creating a manual CI/CD workflow that can re-deploy a previously successful artifact or rebuild from a specific Git tag/commit. Re-deploying a Previous Artifact (If Stored): Concept: If your CI/CD pipeline stores artifacts from successful Dev/Staging deployments (e.g., in CI artifact storage, Artifactory, Cloud Storage), create a workflow that lists recent successful builds and allows re-deploying a selected one. Implementation: Requires robust artifact storage and naming conventions (e.g., app-dev-debug-1.2.0+55.apk). The rollback workflow would need logic to: List available artifacts for the target environment (e.g., query artifact repository API, list files in storage). Accept user input to select an artifact version/build number. Download the selected artifact. Run the deployment step (e.g., firebase appdistribution:distribute) using the downloaded artifact and targeting the correct environment/group. Pros: Fastest rollback, uses the exact binary previously deployed. Cons: Requires managing artifact storage and retention; pipeline logic can be more complex. Re-building and Deploying from a Git Tag/Commit (More Common): Concept: Create a manual workflow similar to the "Single-Click Deployment" (Item 51), but specifically designed for rollback. It takes a known-good Git tag or commit hash as input and runs the build and deploy process using that specific code version. Implementation (GitHub Actions Example): name: Rollback Non-Prod Environment on: workflow_dispatch: inputs: git_ref: description: 'Known-good Git Tag or Commit SHA to roll back to (e.g., v1.1.0+45, abc1234)' required: true environment_target: description: 'Target environment to roll back (dev or staging)' required: true type: choice options: - dev - staging default: 'dev' jobs: rollback: runs-on: ubuntu-latest # Or macos-latest if needed environment: ${{ github.event.inputs.environment_target }} steps: - name: Checkout specific ref for rollback uses: actions/checkout@v3 with: ref: ${{ github.event.inputs.git_ref }} # Checkout the known-good tag/commit # ... Setup Flutter/FVM ... # IMPORTANT: Need to determine the Build Name & Number for this older ref # Option 1: Extract from tag input (if tag format is consistent) # Option 2: Read from pubspec.yaml *at that specific commit* # Option 3: Use a combination (e.g., pubspec version + short commit SHA) - name: Determine Version Info (Example: Read from pubspec) id: package_version uses: CumulusDS/get-package-version-action@v1.3.0 with: path: ./pubspec.yaml # Reads from checked-out commit - name: Set Build Number (Example: using commit SHA for uniqueness) id: build_info run: echo "::set-output name=number::$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)" - name: Build App (Conditional Config) run: | # Logic similar to Item 51 to get API_ENDPOINT etc. based on environment_target API_ENDPOINT="..." FIREBASE_APP_ID="..." # ... fvm flutter build apk --debug \ --build-name=${{ steps.package_version.outputs.version }} \ --build-number=${{ steps.build_info.outputs.number }} \ --dart-define=API_ENDPOINT=$API_ENDPOINT - name: Deploy Rolled-Back Version run: | # Logic similar to Item 51 to get DISTRIBUTION_GROUP etc. DISTRIBUTION_GROUP="..." # ... firebase appdistribution:distribute build/app/outputs/flutter-apk/app-debug.apk \ --app $FIREBASE_APP_ID \ --token ${{ secrets.FIREBASE_CLI_TOKEN }} \ --groups "$DISTRIBUTION_GROUP" \ --release-notes "ROLLBACK to ${{ github.event.inputs.git_ref }} on ${{ github.event.inputs.environment_target }}" # ... Notifications ... How it works: User selects the target environment and provides the specific Git tag or commit hash representing the desired stable state. The workflow checks out that code, builds it with the correct environment configuration, and deploys it. Pros: Doesn't require separate artifact storage; always builds from the source of truth (Git). Cons: Rollback takes as long as a normal build; need a reliable way to identify known-good tags/commits; need to handle version/build numbers correctly for the older code.

Identifying Known-Good Refs: How do you easily find the tag/commit hash for the last successful deployment? CI/CD logs should clearly state the commit hash deployed. Use consistent Git tagging for successful staging/dev builds. Tools like GitHub Deployments API can track deployments per environment. Database: This process typically only rolls back the application code. It does not automatically roll back database changes. If a rollback is needed due to incompatible DB changes, the backend database must be rolled back separately (Item 48), usually manually for non-prod environments or by restoring a DB backup (Item 13). Coordination is key. Permissions: Restrict who can trigger rollback workflows.

Document the rollback procedure for non-prod environments in your CI/CD guide. Explain how to identify the correct Git tag/commit hash or artifact version to roll back to. Clarify that this process does not automatically handle database rollbacks. Providing a simple rollback mechanism for non-production environments allows the team to quickly recover from problematic builds and maintain stable testing environments.

Item: 24 | Architecture Definition | Communication & Alignment | SETUP | 3 | "There is a goal in terms of target automated
test coverage percentage and this target is aligned with the team and the key project sponsors." | Formally agree with the PO and team on a target (e.g., 80% line coverage for unit/widget tests). Configure CI to fail if coverage drops below this. | | This guide explains how to define, agree upon, and document a target for automated test coverage (specifically line coverage for unit and widget tests) in your Flutter project.
documents.s: Completing Item 24: Align on Test Coverage Goal

documents.t: Measurable Quality Target: Provides a quantifiable goal for testing efforts, moving beyond vague statements like "well-tested." Focuses Effort: Helps the team prioritize writing tests, especially for critical business logic. Regression Prevention: Higher coverage generally correlates with a lower chance of regressions. Stakeholder Communication: Gives stakeholders (like the PO) a tangible metric related to code quality and stability. CI Enforcement: Allows you to automatically enforce a minimum quality bar in your CI pipeline.

Line Coverage: The percentage of executable lines of code that were run during the execution of your automated test suite (flutter test --coverage). What it Measures: Whether a line of code was executed by a test. What it Doesn't Measure: If the test assertions were meaningful or correct. If all logical branches (e.g., edge cases within an if statement) were tested. (Branch coverage is a separate metric, often harder to track with standard Flutter tooling). The overall quality or maintainability of the code or tests. Coverage is a useful indicator but not a guarantee of quality. Aiming for 100% is often impractical and leads to diminishing returns.

Understand Your Starting Point (Optional but Recommended): If the project has existing code, run flutter test --coverage and generate an initial coverage report (e.g., using genhtml lcov.info --output-directory coverage_report). Analyze the current coverage percentage and identify areas with low coverage. This provides context for setting a realistic target. Propose a Target: Common Targets: For Flutter unit and widget tests (excluding integration/E2E tests), a common and reasonable target for line coverage is often between 70% and 85%. Considerations: Project Criticality: Higher criticality might warrant a higher target. Team Experience: Teams new to testing might start lower (e.g., 60-70%) and increase gradually. Code Complexity: Highly complex business logic requires more thorough testing. UI-heavy code might naturally have slightly lower unit/widget test coverage (relying more on integration/manual tests). Scope: Be clear that this target applies primarily to Unit Tests (test/**) and Widget Tests (test/**), not necessarily Integration Tests (integration_test/**) or generated code. Discuss and Align with the Team: Present the proposed target to the development team. Explain what coverage means and its limitations. Discuss the feasibility and the effort required to reach and maintain the target. Adjust the target based on team consensus. Ensure the team buys into the goal. Align with Product Owner / Key Sponsors: Schedule a brief meeting with the PO and potentially other key stakeholders. Explain the concept of code coverage in simple terms ("It's a measure of how much of our code is checked by automated tests when we make changes"). Present the team-agreed target (e.g., "We're aiming for 80% line coverage for our core logic"). Explain the trade-offs: "Achieving and maintaining this coverage level means dedicating a portion of our development time to writing tests, which might slightly slow down new feature delivery initially but will improve stability and reduce bugs long-term." Get formal agreement or acknowledgment from the PO/sponsors. This ensures they understand the investment in quality. Document the Goal: Create an "Automated Test Coverage Goal" page on your wiki or add a section to your "Testing Guide" (Item 15). Clearly state the agreed-upon target percentage (e.g., "The target line coverage for unit and widget tests is 80%."). Specify what code is included/excluded (e.g., "This target applies to code in the lib/ directory, excluding generated files (*.g.dart, *.freezed.dart)"). Mention the tool used to measure coverage (flutter test --coverage producing lcov.info).
