Implement Measurement and Enforcement: CI Pipeline: Ensure your CI pipeline runs flutter test --coverage on every PR. Use tools to parse the lcov.info report (e.g., lcov command-line tool, GitHub Actions like coverallsapp/github-action or codecov/codecov-action, or SonarQube integration). Quality Gates (Recommended): Configure your CI tool or SonarQube (Item 6) to fail the build if: Overall project coverage drops below the target (use with caution, can be annoying). Coverage on New Code within a Pull Request is below the target (this is often the most effective gate). Set this threshold in SonarQube or using CI coverage tools. Monitor and Review: Regularly review coverage reports (e.g., bi-weekly during tech backlog refinement - Item 138). Discuss trends and identify areas needing more tests. Revisit the target annually or if project circumstances change significantly.

Item: 99 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Monitoring | RELEASE | 3 | "At least key members in the team can see the application monitoring metrics.
" | Give all developers and the PO "Viewer" access to the Firebase Crashlytics and Performance dashboards. | | This guide explains how to ensure that essential team members have the necessary access to view application monitoring metrics, enabling them to understand application health and troubleshoot issues.
documents.s: Completing Item 99: Ensure Key Team Members Can View App Monitoring Metrics

documents.t: Faster Troubleshooting: Developers can directly investigate crashes or performance issues reported by users or alerts. Informed Development: Understanding real-world performance and stability helps developers make better technical decisions. Quality Ownership: Gives developers and QAs visibility into the impact of their work on production stability and performance. PO Visibility: Allows the Product Owner to see objective data on application health, influencing prioritization and release decisions.

Typically, this includes: All Flutter Developers working on the application. QA Lead/Engineers responsible for testing the application. Tech Lead / Architect. Product Owner (PO). Relevant DevOps/SRE personnel (if applicable).

Identify Monitoring Tools: Confirm the primary tools used for application-specific monitoring (as opposed to infrastructure). For Flutter, this commonly includes: Firebase Crashlytics: For crash reporting and stability metrics (Crash-free users/sessions). Firebase Performance Monitoring: For app startup time, screen render times, and custom traces. Firebase Analytics: For user behavior patterns (though sometimes considered business monitoring). Third-Party APM/RUM: Datadog RUM, Sentry, New Relic Mobile, etc., if used. Determine Required Access Level: For most key members (Devs, QA, PO), "Viewer" or equivalent read-only access is usually sufficient. They need to see the data but not necessarily configure alerts or change settings. Tech Leads, Architects, or dedicated DevOps personnel might require higher privileges (e.g., "Editor," "Admin") to manage settings, configure custom traces, or manage alerts. Grant Access via Tool's Console/Settings: Firebase: Go to your Firebase project settings (⚙️ > Project settings). Navigate to Users and permissions. Click Add member. Enter the email addresses (usually Google accounts) of the team members. Assign the appropriate role (e.g., Viewer for most, Editor or Owner for leads if needed). Note: Access is often granted at the Firebase project level, giving access to multiple services (Crashlytics, Performance, Analytics, etc.). Datadog, Sentry, New Relic, etc.: Follow the specific tool's documentation for adding users and assigning roles (e.g., Read Only, Standard User, Admin). These platforms often have more granular permission models. Document Access Information: On a central project wiki page (e.g., "Monitoring & Alerting"), list the key monitoring tools used. Provide direct links to the relevant dashboards (e.g., link to the Firebase Crashlytics dashboard, the Firebase Performance dashboard). Briefly explain who has access and how to request access if needed (e.g., "All team members have Viewer access via their company Google account. Contact [Tech Lead Name] for issues."). Communicate and Onboard: During onboarding, show new team members where to find the monitoring dashboards and briefly explain how to interpret the key metrics (e.g., "Here's Crashlytics, look at the crash-free user rate. Here's Performance, check the app start time."). Encourage developers and QA to proactively check these dashboards, especially after releases or when investigating issues. By ensuring appropriate access, you empower the team to take ownership of application quality and stability based on real user data.

Item: 46 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Deployment | PREPARATION (Sprint 0) | 4 | "The deployment to the pre-production environment is automated and executed in a CI/CD server (Jenkins, Azure DevOps, etc)." | Create a separate workflow that deploys to a "Staging" track (e.g., separate Firebase project, or "Internal Testing" track on Play Store) from a release/* branch. | | This guide explains how to set up an automated pipeline to deploy your Flutter app to a pre-production environment (often called Staging, UAT, or Release Candidate), which closely mirrors the production environment. This deployment typically happens less frequently than dev deployments, often triggered by creating a release branch or tag.
documents.s: Completing Item 46: Automate Pre-Production Environment Deployment

documents.t: Production-Like Testing: Provides an environment closely resembling production for final QA, UAT, performance testing, and regression testing before a production release. Reduces Manual Effort: Automates the build and deployment process for release candidates. Consistency: Ensures release candidate builds are created using a standardized, repeatable process. Risk Reduction: Catches issues related to production-like configurations or infrastructure before hitting actual users.

Trigger: Often triggered manually, by pushing to a specific release/* branch, or creating a Git tag, rather than on every merge to main. Configuration: Uses configuration (API endpoints, keys via dart-define or .env) specific to the Staging/Pre-Prod environment. Build Mode: Typically builds are done in release mode (--release) to accurately reflect production performance and code optimization (unlike dev builds which might use debug mode). Signing (Optional but Recommended): May use signing keys/profiles that are closer to production (e.g., Ad Hoc or Enterprise distribution for iOS, separate staging keys for Android) compared to debug builds. Still not the final production keys. Distribution: Might use slightly different distribution tracks (e.g., TestFlight External Testing, Play Store Closed Testing/Beta Track, separate Firebase App Distribution project/group).

Choose Triggering Strategy: Release Branch: Create a workflow that triggers when a branch matching release/v*.*.* is pushed. (Good for stabilizing a release). Git Tag: Create a workflow that triggers when a tag matching v*.*.*+* (or similar release candidate pattern) is pushed. (Good for specific release candidate builds). Manual Trigger: Create a workflow with workflow_dispatch allowing manual triggering, potentially requiring the branch/tag name as input. (Good for controlled RC builds). Create a Separate CI/CD Workflow: Duplicate your dev deployment workflow (Item 45) or create a new one (e.g., .github/workflows/deploy_staging.yaml). Update the on: trigger section based on your chosen strategy (release branch, tag, manual). Configure Build Steps for Pre-Prod: Check out the correct code (based on the trigger event - branch or tag). Set up Flutter, platform SDKs, dependencies as usual. Crucially: Build the artifacts in release mode (--release) using the Staging/Pre-Prod configuration via --dart-define or .env.staging. Android Example: fvm flutter build appbundle --release --build-name=... --build-number=... --dart-define=API_ENDPOINT=https://staging-api.example.com ... (AAB might be preferred here to test the format used for production). iOS Example: fvm flutter build ipa --release --build-name=... --build-number=... --dart-define=API_ENDPOINT=https://staging-api.example.com --export-options-plist=path/to/ExportOptionsStaging.plist ... (Ensure appropriate staging/AdHoc signing). Configure Deployment Step for Pre-Prod: Choose the appropriate distribution target for this environment: Firebase App Distribution: Use a separate group (e.g., uat-testers) or even a separate Firebase project for staging builds. TestFlight: Upload to App Store Connect for distribution to Internal or External Testers. Requires production-like signing. fastlane pilot can automate this. Google Play Closed Testing: Upload to a Closed Testing track (Alpha/Beta) in the Play Console. Requires production-like signing. fastlane supply can automate this. Update the deployment step in your CI/CD workflow to target the chosen platform/track using staging credentials/secrets. Example (Firebase App Dist Staging Group): - name: Upload to Firebase App Distribution (Staging) run: | firebase appdistribution:distribute build/app/outputs/flutter-apk/app-release.apk \ --app ${{ secrets.FIREBASE_APP_ID_ANDROID }} \ --token ${{ secrets.FIREBASE_CLI_TOKEN }} \ --groups "uat-testers" \ # Target specific group --release-notes "Staging Build ${{ github.ref_name }} - ${{ github.sha }}" Example (using Fastlane for TestFlight/Play Console): # (Assuming fastlane is set up) - name: Deploy to TestFlight (iOS) run: bundle exec fastlane beta_ios - name: Deploy to Play Store Closed Testing (Android) run: bundle exec fastlane beta_android Add Notifications: Notify relevant stakeholders (QA, UAT testers, PO) via chat/email when a new staging build is available, providing access instructions/links. Document the Process: Update your CI/CD/Release documentation (Item 26) to include the staging deployment workflow, trigger mechanism, and how testers access these builds. Automating pre-production deployments ensures a reliable process for getting release candidates into a production-like environment for final validation before impacting end-users.

Item: 30 | Architecture Definition | Non-functional requirements | SETUP | 4 | "There is a target for the NFR metrics.
The target is defined and documented." | Quantify NFRs (e.g., "99.9% crash-free users" via Firebase Crashlytics; "P95 API response time < 500ms" via backend monitoring). | | This guide details the crucial step of assigning specific, measurable targets to the Non-Functional Requirements (NFRs) identified previously (Item 27) and documented (often using a template from Item 28). This step makes NFRs actionable and verifiable.
documents.s: Completing Item 30: Define Targets for NFR Metrics

documents.t: Measurability: Turns vague goals ("fast app") into concrete, testable criteria ("startup < 2s"). Objectivity: Removes ambiguity and subjectivity in assessing whether a requirement has been met. Focus: Guides development and testing efforts towards achieving specific outcomes. Quality Gates: Enables automated checks in CI/CD or release processes based on hitting these targets. Clear Communication: Provides unambiguous quality goals for the team and stakeholders.

Revisit Collected NFRs: Use the NFR list (Item 27) or the populated NFR template (Item 28) as your input. For Each Key NFR, Define Metric, Target, and Tool: Go through each NFR statement and determine: How can we measure this? (Metric): Identify a specific, quantifiable indicator. What is the acceptable value? (Target): Define the precise threshold, number, or state that signifies success. How will we perform the measurement? (Tool/Method): Specify the tool or process used to measure the metric. Quantify Common Flutter NFRs (Examples - expand on Item 28): Performance: NFR: "App starts quickly." Metric: Cold App Startup Time (P90 or P95 - percentile ensures most users have this experience). Target: < 2.0 seconds. Tool: Firebase Performance Monitoring. NFR: "Screens load fast." Metric: Screen Trace Duration (P90) for critical screens (e.g., Home, Product Detail). Target: < 500ms. Tool: Firebase Performance Monitoring (Custom Traces). NFR: "Scrolling is smooth." Metric: Frames Per Second (FPS) during scroll / Number of Jank Frames. Target: Maintain ~60 FPS / 0 Jank frames on target devices. Tool: Flutter DevTools (Performance Overlay, Track Widget Builds). Note: Hard to automate fully, often requires manual profiling. NFR: "App uses reasonable memory." Metric: Memory usage after specific flow. Target: < 250 MB on mid-range device (example target). Tool: Flutter DevTools (Memory tab), Android Studio Profiler, Xcode Instruments. Reliability: NFR: "App doesn't crash often." Metric: Crash-Free User Rate. Target: > 99.9%. Tool: Firebase Crashlytics. NFR: "Backend is available." Metric: API Endpoint Uptime / Availability. Target: > 99.9%. Tool: Backend monitoring (Datadog, GCP Monitoring uptime checks). NFR: "Network errors are handled gracefully." Metric: Percentage of failed network requests showing user-friendly error messages. Target: 100%. Tool: Manual testing, Code review. Maintainability: NFR: "Code is easy to test." Metric: Line Coverage on New Code (Unit/Widget Tests). Target: > 80%. Tool: flutter test --coverage, SonarQube/lcov report. NFR: "Code follows standards." Metric: Number of New Major/Critical Code Smells. Target: 0. Tool: SonarQube Quality Gate. NFR: "Build process is fast." Metric: CI Pipeline Duration (PR check). Target: < 15 minutes. Tool: CI/CD Platform (GitHub Actions logs, etc.). Security: NFR: "Dependencies are secure." Metric: Number of New Critical/High Vulnerabilities detected in dependencies. Target: 0. Tool: Snyk / Dependabot / SonarQube vulnerability scan. NFR: "Data is encrypted in transit." Metric: Usage of HTTPS (TLS 1.2+). Target: 100% of external API calls. Tool: Code review, Network proxy inspection (during testing), Pen-Test report. Compatibility: NFR: "Supports target OS versions." Metric: Minimum Supported OS Version. Target: Android API 23+, iOS 13.0+ (example targets). Tool: build.gradle (minSdkVersion), Podfile (platform :ios). Document the Targets: Fill in the Metric, Target, and Measurement Method/Tool columns in your NFR spreadsheet (from Item 28). Ensure the wiki page or document summarizing NFRs (Item 27) also includes these specific targets for key requirements. Review and Approve: Review these quantified targets with the development team for feasibility. Present and get approval from the Product Owner/stakeholders (as per Item 29), ensuring they understand what is being promised and measured. Defining these targets is essential for turning quality requirements into actionable, verifiable goals.

Item: 104 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Monitoring | RELEASE | 4 | There are business monitoring tools for production and there is a team in charge of following up. | (Business) Work with the PO to set up a dashboard (e.g., Looker/Data Studio) showing key business KPIs (e.g., "Daily Active Users," "Signups"). | | This guide outlines the process of establishing tools and dashboards for monitoring key business metrics (KPIs - Key Performance Indicators) related to the Flutter mobile application, and ensuring someone is responsible for tracking them.
documents.s: Completing Item 104: Set Up Business Monitoring Tools

documents.t: Measure Success: Tracks whether the application is achieving its intended business goals (e.g., user growth, engagement, conversion). Data-Driven Decisions: Provides objective data to inform product strategy, feature prioritization, and marketing efforts. Identify Problems/Opportunities: Sudden drops or unexpected trends in KPIs can indicate underlying technical issues, usability problems, or market shifts. Connect Tech to Business: Helps the development team understand the business impact of the features they build.

The specific KPIs depend heavily on the app's purpose, but common examples include: Acquisition: Downloads, Sign-ups/Registrations, Installation Source. Activation: Onboarding completion rate, First key action taken (e.g., first purchase, first post). Engagement: Daily Active Users (DAU), Monthly Active Users (MAU), Session duration, Session frequency, Key feature usage rates (e.g., searches performed, items added to cart). Retention: Day 1/7/30 retention rates, Churn rate. Revenue (if applicable): Average Revenue Per User (ARPU), Conversion Rate (e.g., view-to-purchase), Subscription renewals. App Store Ratings/Reviews.
documents.s: Key Business Metrics for Mobile Apps (Examples)

documents.t: Define Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) with PO/Stakeholders: Crucial Step: Work closely with the Product Owner and key business stakeholders to identify the most important metrics that define success for this specific application. Ask: "How do we know if this app is successful?", "What user behaviors drive business value?", "What are our growth/engagement goals?" Focus on a manageable number of primary KPIs (e.g., 5-10) rather than trying to track everything. Ensure each KPI is SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound). Implement Analytics Tracking in the App: Ensure an analytics platform is integrated into the Flutter app to capture the raw data needed for the KPIs. Common choices: Firebase Analytics: Good general-purpose tool, integrates well with other Firebase services, often sufficient. Mixpanel, Amplitude: More advanced product analytics platforms. Google Analytics for Firebase. Event Tracking: Instrument the app code to log relevant events corresponding to the KPIs (e.g., analytics.logEvent(name: 'sign_up'), analytics.logEvent(name: 'add_to_cart', parameters: {...}), analytics.logScreenView(...)). User Properties: Set user properties (e.g., user role, subscription status) where appropriate (respecting privacy). Choose and Configure a Business Intelligence (BI) / Dashboarding Tool: While Firebase Analytics has its own dashboard, a dedicated BI tool often provides more flexibility for visualizing KPIs and combining data sources. Options: Google Looker Studio (formerly Data Studio): Free, integrates well with Google Analytics/Firebase, BigQuery. Good starting point. Tableau, Power BI, Looker (Google Cloud): More powerful, enterprise-grade BI tools. Mixpanel, Amplitude Dashboards: If using these platforms, their built-in dashboards are often sufficient. Connect Data Sources: Configure the BI tool to connect to your analytics data source (e.g., Firebase via BigQuery export, direct integration). Build the Dashboard: Create a dashboard specifically for the defined KPIs. Use clear visualizations (line charts for trends, scorecards for current values, bar charts for comparisons). Organize it logically. Assign Ownership for Monitoring: Designate who is primarily responsible for regularly reviewing the business monitoring dashboard and reporting on trends or anomalies. This is often the Product Owner or a dedicated Data Analyst. The development team lead should also be aware of major trends, but day-to-day monitoring usually falls to the product/business side. Establish Reporting/Review Cadence: Define how often the KPIs will be reviewed and discussed (e.g., weekly check-in, monthly business review). Incorporate KPI review into relevant team meetings (e.g., Sprint Review). Document and Share: Document the defined KPIs, their meaning, and how they are calculated on the project wiki. Share the link to the primary business monitoring dashboard widely with the team and stakeholders (Item 105). Setting up business monitoring closes the loop, allowing the team and stakeholders to see the real-world outcomes of the application's development and usage.

Item: 58 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Deployment | PREPARATION (Sprint 0) | 4 | The deployment can be executed in a single click for Production environment. | Create a release-productionworkflow (e.g., usingfastlane) that can be manually triggered to build, sign, and upload the final app artifacts to the stores. | | (Note: In mobile context, "deployment to Production environment" typically means building the final artifacts and submitting them to the App Store / Play Store for review and subsequent release. The actual release to users is often a separate manual step - Item 55). This guide explains how to create a manually triggerable CI/CD workflow ("single-click") that automates the entire process of building, signing, and submitting your Flutter app's production version to the app stores.
documents.s: Completing Item 58: Enable Single-Click Production Deployment (Submission)

documents.t: Reduces Manual Errors: Automates the complex and error-prone steps of production building, signing, versioning, and uploading. Consistency: Ensures every production submission uses the exact same, verified process. Speed & Efficiency: Drastically reduces the time and effort required from developers or release managers to prepare and submit a release. Control: Keeps the trigger manual, allowing a designated person (e.g., Release Manager, Tech Lead) to initiate the production submission deliberately. Traceability: The entire submission process is logged within the CI/CD system.

Prerequisites: All steps from Item 55 ("Automate Production Deployment (with Approval)") are implemented, particularly: Secure management of production signing credentials and store API keys in CI/CD secrets. A clear Git tagging strategy for production releases (e.g., vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH+BUILD). Automation tools like fastlane configured for store uploads (supply, pilot/deliver). Create/Adapt the "Release Production" Workflow: Use the dedicated production release workflow created in Item 55 (e.g., .github/workflows/release_production.yaml). Ensure Manual Trigger: Configure the primary trigger to be manual. GitHub Actions: Use workflow_dispatch with necessary inputs. GitLab CI: Use when: manual for the relevant job(s) and potentially CI/CD variables for input. Jenkins: Configure the job as parameterized and manually triggered. Inputs: The workflow must require the exact Git tag representing the approved release candidate as input. This ensures you build from the correct, tested codebase. # GitHub Actions Example Trigger on: workflow_dispatch: inputs: release_tag: description: 'Exact Git tag to build and submit (e.g., v1.2.0+55)' required: true Workflow Steps (Consolidate from Item 55): Checkout: Checkout code using the release_tag provided as input. - name: Checkout Release Tag uses: actions/checkout@v3 with: ref: ${{ github.event.inputs.release_tag }} Setup: Set up Flutter, platform SDKs, dependencies. Credentials: Securely decode/install production signing credentials. Versioning: Extract version name and build number from the release_tag or the pubspec.yaml at that tag. Build: Build the release artifacts (.aab, .ipa) using --release, production --dart-define variables, and production signing. Submit: Run fastlane (or equivalent) lanes to upload the artifacts and associated metadata to the Google Play Console (Production Track) and App Store Connect (Submit for Review). Notifications: Notify the team/release manager upon successful submission or failure. Tagging (Alternative Trigger): If triggering automatically on tag push, the checkout step simplifies to ref: ${{ github.ref }}. However, ensure only authorized personnel can push production tag patterns. A manual trigger (workflow_dispatch) often provides better control. Permissions and Access Control: Restrict Triggering: Use CI/CD platform features to restrict who can trigger this production submission workflow (e.g., specific users, teams, or roles). Secret Access: Ensure production secrets are only exposed to this specific production workflow and protected from other builds (e.g., using GitHub Environments protection rules). Documentation: Clearly document the "Production Release Submission" process in your release runbook. Specify who is authorized to trigger the workflow. Provide step-by-step instructions on how to trigger it (e.g., "Go to GitHub Actions > Release Production Workflow > Run workflow > Enter the approved Git Tag > Click Run"). Remind users that this submits the app for review, and the final release to users still requires manual steps in the store consoles (Item 55). By creating a manually triggered, fully automated production submission workflow, you combine the safety of human oversight for the initiation with the reliability and speed of automation for the execution.

Item: 59 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Deployment | PREPARATION (Sprint 0) | 4 | The rollback can be executed in a single click for Production environment. | Document how to use the App Store Connect / Play Console to select a previous version and "promote" it to 100% of users, effectively rolling back. | | (Note: As established in Item 7 & 48, true "single-click rollback" for live mobile users isn't possible due to app store mechanisms. This item likely refers to either a) the manual store console actions, or b) a "single-click" trigger to build the necessary rollback artifact, which then needs manual submission.) This guide focuses on Option B: Creating a "single-click" CI/CD workflow to build the correct rollback artifact, preparing it for manual submission, and documenting the necessary manual store console actions.
documents.s: Completing Item 59: Enable Single-Click Production Rollback (Build Trigger)

documents.t: Reduces Panic Errors: During a production incident requiring rollback, automating the build of the correct artifact under pressure reduces the chance of manual errors (checking out wrong code, using wrong signing keys, wrong version numbers). Speed: Quickly generates the required .aab/.ipa file based on the last known good state. Consistency: Uses a defined, tested process for creating the rollback build.

Prerequisites: Clear Git tagging strategy for production releases (e.g., vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH+BUILD). Access to previous production artifacts or the ability to rebuild from tags. Secure management of production signing credentials in CI/CD. Understanding of the manual rollback procedures in Google Play Console and App Store Connect (Item 48). Create a Dedicated "Prepare Production Rollback" Workflow: Create a new CI/CD workflow file (e.g., .github/workflows/prepare_rollback.yaml). Trigger: Configure for manual triggering (workflow_dispatch in GitHub Actions). Inputs: lkg_tag: The exact Git tag of the Last Known Good version to roll back to (e.g., v1.2.0+55). new_version_name: (Required for iOS) The new semantic version for the rollback build (e.g., 1.2.2). Must be higher than the faulty version. new_build_number: The new build number for the rollback build (e.g., 61). Must be higher than the faulty version's build number. # GitHub Actions Example Trigger on: workflow_dispatch: inputs: lkg_tag: description: 'Last Known Good Git tag to build FROM (e.g., v1.2.0+55)' required: true new_version_name: description: 'NEW SemVer for this rollback build (e.g., 1.2.1 or 1.3.0) - MUST be > faulty version' required: true new_build_number: description: 'NEW Build Number for this rollback build (e.g., 61) - MUST be > faulty version build no.' required: true Workflow Steps: Checkout LKG Code: Checkout the exact code specified by the lkg_tag input. - name: Checkout Last Known Good Code uses: actions/checkout@v3 with: ref: ${{ github.event.inputs.lkg_tag }} Setup: Set up Flutter, platform SDKs, dependencies. Credentials: Securely decode/install production signing credentials. Versioning: Use the new_version_name and new_build_number inputs for the build command. Do not use the version from the checked-out pubspec.yaml of the old tag. Build: Build the release artifacts (.aab, .ipa) using --release, production --dart-define variables, production signing, and the new version info. - name: Build Rollback Android App Bundle run: | fvm flutter build appbundle --release \ --build-name=${{ github.event.inputs.new_version_name }} \ --build-number=${{ github.event.inputs.new_build_number }} \ --dart-define=API_ENDPOINT=[https://api.example.com](https://api.example.com) # PRODUCTION Config # ... signing config ... - name: Build Rollback iOS IPA run: | # Update Info.plist or use Fastlane to set version before build if needed fvm flutter build ipa --release \ --build-name=${{ github.event.inputs.new_version_name }} \ --build-number=${{ github.event.inputs.new_build_number }} \ --dart-define=API_ENDPOINT=[https://api.example.com](https://api.example.com) # PRODUCTION Config --export-options-plist=path/to/ExportOptionsProd.plist # ... signing config ... Store Artifacts: Upload the generated .aab and .ipa as build artifacts within the CI/CD job, making them easily downloadable. Do NOT automatically submit these to the stores. Document the Full Rollback Process: Create or update a "Production Rollback Runbook" on the wiki. Step 1: Trigger Rollback Build: Explain how to run the "Prepare Production Rollback" workflow, providing the LKG Tag and the required new version/build numbers. Step 2: Download Artifacts: Explain how to download the .aab and .ipa from the completed workflow run. Step 3: Manual Store Submission: Link to or reiterate the manual steps required in Google Play Console and App Store Connect (from Item 48) to upload these downloaded artifacts and release them (requesting expedited review for iOS if needed). Step 4: Verification: Describe how to monitor the stores and application metrics to confirm the rollback was successful. Permissions and Testing: Restrict who can trigger the "Prepare Production Rollback" workflow. Test the workflow periodically by building artifacts for an older tag (deploy them to a test track if possible, but at least verify the build completes successfully with correct signing and versioning). This approach provides a "single-click" way to generate the necessary rollback artifacts reliably, significantly simplifying the most error-prone part of the mobile rollback process, while still leaving the final store submission and release decision as deliberate manual steps.

Maturity Level 4: Continuous Deployment Area: Architecture Execution Practice: Continuous Deployment Phase: DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) Index: 136 Criteria "It is possible to check the deployment status through smoking test scripts." E-commerce App Context (Flutter) A "smoke test" is a basic, automated test that runs after deployment to ensure the app isn't fundamentally broken. It answers the question, "Did the deployment work?" For an e-commerce app, a good smoke test would be: "Can the app start, log in, and load the home screen?" If it fails, the build is marked as "bad" immediately. How to Achieve This (Flutter/E-commerce) Required Tooling UI Testing Framework: Patrol (recommended) or flutter_driver + integration_test. CI/CD Server: GitHub Actions, Codemagic, etc. Device Farm (Optional but best): Firebase Test Lab, AWS Device Farm, or BrowserStack. Implementation Steps Step 1: Write the Smoke Test Script Using Patrol, create a new test file (e.g., test/smoke_test.dart). This test should be simple and fast. It should not test business logic, only that the core app flow is functional. // Example using Patrol framework import 'package:flutter_test/flutter_test.dart'; import 'package:patrol/patrol.dart'; import 'package:my_ecommerce_app/main.dart' as app; // Your app's entry void main() { patrolTest( 'Smoke Test: App Login and Home Screen', (PatrolIntegrationTester $) async { await app.main(); // Start the app await $.pumpAndSettle(); // Wait for app to load // 1. Find and tap the "Login" button await $(#loginButton).tap(); await $.pumpAndSettle(); // 2. Enter credentials (use environment variables) await $(#emailField).enterText(PatrolTester.env['TEST_USER_EMAIL']); await $(#passwordField).enterText(PatrolTester.env['TEST_USER_PASS']); await $(#submitLoginButton).tap(); await $.pumpAndSettle(timeout: Duration(seconds: 10)); // Wait for network // 3. Verify we are on the Home Screen // This confirms login worked and the home screen loaded. expect($(#homeScreenTitle), findsOneWidget); expect($(#productCarousel), findsOneWidget); }, ); } Step 2: Integrate into CI/CD Pipeline This test should run as a post-deploy step. Flow: CI/CD builds and deploys the "Dev" app to Firebase App Distribution (from Item 135). New Step: The CI/CD job then triggers the smoke test. Option A (Device Farm - Recommended): Your CI/CD job uses the Firebase CLI to upload your test script and the newly-built APK/IPA to Firebase Test Lab. Test Lab runs your smoke_test.dart on a real, physical device. The CI/CD job waits for Test Lab to return "PASS" or "FAIL". Option B (Emulator - Good): Your CI/CD job starts an Android emulator. It runs patrol_cli test --target=test/smoke_test.dart (or the flutter_driver equivalent) inside the emulator. It waits for the test to pass or fail. Step 3: Alert on Failure If the smoke test fails, the CI/CD job must: Mark the entire build/deployment as "FAILED". Send an urgent alert to the team's Slack channel: "Smoke test failed for build 1.2.4. App may be broken." (Advanced) Automatically roll back the deployment or mark it as "bad".

Item: 103 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Monitoring | RELEASE | 4 | The team can fix the issue when application monitoring is showing any problems. | Ensure all Flutter developers are trained to read Firebase Crashlytics stack traces to identify and fix bugs in the app. | | This guide focuses on ensuring the Flutter development team has the skills and processes to effectively identify, diagnose, and fix issues surfaced by application-specific monitoring tools (like Firebase Crashlytics).
documents.s: Completing Item 103: Ensure Team Can Fix Application Monitoring Issues

documents.t: Direct Responsibility: The team that writes the code is best equipped to fix bugs within that code. Faster Bug Fixes: Developers can directly analyze crash reports or performance regressions without hand-offs. Improved Code Quality: Understanding production failures provides direct feedback, leading developers to write more resilient code. Reduced Support Load: Enables the team to proactively fix issues before they generate numerous user support tickets.
documents.s: Why Ensure Team Can Fix App Issues?

documents.t: Ensure Access to Monitoring Tools: Verify that all Flutter developers have at least "Viewer" access to the primary application monitoring tools: Firebase Crashlytics: Essential for viewing crash reports, stack traces, affected user counts, and trends. Firebase Performance Monitoring: For diagnosing performance regressions (slow startup, laggy screens). Other tools (Sentry, Datadog RUM) if used. (Refer to Item 99 for granting access). Training on Monitoring Tools: Crashlytics: Conduct a training session (or provide documentation/videos) covering: How to navigate the Crashlytics dashboard. How to interpret crash reports (reading stack traces, understanding context like OS version, device, background/foreground). How to use filtering (by version, build, date, event). How to read custom logs and keys attached to crash reports (if implemented). How to identify crash trends and prioritize issues (by user impact, version). How to use the "Link to Jira" feature (if configured). Performance Monitoring: Explain how to read the dashboards for App Start Time, Screen Traces, and Network Requests. Show how to filter data (by version, country, device, etc.). Explain how to interpret percentiles (P50, P90, P95). If using Custom Traces, show how to analyze them. Debugging Techniques: Include refreshers on using Flutter DevTools for profiling performance and memory issues identified via monitoring. Implement Robust Logging and Context: To make crash reports more useful: User Identification: Set a user identifier (FirebaseCrashlytics.instance.setUserIdentifier(userId);) after login so crashes can be linked to specific users if needed (respecting privacy). Custom Logging: Use FirebaseCrashlytics.instance.log('User navigated to $screenName'); to add breadcrumbs leading up to a crash. Custom Keys: Set key-value pairs (FirebaseCrashlytics.instance.setCustomKey('last_api_call', '/products/123');) to record relevant state information. Train developers on how and what to log effectively. Establish Bug Triage and Fixing Process: Monitoring Review: Designate someone (e.g., Tech Lead, rotating dev) to regularly review Crashlytics (e.g., daily or every few days) for new or spiking issues, especially after releases. Ticket Creation: For significant new crashes or regressions: Create a bug ticket in Jira. Link directly to the specific issue in Crashlytics/Performance Monitoring. Include key information (affected version, estimated user impact, stack trace snippet). Prioritization: Prioritize these production bugs based on user impact (crash rate, number of users affected) and severity, in collaboration with the PO. Assignment: Assign the bug ticket to a developer for fixing. Verification: After deploying a fix, monitor Crashlytics/Performance Monitoring to confirm the issue is resolved in the new version. Close the issue in Crashlytics. Post-Mortem for Major Issues (Optional): For severe or recurring production issues, conduct a brief post-mortem to understand the root cause and identify preventative measures (e.g., "Need more testing around X," "Improve error handling in Y module"). By ensuring developers have the access, skills, and processes to utilize application monitoring data, you enable them to take direct ownership of fixing production issues in their code.

Item: 102 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Monitoring | RELEASE | 4 | The team can fix the issue when infrastructure monitoring is showing any problems. | (Infra) Ensure developers have the necessary (but limited) access and runbooks to debug and redeploy backend services when an issue is found. | | (Note: This item implies a higher level of DevOps maturity where the development team has some capability to address infrastructure/backend issues, not just the mobile app itself. The scope depends heavily on team structure and responsibilities.) This guide outlines steps to empower the development team (potentially including Flutter developers if they have backend responsibilities or the team is full-stack) to diagnose and potentially fix issues related to the backend infrastructure supporting the mobile app.
documents.s: Completing Item 102: Enable Team to Fix Infrastructure Issues

documents.t: Faster Resolution (MTTR): Reduces hand-offs and waiting times for a separate Ops/Infra team, especially for common or well-understood issues. Increased Ownership: Fosters end-to-end responsibility for the service, from code to production operation. Better Root Cause Analysis: Developers who understand the code and can see the infrastructure behavior are often better positioned to find the root cause of problems. Skill Development: Encourages developers to learn more about the operational aspects of their services.

Team Structure: This is most applicable to teams with a DevOps culture, full-stack developers, or embedded SREs/Ops personnel. It's less relevant if there's a strict separation between Dev and Ops. Infrastructure: Assumes infrastructure is managed via code (IaC - Terraform, etc.) and deployments are automated via CI/CD pipelines. Access Control: Requires carefully defined, least-privilege access controls (IAM roles). Training & Documentation: Developers need appropriate training and clear documentation (runbooks).

Define Scope of "Fixable" Issues: Identify common, well-understood infrastructure/backend issues the development team could potentially resolve themselves. Examples: Service Restart: A specific backend service (pod/container) becomes unresponsive and needs restarting. Rollback Deployment: Rolling back a recent backend deployment that introduced instability. Scaling: Manually triggering a scale-up/down action if autoscaling is misconfigured or too slow (less ideal, but sometimes necessary). Clearing Cache: Flushing a problematic cache. Known Application Bug Remediation: Running a predefined script to correct data corrupted by a known bug. Exclude: Clearly define issues that must be escalated to a dedicated Infra/Ops/DBA team (e.g., underlying hardware failures, network configuration, database schema changes, major security incidents). Provide Necessary (Limited) Access: Work with the Infra/Security team to grant developers least-privilege access required to perform the defined actions. Examples: Permission to trigger specific CI/CD pipeline jobs (e.g., "Redeploy Staging Backend," "Rollback Production Backend"). Read-only access to logs and monitoring dashboards (Item 101). Permission to restart specific pods/containers in Kubernetes (e.g., via kubectl rollout restart deployment). Permission to run specific, pre-approved scripts via an automation tool (e.g., Jenkins job, Rundeck). AVOID: Granting broad access like SSH to servers, direct database write access, or admin privileges in the cloud console. Develop Clear Runbooks/Playbooks: For each type of issue the team is expected to handle, create a detailed runbook (a step-by-step guide). Store these on the team wiki. Runbook Content: Symptom: How the issue manifests (e.g., specific alert message, monitoring graph pattern, user report). Diagnosis: Steps to confirm the issue (e.g., "Check logs for error X," "Verify API endpoint Y returns 503"). Resolution Steps: Exact commands or UI clicks needed to fix the issue (e.g., kubectl rollout restart deployment <service-name> -n <namespace>, "Click 'Run Job' on Jenkins job 'Clear-Product-Cache'"). Include screenshots if helpful. Verification: How to confirm the fix worked (e.g., "Check monitoring graph Z returns to normal," "Verify API endpoint Y now returns 200 OK"). Escalation: Crucially: Define when to stop and escalate to the Infra/Ops team if the runbook steps don't resolve the issue. Include contact information/procedures for escalation. Training: Conduct training sessions to walk developers through the common issues, the monitoring tools, the available actions, and the runbooks. Ensure developers understand the potential impact of the actions they can take and the importance of following the runbooks precisely. Logging and Auditing: Ensure all actions taken by developers (pipeline triggers, commands) are logged and auditable. Review and Iterate: After incidents, review the effectiveness of the runbooks and the team's ability to resolve the issue. Update runbooks based on lessons learned. Use retrospectives to discuss challenges or successes in handling infrastructure issues. Empowering the team requires trust, clear procedures (runbooks), appropriate tooling, and careful access control. When done correctly, it can significantly improve incident response times.

Item: 105 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Monitoring | RELEASE | 4 | Everyone in the team can see the business monitoring metrics. | Share the link to the business KPI dashboard (Looker/Data Studio) with the entire team to connect their work to business outcomes. | | This guide explains how to ensure the entire development team (including developers, QA, etc.) has visibility into the key business metrics (KPIs) being tracked for the application.
documents.s: Completing Item 105: Ensure Team Can View Business Monitoring Metrics

documents.t: Connects Work to Value: Helps developers and QA understand why they are building certain features and how their work contributes to business goals (e.g., "This feature aims to increase the conversion rate, which we can see here on the dashboard"). Informed Decision Making: Understanding user behavior patterns (e.g., feature adoption rates, drop-off points) can inform technical design and prioritization decisions. Motivation and Ownership: Seeing the positive (or negative) impact of their work on business metrics can increase team engagement and ownership. Faster Identification of Issues: Sometimes, unexpected changes in business metrics can be the first indicator of a subtle technical bug or performance issue that isn't triggering technical alerts. Transparency: Fosters a culture of openness and shared goals between the technical team and business stakeholders.

Identify the Primary Business Monitoring Dashboard: Confirm where the key business KPIs (defined in Item 104) are being visualized. This is typically a dashboard in a tool like: Google Looker Studio (Data Studio) Tableau / Power BI / Looker Mixpanel / Amplitude Firebase Analytics console (for simpler cases) Ensure Appropriate Access Level: For the development team (Devs, QA, Architect, Tech Lead), "Viewer" or read-only access to the dashboard is usually sufficient. They need to see the data, not modify the dashboard structure or underlying data sources. Work with the dashboard owner (PO, Data Analyst) or tool administrator to grant this access. Access methods vary by tool (e.g., sharing link, adding specific user emails, group-based permissions). Share the Dashboard Link: Central Location: Post the direct link to the main business KPI dashboard in a highly visible, permanent location: Pin it in the main project chat channel (#proj-mobile-general or #proj-mobile-tech). Add it to the project's main README file. Include it on the central project overview page on the wiki. Announcement: Announce the availability of the dashboard and the link to the entire team. Provide Context and Guidance: Introduce the Dashboard: During a team meeting (e.g., Sprint Review, dedicated sync), have the PO or Data Analyst briefly walk the team through the dashboard. Explain Key Metrics: Explain what the primary KPIs mean in business terms and how they relate to the app's goals. How to Interpret: Offer guidance on interpreting the charts (e.g., "This line shows Daily Active Users, we want to see it trending up."). Encourage Viewing: Encourage team members to look at the dashboard periodically (e.g., weekly) to stay informed. Integrate into Team Rituals (Optional): Consider briefly showing 1-2 key KPI trends during Sprint Reviews to connect the completed work to business outcomes. Refer to the dashboard when discussing priorities or the potential impact of new features. By making business metrics easily accessible and understandable for the entire team, you foster a stronger connection between technical execution and business success.

Item: 101 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Monitoring | RELEASE | 4 | Everyone in the team can see the infrastructure monitoring metrics. | Create a shared, read-only dashboard in Datadog/GCP for infrastructure metrics and share the link with the entire team. | | This guide explains how to provide the entire development team (including Flutter developers) with read-only access to relevant infrastructure monitoring metrics.
documents.s: Completing Item 101: Ensure Team Can View Infrastructure Monitoring Metrics

documents.t: Context for App Issues: Mobile app performance and reliability often depend heavily on backend infrastructure health. Seeing infrastructure metrics (CPU, memory, DB load, API latency) helps developers understand if an app issue might be caused by a backend problem. Performance Troubleshooting: When investigating app slowness, developers can check if corresponding backend services are under stress. Shared Understanding: Fosters a broader understanding of the entire system, not just the mobile frontend. Transparency: Increases visibility into the operational health of the platform the app relies on.

Focus on metrics directly impacting the mobile app's experience: API Gateway/BFF: Request latency (P50, P90, P99), error rates (4xx, 5xx), request volume. Core Backend Services: CPU utilization, memory utilization, container/pod counts (if applicable), request latency, error rates. Database: CPU utilization, active connections, read/write latency, disk space/IOPS. Authentication Service: Latency, error rates. Avoid overly detailed or obscure infrastructure metrics that aren't directly relevant to the app's interaction with the backend.

Identify Infrastructure Monitoring Tools: Determine where backend and infrastructure metrics are collected (e.g., Datadog, GCP Cloud Monitoring, AWS CloudWatch, Prometheus/Grafana, New Relic APM). Create a Shared, Curated Dashboard: Within the monitoring tool, create a new dashboard specifically designed for the entire team (including mobile devs). Don't just link them to complex, admin-focused dashboards. Title: "Mobile App Backend Health Overview" or similar. Widgets: Add widgets displaying the key relevant metrics identified above (API latency, error rates, CPU/memory for key services, DB load). Timeframe: Set a reasonable default timeframe (e.g., "Last 1 hour," "Last 6 hours"). Clarity: Use clear titles for graphs and widgets. Keep the layout uncluttered. Focus on providing a quick health overview. Read-Only: Ensure the dashboard itself doesn't require special permissions beyond basic viewing rights. Configure Read-Only Access: Work with your DevOps/Infra team or tool administrators to grant "Viewer" or equivalent read-only access to the monitoring tool for all members of the mobile development team (Devs, QA, PO, Leads). This might involve adding them to specific groups or roles within the tool (e.g., a "Developers" role in Datadog with limited dashboard viewing permissions). Avoid granting permissions that allow modification of monitors, alerts, or infrastructure settings. Document and Share: On your central project wiki page ("Monitoring & Alerting" or "Architecture Overview"), add a section for "Infrastructure Monitoring." Provide a direct link to the shared, curated dashboard created in Step 2. Briefly explain the purpose of the dashboard (e.g., "Use this dashboard to check the health of the backend APIs and services our mobile app depends on."). Explain how team members can access the tool (e.g., "Log in via SSO using your company account."). Communicate and Guide: Announce the availability of the dashboard to the team. During onboarding or team syncs, briefly walk through the dashboard, explaining what the key graphs represent and how they might relate to mobile app behavior (e.g., "If you see API latency spiking here, it might explain why the app feels slow."). Encourage developers to consult this dashboard when troubleshooting app performance or reliability issues. By providing easy, read-only access to a curated view of relevant infrastructure metrics, you give the mobile team valuable context for understanding and debugging application behavior.

Item: 109 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Monitoring | RELEASE | 5 | "The team can take actions when business monitoring is showing any problems (for example, contact the business responsible)." | Create a process: If a business KPI alert fires, the PO and tech lead immediately huddle to triage (is it a bug, marketing issue, or external factor?). | | This guide outlines how to establish a process for the team (primarily involving the Product Owner and Tech Lead) to triage and take appropriate action when business monitoring alerts (Item 108) indicate potential problems.
documents.s: Completing Item 109: Enable Team Actions on Business Monitoring Issues

documents.t: Timely Response: Ensures alerts aren't ignored and potential issues are investigated promptly. Correct Routing: Helps determine if the root cause is likely technical, related to user behavior, a data tracking error, or an external factor, directing the investigation accordingly. Collaboration: Facilitates quick collaboration between product/business and technical leads to understand the context and potential impact. Avoid Unnecessary Panic: Provides a structured way to assess if an alert represents a genuine critical issue requiring immediate technical action or something else.

Define Primary Responders: Identify who is primarily responsible for acknowledging and initially investigating business KPI alerts. This is typically the Product Owner (PO), possibly supported by a Data Analyst if available. Identify the primary technical contact to involve if a technical cause is suspected: the Tech Lead or Architect. Establish Triage Workflow (Triggered by Alert - Item 108): Step A: Initial Assessment (PO / Data Analyst): Acknowledge: Acknowledge the alert (e.g., emoji reaction in the #biz-alerts channel, note in an incident log). Check Dashboard: Immediately go to the relevant business monitoring dashboard (linked from the alert). Contextualize: Is this a known event (e.g., end of a marketing campaign, holiday dip)? Is it a small blip or a significant, sustained trend? Does it correlate with a recent app release, backend deployment, or feature flag change? (Check deployment logs/calendar). Are other related KPIs also affected? Could it be a data tracking/pipeline issue? (Check analytics platform status). Step B: Huddle & Hypothesis (PO + Tech Lead): If the initial assessment doesn't reveal an obvious non-technical cause OR if a technical issue is suspected (e.g., drop correlates with a release), the PO immediately contacts the Tech Lead (e.g., via direct message or call, then posts summary in #biz-tech channel). Quick Huddle (5-15 min): PO shares the KPI alert and initial assessment. Tech Lead checks relevant technical monitoring (Crashlytics, backend performance, recent deployment status). Form Hypothesis: Together, form a quick hypothesis: Is it likely a technical bug (app/backend)? A performance issue? A tracking error? A usability issue introduced? Or non-technical? Step C: Action/Investigation: If Technical Cause Likely: Tech Lead initiates technical investigation (e.g., checks detailed logs, assigns a developer to reproduce, reviews recent relevant PRs). Create a high-priority Jira Bug Ticket, linking the business alert/dashboard and technical findings. Proceed with standard incident response/hotfix process if needed. If Tracking/Data Issue Likely: Assign someone (e.g., Data Analyst, relevant Dev) to investigate the analytics implementation or data pipeline. If Usability/Product Issue Likely: PO initiates further investigation (e.g., check user feedback channels, plan usability testing). If Non-Technical/External Factor Likely: PO investigates further (e.g., check with marketing, check competitor activity) and documents the likely cause. If Unknown: Agree on next steps for investigation, assign owners, and set a time to regroup. Document the Process: Create a "Business KPI Alert Handling Process" page on the wiki. Outline the steps: Initial Assessment (PO), Huddle (PO+Lead), Action/Investigation paths. Clearly define roles and responsibilities (who does the initial check, who gets involved when). Specify communication channels (e.g., Use #biz-tech for discussion after initial huddle). Communicate and Train: Ensure the PO, Tech Lead, and potentially Data Analyst understand and agree on this process. Inform the wider team about the process so they understand how business alerts are handled. Review and Refine: After handling a few alerts, review the process during a team meeting or retrospective. Was it efficient? Was the right action taken? Adjust as needed. This structured process ensures that critical business alerts are quickly assessed by the right people, leading to faster diagnosis and resolution whether the root cause is technical or not.

Item: 55 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Deployment | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 5 | The deployment can be executed automatically for Production environment (Except for release approval) | Automate the build and *upload* to App Store Connect / Google Play Console (e.g., using fastlane). The final "release to users" step remains manual. | | This guide explains how to automate the build and submission process for production releases of your Flutter app, while retaining a crucial manual approval step before the app actually goes live to all users.
documents.s: Completing Item 55: Automate Production Deployment (with Approval)

documents.t: Reduces Manual Errors: Building, signing, and uploading production artifacts manually is complex and prone to errors (using wrong keys, profiles, configurations). Consistency: Ensures every production submission follows the exact same verified process. Speed: Significantly speeds up the process of getting an approved build ready for release in the app stores. Traceability: The automated process is logged and version-controlled (Item 54).

Business Control: Allows the Product Owner or Release Manager to decide the exact timing of the release based on business factors (marketing alignment, support readiness, user impact). Final Sanity Check: Provides a final checkpoint before impacting all users. Phased Rollout Management: The manual step is where the phased rollout (Item 9) is typically initiated and managed. App stores require manual intervention to start/manage these rollouts.

Prerequisites: A reliable CI/CD platform is set up. Pipeline-as-code is used (Item 54). Secure management of production signing keys, certificates, and API keys within the CI/CD platform's secrets management. This is critical and platform-specific (e.g., GitHub Secrets, Codemagic encrypted environment variables, secure files). Access to production secrets should be tightly controlled. A dedicated Git tag naming convention for production releases (e.g., vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH+BUILD) (Item 42). Create a Dedicated "Release Production" Workflow: Create a new CI/CD workflow file (e.g., .github/workflows/release_production.yaml). Trigger: Configure this workflow to run only when triggered manually (e.g., workflow_dispatch in GitHub Actions) or automatically when a specific production tag pattern (e.g., v*.*.*+*) is pushed. Do not trigger this automatically on merges. Inputs (if manual trigger): Require the exact Git tag to build from as input. Automate Production Build: The workflow must perform the following steps: Checkout the exact Git tag specified for the release. Set up Flutter, platform SDKs, dependencies. Securely access and configure production signing credentials (e.g., decode Android Keystore from secrets, set up iOS certificates/profiles using fastlane match or manual certificate installation from secrets). Build the artifacts (.aab for Android, .ipa for iOS) in release mode (--release). Inject production configuration using --dart-define (Item 44). Use the correct version name and build number derived from the Git tag or pubspec.yaml (Item 42). Automate Submission to Stores: Use Automation Tools: Leverage tools specifically designed for app store interaction, most commonly fastlane. fastlane supply: Automates uploading Android builds (.aab) and metadata/screenshots to the Google Play Console. Configure it to upload to the Production track (or potentially start a staged rollout directly if the API supports it). fastlane pilot or fastlane deliver: Automates uploading iOS builds (.ipa) and metadata/screenshots to App Store Connect TestFlight (for final testing) or directly for review. Configure it to submit for review. CI/CD Integration: Add steps to your "Release Production" workflow to execute the appropriate fastlane lanes after the build is complete. # Example steps after build (assuming Fastlane setup) - name: Upload Android to Play Store Production Track run: bundle exec fastlane deploy_android_production working-directory: ./android # Or wherever Fastfile is - name: Upload iOS to App Store Connect for Review run: bundle exec fastlane deploy_ios_production working-directory: ./ios # Or wherever Fastfile is Secrets: Securely provide fastlane with the necessary API keys or authentication credentials (e.g., Google Play Service Account JSON, App Store Connect API Key) via CI/CD secrets. Define the Manual Approval/Release Step: The automated workflow STOPS after successful upload/submission. Document the manual steps required in the Google Play Console and App Store Connect to actually release the submitted build to users: Google Play: Go to the Production track, review the release created by the pipeline, and click "Start rollout" (initiating the phased rollout - Item 9). Monitor and increase percentage manually. App Store Connect: Wait for the build to pass review ("Waiting for Review" -> "Ready for Sale"). Go to the approved version, select the phased release option (Item 9), and click "Release". Monitor and manage the phased release manually if needed. Clearly define who is responsible for performing this final manual release step (e.g., Release Manager, PO, Tech Lead). Notifications and Logging: The automated workflow should notify the responsible person(s) upon successful submission to the stores. Ensure the workflow logs clearly indicate the version submitted and the target track/status. By automating the build and submission but keeping the final release step manual, you balance efficiency and consistency with necessary business control over production deployments.

Item: 43 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Deployment | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 5 | "The same package, that was tested in Dev and Stage environments is promoted to production, (Build once, deploy anywhere) (Except for Mobile, SPA applications)" | (N/A for Mobile) Action: "Ensure the *exact same Git commit* that was tested on Staging is used to build the production artifact (.aab/.ipa) for store submission." | | This guide clarifies the "Build Once, Deploy Anywhere" principle in the context of mobile (Flutter) development and outlines the practical steps to achieve its intent, acknowledging the platform-specific nuances.
documents.s: Completing Item 43: Apply "Build Once, Deploy Anywhere" (Mobile Context)

documents.t: The core idea is that you build your application artifact once, and then deploy that exact same immutable artifact to various environments (Dev, Test, Staging, Production) by only changing external configurations (like database connection strings, API endpoints). This guarantees that what you test is exactly what you deploy.

True "Build Once, Deploy Anywhere" is difficult for mobile apps because: Environment Configuration Embedding: Configuration (like API endpoints) is often embedded at build time using dart-define or similar mechanisms. You cannot easily change the API endpoint of an already built .aab or .ipa file. Platform Signing: Production artifacts (.aab/.ipa) require specific signing keys/certificates that are different from debug or internal distribution builds. You cannot simply promote a "staging-signed" artifact to production. Platform-Specific Builds: You inherently build separate artifacts for Android (.aab/.apk) and iOS (.ipa).

While you can't deploy the exact same binary file, you can achieve the intent of the principle – ensuring the code tested is the code released – by focusing on the source code commit and build process consistency. The Goal: Ensure the exact same Git commit hash that was successfully tested and approved on your Staging/QA environment is used as the source for building the final production-signed artifacts.

Source Control Discipline: Use a clear branching strategy (e.g., Trunk-Based Development - Item 1). Ensure that builds deployed to your primary testing environment (e.g., Staging, deployed via Firebase App Distribution from main) correspond directly to a specific Git commit hash on main. Identify the "Release Candidate" Commit: After QA testing is complete on a build deployed from main (e.g., version 1.2.0+55 deployed to Firebase App Distribution from commit abc1234), and the PO approves it for release, that specific commit (abc1234) becomes your release candidate. Tag the Release Candidate Commit: Create a Git tag pointing exactly to this approved commit hash (Item 42): git tag v1.2.0+55 abc1234 git push origin v1.2.0+55 Dedicated Production Build Workflow: Create a separate CI/CD workflow (e.g., release_production.yaml) specifically for building production-signed artifacts. This workflow should only be triggerable manually (or automatically based on creating the Git tag). Crucially, configure this workflow to check out the code based on the provided Git tag. GitHub Actions Example (Triggered by Tag): name: Release Production Build on: push: tags: - 'v*.*.*+*' # Trigger when a version tag is pushed jobs: build_prod: # Ensure proper secrets for signing are available secrets: ANDROID_KEYSTORE_BASE64: ${{ secrets.ANDROID_PROD_KEYSTORE_BASE64 }} ANDROID_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.ANDROID_PROD_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD }} ANDROID_KEY_ALIAS: ${{ secrets.ANDROID_PROD_KEY_ALIAS }} ANDROID_KEY_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.ANDROID_PROD_KEY_PASSWORD }} # Add iOS signing secrets/certs via match/fastlane etc. runs-on: macos-latest # Need macOS for both Android & iOS builds steps: # Checkout the *exact code* associated with the tag - uses: actions/checkout@v3 with: ref: ${{ github.ref }} # Checks out the tag that triggered the workflow # Extract version info from tag if needed (or pubspec) # Setup Flutter (FVM) # Setup Java/Android SDK # Setup iOS Certs/Provisioning (e.g., using fastlane match) - name: Decode Android Keystore # ... steps to decode base64 secret into a file ... - name: Build Production Android App Bundle run: | # Extract version/build number from tag or pubspec # Example: VERSION_NAME=$(echo $GITHUB_REF_NAME | cut -d'+' -f1 | sed 's/v//') # Example: BUILD_NUMBER=$(echo $GITHUB_REF_NAME | cut -d'+' -f2) fvm flutter build appbundle \ --release \ --build-name=$VERSION_NAME \ --build-number=$BUILD_NUMBER \ --dart-define=API_ENDPOINT=[https://api.example.com](https://api.example.com) \ # PRODUCTION Endpoint # Pass keystore properties # ... commands to use signing secrets ... - name: Build Production iOS IPA run: | # Extract version/build number from tag or pubspec fvm flutter build ipa \ --release \ --build-name=$VERSION_NAME \ --build-number=$BUILD_NUMBER \ --dart-define=API_ENDPOINT=[https://api.example.com](https://api.example.com) \ # PRODUCTION Endpoint --export-options-plist=path/to/ExportOptionsProd.plist # ... ensure correct production signing certs/profiles are used ... # ... Steps to upload artifacts to App Store Connect / Google Play Console (e.g., using fastlane) ... Environment Configuration at Build Time: Notice in the example above, the Production build workflow explicitly uses --dart-define (or equivalent) to inject production-specific configurations (like the API endpoint). This is the necessary deviation from true "Build Once" for mobile. The codebase is identical (from the tag), but the build configuration differs per environment. Verification: Ensure build logs clearly show the Git tag/commit hash being built. Verify that the production build uses the correct production configuration. By using the same Git tag (representing the tested code) as the input for both your Staging/QA builds and your final Production build workflow (which handles production signing and configuration), you achieve the core goal of ensuring that what was tested is what gets released, adapting the "Build Once" principle effectively for mobile development.

Item: 9 | Architecture Definition | Architecture & Coding Guidance | SETUP | 5 | "There is a strategy that helps to reduce the risk of production deployments (blue-green deployment, canary release, feature toggle, etc)." | Implement a feature toggle system (e.g., Firebase Remote Config). Use the phased rollout capabilities in the Google Play Console and App Store Connect. | | This guide explains strategies to reduce the risk associated with deploying new versions of your Flutter mobile app to production users. Unlike web applications, true blue-green or canary deployments are difficult, so the focus shifts to phased rollouts and feature toggles.
documents.s: Completing Item 9: Implement Deployment Risk Reduction Strategy

documents.t: Phased Rollouts (Google Play & App Store Connect): Concept: Gradually release the new app version to a small percentage of users first. Monitor for issues (crashes, performance regressions, negative feedback) before increasing the percentage. Implementation (Google Play - Android): When creating a Production release in the Google Play Console, choose Staged rollout. Start with a small percentage (e.g., 1%, 5%, 10%). Monitor: Closely watch Firebase Crashlytics, Firebase Performance Monitoring, and user feedback channels during the rollout. Increase Percentage: If no critical issues arise after a period (e.g., 24-48 hours), increase the percentage (e.g., to 25%, 50%, 100%). Halt Rollout: If critical issues are found, click Halt rollout in the Play Console. Fix the issues, upload a new version, and start a new staged rollout. Implementation (App Store Connect - iOS): After your app version is approved, go to the version details page. Under "Phased Release for Automatic Updates," select Release over a 7-day period. iOS will automatically manage the rollout percentage over 7 days (e.g., Day 1: 1%, Day 2: 2%, Day 3: 5%, etc.). Monitor: Closely watch Firebase Crashlytics, Performance Monitoring, and user feedback. Pause/Resume: You can Pause the phased release in App Store Connect if issues are found. After fixing and potentially submitting an expedited review for a patch, you can Resume or release the fixed version to all users. Documentation: Document the standard phased rollout plan (percentages, monitoring period) in your release process documentation. Feature Toggles (Feature Flags): Concept: Deploy new features hidden behind a remotely configurable flag. This allows you to deploy the code to production but only enable the feature for specific users (testers, internal team) or gradually roll it out, independent of app store releases. It also provides an immediate "kill switch" if the feature causes problems. Implementation: Choose a Service: Use a feature flagging service like: Firebase Remote Config: Simple, free, integrates well with Firebase. Good for basic on/off toggles and gradual rollouts by user percentage or properties. LaunchDarkly, ConfigCat, Statsig: More advanced features (targeting, A/B testing, SDKs). Integrate the SDK: Add the chosen service's Flutter SDK to your pubspec.yaml. Implement Toggles in Code: // Example using Firebase Remote Config final remoteConfig = FirebaseRemoteConfig.instance; await remoteConfig.setConfigSettings(...); // Set fetch intervals await remoteConfig.fetchAndActivate(); // In your widget or bloc: bool isNewFeatureEnabled = remoteConfig.getBool('show_new_checkout_flow'); if (isNewFeatureEnabled) { // Show new UI or execute new logic return NewCheckoutScreen(); } else { // Show old UI or execute old logic return OldCheckoutScreen(); } Wrap Major Features: Enclose significant new features or risky changes within if (isFeatureEnabled) blocks. Remote Configuration: Configure the flags (show_new_checkout_flow) in the service's dashboard (e.g., Firebase Console). Set the default value (usually false). Rollout Strategy: Deploy the app with the new feature code, but the flag turned OFF. Enable the flag for internal testers/QA first via the service dashboard. Gradually increase the percentage of production users who have the flag enabled (e.g., 1%, 10%, 50%, 100%) via the service dashboard. Monitor for issues. If problems arise, turn the flag OFF immediately in the dashboard – no app store update needed! Cleanup: Once a feature is fully rolled out and stable, schedule tech debt tickets to remove the old code path and the feature flag check to avoid clutter. Documentation: Document which features are currently behind toggles and the process for rolling them out. Thorough Testing (Pre-Deployment): While not a deployment strategy itself, robust automated testing (unit, widget, integration) and manual QA on staging environments significantly reduce the risk of deploying bugs.

Update your project's wiki or deployment documentation: Detail the standard phased rollout percentages and monitoring periods for both Android and iOS. Explain how to use the feature toggle system (Firebase Remote Config or other). List any currently active feature toggles and their status. Emphasize the importance of monitoring during rollouts. By combining phased rollouts and feature toggles, you gain significant control over production releases, minimizing the blast radius of potential issues.

Item: 54 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Deployment | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 5 | Deployment scripts are kept as code in repository. | Store all CI/CD pipeline definitions (e.g., .github/workflows/main.yamlorcodemagic.yaml) in the root of the Flutter project's Git repository. | Apply gitops using ArgoCD following OTSK SA | (Note: GitOps/ArgoCD is typically for backend/infrastructure, not directly for Flutter mobile app deployment itself, but the principle of storing CI/CD definitions in Git applies universally). This guide explains the practice of storing your CI/CD pipeline definitions and any custom deployment scripts directly within your application's source code repository (Git).
documents.s: Completing Item 54: Keep Deployment Scripts as Code

documents.t: Version Control: Your deployment process is versioned alongside the application code it deploys. You can see how the deployment process evolved over time. Visibility & Collaboration: Everyone on the team can see, review, and propose changes to the deployment process via standard Git workflows (branches, PRs). Reproducibility: You can easily check out an older version of the code and see the exact pipeline definition that was used to deploy it. Disaster Recovery: If your CI/CD server configuration is lost, the pipeline definition can be quickly reapplied from the Git repository. Infrastructure as Code Principle: Extends the IaC principle to the deployment pipeline itself.
documents.s: Why Keep Deployment Scripts as Code?

documents.t: Use Pipeline-as-Code Features: Leverage the native pipeline-as-code features of your chosen CI/CD platform. Most modern platforms support defining pipelines in YAML or Groovy files stored in the repository: GitHub Actions: .github/workflows/*.yaml files. GitLab CI/CD: .gitlab-ci.yml file. Codemagic: codemagic.yaml file. Jenkins: Jenkinsfile (declarative or scripted pipeline). Azure DevOps: azure-pipelines.yml file. Bitbucket Pipelines: bitbucket-pipelines.yml file. Avoid UI-Only Configuration: Do not define critical build and deployment logic solely through the CI/CD platform's web interface if a code-based alternative exists. The UI might be used for initial setup or secret management, but the core process should be in the file. Store Pipeline Files in Repository: Place the pipeline definition file(s) in the root directory or a standard location (like .github/workflows/) of your Flutter application's Git repository. Ensure these files are committed and pushed just like any other source code file. Store Custom Scripts in Repository: If your pipeline relies on custom shell scripts, Python scripts, or tools like fastlane (Fastfile), store these scripts within the repository as well (e.g., in a /scripts or /fastlane directory). Call these version-controlled scripts from your main pipeline definition file (e.g., run: ./scripts/deploy_firebase.sh staging, run: bundle exec fastlane beta_android). This keeps the main pipeline file cleaner and allows for more complex logic in familiar scripting languages. Manage Secrets Securely: NEVER commit secrets (API keys, passwords, signing keys) directly into the pipeline definition files or scripts in Git. Use the secrets management features provided by your CI/CD platform (e.g., GitHub Secrets, GitLab CI Variables, Codemagic Environment Variables). Inject these secrets into the pipeline environment at runtime (as shown in previous examples using ${{ secrets.MY_SECRET }}). Review Changes via Pull Requests: Treat changes to pipeline definition files (*.yaml, Jenkinsfile, etc.) and deployment scripts (.sh, Fastfile) like any other code change. Submit changes via Pull Requests. Require code reviews for modifications to the deployment process. This prevents accidental breakages and ensures team awareness. (Context: GitOps/ArgoCD - Backend/Infra): While not directly for the Flutter app artifact deployment (which goes to app stores), GitOps tools like ArgoCD are used for deploying backend services, often to Kubernetes. ArgoCD works by monitoring a Git repository containing Kubernetes manifest files (or Helm charts/Kustomize definitions). When changes are merged to a specific branch in that configuration repository, ArgoCD automatically applies those changes to the Kubernetes cluster. This fully embraces the "Git as the source of truth" principle for infrastructure and backend application state, complementing the pipeline-as-code approach used for building the artifacts. By storing all aspects of your build and deployment process as code within your Git repository, you create a transparent, versioned, and collaborative approach to CI/CD.

Item: 10 | Architecture Definition | Architecture & Coding Guidance | SETUP | 5 | "There are established metrics to measure how effective the DevOps practices are (lead time, deployment frequency, time to recovery, etc)." | Configure CI/CD (e.g., Codemagic, GitHub Actions) to log 'Cycle Time' (PR open to merge) and 'Deployment Frequency'. Use Firebase Crashlytics for 'Change Fail Rate'. | | This guide explains how to establish and track key DevOps metrics (often called DORA metrics) to measure the effectiveness of your Flutter development and deployment processes.

These metrics provide objective insights into your team's velocity and stability, helping you identify bottlenecks and measure the impact of process improvements. High-performing teams generally excel in these areas.

Deployment Frequency (DF): How often does your team successfully release to production? Goal: Higher frequency is generally better (indicates smaller batch sizes, faster feedback). For mobile, "release to production" often means submitting to the app stores. How to Measure: Manual Tracking: Record the date of each production submission in a spreadsheet or wiki page. Calculate the average frequency (e.g., releases per week/month). CI/CD Integration: If your CI/CD pipeline has a dedicated "submit-to-store" job/workflow, log the successful completion timestamp of this job to a monitoring tool (Datadog, Grafana) or a simple log file. Dashboard tools can then calculate the frequency. Target (Example): Aim for at least one production submission per sprint (bi-weekly). Lead Time for Changes (LT): How long does it take to get a commit successfully into production? Goal: Shorter lead time is better (indicates efficient development, review, testing, and deployment processes). How to Measure: Git History: Track the time from the first commit on a feature branch to the merge of the PR into main. This is often called Cycle Time and is a good proxy, especially if merges to main trigger a staging deploy. CI/CD & Git Tags: Measure the time from a Git commit/tag (e.g., release/v1.2.0) to the successful submission/release in the App Store/Play Store. Tools: Some CI/CD platforms or value stream management tools can calculate this automatically by integrating with Git and deployment events. GitHub Actions can provide workflow run times. Target (Example): Aim for an average Cycle Time (commit to merge) of < 2 days. Change Failure Rate (CFR): What percentage of deployments to production cause a failure? Goal: Lower failure rate is better (indicates higher quality and better testing). How to Measure (Mobile Specific): Define "failure": A production release requiring an immediate hotfix due to critical bugs (e.g., crashes, major functionality broken), or needing to be halted/rolled back.
