Manual Tracking: Maintain a log of production releases. Mark those that required a hotfix or rollback. Calculate: (Number of Failing Releases / Total Number of Releases) * 100%. Monitoring Integration: Correlate spikes in Firebase Crashlytics (crash rate) or critical alerts in your monitoring system (Datadog) immediately following a release. If a spike necessitates action, count it as a failure. Target (Example): Aim for a CFR < 15%. Time to Restore Service (TTRS) / Mean Time to Recovery (MTTR): How long does it generally take to recover from a failure in production? Goal: Shorter recovery time is better (indicates effective monitoring, alerting, and rollback/hotfix processes). How to Measure: When a production failure occurs (as defined for CFR): Record the time the issue was detected (e.g., alert fired, critical user report). Record the time the issue was resolved (e.g., rollback completed via app stores, hotfix successfully deployed and verified). Calculate the duration. Track these durations over time and calculate the average (mean or median). Target (Example): Aim for an average TTRS < 24 hours (considering app store review times for hotfixes). Focus heavily on improving detection time via monitoring (Item 95-97).

Define Measurement Methods: Decide exactly how you will measure each metric (manual logs, CI/CD data, monitoring tools). Start simple (manual tracking) if needed. Establish Baselines: Track the metrics for a few sprints/releases to understand your current performance before setting firm targets. Set Initial Targets: Based on baselines and team goals, set realistic, achievable targets. Integrate Data Collection: Configure CI/CD jobs to log timestamps or send events to monitoring systems. Ensure robust production monitoring (Firebase Crashlytics, Performance) is in place. Maintain manual logs diligently if required. Visualize and Review: Create simple charts or use dashboards (Grafana, Datadog, internal tools) to visualize trends over time. Review the metrics regularly (e.g., monthly or quarterly) with the team. Discuss trends and identify areas for improvement (e.g., "Our lead time is increasing, why? Is the PR review process too slow?").

Create a wiki page documenting: The definition of each metric in the context of your project. How each metric is measured (tools, process). The current targets for each metric. Links to dashboards or reports where the metrics can be viewed. Tracking these metrics provides valuable feedback on the health and efficiency of your entire development lifecycle.

Item: 110 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Monitoring | RELEASE | 5 | There is flexibility to create new business indicators and dashboards whenever it is necessary. | (Business/Data) Ensure the data pipeline to the business dashboard (Looker) is flexible and that the PO/Data Analyst can add new charts without developer intervention. | | This guide focuses on ensuring that the system for business monitoring (analytics tracking, data pipeline, and dashboarding tool) is flexible enough to allow the Product Owner (PO) or Data Analyst to create new charts, reports, and potentially dashboards without requiring significant intervention from the core application developers.
documents.s: Completing Item 110: Ensure Flexibility in Business Dashboards

documents.t: Agility: Allows the business/product team to quickly explore new questions, track new initiatives, or visualize data in different ways as needs evolve, without being blocked by development team capacity. Self-Service Analytics: Empowers the PO/Analyst to answer their own questions using data. Reduced Developer Bottleneck: Frees up application developers to focus on building product features rather than constantly tweaking dashboards. Faster Insights: Shortens the time from identifying a business question to getting a data-driven answer.

Comprehensive Event Tracking: The foundation is having the necessary raw data. The Flutter app (and potentially backend) must be instrumented to send rich, well-defined analytics events covering key user interactions (Item 104). Use a clear event naming convention and include relevant parameters (e.g., event: 'product_viewed', params: {'product_id': '123', 'category': ' जूते', 'source': 'search'}). Track screen views, button clicks, form submissions, errors, and key workflow steps. Robust Data Pipeline: Ensure the raw event data flows reliably from the analytics platform (e.g., Firebase Analytics) into a data warehouse or queryable store that the BI tool can access. Firebase -> BigQuery Export: This is a common, powerful pattern. Enabling the export makes all raw Firebase Analytics event data available in BigQuery for complex querying. ETL/ELT Processes: If data needs cleaning, transformation, or joining with other data sources (e.g., backend database data), ensure these data pipeline processes are automated and reliable. User-Friendly BI / Dashboarding Tool: The chosen tool (Looker Studio, Tableau, Power BI, Mixpanel, Amplitude - Item 104) should have an interface that allows non-developers (PO, Analyst) to: Explore data sources. Create new charts and visualizations (line, bar, pie, funnel, retention charts). Combine charts into new dashboards. Apply filters and segment data. Share dashboards easily. Well-Structured Data Model (in Data Warehouse / BI Tool): The data presented to the BI tool should be reasonably well-structured and understandable. This might involve creating specific views or curated tables in the data warehouse (e.g., BigQuery) that simplify common queries or pre-join data, making it easier for the PO/Analyst to use. Training and Support: Ensure the PO or Data Analyst receives adequate training on how to use the chosen BI tool effectively. Provide ongoing support from data engineers or analysts (if available) for complex queries or data source issues, but the goal is self-service for standard dashboarding.

Review Analytics Implementation: Periodically review the analytics events being tracked in the Flutter app with the PO/Analyst. Are there gaps? Is the data clean? Ensure new features include appropriate tracking. Verify Data Pipeline: Ensure the data export (e.g., Firebase -> BigQuery) is active and data is flowing correctly. Monitor ETL jobs if applicable. Choose Appropriate BI Tool: Select a tool that balances power with usability for the intended users (PO/Analyst). Looker Studio is often a good starting point due to its usability and Firebase integration. Provide Training: Invest time in training the PO/Analyst on the BI tool. Empowerment: Grant the PO/Analyst the necessary permissions within the BI tool to create and edit their own reports and dashboards (typically "Editor" or equivalent role). Developer Role: Developers focus on instrumenting the app to produce the raw data. POs/Analysts focus on consuming and visualizing that data. Developers should generally not be the primary creators of business dashboards. Feedback Loop: Have regular check-ins between Devs and POs/Analysts to ensure the tracked data meets the evolving business analysis needs. By setting up this separation of concerns and empowering the product side with self-service tools, you create a flexible and agile business monitoring capability.

Item: 57 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Deployment | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 5 | The lead time (from development to deployment on production) is no longer than one sprint. | (N/A for Mobile) Action: "Ensure 'code commit to store submission' time is < 1 day. Track 'App Store Review Time' as a separate metric." | | This guide addresses the "Lead Time for Changes" DevOps metric (Item 10) in the specific context of mobile app development, acknowledging that the final deployment to users is gated by app store reviews.
documents.s: Completing Item 57: Track Lead Time (Mobile Context)

documents.t: Definition: Lead Time for Changes typically measures the time from the first commit on a feature branch to that change being successfully running in production. Mobile Challenge: The final step, "running in production," is dependent on app store review times (Apple, Google), which are outside the team's direct control and can vary significantly (hours to days, sometimes weeks). Adapting the Metric: For mobile teams, it's more practical to measure lead time up to the point the team completes its controllable actions, which is submission to the app stores for review. App Store Review Time should be tracked as a separate, external dependency metric. Revised Mobile Lead Time: Time from first commit on a feature branch to successful submission to App Store Connect / Google Play Console production track. Alternative / Complementary Metric: Cycle Time: Time from first commit on a feature branch to merge into the main branch (main/develop). This measures the core development process efficiency (coding, review, CI checks).

Measure Process Efficiency: Identifies bottlenecks in the development workflow (e.g., long code review times, slow CI, complex merge processes). Improve Predictability: Shorter, consistent lead/cycle times make release forecasting more reliable. Faster Feedback: Highlights delays in getting features integrated and tested. Benchmarking: Allows comparison with industry DORA metrics (understanding the mobile caveat).
documents.s: Why Track (Adapted) Lead Time / Cycle Time?

documents.t: Define Which Metric(s) to Track: Cycle Time (Commit to Merge): Highly recommended. This measures the internal development loop efficiency, which the team directly controls. Lead Time (Commit to Store Submission): Also valuable. Measures the full internal pipeline including integration, QA on staging, and the production submission build/upload process. App Store Review Time: Track this separately. Time from "Submitted to Store" to "Approved/Ready for Sale". Implement Measurement: Cycle Time (Commit to Merge): Manual: Tedious. Requires recording first commit time and merge time for each PR. Automated (Recommended): Git Analytics Tools: Tools like GitKraken Insights, Waydev, LinearB, or custom scripts analyzing Git history can calculate this. Project Management Tools: Some Jira/Azure DevOps integrations or plugins can track PR cycle times. CI/CD Data: While harder, some CI systems might allow tracking time from branch creation to PR merge event. Lead Time (Commit to Store Submission): Requires correlating the first commit time (from Git) with the timestamp of the successful "submit-to-store" job completion in your CI/CD pipeline (Item 55). This often requires custom scripting or dedicated value stream management tools. A simpler proxy: Merge to Store Submission Time. Measure time from PR merge into main to successful store submission. This focuses on the integration-to-release pipeline efficiency. App Store Review Time: Manual Tracking: Record the submission timestamp (from CI/CD log) and the approval timestamp (from App Store Connect / Play Console notifications or dashboards) in a spreadsheet. Calculate the duration. Establish Baselines and Targets: Track the chosen metrics for several releases/sprints to establish a baseline average. Set realistic targets based on the baseline and desired improvements. Cycle Time Target (Example): < 2 business days. Lead Time (Commit to Submission) Target (Example): < 5 business days (allowing time for QA on staging). Or Merge to Submission Time Target: < 1 business day. App Store Review Time Target: Not applicable (external), but track the average. Visualize and Review: Use dashboards (if using analytics tools) or simple charts (if tracking manually) to visualize trends over time. Review the metrics regularly (e.g., monthly) with the team. Analyze bottlenecks: If Cycle Time is high, are PR reviews slow? If Merge-to-Submission Time is high, is the QA or release build process inefficient? Document: Update your DevOps Metrics documentation (Item 10) to clearly define how Lead Time and Cycle Time are measured for your mobile project, acknowledging the exclusion of app store review time from the primary Lead Time metric. Document the current targets. By tracking adapted Lead Time (or Cycle Time) and separating out App Store Review Time, mobile teams can gain valuable insights into their internal process efficiency and identify areas for improvement.

Item: 133 | Architecture Management | Risks & Blocks management | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 1 | The Architecture maturity level C&A meetings are being conducted by the System Architect monthly basis. | Schedule a recurring monthly "Architecture Maturity Review" meeting to go through this exact checklist. | | (Note: "C&A" likely refers to "Check and Act" or a similar continuous improvement concept, often used in maturity assessments). This guide explains how to establish and conduct regular meetings specifically focused on reviewing the team's adherence to and maturity against the defined architecture processes (like the checklist you provided initially).
documents.s: Completing Item 133: Conduct Architecture Maturity C&A Meetings

documents.t: Continuous Improvement: Provides a dedicated forum to systematically review current practices against defined standards or goals. Identify Gaps & Weaknesses: Highlights areas where the team is falling short of desired maturity levels or where processes are not being followed effectively. Track Progress: Shows progress over time as the team implements improvements and matures its practices. Reinforce Standards: Regularly reviewing the process checklist reinforces its importance and keeps best practices top-of-mind. Generate Actionable Insights: Leads directly to identifying specific action items needed to improve maturity (linking to Item 135). Team Alignment: Ensures the whole team is aware of the process goals and current status.

Use a Defined Checklist/Framework: The spreadsheet you initially provided serves as an excellent checklist or maturity assessment framework. It covers various areas (Architecture Definition, Execution, Management, Validation) and specific practices with maturity levels. Schedule a Recurring Meeting: Cadence: Monthly is a good starting point, as suggested by the item description. Adjust frequency based on project phase and team needs (e.g., might be more frequent initially, less frequent once stable). Duration: 60-90 minutes, depending on the number of items and depth of discussion. Name: "Architecture Process Review," "DevOps Maturity Sync," "Architecture C&A Meeting." Attendees: System Architect (typically facilitates), Tech Lead, and representatives from the Development and QA team. The PO is usually optional unless specific process-product interactions need discussion. DevOps/Infra representation is valuable. Rotate attendees if needed to get broader input without making the meeting too large. Prepare for the Meeting (Facilitator): Review the checklist/spreadsheet beforehand. Gather any relevant data or observations related to specific items since the last meeting (e.g., recent CI/CD failures, feedback from code reviews, status of previous action items). Select a subset of items to focus on if reviewing the entire list every month is too time-consuming. Prioritize areas where issues were noted previously or where changes have occurred. Conduct the Meeting: Review Previous Action Items (Briefly): Check the status of actions identified in the last meeting. Go Through Checklist Items: For each item (or the selected subset), review the criteria and the defined maturity level goal. Discuss Current State: Facilitate an open discussion: "Are we currently meeting this criterion?", "What is our perceived maturity level here (1-5)?", "What evidence do we have?". Identify Gaps: Where does the current state fall short of the goal or best practice? Why? Capture Observations: Note down key discussion points, evidence, and identified gaps. Focus on System, Not Individuals: Keep the discussion focused on processes, tools, and team practices, not on blaming individuals. Identify Action Items: For each identified gap or area for improvement, define specific, actionable steps. Assign an owner responsible for driving the action item. Set a realistic due date or target sprint. Example Action: "Gap: Rollback strategy not fully documented. Action: Tech Lead to update Confluence SCM page with App Store rollback steps. Due: Next Sprint." Document Outcomes: Update the maturity assessment checklist/spreadsheet with the current evaluation for the reviewed items. Record the meeting minutes, highlighting key discussions and the agreed-upon action items (with owners and due dates). Store this on the team wiki. Follow Up (Links to Item 135): Track the action items (e.g., by creating Jira tasks). Review their progress at the start of the next maturity assessment meeting. By systematically reviewing your architecture processes against a defined framework, you create a powerful engine for continuous improvement and drive your team towards higher levels of DevOps maturity. 📈

Item: 134 | Architecture Management | Risks & Blocks management | RELEASE | 1 | "The Solution Review meeting
is always conducted when project have signicificant technical issue/technical decission, and other Software Architects from different projects are invited to join." | The discussion was conducted in AC meeting. | | (Note: The user note "conducted in AC meeting" suggests an existing practice, possibly within an "Architecture Community" or similar group. This guide formalizes it.) This guide explains the purpose and process of conducting Solution Review meetings, especially for significant technical decisions or issues, involving architects from outside the immediate project team.
documents.s: Completing Item 134: Conduct Solution Review Meetings

documents.t: Fresh Perspectives: Architects from other projects bring different experiences, domain knowledge, and technical backgrounds, offering insights the project team might overlook. Identify Blind Spots: External reviewers can more easily spot assumptions, potential risks, or missed requirements. Cross-Pollination of Ideas: Shares solutions and patterns across different teams, promoting consistency and reuse within the organization. Validation & Confidence: Getting positive feedback from experienced peers can increase confidence in a proposed solution. Constructive criticism helps refine it. Mentoring Opportunity: Provides a learning opportunity for both the presenters and the reviewers. Breaking Silos: Encourages collaboration and communication between architects across the organization.
documents.s: Why Conduct Solution Reviews with External Architects? 🤔

documents.t: Trigger these reviews for: Significant New Features: Especially those with complex architecture (e.g., implementing offline sync, a new major integration). Major Architectural Changes: Proposing a shift in core patterns (e.g., changing state management approach across the app). Adopting New Core Technologies: Evaluating and deciding on significant new frameworks or platforms. Complex Technical Problems: When the team is stuck on a difficult technical challenge and needs external input. High-Risk Areas: Solutions involving critical security, performance, or scalability requirements.
documents.s: When to Conduct a Solution Review

documents.t: Identify the Need: The project architect or tech lead identifies a topic (as listed above) that warrants broader review. Prepare the Presentation/Documentation: Create a concise presentation or document (similar to a detailed ADR or the output of Item 41) explaining: Problem/Context: What is the challenge or goal? Proposed Solution: Describe the technical approach clearly, using diagrams. Alternatives Considered: Briefly mention other options explored and why they were discarded. Key Assumptions & Risks: Highlight potential challenges or uncertainties. Specific Questions: List any particular areas where feedback is sought. Share in Advance: Send the material to the invited reviewers at least 1-2 days before the meeting to allow them time to prepare. Schedule the Meeting: Invitees: Project Architect / Tech Lead (presenting). Key developers from the project team involved in the solution. Crucially: 2-4 experienced Software Architects from other projects or teams within the organization. Choose reviewers with relevant expertise if possible. (Leverage the "Architecture Community" or similar group if one exists). Timebox: 60-90 minutes is typical. Clear Goal: State the purpose (e.g., "Review proposed architecture for Offline Sync feature and gather feedback"). Conduct the Meeting: Presentation (15-30 min): The project architect/lead presents the problem and proposed solution concisely. Focus on the core concepts and decision points. Clarifying Questions (10-15 min): Allow reviewers to ask questions to ensure they understand the proposal. Feedback & Discussion (30-45 min): This is the core of the meeting. Facilitate an open discussion where external architects provide feedback, challenge assumptions, suggest alternatives, and share relevant experiences. Encourage constructive criticism. Keep the discussion focused on the technical solution and its trade-offs. The project team should primarily listen and take notes, asking clarifying questions about the feedback received. Capture Notes: Designate someone to take detailed notes of the feedback, suggestions, and any action items. Follow Up: Summarize & Share: Distribute the meeting notes (especially the feedback and suggestions) to all attendees and the project team. Evaluate Feedback: The project architect/lead reviews the feedback with the team. Decide on Actions: Determine which suggestions to incorporate, which require further investigation (potentially a spike), and which might be disregarded (documenting the reason). Update Design: Revise the solution design document/ADR based on the adopted feedback. Communicate Outcome: Briefly inform the reviewers of the final decisions made based on their input, closing the loop. Solution Reviews are a powerful tool for leveraging collective architectural expertise, improving solution quality, and mitigating risks before significant implementation effort is invested. 💡

Item: 137 | Architecture Management | Technical Backlog management | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 1 | The architecture backlog is being managed through follow-up meetings and the architecture tasks are being prioritized in an acceptable frequency (at least bi-weekly). | Hold a bi-weekly "Technical Backlog Refinement" (separate from feature refinement) with the tech lead and senior devs to prioritize tech debt and infra tasks. | | This guide explains how to establish and manage a dedicated "Architecture Backlog" (often called the Technical Backlog) and the process for regularly refining and prioritizing the work within it.
documents.s: Completing Item 137: Manage the Architecture Backlog

documents.t: It's a prioritized list of technical work items needed to maintain and improve the health, quality, and sustainability of the codebase and development infrastructure. It runs parallel to the Product Backlog (which focuses on user features). Items typically include: Technical Debt: Refactoring complex code, improving test coverage, fixing non-critical bugs found in code reviews (Item 5). Architecture Improvements: Implementing changes identified in ADRs, evolving core patterns. Process Improvements: Action items from Maturity Assessments (Item 136) or Risk Meetings (Item 135). Infrastructure Tasks: Setting up new monitoring, improving CI/CD pipelines, automating environment setup. Dependency Updates: Upgrading Flutter versions, major libraries, or backend dependencies. Non-Functional Requirements: Tasks specifically aimed at meeting NFR targets (e.g., performance optimizations, security hardening). Tooling: Evaluating or implementing new development tools.

Visibility: Makes important technical work visible and prevents it from being constantly overshadowed by urgent feature requests. Prioritization: Allows for conscious decisions about which technical improvements provide the most value or mitigate the most risk. Capacity Allocation: Facilitates allocating a specific portion of the team's capacity to this work each sprint (Item 138). Strategic Improvement: Enables a more planned, strategic approach to improving the codebase and infrastructure over time.

Establish the Backlog Location: Use Your Existing Tool (Jira/Azure DevOps): This is usually the best approach. Method 1: Specific Label/Tag: Use a dedicated label like tech-backlog or technical-debt on standard Task/Story issue types. Create a specific board filter or backlog view for this label. Method 2: Dedicated Issue Type: Create a specific issue type like "TechDebt" or "Improvement". Method 3: Separate Project/Board (Use with caution): Only recommended if the volume is very high or managed by a separate platform team; usually better to keep it visible alongside feature work. Populate the Backlog: Continuously add items identified from: Code Reviews (non-trivial fixes) Retrospectives Architecture Maturity Assessments (Action Items) Risk Management Meetings (Mitigation Actions) Developer observations (TODO comments, pain points) NFR monitoring (performance regressions, low coverage areas) Planned upgrades/migrations Schedule Regular Technical Backlog Refinement Meetings: Cadence: Bi-weekly (every other week) is a good frequency, often alternating with feature refinement. Duration: 60 minutes typically. Attendees: Tech Lead (facilitator), Architect (if applicable), Senior Developers, potentially QA or DevOps representatives. The PO is usually not required unless discussing trade-offs affecting feature delivery. Purpose: Review new items, clarify scope, discuss technical approach, estimate effort (Story Points or time), and prioritize the backlog. Prioritize the Backlog: During the refinement meeting, prioritize items based on factors like: Impact/Value: How much will this improve development speed, reduce bugs, enhance performance/security, or mitigate risk? Effort: How much work is involved? (Look for high-value, low-effort items first). Urgency: Is this blocking other work? Is there a deadline (e.g., dependency deprecation)? Frequency of Pain: How often does the team encounter issues related to this item? Alignment with Roadmap: Does this enable upcoming features or NFRs? Maintain a ranked order for the top items in the backlog. Integrate with Sprint Planning: Allocate Capacity: Agree with the PO on allocating a certain percentage of the team's capacity each sprint to technical backlog items (e.g., 15-20%). Select Items: During Sprint Planning, after selecting feature stories, the Tech Lead or team pulls the top-priority items from the refined technical backlog that fit within the allocated capacity. Treat as Regular Work: These items become part of the sprint commitment and are tracked on the sprint board just like feature stories. Review and Adapt: Periodically review the effectiveness of the technical backlog management process in retrospectives. Is the refinement happening effectively? Are items getting prioritized and completed? Is the allocated capacity appropriate? By actively managing a technical backlog, you ensure that continuous improvement and codebase health are treated as first-class citizens in your development process. ✨

Item: 89 | Architecture Management | People & Technical Skills Development | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 2 | The knowledge map is maintained by the team members and updated in a frequency considered adequate. | Review and update the knowledge map quarterly as part of performance reviews or team development goals. | | This guide explains how to maintain the team knowledge map (created in Item 124) to ensure it remains an accurate and useful tool for understanding team capabilities and identifying skill gaps.
documents.s: Completing Item 89: Maintain the Team Knowledge Map

documents.t: Accuracy: An outdated map gives a false picture of the team's skills and weaknesses. Track Growth: Shows how skills have developed over time, both individually and for the team. Identify Current Gaps: Helps continuously identify areas where knowledge is concentrated in too few people (bus factor) or where the team lacks necessary expertise. Inform Training & Development: Provides input for planning training, pairing sessions, or assigning tasks to help individuals grow. Resource Allocation: Can assist leads in assigning tasks to appropriate team members or identifying mentorship opportunities.

Establish Ownership and Cadence: Ownership: While individuals should contribute, designate someone (e.g., Tech Lead, Engineering Manager, Scrum Master) to be responsible for ensuring the map is reviewed and updated regularly. Cadence: Define a regular review frequency. Quarterly is often a good balance. Aligning it with performance review cycles or team goal-setting periods can be effective. Ad-hoc updates should also be encouraged. Define the Update Process: Self-Assessment: Encourage team members to periodically review their own skills on the map and update their proficiency levels (e.g., using a simple scale like 1-Beginner, 2-Intermediate, 3-Advanced, 4-Expert/Mentor) or add new skills they've acquired. Manager/Lead Review: During 1-on-1s or performance reviews, managers/leads should discuss skill development with team members and collaboratively update the map based on observed performance and growth. Peer Feedback (Optional): Incorporate feedback from peers if your team culture supports it. Dedicated Review Session: Hold a brief team session (e.g., 30 minutes quarterly) where the designated owner reminds everyone to update the map and potentially discusses overall team skill trends or identified gaps. Integrate with Development Goals: Use the knowledge map during goal-setting discussions (individual or team level). Identify skills an individual wants/needs to develop. Identify team-level gaps that require focused training, hiring, or cross-skilling efforts. Plan actions (e.g., "Pair programming on CI/CD tasks," "Attend Flutter animation workshop," "Assign next authentication story to Developer X with mentorship from Developer Y") based on these goals and track progress against the map. Keep it Simple and Accessible: Ensure the map format (wiki page, spreadsheet) remains easy to understand and update. Avoid overly complex scoring systems. Make sure everyone knows where the map is located and how to update it. Focus on Key Skills: Don't try to map every possible skill. Focus on the technologies, architectural areas, and process domains most critical to the project's success (as defined in Item 124). Add or remove skills from the map as the project evolves. Use the Map Actively: The map is only useful if it's referenced. Tech leads should consult it when: Assigning complex tasks. Identifying mentorship opportunities. Assessing the "bus factor" (risk if a key person leaves). Planning team training. Regular maintenance, driven by self-assessment and manager reviews, and integrated with development goals, ensures the knowledge map remains a valuable asset for team growth and risk management.

Item: 131 | Architecture Management | Project Plan & Architecture Roadmap | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 2 | "All big technical decisions are being taken through engagement and awareness of all technical team members, architects and developers." | Don't make decisions in a vacuum. Post an ADR proposal in the dev channel for 24 hours for feedback *before* finalizing it. | | This guide explains the importance of involving the entire technical team (architects and developers) in major technical decision-making processes.
documents.s: Completing Item 131: Engage Team in Major Technical Decisions

documents.t: Diverse Perspectives: Developers working directly with the code often have valuable insights into the practical implications, potential challenges, or alternative solutions that might not be immediately obvious to an architect working at a higher level. Increased Buy-in & Ownership: When the team feels involved in a decision, they are more likely to understand the rationale, support the chosen path, and take ownership of its successful implementation. Decisions imposed from the top down can sometimes face passive resistance. Knowledge Sharing: The discussion process itself is a valuable learning opportunity, spreading understanding of architectural concepts and trade-offs throughout the team. Better Decisions: Collective intelligence and constructive debate often lead to more robust and well-considered technical solutions than decisions made in isolation. Early Risk Identification: Team members might identify risks or edge cases related to a proposed solution based on their specific areas of expertise.
Refer back to Item 19. This includes choices like core frameworks, major pattern changes, significant third-party integrations, large refactoring efforts, or decisions with major NFR impacts.

Identify the Decision Point: When a "big" technical decision needs to be made (often identified during backlog refinement, spike investigations, or architectural planning), flag it for broader team discussion. Research & Propose (Architect/Lead): The architect or tech lead should typically perform initial research, identify viable options, and form a proposal or recommendation. This provides a starting point for discussion. Document the Proposal (e.g., Draft ADR): Create a concise document (a draft Architecture Decision Record - ADR is ideal, see Item 128) outlining: Problem/Context: What needs to be decided and why? Options Considered: Briefly list the main alternatives. Proposed Solution: Clearly state the recommended approach. Rationale: Explain the reasoning, pros, and cons (technical & potentially business impact). Share Asynchronously for Feedback: Post the draft ADR or proposal summary in the main technical team chat channel (e.g., #proj-mobile-tech). Set a Timebox: Clearly state a deadline for feedback (e.g., "Please review this proposal for our state management approach and provide feedback/questions within the next 24-48 hours."). This prevents indefinite delays. Encourage Discussion: Prompt team members to add comments directly on the document (if possible) or discuss in a dedicated chat thread. Facilitate Discussion (Synchronous if Needed): If the asynchronous feedback reveals significant disagreement, complex questions, or requires deeper debate, schedule a timeboxed meeting (e.g., 30-60 minutes). Meeting Goal: Focus specifically on discussing the feedback, clarifying points, debating trade-offs, and reaching a consensus or final decision. Facilitation: Ensure everyone has a chance to speak, keep the discussion focused, and steer towards a decision. Make the Final Decision: While consensus is ideal, the architect or tech lead ultimately needs to make the final call, considering all the input gathered. Clearly communicate the final decision back to the team, explaining how their feedback influenced the outcome (even if their preferred option wasn't chosen). Finalize Documentation: Update the ADR status to "Accepted." Incorporate any refinements or clarifications arising from the discussion into the final ADR document. By making major technical decisions a collaborative process, you leverage the collective expertise of your team, foster ownership, and ultimately arrive at better, more sustainable solutions. ✨

Item: 94 | Architecture Management | Technical Backlog management | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 2 | The technical gaps are being managed so the technical debts are not increasing over the time. | Allocate a fixed capacity (e.g., 15% of sprint velocity) to "Technical Backlog" items (tech debt, refactoring, pipeline improvements) every sprint. | | This guide explains how to actively manage technical gaps (missing capabilities, needed refactoring, areas for improvement) and technical debt to prevent them from accumulating and negatively impacting the project over time.
documents.s: Completing Item 94: Manage Technical Gaps and Debts

documents.t: Prevents Snowballing: Unaddressed debt makes future development slower and more difficult as developers constantly work around existing issues. Improves Maintainability: Refactoring complex code, improving tests, and upgrading dependencies makes the codebase easier and safer to change. Boosts Velocity: A cleaner codebase and better tooling often lead to increased development speed in the long run. Reduces Bugs: Addressing underlying issues (poor design, lack of tests) often fixes or prevents bugs. Improves Developer Morale: Working in a clean, well-maintained codebase with up-to-date tools is more satisfying.

Identify and Track Gaps/Debts (Input): Use inputs from various sources: Technical Debt Tickets (Item 5): Specific issues identified during code reviews, retrospectives, or development. Static Analysis Issues (Item 25): Code smells, complexity warnings from SonarQube. Low Code Coverage Areas (Item 24): Modules lacking sufficient unit/widget tests. Outdated Dependencies: Regularly check flutter pub outdated. Using old packages can pose security risks or cause compatibility issues. Missing Automation: Manual steps in the build, test, or deployment process that could be automated. Performance Bottlenecks: Areas identified through profiling (Firebase Performance, DevTools) needing optimization (Item 140). Architectural Deviations: Code not conforming to established patterns (Item 87). Risk Meeting Action Items (Item 93): Tasks identified to mitigate technical risks. Maintain a Technical Backlog: Use your project management tool (Jira). Create specific tickets (e.g., Issue Type "TechDebt" or "Task" with a tech-backlog label) for each identified gap or debt. Ensure tickets clearly describe the problem, its impact, and ideally a suggested solution (as per Item 5). Prioritize the Technical Backlog: Hold regular Technical Backlog Refinement meetings (Item 136) involving the Tech Lead, Architect, and senior developers. Prioritize items based on: Impact/Pain: How much does this issue slow down development, increase risk, or affect users? Effort: How complex is the fix? Urgency: Is this blocking other work? Is it a security risk? Strategic Alignment: Does this enable future features or align with the technical roadmap (Item 129)? Focus on high-impact items and those related to areas currently under active development ("Boy Scout Rule"). Allocate Dedicated Capacity (Crucial Step): Agree on Percentage: Negotiate and agree with the Product Owner and the team to allocate a fixed percentage of each sprint's capacity specifically for working on items from the prioritized technical backlog. Common allocations range from 10% to 25% of the team's velocity. Example: If team velocity is 40 points, allocate 6 points (15%) per sprint for tech backlog items. Treat as Real Work: Pull these prioritized tech backlog tickets into the sprint during Sprint Planning, just like user stories. Assign owners and track progress. Justify to PO: Explain to the PO that this investment is necessary for long-term health and velocity, comparing it to "paying interest on a loan." Frame it in terms of reducing future bugs and enabling faster feature delivery later. Track Progress and Adjust: Monitor the size and age of the technical backlog. Is it growing, shrinking, or stable? Track the amount of effort spent on tech backlog items each sprint. Use retrospectives to discuss if the allocated capacity is sufficient and if the prioritization is effective. Adjust the percentage if necessary based on project health and upcoming deadlines. By consistently identifying, prioritizing, and allocating specific capacity to address technical gaps and debts each sprint, you actively manage the health of your codebase and prevent the accumulation of issues that hinder future progress.

Item: 135 | Architecture Management | Risks & Blocks management | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 2 | "The technical risks are raised through monthly risk meetings that are conducted together with the Development team;
the action plans raised during the meeting are included as tasks in the ticket system (JIRA, Azure DevOps) and followed up in the next meeting.
" | Create a "Risk Register" in Confluence. Review it monthly, identifying new risks (e.g., "A key package is no longer maintained") and action plans. | | This guide explains how to establish a process for proactively identifying, assessing, and managing technical risks throughout the project lifecycle, primarily through regular risk management meetings.
documents.s: Completing Item 135: Manage Technical Risks via Risk Meetings

documents.t: Avoid Surprises: Prevents technical issues from unexpectedly derailing sprints or releases. Reduce Impact: Allows the team to plan mitigation strategies before a risk becomes a major problem. Informed Decisions: Makes risks visible, enabling better decisions about priorities, resource allocation, and technical choices. Improved Planning: Feeds into backlog refinement and sprint planning (e.g., scheduling work to mitigate a high-priority risk). Stakeholder Communication: Provides a structured way to communicate significant technical risks to the PO and other stakeholders.

Potential problems related to the technology, architecture, implementation, or development process that could negatively impact the project's timeline, budget, quality, or success. Examples: Technology: A chosen library becomes unmaintained, a framework introduces breaking changes, performance limitations of a chosen tool. Architecture: Scalability bottlenecks, poor component coupling leading to difficult changes, security vulnerabilities in the design. Implementation: Overly complex code, lack of test coverage in critical areas, performance issues in specific features. Process: Insufficient testing, unstable CI/CD pipeline, knowledge silos within the team, dependencies on external teams/APIs not being ready. External: Changes in platform (iOS/Android) requirements, third-party service outages or deprecations.

Establish a Risk Register: Create a central document, typically a Risk Register, on your team's wiki (Confluence). This register will be the single source of truth for tracking identified risks. Columns should include: Risk ID: Unique identifier. Risk Description: Clear statement of the potential problem ("What could go wrong?"). Date Identified: When the risk was first logged. Category: (e.g., Technology, Architecture, Process, External). Likelihood: How likely is this risk to occur? (e.g., High, Medium, Low; or 1-5 scale). Impact: If it occurs, what is the severity of the consequence? (e.g., High, Medium, Low; or 1-5 scale; consider impact on Cost, Schedule, Quality). Risk Score/Priority: Calculated from Likelihood x Impact (helps prioritize). Mitigation Strategy: What actions can be taken now to reduce the likelihood or impact? (e.g., "Add monitoring," "Write more tests," "Investigate alternative library"). Contingency Plan: What actions will be taken if the risk occurs? (e.g., "Rollback deployment," "Allocate extra time for refactoring"). Owner: Who is responsible for monitoring this risk and driving mitigation actions? Status: (e.g., Open, Mitigating, Monitoring, Closed). Last Reviewed: Date the risk was last discussed. Schedule Regular Risk Management Meetings: Cadence: Monthly is a common starting point. Adjust based on project phase (more frequent during early stages or high uncertainty). Can sometimes be combined with the Architecture Maturity meeting (Item 133). Duration: 45-60 minutes. Attendees: Architect/Tech Lead (facilitator), Development Team representatives, QA representative. PO is optional but useful for understanding business impact. Conduct the Risk Meeting: Review Existing Risks: Go through the Open risks in the Risk Register. Discuss any changes in Likelihood or Impact. Review progress on Mitigation Strategy action items. Are they complete? Effective? Update the Status and Last Reviewed date. Identify New Risks: Brainstorm potential new risks based on recent events, upcoming work, or changes in technology/requirements. Ask: "What are we worried about?", "What could go wrong in the next month/quarter?". Assess New Risks: For each new risk, determine its Description, Category, Likelihood, and Impact. Calculate the Priority. Define Mitigation/Contingency: For high-priority new risks (and potentially medium ones), define Mitigation Strategies and Contingency Plans. Assign an Owner. Create Action Items in Ticket System: Crucial Step: For every Mitigation Strategy defined that requires specific work (e.g., "Investigate alternative library," "Add specific performance tests"), create a corresponding task in your ticket system (Jira). Link: Link the Jira task back to the Risk ID in the register. Assign: Assign the Jira task to the Risk Owner. Prioritize: These tasks should be prioritized alongside other technical backlog items (Item 137). Follow Up: Track the progress of the mitigation tasks in Jira. Review the status of these tasks at the beginning of the next risk meeting. Communicate High-Priority Risks: Ensure the Product Owner and relevant stakeholders are aware of high-priority risks and the planned mitigation efforts, especially those that might impact timelines or require resource allocation. By systematically identifying, assessing, and planning responses to technical risks, you move from reactive firefighting to proactive risk management, increasing the predictability and success rate of your project. 🛡️

Item: 93 | Architecture Management | Risks & Blocks management | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 2 | "The technical risks are raised through monthly risk meetings that are conducted together with the Development team;
the action plans raised during the meeting are included as tasks in the ticket system (JIRA, Azure DevOps) and followed up in the next meeting.
" | Create a "Risk Register" in Confluence. Review it monthly, identifying new risks (e.g., "A key package is no longer maintained") and action plans. | | This guide explains how to establish and conduct regular risk management meetings involving the development team to proactively identify, assess, and plan mitigation for technical risks.
documents.s: Completing Item 93: Conduct Monthly Risk Management Meetings

documents.t: Proactive Identification: Creates a dedicated space to think about potential problems before they occur, rather than just reacting to issues. Shared Awareness: Ensures the entire team is aware of potential technical challenges and uncertainties. Collective Brainstorming: Leverages the team's collective experience to identify risks and brainstorm mitigation strategies. Prioritization: Helps prioritize which risks require active mitigation versus those that can be accepted or monitored. Actionable Plans: Translates identified risks into concrete action items with owners and due dates. Improved Predictability: Reduces the likelihood of unforeseen technical issues derailing sprints or releases.

Schedule a Recurring Monthly Meeting: Cadence: Monthly is a common and effective frequency. Duration: 45-60 minutes. Attendees: Entire development team (Flutter, Backend, QA), Architect/Tech Lead, potentially the Product Owner (especially for risks related to scope or external dependencies). Name: "Technical Risk Review," "Project Risk Meeting." Create and Maintain a Risk Register: Tool: Use a shared document, typically a table on a wiki page (Confluence) or a dedicated spreadsheet. Columns: Include columns for: Risk ID: Unique identifier. Risk Description: Clear statement of the potential problem (e.g., "Unmaintained xyz_package might become incompatible with future Flutter versions"). Date Identified: When the risk was first raised. Likelihood: Estimate of how likely the risk is to occur (e.g., Low, Medium, High; or 1-5 scale). Impact: Estimate of the negative consequences if the risk occurs (e.g., Low, Medium, High; or 1-5 scale; consider impact on timeline, cost, quality, security). Risk Score/Level: Calculated based on Likelihood x Impact (helps with prioritization). Mitigation Strategy: The plan to reduce the likelihood or impact (e.g., Avoid, Reduce, Transfer, Accept). Action Plan: Specific steps to implement the mitigation strategy (e.g., "Research alternative packages for xyz_package," "Implement additional monitoring for API X," "Write ADR to document workaround"). Owner: Who is responsible for executing the action plan? Due Date: When should the action plan be completed? Status: (e.g., Open, In Progress, Mitigated, Accepted, Closed). Conduct the Monthly Meeting: Facilitator: Assign a facilitator (e.g., Tech Lead, Scrum Master). Agenda: Review Action Items (10 min): Go through action items from the previous meeting. Owners provide status updates. Mark completed actions. Review Existing Risks (15-20 min): Briefly review the open risks in the register, starting with the highest score/level. Update likelihood/impact estimates if circumstances have changed. Discuss if mitigation plans are still appropriate. Identify New Risks (15-20 min): Brainstorm new potential technical risks. Consider upcoming features, changes in technology, team changes, external dependencies, performance concerns, security threats, etc. Encourage everyone to contribute. Assess New Risks & Define Actions (10 min): For newly identified risks, assess likelihood and impact. Brainstorm initial mitigation strategies and define concrete action items with owners and target due dates. Add them to the register. Integrate Action Plans into Backlog: Create Tickets: Immediately after the meeting, create tasks (e.g., Spike, Task, Bug, TechDebt) in your project management tool (Jira) for all new action items identified. Link Tickets: Link these Jira tickets back to the Risk Register (and vice-versa if possible). Prioritize: Treat these action items as part of the technical backlog. Prioritize them alongside other technical work based on the associated risk level. Ensure owners have capacity allocated to work on them. Communicate: Share the updated Risk Register or meeting minutes with relevant stakeholders (e.g., PO, Project Manager) especially for risks with significant business impact. By dedicating time each month to systematically review and manage technical risks, the team can proactively address potential problems, leading to a smoother and more predictable development process.

Item: 90 | Architecture Management | Project Plan & Architecture Roadmap | PREPARATION (Sprint 0) | 2 | "Pros and Cons of technical decisions, comparing to the others solutions, are recorded for later reference." | Implement a lightweight Architecture Decision Record (ADR) process. Create an "ADR" folder in the Git repo or Confluence for decisions like "Why we chose BLoC." | | (Note: This item is essentially describing the core purpose and content of an Architecture Decision Record (ADR), which is also covered in more detail by Item 128. This focuses specifically on capturing the comparison aspect during the decision-making process.) This guide explains the importance of recording not just what technical decisions were made, but also why, including the alternatives considered and their pros and cons. The primary mechanism for this is using Architecture Decision Records (ADRs).
documents.s: Completing Item 90: Record Pros and Cons of Technical Decisions

documents.t: Context & Rationale: Provides crucial context for future developers (or even the original authors later) to understand why a particular technology or pattern was chosen. Prevents "Why did we do it this way?" questions. Avoids Re-Litigation: When the same questions or alternatives come up again later, the ADR shows they were already considered and provides the reasoning for the original choice. Informed Future Decisions: If circumstances change (e.g., team skills evolve, new technology emerges, requirements shift), the ADR provides the original context needed to re-evaluate the decision effectively. Knowledge Sharing: Captures the valuable thinking and trade-off analysis that went into the decision. Onboarding: Helps new team members understand the history and rationale behind key architectural choices.
documents.s: Why Record Pros, Cons, and Alternatives?

documents.t: ADRs are lightweight text documents that capture a single significant architectural decision. Choose an ADR Format/Template: Use a simple, standard template. Markdown is common. Key sections include: Title: Short noun phrase describing the decision (e.g., "ADR-001: Use BLoC for State Management"). Status: (e.g., Proposed, Accepted, Deprecated, Superseded by ADR-XXX). Date: When the decision was made. Context: What problem or situation is being addressed? What are the constraints or requirements? Decision: Clearly state the chosen solution/technology/pattern. Alternatives Considered: List the other viable options that were evaluated. Pros and Cons: (Key Section for this Item) For each alternative (including the chosen one), briefly list the main advantages (Pros) and disadvantages (Cons) considered in the context of this project. Rationale/Argument: Explain why the chosen decision was made, referencing the pros and cons. Why did the chosen option win out over the alternatives? Consequences: What are the results of this decision (positive and negative)? What new problems might it introduce? What future work might be needed? Store ADRs: Create a dedicated location, easily accessible to the team: Recommended: A directory within the project's Git repository (e.g., docs/adr/, doc/architecture/decisions/). This versions the decisions alongside the code. Files are typically named like 001-use-bloc-for-state-management.md. Alternative: A dedicated space in the team's wiki (Confluence). Establish the Process: When to Write an ADR: For significant architectural decisions (see Item 19 for examples: core frameworks, major patterns, key integrations, impactful refactoring). Not needed for trivial choices. Who Writes: Typically the Tech Lead, Architect, or the developer(s) who did the research/spike. Review: Discuss proposed ADRs with the team (or relevant senior members/architect) before marking them as "Accepted." Use PRs if storing ADRs in Git. Keep it Lightweight: Focus on capturing the essential context, options, trade-offs, and rationale concisely. Avoid overly long or complex documents. Focus on Pros and Cons Analysis: When creating the ADR, explicitly dedicate time to list the pros and cons of each option relative to your project's specific goals and constraints. Example snippet for "State Management Choice": ## Alternatives Considered - **Provider:** - Pros: Simple for basic cases, less boilerplate initially. - Cons: Can become complex to manage dependencies and testing for larger features, less prescriptive structure. - **BLoC/Cubit:** - Pros: Clear separation of logic/UI, highly testable, prescriptive structure good for team consistency, good tooling (`bloc_test`). - Cons: More boilerplate required compared to Provider, steeper learning curve initially. - **Riverpod:** - Pros: Compile-safe dependency injection, flexible, testable, avoids `BuildContext` dependency. - Cons: Newer than BLoC/Provider (at the time of decision), team less familiar initially. ## Rationale BLoC/Cubit was chosen due to its strong emphasis on testability and clear separation of concerns, which were deemed critical for the long-term maintainability of this complex application. The prescriptive nature helps ensure consistency across a growing team, despite the initial boilerplate overhead. Riverpod was considered a strong contender but team familiarity with BLoC was higher at project start. By systematically recording the pros, cons, and rationale for significant technical decisions using ADRs, you create a valuable, lasting record of your project's architectural evolution.

Item: 92 | Architecture Management | Project Plan & Architecture Roadmap | SETUP | 2 | "All team members, including the team responsible for the development, infrastructure, business and project sponsors are aware about the planned activities for the project." | Hold a quarterly "Roadmap Review" meeting with the PO, tech team, and stakeholders to review the upcoming business and technical epics. | | This guide explains the importance of ensuring that the entire project team (developers, QA, infrastructure, PO) and key sponsors are aware of the overall project plan and upcoming activities, including both business features and technical initiatives.
documents.s: Completing Item 92: Ensure Team Awareness of Project Plan

documents.t: Alignment: Ensures everyone understands the project's goals, priorities, and direction. Context: Provides developers with context for why they are building certain features, which can lead to better implementation decisions. Proactive Planning: Allows technical team members (including infrastructure) to anticipate upcoming needs (e.g., new backend services, required infrastructure changes, necessary refactoring) before development starts on dependent features. Dependency Management: Helps identify and manage dependencies between different workstreams or teams. Motivation: Understanding the bigger picture and upcoming milestones can be motivating for the team. Transparency: Builds trust with sponsors and stakeholders by keeping them informed of the planned trajectory.

Project Kickoff Meeting: Initial Communication: The initial project plan, high-level goals, scope, and roadmap should be clearly presented to the entire team and key sponsors during the project kickoff. Accessible Roadmap Document: Business Roadmap: Maintain a high-level roadmap (e.g., quarterly view) showing major business features, epics, or themes. This is typically owned by the Product Owner. Make it easily accessible (e.g., on the project wiki, in Jira). Technical Roadmap (Item 129): Maintain a parallel technical roadmap showing major technical initiatives, architectural changes, large refactoring efforts, or infrastructure upgrades. This is often owned by the Architect or Tech Lead. Ensure it aligns with the business roadmap. Combined View: Ideally, present a combined view or ensure both roadmaps are easily accessible from a central project overview page. Regular Roadmap Review Meetings: Cadence: Hold periodic (e.g., Quarterly or aligned with major planning increments) "Roadmap Review" or "Look Ahead" meetings. Attendees: Include the Product Owner, the entire development team (Flutter, Backend, QA), Infrastructure/DevOps representatives, Architect/Tech Lead, and key sponsors/stakeholders. Agenda: Review progress against the previous period's roadmap. PO presents the updated Business Roadmap for the upcoming period(s), explaining the goals and priorities. Architect/Tech Lead presents the updated Technical Roadmap, highlighting necessary enablers, planned refactoring, or infrastructure work needed to support the business goals. Discuss alignment, dependencies, potential risks, and required resources. Allow time for Q&A from all attendees. Sprint Reviews / Demos: While focused on the completed sprint increment, use the Sprint Review to briefly contextualize how the completed work fits into the larger roadmap and what's coming next. Backlog Refinement: During refinement, the PO should provide context for upcoming features by relating them back to the overall roadmap goals. Team Communication Channels: Share links to updated roadmaps or summaries of roadmap review meetings in the main project chat channel.

Major features/epics planned for the next ~1-3 months (or relevant planning horizon). Key milestones or release dates. Significant technical initiatives or prerequisites. Known cross-team dependencies. High-level project goals and objectives. By regularly communicating the overall project plan and roadmap to everyone involved, you foster alignment, enable proactive technical planning, and ensure the entire team is working towards the same strategic goals.

Item: 132 | Architecture Management | Project Plan & Architecture Roadmap | SETUP | 2 | "All team members, including the team responsible for the development, infrastructure, business and project sponsors are aware about the planned activities for the project." | Hold a quarterly "Roadmap Review" meeting with the PO, tech team, and stakeholders to review the upcoming business and technical epics. | | This guide focuses on ensuring that everyone involved in the project, across different roles (development, infrastructure, business, sponsors), has visibility into the overall project plan and upcoming activities.
documents.s: Completing Item 132: Ensure Team Awareness of Project Plan

documents.t: Alignment: Helps everyone understand how their individual work contributes to the larger project goals and roadmap. Context: Provides context for upcoming features, technical work, or potential dependencies. Proactive Planning: Allows teams (like infrastructure or backend) to anticipate needs arising from the mobile team's roadmap (e.g., preparing new services, scaling resources). Dependency Management: Surfaces potential cross-team dependencies early. Transparency & Trust: Builds trust and keeps everyone informed about the project's direction and progress. Motivation: Seeing the bigger picture can be motivating for team members.

Focus on the medium-to-long term plan, not just the current sprint: Product Roadmap: High-level overview of major features, themes, or business milestones planned for the upcoming quarters. (Owned by PO). [Image of a simple product roadmap] Technical Roadmap: Key technical initiatives, major refactoring, framework upgrades, infrastructure changes planned. (Owned by Architect/Tech Lead - Item 129). Key Milestones & Deadlines: Any significant project deadlines or target release dates. Major Dependencies: Known dependencies on other teams, external vendors, or infrastructure readiness.

Maintain Accessible Roadmaps: Ensure both the Product Roadmap (managed by the PO) and the Technical Roadmap (managed by the Tech Lead/Architect) are documented and accessible to the entire team (e.g., on Confluence, Jira roadmaps, a shared slide deck). Regular Roadmap Review Meetings: Cadence: Hold these meetings periodically, aligning with planning cycles (e.g., Quarterly is common, or perhaps before each Program Increment in SAFe). Attendees: Invite representatives from all relevant groups: Mobile Development Team (including QA) Product Owner / Business Analysts Infrastructure / DevOps Team representative Backend Team representative(s) Project Manager / Scrum Master Key Project Sponsors / Business Stakeholders Agenda: Review Recent Progress: Briefly recap major accomplishments from the previous period. Product Roadmap Update (PO): Present the planned features/themes for the upcoming quarter(s). Explain the business value and priorities. Technical Roadmap Update (Architect/Lead): Present planned technical initiatives, explaining their necessity (e.g., "Upgrading Flutter to support new OS features," "Refactoring payment module for stability"). Discuss Dependencies & Risks: Open forum to discuss potential dependencies between teams, infrastructure needs, or risks related to the plan. Q&A: Allow time for questions from all attendees. Integrate into Regular Cadences: Sprint Reviews/Demos: Briefly mention how the completed sprint work contributes to the larger roadmap goals. Team Syncs: Tech Lead/Architect can provide brief updates on progress towards technical roadmap items. Visual Communication: Use clear visual aids (roadmaps, timelines) during review meetings. Consider posting simplified roadmap visuals in shared team spaces (physical or virtual). Documentation Links: Ensure links to the latest roadmap documents are easily accessible from the main project wiki page or team handbook. By establishing regular communication forums that bring together different parts of the project team and stakeholders to review the overall plan, you foster alignment, enable proactive planning, and ensure everyone is pulling in the same direction. 🗺️

Item: 91 | Architecture Management | Project Plan & Architecture Roadmap | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 2 | "All big technical decisions are being taken through engagement and awareness of all technical team members, architects and developers." | Don't make decisions in a vacuum. Post an ADR proposal in the dev channel for 24 hours for feedback *before* finalizing it. | | This guide focuses on fostering a culture and process where significant technical decisions are made collaboratively, involving the broader development team, rather than being dictated solely by an architect or lead.
documents.s: Completing Item 91: Ensure Team Engagement in Technical Decisions

documents.t: Better Decisions: Leverages the collective knowledge, experience, and diverse perspectives of the entire team, potentially identifying issues or alternatives missed by individuals. Increased Buy-in: Developers who participate in or understand the reasoning behind a decision are more likely to accept, adopt, and adhere to it. Reduces resistance. Shared Ownership: Fosters a sense of collective ownership over the architecture and technical direction. Knowledge Sharing & Growth: The discussion process itself helps educate the entire team on architectural considerations, trade-offs, and new technologies. Empowers team members. Improved Morale: Developers feel valued and trusted when their input is sought on important technical matters.

Transparency in Proposal (ADRs): When a significant technical decision needs to be made (Item 19, 90), use the Architecture Decision Record (ADR) process. Draft and Share: The architect, tech lead, or developer proposing the solution writes a draft ADR, including context, alternatives, pros/cons, and the proposed decision/rationale. Circulate for Feedback: Share this draft ADR with the entire development team via: Posting a link in the main technical chat channel (e.g., #proj-mobile-tech). Sending an email notification. If using Git for ADRs, opening a Pull Request for the new ADR file. Timebox for Feedback: Explicitly state a deadline for feedback (e.g., "Please provide feedback on this ADR proposal by end-of-day tomorrow" or "Allowing 24-48 hours for comments"). Dedicated Discussion Forums: Architecture Sync Meetings: Use regular architecture sync meetings (Item 88) as a primary forum to discuss proposed ADRs or complex technical challenges requiring team input. Ad-Hoc Design Meetings: For urgent or particularly complex decisions, schedule specific meetings inviting relevant team members to brainstorm and discuss options. Chat Channel Discussions: Encourage follow-up questions and discussions related to the ADR proposal directly in the technical chat channel (using threads). Encourage Participation: Psychological Safety: Create an environment where developers feel safe to voice opinions, ask questions, or challenge proposals respectfully, regardless of seniority. Leaders should actively solicit input from quieter members. Value Input: Acknowledge and consider all feedback provided, even if it doesn't change the final decision. Explain why certain suggestions were or weren't incorporated when finalizing the ADR. Delegate Research: Empower developers to research specific options or create proof-of-concepts (Spikes) to inform decisions. Clear Decision-Making Process: While engagement is crucial, clarify who makes the final decision after feedback is gathered (usually the Architect or Tech Lead, potentially in consultation with senior devs). This avoids analysis paralysis. Clearly communicate the final decision and update the ADR status to "Accepted." Accessibility of Information: Ensure all ADRs (and supporting documentation) are stored in a location easily accessible to the entire team (Item 90). Avoid making significant technical decisions in isolation ("ivory tower architect"). By involving the team in the process through transparent proposals (ADRs) and open discussion forums, you arrive at better, more widely accepted technical solutions.

Item: 140 | Architecture Management | Technical Backlog management | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 3 | Recurrent follow-up meetings are conducted by the technical responsible in order to discuss the goals and issues that came from the test automation and coverage percentage. | Review the code coverage report (e.g., from lcov) in the same bi-weekly tech meeting. If coverage is dropping, create tasks to add tests. | | This guide explains how to establish a regular cadence for discussing goals, progress, and issues related to test automation and code coverage in your Flutter project.
documents.s: Completing Item 140: Hold Test Automation Follow-up Meetings

documents.t: Maintain Focus on Coverage Goal: Keeps the team accountable for the agreed-upon test coverage target (Item 24). Identify Coverage Gaps: Highlights areas of the codebase with insufficient test coverage, indicating higher risk for regressions. Track Automation Progress: Monitors progress on implementing higher-level automated tests (Integration, E2E) if that's a team goal (Item 157). Discuss Test Quality & Flakiness: Provides a forum to discuss not just quantity (coverage) but also the quality and reliability (flakiness) of automated tests. Share Best Practices: Allows team members to share effective testing patterns or troubleshoot common testing problems. Generate Improvement Actions: Leads to specific tasks like adding tests to low-coverage areas, refactoring untestable code, or improving the CI testing environment.

Integrate into Existing Meetings (Recommended): Similar to code quality follow-ups (Item 139), leverage existing technical team meetings. Technical Backlog Refinement (Item 137): Dedicate 10-15 minutes (potentially right after the code quality review segment) of this bi-weekly meeting to test automation and coverage. Team Technical Sync-up: If applicable. Prepare for the Review (Tech Lead/QA Lead): Before the meeting: Generate or locate the latest code coverage report (e.g., the HTML report generated from lcov.info, or the coverage view in SonarQube/SonarCloud). Review the overall coverage percentage and the coverage on new code. Is it meeting the target (Item 24)? What are the trends? Identify specific modules, features, or critical files with significantly low coverage. Check the CI pipeline logs for any recent test failures or flaky tests. Review progress on any ongoing UI/E2E test automation efforts. Prepare 1-2 key talking points. Conduct the Test Automation Review Segment: Share Screen: Display the coverage report (HTML or SonarQube). Review Coverage Metrics: State the current overall coverage and coverage on new code. Compare against the target. Celebrate meeting the goal! Highlight trends (improving, stable, decreasing?). Discuss Low-Coverage Areas: Point out 1-2 critical areas with low coverage. Discuss why coverage is low (difficult to test? recent feature without tests? oversight?). Discuss Test Reliability: Ask the team: "Have there been any flaky tests in CI recently?", "Are tests running reliably locally?". Discuss potential causes and fixes for flaky tests (e.g., timing issues, improper setup/teardown, external dependencies). Review Automation Progress (if applicable): Briefly discuss the status of any work being done on integration or E2E tests. Are there blockers? Is the chosen framework working well? Identify Action Items: Capture specific actions needed. Create and Track Action Items: Add Missing Tests: For critical areas with low coverage, create specific Jira tasks (e.g., "Increase test coverage for payment_bloc.dart") and add them to the Technical Backlog (Item 137). Fix Flaky Tests: Create high-priority bug tickets or tasks to investigate and fix unreliable tests. Flaky tests erode trust in the test suite. Refactor Untestable Code: If code is difficult to test, create tech debt tickets to refactor it for better testability. Improve CI Environment: If tests fail in CI but pass locally, create tasks to investigate and stabilize the CI test environment. Assign owners and prioritize these tasks in the technical backlog refinement. Keep it Focused and Actionable: Stick to the timebox (10-15 min). Focus on trends, critical gaps, and reliability issues. Avoid debugging specific failing tests during this meeting. The goal is to maintain visibility, ensure accountability for the coverage target, improve test reliability, and generate prioritized actions for the backlog. Regularly reviewing test automation and coverage ensures that testing remains a priority and that your test suite provides reliable protection against regressions. ✅

Item: 136 | Architecture Management | Risks & Blocks management | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 3 | "The action plans originated from the Architecture maturity level C&A are tracked in the ticket system (JIRA, Azure DevOps) and the progress is followed up in the next meeting." | Create Jira tasks for all "No" or "Needs Improvement" items from the maturity review and add them to the technical backlog. | | This guide explains how to ensure that the action plans identified during Architecture Maturity Assessment meetings (Item 133) are effectively tracked and followed up on, driving actual improvement.
documents.s: Completing Item 136: Track Maturity Assessment Action Plans

documents.t: Accountability: Assigning actions to owners in a tracking system makes responsibility clear. Visibility: Makes the planned improvement efforts visible to the team and stakeholders. Prioritization: Allows improvement tasks to be prioritized alongside other technical work in the backlog. Progress Monitoring: Enables tracking the status of improvements over time. Prevents Stagnation: Ensures that the output of maturity assessment meetings translates into tangible changes, rather than just discussion points that get forgotten. Closes the Loop: Provides concrete items to review at the start of the next assessment meeting.

Identify Action Plans During Maturity Meeting: As you review the architecture process checklist (Item 133) and identify gaps or areas where the current state doesn't meet the desired maturity level, define specific, actionable steps to address them. Example: Maturity Item: "Automated testing is integrated into the build..." (Item 159) Current State: "Tests run, but coverage isn't checked/enforced." Action Plan: "Configure SonarQube Quality Gate to fail PR builds if Coverage on New Code is < 80%." Owner: Tech Lead Target: End of next sprint Create Tasks in Ticket System (Jira/Azure DevOps): Immediately After the Meeting: The meeting facilitator or designated person should create tasks in your primary ticket tracking system (e.g., Jira) for every action plan identified. Task Details: Type: Use a specific type (e.g., "Task", "Improvement") or a dedicated label (e.g., arch-maturity, process-improvement). Title: Make it clear and action-oriented (e.g., "Configure SonarQube Coverage Gate for PRs"). Description: Briefly explain the gap identified in the maturity assessment and the goal of the action. Link back to the specific maturity checklist item number and the meeting notes. Assignee: Assign the task to the Owner identified in the meeting. Estimate (Optional but Recommended): Roughly estimate the effort involved (Story Points or time) to help with prioritization. Target Sprint/Due Date: Set a realistic target for completion. Add Tasks to the Backlog: These newly created tasks should be added to the team's Technical Backlog (alongside tech debt, refactoring, etc. - see Item 137). Prioritize and Plan: During Technical Backlog Refinement meetings (Item 137), these improvement tasks should be discussed and prioritized along with other technical work. Relevant tasks should be pulled into upcoming sprints based on priority and team capacity, just like any other work item. Track Progress: Monitor the status of these tasks in Jira/Azure DevOps like any other development task. Owners should provide updates during daily stand-ups if they are actively working on an improvement task. Follow Up in Next Maturity Meeting: Crucial Step: At the beginning of the next Architecture Maturity Assessment meeting, review the list of action items from the previous meeting. Check the status of the corresponding Jira tasks. Discuss completed items – did the action achieve the desired improvement? Update the maturity assessment accordingly. Discuss blocked or overdue items – what are the impediments? Does the action need to be redefined or reprioritized? By integrating architecture maturity improvements into your regular backlog management and sprint workflow via a ticket system, you ensure these important, but often non-urgent, tasks receive the necessary attention to drive continuous improvement. ✅

Item: 141 | Architecture Management | Technical Backlog management | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 4 | Recurrent follow-up meetings are conducted by the technical responsible in order to discuss the goals and issues that came from the performance test metrics. | Review the Firebase Performance Monitoring dashboard (App Start, Screen Load) monthly. Create tasks for any regressions. | | This guide explains how to establish a regular process for reviewing performance metrics and discussing issues identified through performance monitoring or testing for your Flutter application.
documents.s: Completing Item 141: Hold Performance Test Follow-up Meetings

documents.t: Maintain Performance Goals: Keeps the team focused on achieving and maintaining the agreed-upon performance NFR targets (Item 30). Early Detection of Regressions: Allows for quicker identification of performance degradations introduced by recent code changes. Catching these early is much cheaper than fixing them later. Analyze Trends: Helps understand performance characteristics across different app versions, OS versions, devices, and user segments. Prioritize Optimizations: Provides data to prioritize performance improvement efforts on the areas with the biggest impact or degradation. Inform Development: Raises awareness among developers about performance-sensitive areas and best practices. Generate Improvement Actions: Leads to specific tasks for profiling, optimizing code, or adjusting configurations, which are added to the technical backlog (Item 137).

Integrate into Existing Meetings or Schedule Dedicatedly: Option A (Integrate): If performance is relatively stable or reviews are straightforward, incorporate a 10-15 minute segment into a monthly technical meeting (e.g., the Architecture Maturity Review - Item 133, or a dedicated monthly Tech Sync). Bi-weekly might be too frequent unless actively chasing performance issues. Option B (Dedicated): If performance is a critical focus or requires deeper dives, schedule a dedicated 30-45 minute "Performance Review" meeting monthly. Attendees: Tech Lead (facilitator), Architect, interested Developers, QA Lead. PO is optional but useful for understanding user impact. Prepare for the Review (Tech Lead/Performance Champion): Before the meeting: Gather Data: Access the primary performance monitoring tool, typically Firebase Performance Monitoring. Review Key Metrics: Focus on the metrics tied to your NFR targets (Item 30): App Start Time: Check trends (Cold, Warm). Filter by country, device, OS version if needed. Look for recent regressions. Screen Traces: Review durations for critical screens (defined via custom traces). Check percentiles (P90, P95). Look for regressions. Slow/Frozen Frames: Check the percentage of sessions experiencing slow or frozen frames. Identify screens with the worst performance. Network Requests: Review durations and failure rates for critical API calls.
