Check Other Sources (if applicable): Review results from any automated performance tests run in CI (Item 175) or manual profiling sessions (Item 179). Correlate with Releases: Compare performance trends against recent app release dates. Did a specific version introduce a regression? Prepare screenshots or links to highlight key trends or specific issues. Conduct the Performance Review Segment/Meeting: Share Screen: Display the Firebase Performance Monitoring dashboard (or other relevant data). Review NFR Targets vs. Actuals: Compare the current performance metrics (App Start, Screen Traces) against the defined NFR targets. Are we meeting them? Highlight Trends & Regressions: Point out significant changes since the last review. "Cold start time increased by 15% in version 1.3.0." "The product detail screen trace duration is exceeding our 500ms target for P90." Discuss Potential Causes: Brainstorm possible reasons for regressions or poor performance. Relate them to recent features or changes if possible. Review Slow/Frozen Frames Data: Identify the screens causing the most jank. Discuss potential UI optimization strategies (e.g., smarter list building, reducing widget rebuilds). Identify Action Items: Capture specific actions needed to address identified issues. Create and Track Action Items: For performance regressions or areas failing to meet NFR targets, create Jira tasks (e.g., "Investigate App Start regression in v1.3.0," "Optimize rendering performance on Product List screen"). Use a performance label. Add these tasks to the Technical Backlog (Item 137). Prioritize: Performance issues impacting core user experience or significantly missing NFR targets should be prioritized highly in the technical backlog refinement. Assign owners for investigation and implementation. Follow Up: Track the progress of performance improvement tasks in Jira. Review the status of previous action items at the start of the next performance review meeting. Monitor the impact of implemented optimizations in subsequent performance data reviews. Regularly reviewing performance metrics transforms performance from an occasional concern into a continuous quality attribute that is actively managed and improved. 💨

Item: 141 | Architecture Management | Technical Backlog management | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 4 | Recurrent follow-up meetings are conducted by the technical responsible in order to discuss the goals and issues that came from the security test metrics. | Review security scan (e.g., Snyk) results as they occur in the CI pipeline. Triage and create tickets for any high-vulnerability findings. | | (Note: Item number seems duplicated with Performance, assuming this is Item 142 based on context) This guide explains how to establish a process for regularly reviewing security metrics and findings from automated scans or manual tests, ensuring vulnerabilities are promptly addressed.
documents.s: Completing Item 141: Hold Security Test Follow-up Meetings

documents.t: Maintain Security Posture: Keeps security visible and ensures vulnerabilities don't slip through the cracks. Timely Remediation: Facilitates prompt triage and fixing of identified security issues, reducing the window of exposure. Analyze Trends & Root Causes: Helps identify recurring vulnerability types (e.g., outdated dependencies, specific coding errors), pointing to needs for training or process changes. Prioritize Security Work: Provides data to prioritize security fixes within the technical backlog based on severity. Compliance & Reporting: Creates a record of security review and remediation efforts, often needed for compliance or audits. Raise Awareness: Increases security awareness among developers by regularly discussing findings.

While dedicated review meetings can be useful, a "shift-left" approach is generally more effective for security: Integrate security checks early and automatically into the development workflow. Automated Scans in CI/CD: Use tools like Snyk, Dependabot, SonarQube/SonarCloud's security features, or mobile-specific SAST (Static Application Security Testing) tools directly within your Pull Request CI pipeline. Fail Builds on Critical Issues: Configure these tools to fail the CI build if new Critical or High severity vulnerabilities are detected in dependencies or code. This prevents vulnerabilities from being merged in the first place. IDE Integration: Use security linting plugins in the IDE (VS Code) to catch issues as developers code. If you implement strong "shift-left" automated checks, dedicated recurring meetings specifically for security test metrics might become less critical, as issues are caught and addressed immediately within the PR workflow. However, a periodic review is still valuable.
documents.s: Shift-Left Approach (More Effective than Meetings Alone)

documents.t: Implement Automated Security Scanning (Shift-Left): Dependency Scanning: Configure Snyk, Dependabot, or SonarQube to scan pubspec.lock (and potentially native dependencies like Podfile.lock or Gradle files) for known vulnerabilities on every Pull Request. Fail the build for new High/Critical findings. Static Code Analysis (SAST): Configure SonarQube/SonarCloud or a dedicated SAST tool to analyze Dart/native code for potential security flaws (e.g., hardcoded secrets, insecure API usage) on every Pull Request. Configure Quality Gates to flag or fail on new security issues (Item 25). Secrets Scanning: Use tools (e.g., GitGuardian, truffleHog, built-in features of GitHub/GitLab) to scan commits and PRs for accidentally committed secrets. Establish Triage Process for Automated Findings: Immediate Action on PRs: If the CI build fails due to a security finding, the PR author is responsible for investigating and fixing it before the PR can be merged. This might involve: Updating a vulnerable dependency. Refactoring insecure code. Marking a finding as a false positive (with justification and potentially review). Tech Lead/Security Champion Review: For complex findings or false positives, involve the Tech Lead or a designated Security Champion for review and approval. Schedule Periodic Security Review (Less Frequent than Code Quality/Tests): Cadence: Monthly or even Quarterly might be sufficient if strong automated checks are in place. Consider integrating a 10-15 minute segment into a monthly Tech Sync or Architecture Maturity Review. A dedicated meeting might only be needed if dealing with many complex findings or post-pen-test results. Attendees: Tech Lead, Architect, Security Champion (if any), interested developers. Purpose: Review overall trends, discuss complex/recurring issues, review findings from manual tests (e.g., penetration tests), and plan larger security initiatives. Prepare for the Periodic Review: Review dashboards from security tools (Snyk, SonarQube Security Reports). Look for: Overall vulnerability count and severity trends. Any High/Critical vulnerabilities that bypassed automated gates (should be rare). Recurring types of vulnerabilities or hotspots. Results from recent manual penetration tests (if applicable). Conduct the Periodic Security Review: Discuss overall trends and posture. Review any critical findings needing attention. Discuss recurring issues and potential root causes (e.g., need for team training on input validation). Review findings from manual tests (e.g., pen-test results) and plan remediation. Identify action items (e.g., update dependencies, schedule refactoring, conduct training). Create and Track Action Items: Create Jira tasks for all required remediation work, security improvements, or tool configuration changes. Use a security label. Add high-priority security fixes (especially Critical/High vulnerabilities) to the Technical Backlog (Item 137) or potentially treat them as urgent bugs. Prioritize security tasks based on severity and risk. By combining aggressive automated security checks in the CI/CD pipeline with a clear triage process and periodic high-level reviews, you can effectively manage security risks without necessarily needing frequent, dedicated "security test metrics" meetings. Focus on fixing issues as they are found in PRs. 🛡️
documents.s: Steps (Assuming Both Shift-Left and Periodic Review)

documents.t:
Item: 142 | Architecture Management | Technical Backlog management | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 5 | "The team's maturity on Architecture Process is known by the entire company, project sponsors and stakeholders;
There is a plan to manage, spread and scale knowledge beyond the project boundaries." | Share the results of the monthly "Architecture Maturity Review" with the engineering manager and project sponsors. | | This guide covers the advanced practice (Maturity Level 5) of communicating your team's architecture process maturity externally and having a plan for sharing knowledge beyond your immediate team.
documents.s: Completing Item 142: Communicate Team Maturity and Knowledge Sharing Plan

documents.t: Visibility & Transparency: Makes the team's commitment to quality processes and continuous improvement visible to leadership and other teams. Builds Confidence: Demonstrates a mature and proactive approach to software development, building confidence among sponsors and stakeholders. Justifies Investment: Helps justify the time and resources invested in DevOps tools, testing, and process improvement by showing tangible maturity progress. Cross-Team Learning: Sharing knowledge, best practices, and lessons learned benefits other teams within the organization, potentially raising the bar for everyone. Scaling Best Practices: Facilitates the adoption of successful processes and tools developed by your team in other parts of the company. Recognizes Team Effort: Highlights the team's achievements in improving their processes.
documents.s: Why Communicate Maturity and Share Knowledge? 🤔

documents.t: Synthesize Maturity Assessment Results: Use the outputs of your regular Architecture Maturity Assessment meetings (Item 133). Don't just share the raw checklist. Create a concise summary highlighting: Overall Maturity Trend: Is the team generally improving, stable, or declining in key areas? Strengths: Areas where the team consistently meets high maturity levels. Areas for Improvement: Key areas where gaps were identified. Key Improvement Initiatives: Briefly mention the top 1-3 action items the team is working on to address gaps. Visualize: Consider using a simple chart (e.g., a radar chart showing scores across different categories like CI/CD, Testing, Monitoring) to provide a quick visual overview of maturity levels. [Image of a maturity model radar chart] Identify the Audience: Engineering Manager / Direct Leadership: Definitely needs to be informed. Project Sponsors / Key Business Stakeholders: Share a higher-level summary focusing on stability, quality, and speed improvements resulting from process maturity. Wider Engineering Organization (Optional): If there's a forum like an Engineering All-Hands or Architecture Guild. Choose Communication Channels: Regular Reports: Include a slide or section in regular project status reports or engineering team updates. Dedicated Updates: Send a brief summary email or present findings briefly in relevant leadership meetings (e.g., quarterly). Internal Blog/Wiki: Post updates on an internal engineering blog or central architecture wiki. Focus on Impact: Whenever possible, connect process maturity improvements to tangible outcomes: "Improving our CI pipeline (Maturity Item X) reduced average build times by 25%, speeding up developer feedback." "Implementing stricter Quality Gates (Maturity Item Y) has correlated with a 10% decrease in production bugs this quarter." "Our increased test coverage (Maturity Item Z) allowed us to confidently release the critical payment feature on time."

Identify Valuable Knowledge/Practices: What has your team learned or built that could benefit others? Successful implementation of a specific architectural pattern (e.g., Clean Architecture in Flutter). Effective CI/CD pipeline setup for Flutter (specific actions, caching strategies). Useful reusable code components or internal libraries. Lessons learned from adopting a new technology (e.g., Riverpod, Isar). Effective testing strategies or custom tools. Well-defined processes (e.g., your refined NFR management, ADR process). Establish Knowledge Sharing Mechanisms: Internal Tech Talks / Brown Bags: Encourage team members to present topics to other teams or the wider engineering org. Community of Practice (CoP) / Guild Meetings: Participate in or help establish CoPs (e.g., Mobile Development CoP, Architecture Guild) where teams can share practices. Internal Blog Posts / Wiki Articles: Document learnings, patterns, or tutorials on shared internal platforms. Reusable Libraries: Package useful, generic code into internal libraries and publish them to a shared artifact repository (Item 80). Provide clear documentation. Code Sharing / InnerSource: Make relevant parts of your codebase visible to other teams (if appropriate within organizational policy) as examples. Pairing / Mentoring: Offer opportunities for developers from other teams to pair with your team members. Allocate Time & Encourage Participation: Recognize knowledge sharing as a valuable activity. Allow team members time to prepare presentations, write articles, or contribute to shared libraries as part of their regular work or dedicated "innovation time." Provide coaching or support for team members who are interested in presenting or writing. Document the Plan: Create a simple "Knowledge Sharing Plan" section on your team wiki outlining the intended mechanisms (e.g., "Aim for one tech talk per quarter," "Contribute reusable widgets to internal library X") and potentially assign owners or champions for different initiatives. By actively communicating your team's process maturity and fostering a culture of sharing knowledge beyond project boundaries, you amplify the impact of your team's improvements and contribute to the growth of the entire engineering organization. 🌟

Item: 143 | Architecture Validation | Architecture Evaluation | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 1 | The code quality is followed by performing code reviews and the process is documented and known by the team members. | Enforce PR reviews using GitHub branch protection rules. Require at least one approval before merging. | | This guide details how to establish, document, and enforce a code review process using Pull Requests (PRs) for your Flutter project.
documents.s: Completing Item 143: Implement Code Review Process

documents.t: Improve Code Quality: Catches bugs, logical errors, performance issues, and security vulnerabilities before they reach the main codebase. Ensure Consistency: Enforces adherence to coding standards, architectural patterns, and best practices (Items 3, 11). Knowledge Sharing: Spreads knowledge about the codebase and different implementation techniques among team members. Reviewers learn from the code they review, and authors learn from the feedback. Mentoring: Provides opportunities for senior developers to mentor junior developers. Collective Ownership: Fosters a sense of shared responsibility for the quality of the codebase. Alternative Solutions: Reviewers might suggest simpler, more efficient, or more robust ways to solve the problem.

Establish the PR Workflow: Branching: Require all changes (features, bug fixes) to be developed on separate branches (feature branches) based off main (or develop if using Gitflow) - (Covered by Item 1). Pull Requests: Mandate that the only way code gets merged into the main branch (main or develop) is through a Pull Request. Direct pushes must be disallowed. Define the Code Review Process and Expectations: Create a "Code Review Guidelines" page on your team wiki. Author's Responsibility: Ensure code compiles, passes all automated checks (lint, tests - Item 6, 159), and works as intended. Write a clear PR title and description using the template (Item 8). Keep PRs small and focused (Item 34). Avoid submitting huge changesets that are difficult to review. Perform a self-review first, looking for obvious errors or areas for improvement. Request reviews from appropriate team members (see below). Respond constructively to feedback and make necessary changes promptly. Reviewer's Responsibility: Goal: Aim to improve the code, not just find flaws. Be constructive and respectful. Timeliness: Aim to provide feedback within a reasonable timeframe (e.g., within 1 business day) to avoid blocking the author. What to Look For: Correctness: Does the code do what the story/bug requires? Does it handle edge cases and errors correctly? Readability & Clarity: Is the code easy to understand? Are variable/function names clear? Is the logic straightforward? Consistency: Does it follow established coding conventions (Item 3) and architectural patterns (Item 11)? Test Coverage: Are there sufficient unit/widget tests for the changes? Do the tests make sense? (Item 15) Performance: Are there any obvious performance bottlenecks (e.g., inefficient loops, unnecessary rebuilds)? (Item 31) Security: Are there any potential security vulnerabilities (e.g., improper input handling, hardcoded secrets)? (Item 32) Maintainability: Is the code overly complex? Is it well-structured? Could it be simplified? Documentation: Are comments added where necessary? Does relevant external documentation need updating (Item 35)? Feedback Style: Be specific. Explain why a change is suggested. Offer concrete suggestions if possible. Distinguish between blocking issues ("Must Fix") and suggestions/nitpicks ("Consider," "Optional"). Use standard prefixes like [Nit] for minor style preferences. Approval: Approve the PR once satisfied with the changes or if only minor, non-blocking suggestions remain. Define Reviewer Assignment: Specify how reviewers are chosen (e.g., "Author requests at least one peer," "Use GitHub's CODEOWNERS file," "Rotate reviewers," "Tech Lead reviews complex changes"). Enforce the Process with Tooling: Protected Branches (Crucial): Configure branch protection rules on main (and develop, release/*) in GitHub/GitLab (Item 8): ✅ Require a pull request before merging. ✅ Require approvals (set to at least 1). ✅ Require status checks to pass (CI build including lint/test must succeed). (Optional but recommended) Dismiss stale approvals when new commits are pushed. (Optional but recommended) Require review from Code Owners for specific files/directories. Document and Communicate: Ensure the "Code Review Guidelines" wiki page is linked from the main SCM policy and onboarding documents. Discuss the guidelines with the team and ensure everyone understands the expectations for both authors and reviewers. Revisit the process during retrospectives if issues arise (e.g., reviews taking too long, inconsistent feedback). By implementing a mandatory, well-defined, and tool-enforced code review process, you establish a critical quality gate that significantly improves the health and stability of your codebase. 👍

Item: 151 | Architecture Validation | Continuous Testing | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 1 | "The application is being validated across different browsers (for web), different devices (for mobile) and resolutions according to the requirements." | Use a device farm (e.g., Firebase Test Lab, AWS Device Farm) to run automated tests on a range of real Android and iOS devices. | | (Note: Item mentions browsers, but action and context are mobile. This guide focuses on mobile devices). This guide explains the importance of validating your Flutter mobile application on a variety of devices and screen resolutions and how to implement this validation.
documents.s: Completing Item 151: Validate on Different Devices/Resolutions

documents.t: Diverse Ecosystem: The Android and iOS ecosystems include a vast range of devices with different screen sizes, aspect ratios, pixel densities, OS versions, and hardware capabilities (CPU, memory). Layout Issues: Flutter's responsive UI capabilities are powerful, but layouts can still break or look awkward on unexpected screen sizes (e.g., text overflow, buttons misplaced, unusable content on very small or very large screens). Performance Differences: Performance (startup time, animation smoothness, memory usage) can vary significantly between low-end and high-end devices. Platform-Specific Bugs: Issues might occur only on specific OS versions or manufacturer customizations (especially on Android). Ensure Reach: Validating on older OS versions and lower-end devices ensures your app is usable by a wider audience (if required by project goals).

Define Target Devices and OS Versions: Requirements: Consult project requirements or market data. What are the minimum supported iOS and Android versions (Item 30 - Compatibility NFR)? Key Segments: Identify representative devices for key user segments: High-End: Recent iPhone, Google Pixel, Samsung Galaxy S series. Mid-Range: Popular mid-range Android devices (e.g., Samsung A series, specific models common in target markets). Low-End (If Supporting): Older iPhones, lower-spec Android devices. Different Form Factors: Include at least one tablet (iPad, Android tablet) if tablet support is required. Consider foldable phones if relevant. Document: List the primary target devices/OS versions for testing in your Test Plan or wiki. Manual Testing Strategy: QA Device Pool: Ensure the QA team has access to a representative range of physical devices from the target list. Emulators/simulators are useful for development but don't catch all hardware or OS-specific issues. Test Execution: During manual testing cycles (before release), QA should execute test cases on a variety of devices, specifically looking for layout, performance, and platform-specific issues. Prioritize testing new UI features across different screen sizes. Exploratory Testing: Encourage exploratory testing on less common devices occasionally to catch unexpected problems. Automated Testing Strategy (Device Farms): Leverage Device Farms: Use cloud-based device farms to run your automated tests (especially Integration Tests or E2E Tests) across a wide range of real physical devices that your team doesn't own. Popular Services: Firebase Test Lab: Good integration with Android (Robo tests, instrumentation tests). iOS support is more limited (XCTests). Can run Flutter integration tests. [Image of Firebase Test Lab device selection] AWS Device Farm: Wide range of Android and iOS devices. Supports various test frameworks including Flutter Integration Tests (with custom test environments). BrowserStack App Automate / Sauce Labs Real Device Cloud: Offer extensive device selections and support for Appium, Espresso, XCUITest (which can sometimes be used to drive Flutter apps, though direct Flutter test support is better). Often used with frameworks like Patrol or Maestro for Flutter E2E testing. Implementation: Choose a device farm service. Write your automated integration/E2E tests (e.g., using package:integration_test, patrol). Configure your CI/CD pipeline: Add steps to build the testable app artifacts (.apk, .ipa). Add steps to upload the artifacts and your test scripts/definitions to the chosen device farm service via its CLI or API. Specify the target device pool or specific devices to run the tests on. Configure the pipeline to wait for results and fail if tests fail on the farm. Frequency: Running extensive device farm tests on every PR can be slow and expensive. Common strategies: Run on a limited set of core devices for PR checks. Run on the full device set nightly against the main branch. Run on the full device set before tagging a release candidate. Layout Preview Tools (Development): Device Preview Package (device_preview): Use this package during development to simulate different screen sizes, orientations, and platform appearances directly within your debug app. Helps catch basic layout issues early. IDE Previews: Utilize layout previews available in Android Studio or VS Code (though device_preview is often more comprehensive). Monitor Production Data: Use Firebase Crashlytics and Performance Monitoring to identify issues occurring on specific devices or OS versions in the wild that might have been missed during testing. Filter data by device model and OS. By combining targeted manual testing on physical devices, automated testing across a device farm, and using preview tools during development, you can significantly increase confidence that your Flutter app provides a consistent and functional experience across the diverse mobile landscape. 🌐

Item: 73 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Integration | PREPARATION (Sprint 0) | 2 | "The build to create artifact for environments are automated, and there is no manual steps, excluding configuring enviroment variables/settings." | Use CI/CD (e.g., GitHub Actions, Codemagic) for all artifact generation. Developers must not build release .aab/.ipa files locally. | | This guide explains the importance of automating the generation of application build artifacts (.apk, .aab, .ipa) using a CI/CD server and why manual local builds for releases should be avoided.
documents.s: Completing Item 73: Automate Build Artifact Generation

documents.t: Consistency & Reproducibility: Ensures that every artifact is built using the exact same environment, tools, Flutter version, and build commands. Eliminates "works on my machine" problems. Reduced Errors: Manual build steps are prone to human error (forgetting a flag, using the wrong signing key, incorrect environment configuration). Automation removes this risk. Efficiency: Frees developers from the time-consuming and often tedious process of manually building, signing, and managing artifacts. Security: Allows sensitive information like code signing keys and passwords to be managed securely within the CI/CD environment's secret management, rather than being stored on developer machines. Traceability: CI/CD logs provide a clear record of how and when each artifact was built, linked to a specific code commit.

Mandate CI/CD for All Release Builds: Establish a firm team policy: Developers MUST NOT create release builds (.aab/.ipa intended for distribution or production) on their local machines. All artifacts intended for QA testing (Staging) or Production release must be generated by the automated CI/CD pipeline. Configure CI/CD Build Jobs: As part of your CI/CD setup (Item 70, Item 45, etc.), create specific jobs or steps responsible for building the release artifacts. Environment Configuration: Use a clean, consistent build environment (Docker image, dedicated runner). Install the exact required Flutter SDK version (use FVM - Item 2). Install any other required dependencies (Java, CocoaPods, Fastlane). Build Commands: Use the correct flutter build commands for each platform: # Android App Bundle (Production) flutter build appbundle --release \ --dart-define=VAR1=ProdValue1 \ --dart-define=VAR2=ProdValue2 # iOS IPA (Production) flutter build ipa --release \ --export-options-plist=path/to/ExportOptionsProd.plist \ --dart-define=VAR1=ProdValue1 \ --dart-define=VAR2=ProdValue2 Ensure environment variables (--dart-define or .env files - Item 69) are correctly injected for the target environment (Staging, Prod). Retrieve sensitive values from CI secrets. Code Signing: Android: Securely provide the upload keystore file (.jks) and its passwords (key password, store password) to the build environment via CI secrets. Configure android/app/build.gradle to use these. iOS: Securely provide the distribution certificate (.p12) and provisioning profile (.mobileprovision) and any associated passwords to the build environment via CI secrets. This is often complex and best managed using tools like fastlane match or specialized CI features (like Codemagic's key management). Configure Xcode settings or ExportOptions.plist accordingly. Artifact Storage: Configure the CI/CD job to automatically archive and store the generated artifacts (.aab, .ipa, build logs, mapping files for Android crash symbolication) in a reliable location: CI/CD platform's built-in artifact storage (often temporary). GitHub Releases / GitLab Packages. Dedicated artifact repository (Artifactory, Nexus). Cloud storage (GCP Bucket, AWS S3). Ensure artifacts are clearly named, versioned, and linked to the corresponding Git commit/tag. Exclude Local Build Files: Ensure your project's .gitignore file includes the build/ directory and any locally generated artifact files to prevent accidental commits. Documentation and Communication: Document in the team's wiki that all official builds come only from the CI/CD pipeline. Explain why local release builds are prohibited (consistency, security, reproducibility). Provide links to where team members can download the latest CI-generated builds for testing (e.g., Firebase App Distribution link). By strictly enforcing automated artifact generation through CI/CD, you significantly improve the reliability, security, and traceability of your build process.

Item: 79 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Integration | PREPARATION (Sprint 0) | 2 | "The current status of the build is visible to everyone in the team and there is immediate feedback when the build run or fail (email, chat message, etc)" | Integrate the CI/CD tool with the team's chat (e.g., Slack/Google Chat) to post notifications for build successes and failures. | | This guide explains how to make the status of your CI/CD builds easily visible to the entire team and ensure immediate feedback is provided upon completion or failure.
documents.s: Completing Item 79: Ensure Build Status Visibility and Feedback

documents.t: Fast Feedback Loop: Immediately informs developers if their changes broke the build or failed tests, allowing for quicker fixes. Team Awareness: Keeps the entire team (including QA, PO) aware of the integration status and the availability of new builds for testing. Reduced Integration Time: Broken builds are identified and fixed faster, preventing them from blocking other developers. Transparency: Makes the CI/CD process less of a "black box." Accountability: Encourages collective ownership of maintaining a green build.
documents.s: Why is Build Visibility and Feedback Important?

documents.t: Choose Visibility Mechanisms: CI/CD Dashboard: Most CI/CD platforms (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Codemagic, Jenkins) provide a web UI showing build history, current status (running, success, failure), and logs. Ensure all team members know how to access this. Pull Request Status Checks: Configure the CI/CD platform to report the status of checks (lint, test, build, quality gate) directly within the Pull Request interface on GitHub/GitLab. This is crucial for blocking merges on failure. [Image of GitHub PR status checks] Real-time Chat Notifications: Integrate the CI/CD platform with the team's primary chat tool (Slack, Google Chat, Teams). This provides immediate, push-based feedback. Build Badges (Optional): Embed status badges (showing build success/failure for the main branch) in the project's README file. Physical Monitors (Optional): In a co-located office, a dedicated monitor displaying the main branch build status can be effective (less common now with remote work). Configure Pull Request Status Checks: In your CI workflow file (e.g., GitHub Actions YAML), ensure jobs corresponding to critical checks (analyze, test, format, build, SonarQube Quality Gate) are configured to run on pull_request triggers. In your Git host (GitHub/GitLab), configure branch protection rules (Item 8) for the main branch to require these status checks to pass before merging. Configure Chat Notifications: Select Target Channel: Choose a dedicated channel for automated notifications (e.g., #proj-mobile-alerts - Item 17) to avoid spamming general channels. Configure Integration: Use built-in integrations or marketplace apps/plugins for your CI/CD platform and chat tool: GitHub Actions: Use actions like rtCamp/action-slack-notify, slackapi/slack-github-action, or specific Google Chat actions. GitLab CI: Built-in Slack/Teams integrations. Codemagic: Built-in Slack/Email integrations. Jenkins: Slack Plugin or others. Configure Notification Triggers: Set up notifications for key events: Build Failure (Most Important): Send an immediate notification on any build failure on the main branch or on a PR. Include a link to the failed build logs and @mention the commit author if possible. Build Success (Main Branch): Notify when the main branch build succeeds after a merge (often coincides with deployment notifications - Item 70). Build Success (PR - Optional): Optionally notify when a PR build passes (can be noisy). Status checks in the PR interface are often sufficient. Deployment Success/Failure: Notify about the status of deployments to Dev/Staging/Prod environments. Message Content: Make notifications clear and concise. Include: Project Name Branch Name / PR Number Status (✅ Success / ❌ Failure) Commit Author (if possible) Link to Build Logs / PR / Deployment Document Access: In your project onboarding guide or wiki, provide links to: The CI/CD dashboard. The chat channel used for notifications. Instructions on interpreting status checks in Pull Requests. Establish Team Norms: Broken Build is Priority #1: Emphasize the "Stop the Line" policy (Item 162). If the main branch build fails, fixing it becomes the team's top priority. Monitor Notifications: Encourage team members (especially the author of the failing commit) to monitor the alerts channel and take action on failures promptly. By ensuring build status is highly visible and feedback is immediate, you reinforce the core principles of Continuous Integration and enable the team to maintain a stable codebase.

Item: 95 | Architecture Validation | Architecture Evaluation | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 2 | The defects identified during the code reviews become defects in the ticket control system (JIRA or similar) and are part of the quality metrics. | If a PR comment is not a simple fix (e.g., "This needs refactoring"), create a new Jira "Tech Debt" ticket for it and link it in the comment. | | This guide explains how to establish a process for tracking significant issues or defects identified during Pull Request (PR) code reviews as formal tickets in your project management system (e.g., Jira).
documents.s: Completing Item 95: Track Defects Found During Code Review

documents.t: Visibility: Makes significant issues visible beyond the context of a single PR comment thread. Ensures they aren't forgotten after the PR is merged. Prioritization: Allows these issues (often representing technical debt or required refactoring) to be prioritized against other work in the technical backlog (Item 94). Work Tracking: Ensures that the effort required to fix these issues is properly accounted for and planned into sprints. Quality Metrics: Provides data on the types and frequency of issues being caught in review, which can inform process improvements or targeted training. Completeness: Ensures that agreed-upon follow-up actions from a code review actually get done.

Not every PR comment needs a separate ticket. Focus on tracking issues that are: Non-Trivial Fixes: Require more effort than a quick change within the current PR (e.g., need significant refactoring, architectural changes, further investigation). Technical Debt: Represent suboptimal code, missing tests, or deviations from standards that are accepted for now to merge the PR but need addressing later (Item 5). Potential Bugs: Identify logic flaws or edge cases not handled, even if not directly related to the PR's core functionality. Actionable Follow-ups: Agreed-upon improvements or investigations arising from the review discussion. Simple suggestions (typos, naming tweaks, minor logic improvements) should typically be addressed directly within the PR itself.

Establish the Triage Process During Code Review: When a reviewer identifies a significant issue (as defined above) in a PR: Comment: Clearly explain the issue in the PR comment. Discuss: Briefly discuss with the PR author. Agree whether it must be fixed before merging this PR, or if it can be addressed as a follow-up. Decision to Track: If agreed that it's a non-trivial follow-up: Create Ticket: The reviewer or the author creates a new ticket in Jira. Ticket Type: Use an appropriate type (e.g., "Bug," "Task," "TechDebt"). Label/Component: Assign a relevant label (e.g., code-review-followup, tech-debt) or component. Description: Copy/paste the context from the PR comment, explaining the issue, location, and suggested fix. Link PR: Link the Jira ticket back to the original PR comment (most Git hosts allow pasting Jira links). Update Comment: The person creating the ticket replies to the original PR comment with a link to the newly created Jira ticket (e.g., "Good point. Created MEC-789 to track this refactoring."). Integrate with Technical Backlog: These newly created tickets automatically become part of the technical backlog. They should be reviewed and prioritized during the regular Technical Backlog Refinement meetings (Item 136) along with other tech debt and improvement tasks. Use as a Quality Metric (Optional but Useful): Periodically analyze the types of issues being created from code reviews (e.g., using Jira labels/queries). Are certain patterns emerging? (e.g., many issues related to error handling, specific architectural pattern misuse, lack of tests). Use this data to inform team training, documentation improvements, or adjustments to coding conventions. Communicate the Process: Ensure the entire team understands when to create a follow-up ticket versus fixing an issue directly in the PR. Document this process briefly in the team's code review guidelines. By systematically tracking significant issues found during code reviews, you ensure they are not lost and can be properly prioritized and addressed, contributing to the continuous improvement of the codebase's quality.

Item: 98 | Architecture Validation | Continuous Testing | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 2 | "Manual test cases follow template to be same page to all team members to execute them .
The content of test cases must be informative (enough step/action, input value, expects etc)" | (QA) Provide QA with a standard test case template in the test management tool (e.g., Zephyr, TestRail). | | This guide explains the importance of using a standardized template for writing manual test cases, ensuring clarity, consistency, and effective execution by the QA team or anyone performing manual testing.
documents.s: Completing Item 98: Use Manual Test Case Template

documents.t: Clarity & Consistency: Ensures all test cases are structured similarly, making them easier to read, understand, and execute consistently by different testers. Completeness: Prompts the test author (usually QA) to include all necessary information (preconditions, steps, expected results), reducing ambiguity. Reproducibility: Well-defined steps make it easier to reproduce bugs found during testing. Test Coverage Tracking: Structured test cases in a Test Management Tool allow for better tracking of test execution status (Pass/Fail/Blocked) and coverage against requirements. Efficiency: Reduces guesswork for the tester executing the case, leading to faster and more accurate testing. Onboarding: Helps new QA team members quickly understand how tests are documented and executed.
documents.s: Why Use a Test Case Template?

documents.t: A good manual test case template, often implemented within a Test Management Tool (like Zephyr, TestRail, Xray, qTest) or even a structured document/spreadsheet, should include fields for: Test Case ID: A unique identifier (e.g., TC-LOGIN-001). Often auto-generated by tools. Requirement/Story Link: Link to the User Story or requirement(s) this test case verifies (e.g., Jira ticket MEC-123). Essential for traceability. Title/Summary: A clear, concise description of the test case's objective (e.g., "Verify successful login with valid credentials"). Priority/Severity: (Optional) Indicates the importance of the test case (e.g., High, Medium, Low). Test Type: (Optional) Category of test (e.g., Functional, UI, Performance, Security, Regression). Preconditions: Any conditions that must be met before starting the test steps (e.g., "User is logged out," "App is installed," "Backend service is running," "User account 'test@example.com' exists with password 'password123'"). Be specific. Test Steps: A numbered list of clear, simple, sequential actions the tester needs to perform. Start with launching the app or navigating to the correct starting screen. Each step should describe a single, distinct action (e.g., "Tap on the 'Email' field," "Enter 'test@example.com'," "Tap the 'Login' button"). Avoid combining multiple actions. Test Data: Specific input values to be used during the test steps (e.g., Username: test@example.com, Password: password123). Can be included within steps or in a separate field. Expected Result: For each test step (or for the final outcome), describe the expected behavior, state, or UI appearance. This must be objective and verifiable. (e.g., "Step 3 Expected: User is navigated to the Home Screen," "Step 3 Expected: 'Welcome, Test User!' message is displayed."). Avoid vague terms like "Works correctly." Actual Result (Execution Field): A field (usually in the test management tool) for the tester to record the actual outcome observed during execution. Status (Execution Field): Pass / Fail / Blocked / Skipped. Bug ID (Execution Field): If the test fails, link to the bug ticket created in Jira. Tester/Date Executed (Execution Field): Who ran the test and when. Environment (Execution Field): On which environment/device/OS version the test was run.
documents.s: Key Elements of a Test Case Template

documents.t: Choose a Test Management Tool (Recommended): Select a tool like Zephyr Scale/Squad (Jira plugin), Xray (Jira plugin), TestRail, etc. These tools provide built-in templates, execution tracking, reporting, and traceability features. If a dedicated tool isn't feasible, use a structured Confluence page template or a shared spreadsheet, but this lacks robust tracking features. Define/Configure the Template: Work with the QA team to define the standard template fields based on the elements listed above. Configure this template within your chosen tool. Train the Team (QA Primarily): Ensure all QA members understand the template fields and the level of detail required. Provide examples of well-written test cases. Emphasize clarity in steps and expected results. Write Test Cases: QA writes test cases for new user stories (often during or after refinement/planning) based on the Acceptance Criteria, using the standard template. Review Test Cases (Optional but Recommended): Have developers or the PO briefly review test cases for key features to ensure they accurately reflect the requirements and cover important scenarios. Execute Using the Template: During the testing phase, testers execute the steps precisely as written, recording actual results and status in the test management tool. By using a standardized template, you improve the quality, consistency, and efficiency of your manual testing efforts.

Item: 152 | Architecture Validation | Continuous Testing | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 2 | Unit tests are coded and planned within each business story. | Add "Unit tests written and passing" (for flutter test) as a mandatory item in the "Definition of Done" for all stories involving business logic. | | This guide explains how to integrate the planning and implementation of unit tests directly into the workflow for developing user stories.
documents.s: Completing Item 152: Code and Plan Unit Tests Within Stories

documents.t: Testability by Design: Thinking about tests while writing the code encourages developers to write more modular, decoupled, and testable code from the start. Immediate Feedback: Writing tests alongside implementation provides immediate confirmation that the logic works as expected and catches regressions early if changes are made later in the story's development. Clearer Definition of Done: Explicitly including unit tests makes the quality expectation clear and ensures testing isn't skipped or deferred. Living Documentation: Well-written unit tests serve as executable documentation, demonstrating how a piece of code is intended to be used and what its expected outcomes are. Reduces End-of-Sprint Rush: Prevents the anti-pattern of trying to add tests for multiple stories just before the sprint ends.
documents.s: Why Integrate Unit Testing with Story Development? ⚙️

documents.t: Remember, unit tests focus on isolating and verifying small pieces of logic: Flutter: BLoCs, Cubits, ViewModels, Notifiers (State Management Logic). Business Logic Classes (Use Cases, Services). Repository implementations (testing their logic, mocking data sources). Utility functions, validators, data mappers/transformers. They do NOT typically involve rendering UI or making real network/database calls. Mocks and stubs are used extensively (Item 15).

Include Unit Testing in Definition of Done (DoD): This is the most critical enforcement mechanism. Add a specific, non-negotiable checklist item to your team's Definition of Done: ✅ Unit tests written and passing for new/modified business logic. (Optional but Recommended) ✅ Unit test coverage meets target (>80% on new/modified code). (Requires measuring coverage per change, often via SonarQube/CI tools - Item 154). A story cannot be considered "Done" (and moved to QA or closed) unless the required unit tests are implemented and passing. Consider Tests During Refinement & Planning: When discussing the technical approach for a story during refinement (Item 37), briefly consider: "How will we unit test this logic?". This thought process can influence the design. If a proposed approach seems hard to unit test, it might be a sign the design needs refinement (e.g., needs more separation of concerns). Include "Write Unit Tests" as one of the standard sub-tasks when breaking down stories during Sprint Planning (Item 38). Write Tests During Implementation: Encourage developers to write unit tests concurrently with writing the implementation code. Test-Driven Development (TDD) (Optional but beneficial): Write a failing unit test for a small piece of required functionality. Write the minimum amount of implementation code needed to make the test pass. Refactor the code while ensuring the test still passes. Repeat for the next piece of functionality. TDD naturally leads to testable code and ensures tests are written. Test-After (More Common): Write the implementation code for a small part (e.g., a method in a Bloc), then immediately write the unit tests for that part before moving on. Avoid: Writing all implementation code for the entire story and then trying to add all the unit tests at the end. Run Tests Locally: Developers must run the relevant unit tests (flutter test path/to/file_test.dart or flutter test) locally to ensure they pass before committing code or opening a Pull Request. IDE integration (VS Code, Android Studio) makes running individual tests or file tests easy. Enforce via CI Pipeline: The CI pipeline triggered on every Pull Request must run the full unit test suite (flutter test) - (Item 159). The build must fail if any unit test fails. (Optional but Recommended) The CI pipeline should check for coverage on new code and fail if it's below the target (Item 154). Review Tests During Code Review: Code reviewers (Item 143) must explicitly check that appropriate unit tests have been added or updated as part of the PR. Review the quality of the tests themselves: Are they testing the right things? Are they readable? Do they cover important edge cases? Are mocks used correctly? By integrating unit testing directly into the user story workflow and making it a required part of the Definition of Done, you ensure that testing is a continuous activity that supports quality and maintainability throughout the development process. 🎯

Item: 96 | Architecture Validation | Architecture Evaluation | PREPARATION (Sprint 0) | 2 | The code quality is measured through static code analysis tools. | Configure flutter analyzewith strict rules inanalysis_options.yaml and run it on every PR. | | (Note: This item is foundational and closely related to Item 6, "Implement Code Style Tools," and Item 25, "Align on Static Analysis Metrics Goal." This focuses on the existence and basic configuration of the tool during setup.) This guide covers the initial setup and integration of static code analysis tools to automatically measure and check code quality in your Flutter project.
documents.s: Completing Item 96: Use Static Code Analysis Tools

documents.t: Automated Quality Checks: Automatically detects potential bugs, style inconsistencies, performance issues, and deviations from best practices without needing to run the code. Early Feedback: Provides immediate feedback to developers as they code (via IDE integration) or when they submit a Pull Request (via CI). Consistency: Enforces coding standards and conventions uniformly across the entire team and codebase. Bug Prevention: Catches common error patterns (e.g., potential null issues, incorrect async usage) before they reach testing or production. Improved Maintainability: Encourages cleaner, more readable, and less complex code.
The primary static analysis tool for Flutter/Dart is built into the Dart SDK and run via flutter analyze.

Configure Analysis Rules (analysis_options.yaml - Crucial Step): This file, placed in the root of your Flutter project, controls which rules the Dart Analyzer enforces. Do not skip this step. Create/Edit analysis_options.yaml: Include Base Rules: Start by including a standard set of recommended rules: # Use the recommended Flutter lint set include: package:flutter_lints/flutter.yaml # Optionally, include stricter sets like package:lints/recommended.yaml or effective_dart Customize Rules: Enable additional lints or customize existing ones based on team preferences and project needs. Refer to the Dart Linter Rules documentation for available rules. analyzer: # Treat certain issues as errors instead of warnings/infos errors: missing_required_param: error # Promote infos/warnings to errors if desired # avoid_print: error exclude: # Exclude generated files from analysis - '**/*.g.dart' - '**/*.freezed.dart' linter: rules: # Enable specific rules not in the base set always_declare_return_types: true avoid_redundant_argument_values: true prefer_final_locals: true # Disable rules if necessary (use with caution) # avoid_catches_without_on_clauses: false Commit the File: Commit analysis_options.yaml to your Git repository so the rules are shared and versioned. Integrate with IDE: Modern IDEs like VS Code (with the Dart/Flutter extensions) automatically use the analysis_options.yaml file. They provide real-time feedback by highlighting analysis issues directly in the code editor. Ensure developers have the necessary extensions installed and enabled. Integrate with CI Pipeline: Add a step to your CI workflow (e.g., GitHub Actions) that runs on every Pull Request. Use the flutter analyze command. Crucially, use flags to fail the CI build if any issues are found. # Example GitHub Actions step - name: Analyze code run: flutter analyze --fatal-infos --fatal-warnings . # --fatal-infos: Treat info-level issues as errors # --fatal-warnings: Treat warning-level issues as errors This prevents merging code that violates the defined quality standards. Consider Additional Tools (Optional - Relates to Item 6 & 25): While flutter analyze is the core, consider tools like SonarQube/SonarCloud for deeper analysis (complexity, duplication, security hotspots) and tracking quality trends over time. SonarQube often incorporates the results from the Dart Analyzer. Document and Communicate: Briefly document the use of flutter analyze and the location of the analysis_options.yaml file in your project's README or onboarding guide. Explain the importance of adhering to the analysis rules during team onboarding and code reviews. By setting up and enforcing static analysis early using flutter analyze and a well-configured analysis_options.yaml, you establish a foundational layer of automated code quality assurance for your project.

Item: 144 | Architecture Validation | Architecture Evaluation | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 2 | The defects identified during the code reviews become defects in the ticket control system (JIRA or similar) and are part of the quality metrics. | If a PR comment is not a simple fix (e.g., "This needs refactoring"), create a new Jira "Tech Debt" ticket for it and link it in the comment. | | This guide explains how to handle significant issues identified during code reviews by tracking them formally in your ticket system (e.g., Jira), rather than letting them get lost in PR comments.
documents.s: Completing Item 144: Track Defects Found During Code Reviews

documents.t: Visibility: Ensures significant issues identified during review aren't forgotten after the PR is merged, especially if they aren't fixed within that PR. Prioritization: Allows these issues (often technical debt or necessary refactoring) to be added to the Technical Backlog (Item 137) and prioritized against other technical work. Tracking: Creates a record of identified issues and their resolution status. Quality Metrics: Allows you to (optionally) track the number or types of significant issues found during reviews as an indicator of code quality trends or areas needing more attention. Avoids PR Bloat: Prevents Pull Requests from becoming blocked indefinitely while developers attempt large refactorings suggested during review. Allows the main feature/fix to be merged while scheduling the larger improvement.
documents.s: Why Track Code Review Defects Formally? 🧐

documents.t: Not every PR comment needs a Jira ticket. Focus on issues that are: Non-Trivial: Require more than a few minutes to fix (e.g., significant refactoring, addressing a complex logical flaw, adding substantial missing test coverage). Architectural Concerns: Deviations from established patterns, performance bottlenecks, potential security risks that need more investigation or rework than a quick fix. Technical Debt: Code that works but is overly complex, hard to understand, poorly tested, or likely to cause problems later. Bugs: Actual logical errors found during review that might be complex to fix or whose fix is deferred. Simple fixes (typos, naming convention violations, minor logic adjustments) should generally be addressed directly within the PR before merging and do not need separate tracking.

Identify Trackable Issues During Code Review: When a reviewer identifies a non-trivial issue (as defined above), they should still add a comment to the Pull Request explaining the problem. Crucially: The reviewer (or the PR author, upon discussion) decides if the fix is simple enough to handle within the current PR or if it should be deferred and tracked separately. Decision Point: Fix Now vs. Track and Defer: Fix Now: If the issue is critical, blocks the core functionality of the PR, or is relatively quick to fix without significantly expanding the PR's scope. The author fixes it, pushes the update, and the review continues. Track and Defer: If the issue represents significant technical debt, requires substantial refactoring, needs more investigation, or fixing it would excessively delay the merging of the primary feature/fix. Create a Ticket in Jira (If Tracking/Deferring): Reviewer or Author: Creates a new task in Jira. Ticket Details: Type: "TechDebt," "Bug," or "Task" (use a consistent type or label like code-review-finding). Title: Clearly describe the issue (e.g., "Refactor OrderService to separate concerns identified in PR #123"). Description: Paste the context: Include the relevant code snippet(s). Explain the problem: Detail why it's an issue (e.g., "Violates SRP," "Hard to test," "Potential performance issue under load"). Link back to the PR comment: Provide a direct link to the specific comment in the Pull Request where the issue was raised. Suggest a potential solution if obvious. Assignee: Assign initially to the original PR author or the Tech Lead for prioritization. Labels: Add relevant labels (tech-debt, refactoring, performance, security, code-review-finding). Link and Update PR: In the PR Comment: The person who created the Jira ticket should reply to the original review comment, stating that the issue is being tracked separately and providing the Jira ticket link. (e.g., "Good point. This requires a larger refactor. Created ticket MEC-789 to track this. Let's merge the current changes and address the refactor separately."). PR Status: This allows the reviewer to potentially resolve their comment (knowing the issue is tracked) and approve the PR, unblocking the merge of the main feature/fix. Manage in Technical Backlog: The newly created Jira ticket automatically enters the Technical Backlog (Item 137). It gets prioritized during Technical Backlog Refinement along with other technical tasks. It will eventually be scheduled into a sprint based on its priority. (Optional) Track Metrics: Use Jira filters or dashboards based on the label/issue type (code-review-finding) to track: Number of significant defects found per sprint/month. Common types of defects being found. Resolution rate of these defects. Discuss these metrics during Architecture Maturity Reviews (Item 133) or Retrospectives to identify trends or areas for process improvement (e.g., if many similar defects are found, maybe coding standards need clarification or training is needed). By formally tracking significant issues found during code reviews, you ensure they are not lost and can be addressed systematically, contributing to long-term code health without unnecessarily blocking feature delivery. Jira ↔️ PR

Item: 97 | Architecture Validation | Continuous Testing | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 2 | Unit tests are coded and planned within each business story. | Add "Unit tests written and passing" (for flutter test) as a mandatory item in the "Definition of Done" for all stories involving business logic. | | This guide explains the practice of writing unit tests as an integral part of implementing a user story, rather than as an afterthought.
documents.s: Completing Item 97: Code Unit Tests Within Stories

documents.t: Testable Code: Encourages writing code that is inherently more testable (modular, loosely coupled) because testing is considered during implementation. Immediate Feedback: Provides developers with fast feedback on the correctness of their logic as they build it. Regression Prevention: Creates a safety net, ensuring that future changes don't break the logic implemented in the story. Living Documentation: Well-written unit tests serve as executable documentation, clarifying how individual components are expected to behave. Part of "Done": Ensures testing isn't skipped or deferred due to time pressure; it's a required part of completing the story.
documents.s: Why Write Unit Tests Within the Story Scope?

documents.t: Focus unit tests on the "logic" parts of your code, typically outside the direct UI rendering: State Management: Blocs, Cubits, Providers, ViewModels (testing state transitions and logic). Use bloc_test or similar helpers (Item 15). Business Logic: Use Cases, Interactors, Services. Data Layer: Repository implementations (mocking data sources), data mappers/transformers. Utility Functions: Validators, formatters, calculation helpers. Widget Tests (flutter test for widgets) are also crucial and often included within the story scope, especially for verifying UI reactions to state changes or simple interactions, but this item often emphasizes logic unit tests.

Include Testing in Definition of Done (DoD): This is the key enforcement mechanism. Add explicit criteria to your team's DoD (Item 86): ✅ Unit tests written for new/modified business logic. ✅ Relevant widget tests written/updated for UI changes. ✅ All unit and widget tests passing (flutter test). (Optional) Meets code coverage target on new code (Item 24). A story cannot be considered "Done" (ready for QA) until these criteria are met. Plan Testing During Refinement/Task Breakdown: When breaking down a story into sub-tasks during Sprint Planning or refinement, explicitly include tasks for writing tests: "Implement login logic in LoginBloc." "Write unit tests for LoginBloc." "Create LoginScreen UI." "Write widget tests for LoginScreen." Factor the time/effort for writing tests into the story's overall estimate. Adopt a Test-Driven Development (TDD) or Test-First Approach (Optional but Recommended): TDD Cycle (Red-Green-Refactor): Red: Write a failing unit test for a small piece of desired functionality. Green: Write the simplest possible production code to make the test pass. Refactor: Improve the production code (and potentially the test code) while ensuring tests still pass. Even if not strictly following TDD, writing tests alongside or immediately after writing the corresponding production code is more effective than writing them much later. Provide Testing Guidance and Examples (Item 15): Ensure developers have clear documentation and examples showing how to write effective unit and widget tests for your project's architecture (e.g., testing Blocs with bloc_test, mocking repositories with mocktail). Enforce During Code Review: Code reviewers must check for the existence and quality of unit/widget tests as part of their PR review. Are the tests meaningful? Do they cover important logic branches and edge cases? Is the test coverage adequate for the changes made? PR approval should be withheld if testing is insufficient. Automate Test Execution in CI: Ensure flutter test runs automatically on every PR (Item 88) and merge to main (Item 83). The build must fail if tests fail. By making unit testing an inseparable part of the development process for each story, you build quality and maintainability into the codebase from the start.

Item: 156 | Architecture Validation | Continuous Testing | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 2 | "Unit test cases, as well as Assert conditions, are always updated every time business logic is changed." | When a dev changes business logic, the "Definition of Done" requires them to update the corresponding unit tests in the same PR. | | This guide focuses on the critical practice of ensuring that automated unit tests (and widget tests) are kept up-to-date whenever the underlying application code or business logic they cover is modified.
documents.s: Completing Item 156: Keep Unit Tests Updated

documents.t: Maintain Accuracy: Outdated unit tests provide a false sense of security. They might pass even if the logic they originally tested is now broken or behaves differently. Prevent Regressions: Updated tests act as a safety net, ensuring that changes to one part of the code don't inadvertently break existing functionality covered by the tests. Guide Refactoring: A comprehensive suite of up-to-date unit tests gives developers confidence to refactor code, knowing the tests will quickly flag any introduced errors. Executable Documentation: Unit tests document the intended behavior of code units. Keeping them updated ensures this documentation remains accurate. Enable CI/CD: Reliable automated checks depend on tests accurately reflecting the current codebase. Failing builds due to outdated tests waste time.

Updates are necessary whenever: Business Logic Changes: The core requirements or rules implemented in a Bloc, Use Case, Repository method, or utility function are modified. Code Refactoring: The internal implementation of a method or class changes, potentially affecting its inputs, outputs, or dependencies, even if the external behavior should remain the same. Tests verify this. Dependency Changes: The way a unit interacts with its mocked dependencies changes (e.g., calling a different repository method, expecting a different data structure). Bug Fixes: When fixing a bug in a logic unit, the corresponding unit test(s) should be reviewed, updated, or added (Item 161) to explicitly cover the bug scenario and prevent its recurrence.
documents.s: When Should Unit Tests Be Updated?

documents.t: Co-locate Tests and Code: Keep test files adjacent to the source files they test (e.g., user_repository.dart and user_repository_test.dart). This makes it easy for developers to find and update tests when modifying the source code. Integrate into Definition of Done (DoD) (Crucial): Add a specific, non-negotiable checklist item to your team's Definition of Done for user stories and bug fixes: ✅ Unit tests updated (or added) for modified/new logic and passing. A story or bug fix is not "Done" until the associated tests accurately reflect the final code state and pass. Update Tests During Implementation/Refactoring: Treat Tests as Part of the Change: Developers must consider updating tests as an integral part of making any code change, not a separate, later task. TDD (Test-Driven Development): If using TDD, this happens naturally. When requirements change, the tests are updated first to reflect the new expected behavior, and then the code is changed to make the new tests pass. Test-After: If writing tests after code, developers must run the existing tests after making code changes. If tests fail because the logic correctly changed, update the tests (assertions, mock setups) to match the new expected behavior. If tests fail because the code change introduced an unintended regression, fix the code, not the test. Refactoring: When refactoring, existing tests should ideally still pass (as external behavior shouldn't change). If refactoring involves changing method signatures or dependencies, update the test setup and calls accordingly. Pull Request (PR) Includes Test Updates: Any PR that modifies application code covered by unit tests must include the corresponding updates to those unit tests within the same PR. Do not allow merging code changes without their accompanying test updates. Enforce During Code Review: Code reviewers (Item 143) must explicitly check that unit tests have been appropriately added or updated as part of the PR. Questions to ask during review: "Does this PR change logic covered by existing tests?", "If so, are the tests updated?", "Are new tests added for new logic paths?", "Do the updated assertions accurately reflect the new requirements?". Withhold PR approval if necessary test updates are missing or incorrect. CI Pipeline Enforcement: The CI pipeline must run all unit tests on every PR (flutter test) and fail the build if any test fails (Item 159). This ensures that broken or outdated tests prevent merging. By making unit test maintenance an inseparable part of the development process, enforced by the DoD, code reviews, and CI, you ensure your test suite remains a reliable asset for quality assurance and safe refactoring throughout the project's lifecycle. ♻️

Item: 99 | Architecture Validation | Continuous Testing | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 2 | "Unit test cases, as well as Assert conditions, are always updated every time business logic is changed." | When a dev changes business logic, the "Definition of Done" requires them to update the corresponding unit tests in the same PR. | | This guide emphasizes the critical practice of updating existing unit tests (and widget tests) whenever the corresponding application code's logic or behavior is modified.
documents.s: Completing Item 99: Update Unit Tests When Logic Changes

documents.t: Maintain Test Relevance: Outdated tests that no longer reflect the current logic provide a false sense of security (they might still pass but test the wrong thing) or fail unnecessarily (requiring investigation or deletion). Prevent Regressions Accurately: Updated tests ensure that the intended new behavior is locked in and that future changes don't
documents.s: Why Update Tests When Code Changes?

documents.t: Item: 50 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Deployment | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 3 | "The backup strategy is automated for all environments (database, files, etc)." | (Infra-focused) Configure automated daily snapshots for the GCP/AWS databases for all environments. | | (Note: This primarily relates to infrastructure and backend components supporting the Flutter app). This guide covers implementing and verifying that backup strategies for critical data assets (like databases) are automated across all relevant environments (Development, Staging, Production).
documents.s: Completing Item 50: Automate Backup Strategy for All Environments

documents.t: Reliability: Manual backups are easily forgotten or performed inconsistently. Automation ensures backups happen regularly as scheduled. Consistency: Uses the same process every time, reducing human error. Reduced Overhead: Frees up team members from performing manual backup tasks. Disaster Recovery Foundation: Automated backups are essential for any effective disaster recovery plan (Items 12 & 13).

Identify Assets Requiring Automated Backups: Focus on stateful components where data loss would be problematic. The most common asset is the database. User-generated content (e.g., files in Cloud Storage/S3) might also require specific backup configurations if versioning/replication isn't sufficient. Application source code and configuration-as-code are typically covered by Git (Items 12 & 13) and don't usually need separate automated backup jobs beyond the Git provider's own redundancy. Leverage Managed Cloud Services (Preferred): If using managed database services (e.g., GCP Cloud SQL, AWS RDS, Azure SQL Database, MongoDB Atlas, Firestore), utilize their built-in automated backup features. This is usually the easiest and most reliable approach. Configuration (Example: GCP Cloud SQL): Navigate to the Cloud SQL instance settings in the GCP Console. Go to the "Backups" section. Enable Automated Backups: Ensure this is checked. Configure Schedule: Set a daily backup window (usually during off-peak hours). Configure Retention: Define how many days backups should be kept (e.g., 7 days for Dev/Staging, 14-30 days for Prod - as defined in Items 12 & 13). Enable Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR): Enable this for Production (and potentially Staging if needed) to allow restoring to any specific minute within the retention window (usually requires Write-Ahead Logs). Location: Choose backup location (e.g., multi-region for production resilience). Configuration (Other Services): Follow the specific documentation for your managed database service (AWS RDS automated snapshots, MongoDB Atlas cloud backups, Firestore backups, etc.). The principles (enable automation, set schedule, set retention) are similar. Implement Custom Backup Scripts (If Managed Services Not Used/Sufficient): If running self-managed databases or needing backups for other assets not covered by cloud features: Scripting: Write scripts using database-native tools (pg_dump, mysqldump, mongodump) or file system tools (rsync, tar) to create backup files. Storage: Securely copy the backup files to a durable storage location (e.g., Cloud Storage, S3), preferably in a different region or account. Scheduling: Use a scheduler (e.g., cron on a dedicated utility VM, Cloud Scheduler, AWS EventBridge Scheduler) to run these scripts automatically on the desired frequency (e.g., daily). Monitoring & Alerting: Implement checks to ensure the scheduled backup jobs run successfully and alert the team if they fail. Retention: Implement scripts or lifecycle policies on the storage bucket to automatically delete old backups according to the retention policy. Verify Automation Across Environments: Go through the configuration for each environment (Development, Staging, Production). Confirm that automated backups are configured and enabled according to the strategy defined in Items 12 and 13. Don't assume dev/staging are automatically configured just because production is. Often, they need separate enablement (perhaps with shorter retention). Monitoring and Verification: Check Backup Status: Regularly (e.g., weekly check via console, or set up automated alerts) verify that automated backups are completing successfully for all environments. Cloud providers usually offer monitoring metrics for backup status. Test Restores: Periodically test restoring from these automated backups (to a non-production environment) to ensure they are valid and the restore process works (as mentioned in Items 12 & 13). Document the Automation: In your Backup Strategy documents (Items 12 & 13), explicitly state how backups are automated for each asset and environment (e.g., "Production Cloud SQL: Automated daily snapshots enabled via GCP console, 30-day retention," "Staging MongoDB: Daily mongodump via cronjob to GCS bucket, 7-day retention via lifecycle policy"). By ensuring backups are fully automated across all environments, you establish a reliable foundation for data recovery and reduce the risk associated with manual processes.

Item: 49 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Deployment | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 3 | The scripts for database changes are automatically deployed in the deployment pipeline. | (Backend-focused) Integrate the DB migration tool (e.g., Liquibase, Flyway) as a step in the backend's deployment pipeline. | | (Note: This primarily concerns the backend deployment pipeline supporting your Flutter app). This guide explains how to integrate the execution of incremental database migration scripts (managed by tools like Liquibase or Flyway, as per Item 47) into the automated deployment pipeline for the backend application.
documents.s: Completing Item 49: Automate Database Script Deployment

documents.t: Consistency: Ensures the correct database schema changes are applied automatically every time the backend application is deployed to an environment. Eliminates manual, error-prone steps. Reliability: Guarantees that the database schema is always in the state expected by the application code being deployed. Speed: Speeds up the deployment process by removing manual handoffs or interventions for database updates. CI/CD Integration: Makes database changes a seamless part of the overall continuous delivery process.

Prerequisites: A database migration tool (Liquibase, Flyway, etc.) is integrated into the backend project (Item 47). Migration scripts are versioned in the backend's Git repository. An automated deployment pipeline exists for the backend application (e.g., deploying to Kubernetes, Serverless, VMs). Choose Integration Point: The database migration command should run before the new application code starts serving traffic but after any necessary infrastructure provisioning or updates. Common Patterns: As part of the application startup script: The application itself runs the migration command upon starting. Simple, but can increase startup time and requires careful handling of multiple instances starting simultaneously (locking). As a dedicated step in the deployment pipeline: Before deploying the new application version, run the migration command against the target database. This is generally preferred for better control and separation. Using Init Containers (Kubernetes): Run the migration command in a Kubernetes Init Container that completes successfully before the main application container starts. This handles locking well in distributed environments. Configure the Pipeline Step: Add a new step to the backend's deployment pipeline (e.g., in Jenkinsfile, gitlab-ci.yml, cloudbuild.yaml, GitHub Actions workflow). This step should execute the chosen migration tool's "update" or "migrate" command. Environment Configuration: Ensure the pipeline step securely provides the correct database connection details (URL, username, password/secret) for the target environment (Dev, Staging, Prod). Use secrets management provided by the CI/CD platform. Example (Conceptual Pipeline Step using Liquibase CLI): # (Assuming Liquibase CLI is installed/available in the build agent) - name: Apply Database Migrations env: DB_URL: ${{ secrets.STAGING_DB_URL }} # From CI/CD Secrets DB_USERNAME: ${{ secrets.STAGING_DB_USERNAME }} DB_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.STAGING_DB_PASSWORD }} run: | liquibase --url="$DB_URL" \ --username="$DB_USERNAME" \ --password="$DB_PASSWORD" \ --changeLogFile=src/main/resources/db/changelog/db.changelog-master.yaml \ update # The command to apply changes Example (Conceptual Pipeline Step using Flyway Docker): - name: Apply Database Migrations env: FLYWAY_URL: ${{ secrets.STAGING_DB_URL }} FLYWAY_USER: ${{ secrets.STAGING_DB_USERNAME }} FLYWAY_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.STAGING_DB_PASSWORD }} run: | docker run --rm -v $(pwd)/src/main/resources/db/migration:/flyway/sql \ flyway/flyway:latest migrate Error Handling: Configure the pipeline step to fail the entire deployment if the database migration command fails. This prevents deploying application code that is incompatible with the database schema. Ensure migration tool logs are captured by the CI/CD system for troubleshooting. Permissions: Ensure the database user configured for the migration tool has sufficient permissions to make schema changes (e.g., ALTER TABLE, CREATE TABLE, CREATE INDEX) in the target database. It might be a different user than the application's runtime user (which might only have CRUD permissions). Testing: Thoroughly test the pipeline integration in non-production environments first. Verify that migrations are applied correctly and that the application starts successfully afterwards. Test the failure scenario (e.g., by introducing a deliberately broken migration script) to ensure the pipeline stops as expected. Documentation: Document this step within the backend's CI/CD pipeline documentation, explaining how database migrations are handled automatically. By integrating database migrations directly into the deployment pipeline, you ensure that database schema evolution is a reliable, automated part of your release process.

Item: 139 | Architecture Management | Technical Backlog management | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 3 | "Recurrent follow-up meetings are conducted by the technical responsible in order to discuss the
goals and issues that came out from the code quality analysis." | Biweekly meetings, syncup meetings | | (Note: User comment suggests incorporating into existing biweekly/syncup meetings) This guide explains how to establish a regular cadence for discussing code quality goals and issues identified through static analysis tools (like SonarQube/SonarCloud or flutter analyze).
documents.s: Completing Item 139: Hold Code Quality Follow-up Meetings

documents.t: Maintain Focus: Keeps code quality visible and top-of-mind for the team, reinforcing its importance. Analyze Trends: Allows the team to look beyond individual PR issues and identify recurring patterns, systemic problems, or areas where quality is degrading over time. Shared Understanding: Ensures the team collectively understands the quality goals (e.g., Quality Gate criteria - Item 25) and how to interpret the analysis results. Identify Root Causes: Provides a forum to discuss why certain issues keep appearing (e.g., misunderstanding a convention, missing documentation, overly complex module) rather than just fixing symptoms. Generate Improvement Actions: Leads to identifying specific actions, such as targeted refactoring (adding to Tech Backlog - Item 137), updating coding conventions (Item 3), or conducting focused training/pairing sessions. Celebrate Successes: Acknowledge improvements in quality metrics.
