Integrate into Existing Meetings (Recommended): Leverage existing technical team meetings rather than creating yet another separate meeting, as suggested by the user note. Good candidates include: Technical Backlog Refinement (Item 137): Dedicate the first 10-15 minutes of this bi-weekly meeting to code quality review. Team Technical Sync-up: If you have a regular internal sync distinct from daily stand-ups. Avoid: Daily stand-ups (too short), Sprint Retrospectives (retros focus on the process of the last sprint, though quality issues can be inputs), Sprint Planning (needs to focus on the upcoming sprint). Prepare for the Review (Tech Lead/Architect): Before the meeting, briefly review the SonarQube/SonarCloud dashboard for the project. Look for: Overall Quality Gate status. Trends in key metrics (Bugs, Vulnerabilities, Smells/Tech Debt Ratio, Coverage, Duplication) - especially on "New Code." Specific modules or files with recurring or high numbers of issues. Any recently introduced "Blocker" or "Critical" issues. Review recent flutter analyze results if not fully captured by SonarQube. Prepare 1-2 key talking points or areas of concern/praise. Conduct the Quality Review Segment: Share Screen: Display the SonarQube/SonarCloud dashboard (or relevant analysis report). Review Overall Status: Briefly mention the current Quality Gate status and overall trends (improving, stable, degrading?). Highlight Key Areas: Focus on 1-2 specific points: "Notice the Maintainability rating dropped slightly this period, mainly due to increased complexity in the X module. Let's discuss if refactoring is needed." "Coverage on new code is consistently hitting our 80% target - great job!" "We saw a couple of new 'Major' bugs related to null safety this week; let's quickly review the pattern that caused them." "This deprecated method is still being used frequently; we need to prioritize replacing it." Discuss Patterns & Root Causes: Encourage a brief discussion (5-10 min) on any recurring issues. Why are they happening? Is documentation unclear? Is more training needed? Identify Action Items: If the discussion reveals needed actions (e.g., refactor module X, update documentation on pattern Y, add specific lint rule), capture these. Create and Track Action Items: For specific code improvements (refactoring, fixing smells), create Jira tasks and add them to the Technical Backlog (Item 137). For process/documentation changes, create tasks or assign owners directly. Follow up on these action items in subsequent meetings or backlog refinements. Keep it Focused and Actionable: Stick to the allocated timebox (10-15 min). Avoid deep dives into specific lines of code unless illustrating a key pattern. Address specific PR issues during code reviews. The goal is trend analysis, shared understanding, and identifying actionable improvements for the backlog. By dedicating a small, regular amount of time to collectively review code quality metrics, you foster a culture of quality ownership and drive continuous improvement in your codebase. ✨

Item: 147 | Architecture Validation | Architecture Evaluation | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 3 | The code quality is visible to everyone in the team and there is immediate feedback whenever the quality has decreased. | Post SonarQube results to a chat channel. Configure the flutter analyze CI job to fail the build on any linter errors. | We set up a weekly SonarQube job to run and report the results to Google Chat. | This guide explains how to make code quality metrics visible to the entire team and provide immediate feedback when quality standards are not met, fostering collective ownership.
documents.s: Completing Item 147: Ensure Code Quality Visibility and Feedback

documents.t: Transparency: Everyone can see the current state of code quality and how it's trending. Collective Ownership: When quality metrics are shared, quality becomes a team responsibility, not just the Architect's or Lead's concern. Fast Feedback Loop: Immediate feedback (e.g., a failing CI build on a PR) allows developers to fix issues while the context is still fresh in their minds, which is much more efficient. Delayed feedback (e.g., finding issues weeks later) is costly. Reinforces Standards: Consistent, automated feedback reinforces adherence to coding standards and quality goals. Motivation: Seeing quality metrics improve can be motivating; seeing them decline can be a call to action.
documents.s: Why Make Quality Visible and Feedback Immediate? 👀

documents.t: Immediate Feedback via CI on Pull Requests (Most Important): Static Analysis (flutter analyze): Configure your CI pipeline to run flutter analyze --fatal-infos --fatal-warnings . on every Pull Request. This job must fail the build if any errors or warnings (based on your analysis_options.yaml - Item 145) are found. Formatting Check (dart format): Configure CI to run dart format --output=none --set-exit-if-changed . on every PR. This must fail if code isn't formatted correctly (Item 6). Unit/Widget Tests (flutter test): Configure CI to run flutter test on every PR. This must fail if any tests fail (Item 159). SonarQube/SonarCloud Quality Gate: If using SonarQube/Cloud (Item 6, 25), configure it to analyze the PR and fail the build if the defined Quality Gate conditions (e.g., coverage on new code < 80%, new critical bugs > 0) are not met. Required Status Checks: Configure your Git host (GitHub/GitLab) branch protection rules (Item 8) to require all these CI checks to pass before a PR can be merged. This provides immediate, blocking feedback. Visibility of CI Results: Ensure CI results (pass/fail status, links to logs, SonarQube reports) are clearly visible directly within the Pull Request interface. Most CI/Git host integrations do this automatically. Developers should see a clear red 'X' or green '✓'. Shareable Dashboards: SonarQube/SonarCloud: Make the project dashboard accessible to the entire team (read-only is usually sufficient). This dashboard shows overall trends for bugs, vulnerabilities, smells, coverage, duplication etc. Test Coverage Reports: If not using SonarQube, configure CI to publish the HTML coverage report (lcov output) as an artifact, so team members can view detailed coverage if needed. Monitoring Dashboards (for NFRs): Share links to Firebase Performance Monitoring, Crashlytics, and relevant backend monitoring dashboards (Datadog, etc.) that track NFRs related to quality (e.g., crash rate, performance targets). Automated Notifications (Use Sparingly but Effectively): CI Failures: Configure CI to post a notification to the main technical chat channel (#proj-mobile-tech or #proj-mobile-alerts) only when a build/check fails on the main branch (e.g., main). PR failures are visible in the PR itself. Over-notifying for every PR failure creates too much noise. SonarQube Summary (Optional): As noted in the item, setting up a periodic (e.g., weekly) summary post from SonarQube to a chat channel can be useful to remind the team of overall trends, but immediate PR feedback is more critical. Daily posts are usually too noisy. Production Alerts: Critical production alerts (crashes, performance spikes) should definitely go to a dedicated alerts channel (Item 100). Discuss During Regular Meetings: Briefly review key quality dashboards (SonarQube, Coverage, Firebase Crashlytics/Performance) during regular technical meetings (e.g., Technical Backlog Refinement, Architecture Maturity Review - Items 139, 140, 141) to discuss trends and identify areas needing attention. Documentation Links: Include links to the key quality dashboards (SonarQube, Firebase, etc.) in your project's main README or development hub wiki page for easy access. By making quality metrics highly visible and integrating immediate feedback directly into the PR workflow, you create a system where quality is constantly monitored and actively managed by the entire team. 📊✅❌

Item: 148 | Architecture Validation | Architecture Evaluation | PREPARATION (Sprint 0) | 3 | The build will fail if the code that was created does not match the code quality goals. | Configure the SonarQube/SonarCloud quality gate to fail the CI pipeline if (e.g.) "New Code Coverage < 80%" or "New Blocker Issues > 0". | | This guide details how to configure your CI/CD pipeline to automatically fail if the code changes in a Pull Request (PR) do not meet the predefined code quality goals, specifically focusing on metrics typically enforced via SonarQube/SonarCloud Quality Gates.
documents.s: Completing Item 148: Fail Build if Quality Goals Not Met

documents.t: Enforcement: Acts as an automated gatekeeper, preventing code that degrades quality (e.g., lowers coverage, introduces critical issues) from being merged into the main codebase. Documentation and guidelines alone are often insufficient. Immediate Feedback: Provides the fastest possible feedback to the developer that their changes do not meet the agreed-upon standards (Item 147). Consistency: Ensures that quality standards are applied consistently to all code changes, regardless of the author or reviewer. Reduces Reviewer Burden: Automates the checking of objective metrics (coverage, bugs, smells), allowing human reviewers to focus on logic, design, and usability. Drives Improvement: Motivates developers to address quality issues early in the development cycle.
documents.s: Why Fail the Build on Quality Goals? 🚫

documents.t: Static Analysis Tools Integrated: You have flutter analyze running in CI (Item 145) and failing the build on errors/warnings. SonarQube/SonarCloud Integrated: SonarQube or SonarCloud is set up to analyze your Flutter project within the CI pipeline (Item 6). Quality Goals Defined: You have defined specific, measurable quality goals, particularly for "New Code" (Code Coverage - Item 24, Static Analysis Metrics - Item 25).

Define the SonarQube/SonarCloud Quality Gate: Log in to your SonarQube/SonarCloud instance. Navigate to Quality Gates. Create a new Quality Gate specific to your project or organization, or edit the default ("Sonar way"). Add Conditions - Focus on "On New Code": Add conditions that apply specifically to the code changed within the Pull Request or since the last release. This is crucial for incremental improvement. Common conditions include: Coverage on New Code | is less than | 80% (Adjust percentage based on Item 24) Maintainability Rating on New Code | is worse than | A Reliability Rating on New Code | is worse than | A Security Rating on New Code | is worse than | A (Alternatively, use counts for new issues) New Bugs | is greater than | 0 New Vulnerabilities | is greater than | 0 New Code Smells | is greater than | 0 (Can be noisy; consider rating or only Blocker/Critical smells) Duplicated Lines (%) on New Code | is greater than | 3% (Or 5%) Security Hotspots on New Code | is greater than | 0 (This condition ensures new hotspots must be reviewed/acknowledged in SonarQube before the gate passes). Assign the Quality Gate: Make sure this Quality Gate is explicitly assigned to your Flutter project within SonarQube/SonarCloud settings. Configure CI Pipeline to Wait for Quality Gate Result: Your CI pipeline step that runs the SonarQube/SonarCloud analysis needs to wait for the analysis results and the Quality Gate status from the SonarQube server. Most official SonarSource CI integrations (like SonarSource/sonarcloud-github-action for GitHub Actions or specific scanner CLI options) handle this automatically. They will: Run the scanner locally in the CI job. Upload the results to SonarQube/SonarCloud. Poll the server for the analysis report and Quality Gate status. Exit the CI job with an error code if the Quality Gate fails. Example (Conceptual GitHub Actions using official action): - name: SonarCloud Scan uses: SonarSource/sonarcloud-github-action@master env: GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} SONAR_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SONAR_TOKEN }} # This action typically waits for the report and fails the job if the Quality Gate fails. # Check the specific action's documentation for options like timeout or polling interval. Verification: Ensure that when you intentionally introduce code that violates a Quality Gate condition (e.g., significantly lower coverage, a critical bug pattern), the SonarQube step in your CI pipeline correctly reports the failure and causes the overall CI check to fail. Enforce CI Checks via Branch Protection: As mentioned in Item 147, ensure that the CI check which includes the SonarQube Quality Gate evaluation is set as a required status check in your branch protection rules for main (Item 8). This physically prevents merging a PR if its changes cause the Quality Gate to fail. Communicate to the Team: Clearly communicate which Quality Gate conditions are active and that they will block PR merges if not met. Ensure developers know how to check the SonarQube report linked in their PR to see why the gate failed and how to fix the issues. By failing the build automatically when quality goals aren't met on new code, you create a strong, immediate feedback loop that enforces your team's quality standards proactively. 💪

Item: 159 | Architecture Validation | Continuous Testing | PREPARATION (Sprint 0) | 3 | "The automated testing is integrated in the build, and the build will fail if the test coverage percentage is not enough ( < 80% ) or if the test is failing." | Add a flutter test --coverage step to the main CI pipeline. The build *must* fail if any test fails. Configure coverage gates in SonarQube. | 2025-03-30 | This guide details how to integrate your automated tests (Unit, Widget) into the main CI build pipeline and configure it to fail if tests fail or if code coverage targets are not met.
documents.s: Completing Item 159: Integrate Automated Testing in Build & Fail on Issues

documents.t: Automated Quality Gate: Provides an automatic check on every proposed code change (Pull Request) to ensure it doesn't break existing functionality or degrade test coverage below acceptable levels. Immediate Feedback: Developers get instant notification if their changes cause test failures or violate coverage rules, allowing them to fix issues quickly (Item 147). Prevents Merging Broken Code: Failing the build prevents code with failing tests or insufficient coverage from being merged into the main branch, protecting codebase stability. Enforces Testing Discipline: Reinforces the expectation that tests must pass and coverage targets must be met for code to be considered complete. Builds Confidence: A consistently "green" build provides confidence that the codebase is in a healthy state.
documents.s: Why Integrate Tests and Fail the Build? ✋

documents.t: Run Unit and Widget Tests in CI: Ensure your main CI pipeline (running on every PR and merge to main) includes a step that executes your unit and widget tests. Command: Use flutter test. Failure Condition: The flutter test command automatically exits with a non-zero exit code if any test fails. The CI pipeline step MUST be configured to fail if the command exits with a non-zero code. This is the default behavior for most CI platforms. Example (GitHub Actions): - name: Run Unit & Widget Tests run: flutter test # This step will automatically fail if any test fails Generate Coverage Report in CI: Add the --coverage flag to the test command to generate the coverage report (lcov.info), which is needed for coverage checks. - name: Run Tests and Generate Coverage run: flutter test --coverage # This still fails if tests fail, but also creates coverage/lcov.info Enforce Coverage Target (Fail Build if Not Met): This requires integrating a tool that analyzes the coverage report and checks against your defined goal (Item 24), specifically focusing on "Coverage on New Code" (Item 154). Using SonarQube/SonarCloud (Recommended): Configure Quality Gate: Ensure your SonarQube/Cloud Quality Gate has a condition like Coverage on New Code is less than 80% (adjust target %) and that this gate is assigned to your project (Item 148). Configure CI Step: Ensure the CI step running the SonarQube/Cloud analysis is configured to wait for the server analysis and fail the CI job if the Quality Gate fails (Item 148). # Example using SonarCloud GitHub Action (assumes previous test step generated coverage) - name: SonarCloud Scan uses: SonarSource/sonarcloud-github-action@master env: GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} SONAR_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SONAR_TOKEN }} # This action fails the job if the SonarCloud Quality Gate fails Using Other Coverage Tools (e.g., Codecov/Coveralls): Configure the tool to analyze the lcov.info report uploaded from CI. Configure coverage targets and thresholds within the tool's settings (e.g., "Fail PR if coverage on new code drops below 80%"). Ensure the tool provides a status check back to your Git host (GitHub/GitLab). Configure Branch Protection Rules: In your Git host (GitHub/GitLab), configure branch protection rules for your main branch (Item 8). Crucially: Add the CI checks corresponding to: Running flutter test. The SonarQube Quality Gate status (or the status from your alternative coverage tool). Mark these checks as required for merging. This physically prevents merging a PR if tests fail or coverage targets aren't met. Communicate Expectations: Ensure the entire team understands that: All tests must pass for a PR to be merged. New code must meet the defined coverage threshold. A failing build due to tests or coverage requires the developer to fix the issues before merging. By integrating tests and coverage checks directly into the build pipeline and configuring them to fail on issues, you create essential automated quality gates that protect your main branch and enforce your team's quality standards. ✅❌

Item: 31 | Architecture Definition | Non-functional requirements | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 3 | The top important non-functional requirements related to performance are defined and mapped within each business story. | Add an "NFR" field or "Acceptance Criteria" bullet point to Jira stories that have performance implications (e.g., "List must load and render 100 items smoothly"). | | This guide explains how to ensure that relevant performance NFRs (Non-Functional Requirements) are considered and explicitly linked to specific user stories during development sprints.
documents.s: Completing Item 31: Map Performance NFRs to Stories

documents.t: Contextual Awareness: Reminds developers and QA to consider performance implications while implementing and testing a specific feature. Targeted Testing: Guides performance testing efforts towards the features where it matters most. Clear Acceptance: Makes performance expectations part of the story's acceptance criteria. Prevents Regressions: Helps catch performance issues related to new features before they reach production.
documents.s: Why Map Performance NFRs to Stories?

documents.t: Identify Performance-Sensitive Stories: During backlog refinement or sprint planning, review upcoming user stories. Identify stories that are likely to have a noticeable impact on performance or where performance is a key aspect of the user experience. Examples: Implementing screens that display large lists of data. Introducing complex animations or transitions. Features involving heavy computations or data processing on the device. Integrating new background processes. Fetching or displaying large images/media. Core user flows (e.g., login, checkout, main dashboard loading). Reference Relevant NFR Targets: Recall the specific, quantified performance NFRs defined for the project (from Item 30), such as: Screen Render Time < 500ms Maintain ~60 FPS during scroll App Startup Time < 2.0s Add Performance Criteria to the Story: Option A: Dedicated NFR Field (if Jira supports it): Link the story to the relevant NFR ID(s) (e.g., PERF-01, PERF-02). Option B: Acceptance Criteria (Most Common): Add specific, performance-related bullet points to the story's Acceptance Criteria (AC). These ACs should be inspired by the NFR targets but tailored to the story's context. Bad AC: "List should be fast." Good AC: "The product list screen must load and display the first 20 items within 500ms on a mid-range Android device (e.g., Galaxy A50)." Good AC: "Scrolling through the product list (up to 100 items) must maintain smooth scrolling (~60 FPS) with no noticeable jank on target devices." Good AC: "Applying the filter should update the list within 300ms." Option C: NFR Checklist in Description: Add a checklist section to the story description: **NFR Considerations:** - [x] Performance: List scrolling smoothness (Target: ~60 FPS) - [ ] Security: N/A - [ ] Accessibility: N/A Discuss During Refinement/Planning: Explicitly discuss the performance ACs or considerations when refining the story. Ensure the team understands the performance expectations and considers them during estimation and technical design. Verify During Development and QA: Developers: Should use Flutter DevTools (Performance view, Performance Overlay) during development to profile and optimize the feature against the criteria. QA: Should perform manual testing on target devices to specifically validate the performance-related ACs (e.g., checking for scroll jank, measuring load times if feasible). Automated Tests: While hard to fully automate FPS checks, automated integration tests can verify load times or item counts within a timeframe. By explicitly mapping performance considerations to relevant stories, you integrate performance awareness directly into the development workflow.

Item: 33 | Architecture Definition | Non-functional requirements | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 3 | "NFR is reviewed everytime business requirement changed (via backlog refinement, planning, customer feedback, etc)" | Add an "NFR Impact" check to the team's "Definition of Ready" for all new user stories during backlog refinement. | | This guide explains how to establish a process for regularly reviewing Non-Functional Requirements (NFRs) in response to changes in business requirements or other project factors.
documents.s: Completing Item 33: Establish NFR Review Cadence

documents.t: Maintain Alignment: Business priorities can shift, potentially changing the importance or target values of certain NFRs (e.g., initial focus on speed-to-market might relax performance NFRs temporarily, while a later focus on scale might tighten them). Impact Assessment: New features or changes to existing ones can impact NFRs (e.g., adding a complex background sync feature impacts performance and battery life). Reviewing NFRs helps identify these impacts early. Proactive Adjustments: Allows the team to adjust architecture, design, or testing strategies if changing requirements put NFR targets at risk. Avoid Surprises: Prevents situations where the team delivers a feature that functions correctly but fails to meet underlying quality expectations because NFRs weren't reconsidered.

Integrate NFR Check into Change Management Processes: The core idea is to make NFR review a trigger-based activity linked to requirement changes. Backlog Refinement/Sprint Planning: This is the most crucial checkpoint. Add an "NFR Impact Assessment" item to your team's Definition of Ready (DoR) checklist for user stories. During refinement, for every story (or at least significant ones), explicitly ask: "Does this feature significantly impact Performance (speed, memory, battery)?" (Refer to NFR targets like PERF-01, PERF-02). "Does this feature handle sensitive Data or affect Authentication/Authorization?" (Refer to SEC-01, SEC-02). "Does this feature impact Reliability (e.g., offline scenarios, complex state)?" (Refer to REL-01). "Does this feature have specific Accessibility requirements?" (Refer to USAB-01). "Does this introduce new Compatibility constraints (e.g., require a newer OS version)?" (Refer to COMP-01). If the answer is YES to any of these, ensure the story includes specific Acceptance Criteria related to that NFR (as per Items 31 & 32). If a new feature fundamentally changes how an NFR should be measured or targeted (e.g., adding offline mode changes how "availability" is perceived), schedule a separate discussion to update the NFR document (Item 28/30). Change Requests: If significant changes to requirements occur mid-sprint or outside the regular planning cycle, the Tech Lead/Architect should perform a quick NFR impact assessment as part of analyzing the change request. Customer Feedback Review: When reviewing user feedback (e.g., app store reviews, support tickets), pay attention to comments related to NFRs (slowness, crashes, security concerns, usability issues). This feedback might trigger a review of specific NFR targets or priorities. Architecture Decision Records (ADRs): When making significant technical decisions (Item 19), explicitly document the expected impact (positive or negative) on relevant NFRs in the ADR. Document the Review Process: Update your team's "Definition of Ready" document on the wiki to include the "NFR Impact Assessment" checkpoint. Briefly mention in your NFR documentation (Item 27/28) that NFRs are reviewed as part of the backlog refinement process. Perform Ad-Hoc Reviews When Necessary: Beyond the regular checkpoints, the Tech Lead or Architect should initiate an NFR review if: Monitoring reveals consistent failure to meet an NFR target (e.g., crash rate increasing). A major technology change occurs (e.g., Flutter major version upgrade, backend platform migration). Significant shifts in business strategy or user expectations are communicated. By embedding NFR consideration into the regular flow of requirements handling, you ensure that quality attributes remain aligned with functional development throughout the project lifecycle.

Item: 32 | Architecture Definition | Non-functional requirements | SETUP | 3 | "The Non-functional requirements related to security are defined and mapped within each individual business story.
" | For stories involving user data or auth (e.g., login, profile), add security-specific Acceptance Criteria (e.g., "Ensure PII is not logged," "Input must be sanitized"). | | (Note: The item phase is listed as SETUP, but the mapping often happens during DEVELOPMENT sprints as stories are refined. The principle applies regardless). This guide explains how to ensure relevant security NFRs (Non-Functional Requirements) are considered and explicitly linked to specific user stories, especially those handling sensitive data or involving authentication/authorization.
documents.s: Completing Item 32: Map Security NFRs to Stories

documents.t: Contextual Security Awareness: Makes security a requirement for specific features, not an afterthought. Reduces Vulnerabilities: Prompts developers to implement security best practices (input validation, proper data handling) precisely where needed. Clear Acceptance: Makes security expectations part of the story's acceptance criteria. Targeted Testing: Guides security testing (manual or automated) towards features with higher risk profiles.
documents.s: Why Map Security NFRs to Stories?

documents.t: Identify Security-Sensitive Stories: During backlog refinement or sprint planning, review upcoming user stories. Identify stories that handle sensitive data, interact with authentication/authorization, involve user input that could be malicious, or modify critical system state. Examples: Login, registration, password reset flows. User profile creation/editing (handling PII - Personally Identifiable Information). Payment processing or handling financial data. Any feature involving user-generated content or input fields. Features modifying permissions or roles. Integration with third-party services requiring API keys or tokens. Reference Relevant Security NFRs/Principles: Recall the specific security NFRs (Item 30) and general security best practices: Input Validation (Prevent XSS, Injection). Output Encoding. Authentication & Session Management. Authorization (Least Privilege). Secure Data Storage (Encryption at rest, avoid storing sensitive data unnecessarily). Secure Data Transmission (HTTPS/TLS). Proper Error Handling (Avoid leaking sensitive info). No Hardcoded Secrets. Avoid Logging Sensitive Data (PII, tokens, passwords). Add Security Criteria to the Story: Option A: Dedicated NFR Field: Link the story to relevant Security NFR IDs (e.g., SEC-01, SEC-03). Option B: Acceptance Criteria (Most Common): Add specific, security-related bullet points to the story's Acceptance Criteria (AC). Story: User Login AC: "Password input must be masked." AC: "Authentication token must be stored securely (e.g., using flutter_secure_storage)." AC: "User credentials must only be sent over HTTPS." AC: "Backend must validate email and password format." (Backend AC, but relevant context) AC: "Login failures must return generic error messages (avoid 'user not found' vs 'wrong password')." Story: Update User Profile AC: "User input (name, bio) must be validated and sanitized to prevent XSS." AC: "Only the logged-in user can update their own profile (backend authorization required)." AC: "User's email address (PII) must not be logged in client or server logs during update." Story: Display Product List from API AC: "API call must use HTTPS." AC: "Authentication token must be included in the request header." Discuss During Refinement/Planning: Explicitly discuss the security ACs or considerations when refining the story. Ensure the team understands the security expectations and potential attack vectors for the feature. Consider if a brief "Threat Model" discussion is needed for particularly sensitive features. Verify During Development, Code Review, and QA: Developers: Implement code considering the security ACs (e.g., using input formatters, secure storage). Code Review: Reviewers must specifically check for adherence to security ACs and best practices (look for input validation, correct API calls, secure data handling, absence of logged secrets). QA: Perform testing to explicitly verify security ACs (e.g., try inputting script tags, check if password fields are masked, use a proxy to verify HTTPS). Security-focused exploratory testing is valuable here. By mapping security requirements directly to stories, you embed security into the development process, making it a shared responsibility rather than a separate phase.

Item: 146 | Architecture Validation | Architecture Evaluation | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 3 | The code review is performed by the development team and they do not depend on the Software Architect. | Encourage "peer reviews" (dev-to-dev) in addition to the tech lead review. The architect should not be the bottleneck for all PRs. | | This guide focuses on fostering a culture where code reviews are primarily conducted by peer developers within the team, rather than relying solely on the Software Architect or Tech Lead as a bottleneck.
documents.s: Completing Item 146: Enable Peer Code Reviews

documents.t: Scalability: The Architect/Lead cannot realistically review every single line of code, especially as the team grows. Peer reviews distribute the workload. Faster Feedback: Developers often get faster feedback from peers who are readily available compared to waiting for a potentially busy Architect/Lead. Knowledge Sharing: This is a major benefit. Reviewing each other's code is one of the best ways for developers to learn different parts of the codebase, understand different approaches, and improve their own skills. Team Ownership: Encourages collective responsibility for code quality across the entire team. Reduced Bus Factor: Prevents the Architect/Lead from becoming a single point of failure for code integration. Frees Up Architect/Lead: Allows the Architect/Lead to focus on higher-level design, complex reviews, mentoring, and strategic technical tasks, rather than reviewing routine changes.

Set Clear Expectations (Code Review Guidelines - Item 143): Your existing Code Review Guidelines should explicitly state that peer reviews are expected and valued. Define the minimum requirement (e.g., "At least one approving review from another developer is required before merging"). Clarify when the Architect/Lead should be involved (e.g., "Add the Tech Lead as a reviewer for changes affecting core architecture, security-sensitive areas, or introducing new major dependencies"). Empower the Team: Trust developers to provide valuable feedback. Provide training or guidance on how to perform effective code reviews if needed (referencing the guidelines). Ensure developers have sufficient understanding of the project's architecture (Item 11) and coding standards (Item 3) to review effectively. Establish a Process for Requesting Reviews: Author Assigns: The PR author should proactively request reviews from 1-2 relevant peers using the GitHub/GitLab reviewer feature. Encourage selecting reviewers familiar with the code area, but also sometimes someone unfamiliar for a fresh perspective. Team Rotations/Assignments (Optional): Some teams assign reviewers on a rotating basis or use tools/bots (like GitHub's auto-assign feature based on CODEOWNERS or round-robin). Start simple with author assignment. Communicate: Authors can post a link to their PR in the team chat channel (#proj-mobile-tech) requesting reviews. Architect/Lead Role Shift: The Architect/Lead shifts from reviewing everything to: Reviewing architecturally significant PRs (as defined in the guidelines). Performing spot-checks on already peer-reviewed PRs occasionally. Mentoring developers on how to give and receive effective feedback. Helping resolve disagreements during reviews. Monitoring overall code quality trends (using tools like SonarQube - Item 139). Configure Tooling (Branch Protection - Item 8): Ensure branch protection rules require at least one (or two, if preferred) approving review before merging. This enforces the process. Consider using a CODEOWNERS file (GitHub/GitLab feature) to automatically request reviews from specific individuals or teams when certain files/directories are modified. This can ensure experts review critical areas, supplementing general peer reviews. Foster a Positive Review Culture: Emphasize that the goal is collective improvement, not criticism. Encourage reviewers to be respectful and constructive. Encourage authors to be open to feedback and not take it personally. Recognize and appreciate thorough reviews during team meetings or retrospectives. Monitor and Adjust: During retrospectives, discuss how the peer review process is working. Are reviews timely? Is the feedback helpful? Is the workload balanced? Adjust the process as needed. By shifting the primary code review responsibility to peers, you create a more scalable, resilient, and collaborative development process that enhances both code quality and team knowledge. 🚀

Item: 38 | Architecture Definition | Technical Refinement & Design | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 3 | "The planning meetings usually go smoothly;
the technical refinement usually is on time and there are no missing definitions;
the team understands the technical documents and are comfortable with the task estimations." | Ensure technical leads prepare for planning by pre-refining complex stories, identifying dependencies, and confirming API contracts. | | This guide focuses on practices that contribute to smooth, efficient, and effective Sprint Planning meetings, building upon the foundation of timely technical refinement (Item 37).
documents.s: Completing Item 38: Ensure Smooth Planning Meetings

documents.t: Efficiency: Respects team members' time by keeping the meeting focused and within its timebox. Effective Commitment: Leads to a realistic sprint backlog that the team is confident they can deliver. Clear Sprint Goal: Allows the team to quickly align on the primary objective for the sprint. Reduced Confusion: Minimizes ambiguity about what needs to be done and how. Positive Sprint Start: Sets a positive and organized tone for the upcoming sprint.

Timely Refinement (Item 37): A sufficient number of stories at the top of the backlog must already be refined, estimated, and meet the Definition of Ready (DoR). This is the most critical factor. Well-Prepared Product Owner: The PO should come with clear sprint goal ideas and have the backlog prioritized beforehand. Stable Team Velocity: The team should have a reasonable understanding of its capacity based on past sprints.

Pre-Planning Preparation (Tech Lead / Senior Devs): Review Top Backlog: Before the planning meeting, the Tech Lead (and potentially other senior devs) should quickly review the "Ready" stories intended for the upcoming sprint. Anticipate Questions: Identify any remaining minor ambiguities or potential technical questions that might arise during planning. Prepare brief answers or pointers to documentation. Complex Story Check: For particularly complex stories (even if refined), quickly re-verify the proposed technical approach and dependencies. API/Dependency Confirmation: Double-check that any required API contracts (even if mock implementations) or critical dependencies are in place or accounted for. Structured Planning Meeting Agenda: Capacity Planning (Briefly): Note team availability (vacations, holidays). Review historical velocity as a guideline. Sprint Goal Proposal: PO presents the proposed business goal(s) for the sprint. Team discusses and refines the goal. Story Selection: PO walks through the prioritized, "Ready" stories from the top of the backlog. For each story: Briefly confirm understanding (allow quick clarifying questions, but avoid re-refining). Team confirms the estimate (usually no change needed if refinement was thorough). Team volunteers (or assigns) initial owners/pairs. Pull the story into the sprint backlog. Capacity Check: Continue selecting stories until the team feels the workload matches their capacity and fulfills the sprint goal. It's okay to slightly under-commit initially. Confirm Sprint Backlog & Goal: Final confirmation from the team that the selected stories form a coherent sprint backlog aligned with the agreed-upon sprint goal. During the Meeting - Keep it Focused: Timebox: Adhere to the agreed-upon timebox for the meeting (e.g., 1-2 hours for a 2-week sprint). Facilitation: The Scrum Master (or designated facilitator) keeps the discussion focused on the agenda items (goal setting, selection, capacity). Defer Deep Dives: If a story unexpectedly requires significant discussion or re-estimation, timebox the discussion (e.g., 5 minutes). If unresolved, remove it from the sprint and flag it for immediate re-refinement after planning. Do not let one problematic story derail the entire meeting. Task Breakdown (Optional): Some teams break stories into technical tasks during planning, others do it after planning or as the first step when a developer picks up the story. Choose what works best, but keep task breakdown efficient if done in the meeting. Post-Planning: Ensure the sprint backlog is correctly reflected in the project management tool (Jira). Team members begin working on tasks, potentially performing detailed task breakdowns for their assigned stories. By ensuring thorough refinement before planning and maintaining focus during planning, teams can make Sprint Planning a smooth, predictable, and effective ritual.

Item: 154 | Architecture Validation | Continuous Testing | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 3 | Code coverage should not be decreased. Any decrease need explaination and approval by architect (consulted with architect team). | Configure the CI pipeline to generate a code coverage report (lcov). Set the SonarQube quality gate to fail if "Coverage on New Code" is < 80%. | All code coverage settings have been established at 80% in SonarQ. Mobile SonarQ | This guide explains how to implement mechanisms to prevent code coverage from decreasing when new code is added or existing code is modified, primarily using automated checks in the CI pipeline.
documents.s: Completing Item 154: Prevent Code Coverage Decrease

documents.t: Maintains Quality Bar: Ensures that the established level of test coverage (your safety net against regressions) doesn't erode over time as the codebase evolves. Enforces Testing Discipline: Requires developers to write tests for new code as part of the implementation, reinforcing the practice of testing alongside development (Item 152). Early Feedback: Provides immediate feedback in Pull Requests if new code lacks sufficient tests, before it gets merged. Avoids "Coverage Debt": Prevents the accumulation of untested code that becomes harder and harder to add tests for later. Supports Coverage Goals: Directly supports the achievement and maintenance of the overall test coverage target (Item 24).

The most effective way to prevent overall coverage from decreasing is to enforce a minimum coverage level specifically on the new or modified lines of code within each Pull Request. It's often impractical or counterproductive to fail a build just because overall coverage dropped slightly due to minor refactoring in an untested legacy area.
documents.s: Key Strategy: Focus on "Coverage on New Code"

documents.t: Generate Coverage Reports in CI: Ensure your CI pipeline (running on every PR) includes a step to run tests and generate a coverage report in a standard format, typically lcov. - name: Run tests and generate coverage run: flutter test --coverage # This creates coverage/lcov.info Integrate Coverage Tooling: Use a tool that can analyze the coverage report and, crucially, calculate coverage specifically on the changed lines within the Pull Request compared to the target branch (main). Recommended Tool: SonarQube / SonarCloud Setup: Ensure SonarQube/Cloud analysis is part of your CI pipeline (Item 6) and is configured to receive the lcov.info report. # In sonar-project.properties sonar.dart.coverage.reportPath=coverage/lcov.info Quality Gate Configuration (Item 148): This is where the enforcement happens. Define a condition in your Quality Gate specifically "On New Code": Coverage on New Code | is less than | 80% (Use the target percentage agreed upon in Item 24). Alternative Tools: Other CI services or dedicated coverage tools (like Codecov, Coveralls) can also compare PR coverage against the base branch and provide status checks. Choose one and configure it. Fail the Build on Insufficient New Code Coverage: Configure your CI pipeline so that the SonarQube Quality Gate status (or the status from your alternative coverage tool) determines the success or failure of a required CI check. If the "Coverage on New Code" is below the threshold, the Quality Gate fails, which in turn fails the CI check. Ensure this CI check is required for merging PRs via branch protection rules (Item 8). This physically prevents merging code that doesn't meet the coverage standard for its changes. Handle Legitimate Exclusions: Configure your coverage generation or analysis tool to exclude files that shouldn't require coverage (e.g., generated code, potentially UI view files if the focus is on logic coverage). # In sonar-project.properties (example) sonar.coverage.exclusions=**/*.g.dart,**/*.freezed.dart,lib/main.dart # Or using /* LCOV_EXCL_START */ and /* LCOV_EXCL_END */ comments # in Dart code for specific sections. Process for Exceptions (Rarely Needed): The item mentions needing explanation/approval for decreases. With the "Coverage on New Code" approach, this is less common, as overall coverage might fluctuate slightly while new code remains well-tested. However, if a situation arises where meeting the new code coverage target is genuinely impractical or impossible for a specific PR (e.g., complex platform-specific integration with no easy testing path): The developer must clearly document the reason in the PR description. An explicit approval from the Architect or Tech Lead should be required to bypass the failing check (e.g., via a temporary override comment in SonarQube, or an admin merge if absolutely necessary). Track this exception: Consider creating a tech debt ticket to find a way to test this code later. This process should be rare and discouraged. Communicate and Educate: Ensure the team understands the "Coverage on New Code" requirement and how the Quality Gate enforces it. Provide guidance on how to check coverage locally and how to address coverage gaps identified by the CI checks. By focusing on enforcing coverage on new code via automated Quality Gates, you create a powerful mechanism to maintain your testing safety net and prevent the gradual erosion of code quality. 📈

Item: 158 | Architecture Validation | Continuous Testing | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 3 | "If there is a gap between the test coverage target and current situation, the necessary tasks are mapped and converted into defects in the ticket system (e.g. JIRA, ADO...)." | Run the coverage report. Identify critical files with low coverage (e.g., payment_bloc.dart) and create specific tech debt tickets to "Add tests for [file]". | | This guide explains the process of identifying specific areas where test coverage falls short of the target and tracking the work needed to address these gaps using your ticket system (e.g., Jira).
documents.s: Completing Item 158: Track Test Coverage Gaps as Defects

documents.t: Makes Gaps Actionable: Transforms a general problem ("low coverage") into specific, assignable tasks. Visibility: Makes the required testing effort visible on the backlog. Prioritization: Allows work to improve coverage to be prioritized alongside other technical debt and features within the Technical Backlog (Item 137). Tracking Progress: Enables monitoring the team's progress in closing specific coverage gaps. Targeted Improvement: Focuses effort on the most critical areas needing better test coverage, rather than trying to improve everything vaguely.
documents.s: Why Track Coverage Gaps as Defects/Tasks? 📊➡️🎫

documents.t: Identify Coverage Gaps Regularly: Source Data: Use the code coverage reports generated by your CI pipeline (lcov.info visualized via HTML report or SonarQube/SonarCloud). Review Cadence: Review coverage reports periodically, typically during the Test Automation Follow-up meeting segment (Item 140) - e.g., bi-weekly or monthly. Analysis: Look for: Overall Coverage vs. Target: Is the overall project coverage below the agreed target (Item 24)? New Code Coverage: Is the coverage on recent changes meeting the target (Item 154)? (Issues here should ideally be caught and fixed in PRs). Critical Modules/Files with Low Coverage: Identify specific files or directories containing important business logic (Blocs, Use Cases, Repositories, complex widgets) that have significantly lower coverage than the target. Prioritize these critical areas. Don't worry initially about low coverage in trivial UI code or generated files (which should be excluded). Create Tickets for Specific Gaps: For each high-priority area identified with a significant coverage gap, create a new task or defect in Jira (or your chosen tool). Ticket Details: Type: "TechDebt," "Task," or "Bug" (use a consistent type or label like test-coverage-gap). Title: Be specific (e.g., "Increase Unit Test Coverage for PaymentBloc.dart", "Add Widget Tests for OrderSummaryCard.dart"). Description: State the current coverage percentage for the file/module (if easily available). Mention the target coverage percentage. Explain why increasing coverage here is important (e.g., "Contains critical payment logic," "High complexity, risk of regression," "Related to recent production bug MEC-456"). Link to the coverage report or SonarQube page showing the gap. Assignee: Assign to the Tech Lead initially, or to the developer(s) most familiar with that code area. Labels: Add relevant labels (tech-debt, testing, coverage, module name e.g., payment). Estimate (Recommended): Estimate the effort required to write the necessary tests. Add to Technical Backlog: Place these newly created coverage improvement tasks into the Technical Backlog (Item 137). Prioritize and Schedule: During Technical Backlog Refinement meetings (Item 137), prioritize these tasks based on: Criticality of the Code: Gaps in core business logic or frequently changing areas are higher priority. Size of the Gap: Larger gaps might be broken down further or prioritized higher. Risk: Areas related to recent bugs or complex logic pose higher regression risks. Allocate capacity (Item 138) and pull prioritized coverage tasks into sprints just like other technical work. Implement and Verify: Developers implement the missing tests as part of the scheduled task. Verify the coverage increase by running coverage reports locally or checking the results after the changes are merged and analyzed by SonarQube/CI. Close the Jira ticket once the coverage gap is adequately addressed (reaching the target or significantly improved). By systematically identifying critical coverage gaps and tracking the remediation work as specific tasks, you ensure that improving test coverage becomes a manageable and prioritized part of your ongoing development efforts. 🎯

Item: 155 | Architecture Validation | Continuous Testing | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 3 | "Test cases are always up to date, updated every time a business logic is changed." | (QA) When a bug is found on a feature, as part of the fix, QA must review and update the original test case for that feature. | | This guide focuses on the process of ensuring that manual test cases are kept up-to-date and accurately reflect the current behavior of the application, especially when business logic changes or bugs are fixed. (Updating automated tests is covered in Item 156).
documents.s: Completing Item 155: Keep Test Cases Updated

documents.t: Accuracy: Outdated test cases lead to incorrect test executions, potentially passing features that are actually broken or failing features that are working correctly according to new requirements. Efficiency: Prevents wasted time executing irrelevant steps or validating against obsolete expected results. Reliability: Ensures regression testing provides meaningful results based on the current state of the application. Living Documentation: Test cases act as a form of documentation for application behavior. Keeping them updated maintains their value. Traceability: Maintains the link between requirements and how they are currently validated.
documents.s: Why Keep Manual Test Cases Updated? 🔄

documents.t: Updates are typically required when: Business Logic Changes: A user story modifies the requirements or behavior of an existing feature (e.g., changing validation rules, altering a workflow step, modifying calculation logic). UI Changes: Significant UI redesigns might require updating test steps to reflect new element names, locations, or interaction flows. Bug Fixes: When a bug is fixed, the test case(s) that should have caught the bug (or the specific bug reproduction steps) need to be reviewed and potentially updated or added to prevent regression. Environment/Data Changes: If tests rely on specific backend data or environment configurations that change.
documents.s: When Should Test Cases Be Updated?

documents.t: Link Test Cases to User Stories/Requirements: Use your test management tool (Zephyr, TestRail, etc.) to establish clear traceability between user stories (in Jira) and the manual test cases designed to verify them (Item 153). This makes it easy to identify which test cases might be affected by a story. Integrate Review into the Workflow: During Story Refinement/Planning: When discussing a story that modifies existing functionality, ask: "Which existing manual test cases will need to be updated for this change?". Note this down. As Part of Story Testing (QA): When QA tests a user story that involves changes to existing logic: They should first locate and review the existing test cases related to that feature area. As they execute tests and validate the new behavior, they should simultaneously edit and update the existing test cases (steps, expected results) to reflect the changes introduced by the story. If new scenarios are introduced, add new test cases. As Part of Bug Fix Verification (QA): When a bug fix is ready for verification, QA should first locate or create a test case that specifically reproduces the bug. Verify the fix using that test case. Crucially, review and update any related existing functional test cases that might have been impacted or made obsolete by the bug or its fix. Ensure the main test suite now accurately reflects the corrected behavior. Definition of Done (DoD) Consideration: Consider adding a checklist item to the DoD for relevant user stories or bug fixes: ✅ Related manual test cases reviewed and updated (if applicable). The QA member closing the story or bug would be responsible for confirming this. Periodic Test Suite Review (Optional but Recommended): Occasionally (e.g., before a major release or quarterly), conduct a higher-level review of entire test suites for major features. Identify and archive or delete test cases that are completely obsolete due to feature removal or major redesigns. Look for redundancy and opportunities to consolidate or improve existing test cases. Clear Communication: Ensure developers are aware that changing logic might require QA to update test cases and factor that small overhead into planning. By making test case maintenance an ongoing activity tightly coupled with development and bug fixing, you ensure your manual test suite remains an accurate and valuable asset for verifying application quality. 🛠️

Item: 160 | Architecture Validation | Continuous Testing | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 4 | "The acceptance tests are automated and integrated into the build (behat, selenium, etc)." | Run the UI test suite (e.g., patrol_cli) as a *separate, nightly* CI pipeline (as they are slow) against the "Dev" environment. | Github runner for patrol automation testing | (Note: Item mentions Behat/Selenium which are web testing tools. For Flutter, focus is on frameworks like Patrol, Maestro, or integration_test.) This guide explains how to automate acceptance tests (typically higher-level Integration or E2E/UI tests) and integrate them into your CI/CD process, although usually not blocking PR builds directly due to their runtime.
documents.s: Completing Item 160: Automate Acceptance Tests and Integrate into Build

documents.t: These tests verify application behavior from an end-user perspective, often testing complete features or user flows. They correspond to the Acceptance Criteria (AC) defined in user stories. In Flutter, this typically involves: Integration Tests: Testing the interaction of multiple components (widgets, Blocs, services) within the Flutter environment, often with mocked backends (Item 16, 157). Uses package:integration_test. End-to-End (E2E) / UI Automation Tests: Driving the actual application UI like a user would (taps, swipes, input). Uses frameworks like Patrol, Maestro, or Appium (Item 157).
documents.s: What are Acceptance Tests in this Context?

documents.t: Validate User Flows: Ensure critical user journeys work as expected after code changes. Catch Integration Issues: Identify problems caused by the interaction between different parts of the application or with external services (if using a test backend). Regression Testing: Provide a broader safety net than unit/widget tests for detecting regressions in user-facing functionality. Reduce Manual QA Effort: Automate repetitive validation of core flows.

Develop Automated Acceptance Tests: Implement tests for critical user flows based on the chosen framework (integration_test, Patrol, Maestro) as part of your Test Automation Plan (Item 157). Focus on stable, high-value scenarios ("happy paths" of core features). Ensure tests have clear setup, actions, and assertions based on story ACs. Use appropriate data strategies (mocking, mock server, test backend - Item 16). Design the CI Integration Strategy: Challenge: E2E/UI

Item: 157 | Architecture Validation | Continuous Testing | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 4 | Have plan to implement automation tests and follow it. The plan is reviewed periodically. | Prioritize and create a backlog for UI automation (e.g., using patrolormaestro). Start with the most critical flows (e.g., "Login," "Checkout"). | | This guide outlines the process for creating, implementing, and periodically reviewing a plan for higher-level automated tests (Integration and End-to-End/UI tests) in your Flutter project, going beyond basic unit and widget tests.
documents.s: Completing Item 157: Implement and Follow Test Automation Plan

documents.t: Broader Validation: Tests interactions between multiple units, widgets, and potentially services (integration tests) or simulates full user journeys through the UI (E2E tests). Confidence in Flows: Validates critical user workflows (e.g., login, registration, purchase) from start to finish. Regression Detection: Catches regressions in interactions and user flows that unit/widget tests might miss. Reduces Manual Effort: Automates repetitive checks, freeing up QA for more valuable exploratory testing. Faster Feedback (than manual): Provides quicker feedback on the health of integrated components or user flows compared to full manual regression cycles.

Integration Tests (package:integration_test): Run within the Flutter execution environment (on a device or emulator). Can interact with widgets, pump frames, and test interactions between different parts of your app (e.g., widget -> Bloc -> Repository). Often use mocked repositories/data sources (Item 16). End-to-End (E2E) / UI Automation Tests: Drive the app's UI externally, simulating real user interactions (taps, swipes, text input). Typically run against a more complete environment (potentially including a mock backend or dedicated test backend - Item 16). Frameworks: Patrol: Leverages package:integration_test but adds native automation capabilities (permissions, notifications, webviews) and convenience features. Often preferred. Maestro: Declarative YAML-based E2E testing framework, known for resilience and ease of writing simple flows. Runs externally to the app. Appium: Older, cross-platform standard, can be complex to set up and maintain for Flutter.
documents.s: Types of Higher-Level Tests for Flutter

documents.t: Define Automation Goals and Scope: What to Automate? Focus on the most critical and stable user workflows. Good candidates: Login / Logout Registration / Onboarding Core feature flows (e.g., viewing product list, adding to cart, basic checkout) Smoke tests (basic app launch, navigation to key screens). What Not to Automate (Initially)? Avoid highly complex UI interactions, visual validation (checking exact pixels/colors), features under heavy development/flux, or edge cases easily covered by manual/exploratory testing. Choose Framework(s): Select the appropriate framework(s) based on your goals (e.g., integration_test + patrol for comprehensive testing, Maestro for simpler E2E smoke tests). Document this choice. Create the Automation Backlog: Identify specific flows or scenarios to automate based on the defined scope. Create tasks (e.g., User Stories or Tasks) in your Technical Backlog (Item 137) for implementing each automated test case/flow. Example Tasks: "Automate Login Success Flow (Patrol)", "Automate Add to Cart from Product List (Patrol)", "Write Integration Test for Profile Update Bloc+Repo Interaction". Prioritize the Backlog: During Technical Backlog Refinement (Item 137), prioritize these automation tasks based on: Criticality: How important is the user flow? Risk: How likely is this flow to break? How severe is the impact if it does? Stability: Is the feature relatively stable, or still undergoing major changes? Manual Effort Saved: How much time does automating this save QA? Prioritize core "happy path" flows first. Allocate Capacity and Implement: Allocate capacity for technical backlog items each sprint, including test automation tasks (Item 138). Assign automation tasks to developers (or dedicated automation engineers if available) and pull them into sprints. Implement the tests using the chosen framework, following best practices for writing maintainable and non-flaky automation code. Ensure tests have clear assertions. Integrate into CI/CD (Carefully): Integration Tests: Can often run as part of the main PR check pipeline if they are fast and use mocks. E2E/UI Tests: These are typically slower and potentially flakier. Run them: On a nightly schedule against the main branch deployed to a stable test environment. As part of the release candidate validation process before submitting to stores. (Avoid running long E2E suites directly on every PR commit, as it slows down the feedback loop too much). Configure CI to run tests on emulators/simulators or, ideally, via a device farm (Item 151). Report test results clearly (failures need investigation). Review the Plan and Results Periodically: Cadence: Monthly or Quarterly. Forum: Can be part of the Test Automation Follow-up (Item 140), Architecture Maturity Review (Item 133), or a dedicated brief session. Discuss: Progress on implementing the automation backlog. Effectiveness of existing automated tests (Are they catching real bugs? Are they reliable/flaky?). Changes in application features that require updating existing tests or adding new ones. Should the scope or priorities of the automation plan be adjusted? Are the chosen frameworks still appropriate? Update: Update the automation backlog and any high-level plan documentation based on the review. Implementing higher-level test automation is an investment. A clear plan, prioritized backlog, regular implementation effort, and periodic review ensure this investment yields valuable returns in quality and confidence. 📈

Item: 149 | Architecture Validation | Architecture Evaluation | DEVELOPMENT (Sprint 1-N) | 4 | The amount of defects identified during the code reviews are reducing over the time. | Track "Bugs found in production" vs. "Bugs found in QA." If production bugs are high, the code review process needs to be stricter. | | (Note: The suggested action in the item description seems slightly mismatched, focusing on bugs found later rather than during review. This guide focuses on reducing issues found during the review itself, implying improved quality before review). This guide focuses on the goal and methods for reducing the number of significant defects or issues identified during the code review process over time. Achieving this indicates that code quality is improving before it even reaches the review stage.
documents.s: Completing Item 149: Reduce Defects Found During Code Reviews Over Time

documents.t: Increased Efficiency: Fewer issues found during review means less back-and-forth between author and reviewer, faster PR approval times, and quicker merges (improved Lead Time - Item 10). Improved Code Quality: Indicates that developers are internalizing coding standards, architectural patterns, and testing practices, producing higher-quality code initially. Effective Automation: Suggests that automated checks (linting, testing, static analysis - Items 145, 148) are successfully catching many issues before human review. Better Use of Reviewer Time: Allows reviewers to focus on more complex aspects like logic, design, and usability, rather than repeatedly pointing out basic standard violations or common errors. Positive Trend Indicator: A downward trend in review defects is a strong sign of improving team practices and code health.
documents.s: Why Aim to Reduce Code Review Defects? 🤔

documents.t: You need a way to track significant issues found during reviews. This often involves: Formal Tracking (Item 144): Using Jira tickets for non-trivial issues found in PRs provides a clear metric (number of code-review-finding tickets created per sprint/month). Informal Tracking: Reviewers could use specific labels or comment conventions in the PR tool (e.g., [BLOCKER], [MAJOR]) and these could be manually tallied or potentially scraped via API. Formal tracking is generally better.

Strengthen Automated Checks (Shift Left): Aggressive Linting: Ensure your analysis_options.yaml is strict and covers common pitfalls and style issues (Item 145). Fail the build on any violation (Item 148). This eliminates entire classes of review comments. Format Checking: Automatically check formatting (dart format) in CI and fail if incorrect (Item 6). Test Coverage Gates: Enforce minimum code coverage on new code via SonarQube/CI (Item 148). This forces developers to add tests before review. SonarQube Quality Gates: Fail builds on new bugs, vulnerabilities, or major code smells identified by SonarQube (Item 148). Improve Clarity of Standards and Architecture: Ensure Coding Conventions (Item 3) and Architecture Foundation documents (Item 11) are clear, accessible, and well-understood by the team. Use examples. If reviewers repeatedly point out violations of the same standard, it might indicate the documentation or communication needs improvement. Enhance Developer Practices: Self-Reviews: Encourage developers to perform a thorough self-review of their code against the code review guidelines (Item 143) before submitting the PR. IDE Integration: Ensure developers utilize IDE features that highlight lints and errors as they type. Testing Habits: Foster a culture where writing unit/widget tests is an integral part of development, not an afterthought (Item 15). Knowledge Sharing and Training: Pair Programming: Pairing can help developers learn standards and best practices from each other, catching issues even before a formal PR. Targeted Training: If reviews consistently reveal misunderstandings in specific areas (e.g., state management, error handling, security), organize brief internal workshops or knowledge-sharing sessions. Review Feedback: Use feedback from code reviews (especially recurring comments) as learning opportunities for the whole team (e.g., discuss a common mistake in a team sync). Analyze Trends and Adapt: Track the Metric: Monitor the number of significant defects tracked from code reviews over time (e.g., monthly). Identify Patterns: During retrospectives or technical meetings, discuss: "What types of issues are reviewers still finding frequently?", "Why are the automated checks not catching these?". Adjust Automation & Guidelines: Use this analysis to: Add new custom lint rules if appropriate. Refine SonarQube rulesets. Clarify sections in the coding guidelines or architecture documents. Identify needs for further team training. Reducing the number of defects found during code review is a sign of a maturing development process where quality is built-in early, supported by strong automation and clear guidelines, allowing human reviewers to focus on higher-level concerns. 📉➡️✅
documents.s: Strategies to Reduce Code Review Defects

documents.t: Item: 107 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Monitoring | RELEASE | 5 | "When an issue has raised from application monitoring systems, there are actions that are automatically triggered that will not require manual intervention in order to fix it." | (Infra) Configure alerts (e.g., in Datadog) that can trigger automated rollbacks (e.g., via ArgoCD) if a new deployment shows a critical error spike. | | (Note: Similar to Item 106, this is an advanced practice. For mobile apps, "automated fixes" usually mean automated backend rollbacks triggered by app monitoring, or potentially remote config changes.) This guide discusses implementing automated responses triggered by application-level monitoring (like crash rates or performance metrics from the mobile app itself), typically involving backend rollbacks or configuration changes.
documents.s: Completing Item 107: Implement Automated Application Issue Response

documents.t: Fastest Reaction to User Impact: Issues detected directly from the app's behavior (e.g., sudden crash spike) can trigger remediation faster than waiting for backend metrics to degrade. Reduced User Pain: Quickly rolling back a bad release or disabling a faulty feature via remote config minimizes the number of users affected. Safety Net for Deployments: Provides an automated safety mechanism, especially for frequent releases.

Automated Backend Rollback: Trigger: Critical spike in mobile app crash rate (e.g., from Firebase Crashlytics Velocity Alert) or severe performance regression (e.g., Firebase Performance Alert for app start time) immediately following a backend deployment (assuming correlation is possible). Action: Automatically trigger the CI/CD pipeline (e.g., ArgoCD, Jenkins) to redeploy the previous stable version of the backend service(s). Implementation: Requires robust integration between app monitoring (Firebase, Sentry, Datadog RUM) and the backend deployment system. Monitoring tools might send webhooks on alerts, which trigger a rollback workflow. Needs careful correlation to ensure the app issue is likely due to the backend change. Automated Feature Toggle Disable: Trigger: Critical spike in crash rate or error logs specifically associated with a feature currently enabled via a feature toggle (e.g., Firebase Remote Config). Requires careful instrumentation (logging/crash reports tagged with active feature flags). Action: Automatically call the feature toggle service's API (e.g., Firebase Remote Config REST API) to disable the problematic feature flag for all users. Implementation: Requires monitoring tools capable of parsing logs/crash reports for feature context and triggering webhooks/functions that interact with the feature flagging service API.
documents.s: Feasible Automated Actions (Triggered by App Monitoring)

documents.t: Correlation: It can be difficult to automatically determine if a mobile app crash spike is definitively caused by a recent backend deployment versus an issue purely within the app code itself. False positive rollbacks can be disruptive. Client-Side Issues: Many crashes or performance issues originate solely within the mobile app code. These cannot be fixed by backend rollbacks or remote config changes; they require a new app release. Automated rollbacks of app releases are generally not feasible (managed by app stores).

Identify Reliable Triggers: Focus on clear indicators from app monitoring that strongly correlate with backend health. Examples: Firebase Crashlytics Velocity Alert for a crash happening deep within the network layer or directly after parsing a response. Firebase Performance alert showing a sudden, massive increase in network request latency across many endpoints. Custom alerts based on specific error logs sent from the app (e.g., "Received unexpected 500 error from /checkout API"). Avoid: Triggering on vague crashes or metrics that could have many causes. Integrate Monitoring with Deployment System: Configure alerts in your app monitoring tool (Firebase, Datadog RUM, Sentry) for the chosen triggers. Set up these alerts to send a webhook to an intermediary service or directly to your CI/CD platform when they fire. Create a specific CI/CD job/workflow (e.g., rollback-backend-on-alert) that: Receives the webhook payload. Parses the payload to confirm it's the expected alert type. Identifies the relevant backend service(s). Triggers the deployment system (e.g., kubectl rollout undo deployment <service>, ArgoCD sync to previous commit) to revert the service(s) to the last known good version. Implement Safeguards: Cooldown Period: Prevent the rollback from triggering repeatedly in a short period. Manual Override: Provide an easy way for engineers to manually disable the automated rollback automation. Clear Notifications: Send prominent notifications to the team chat (#alerts and #tech channels) whenever an automated rollback is triggered, including the triggering alert details. Idempotency: Ensure the rollback action is safe to run multiple times if necessary (though cooldown should prevent this). Backend Deployment Strategy: This automation works best with deployment strategies that allow easy rollbacks (e.g., Blue-Green, Canary with automated rollback support in tools like Argo Rollouts or Flagger). Document the Automation: Clearly document which app monitoring alerts can trigger automated backend rollbacks. Detail the workflow, involved tools (monitoring, webhooks, CI/CD), and safeguards. Explain how to monitor the automation and how to disable it. Test and Iterate: Test the end-to-end flow in a staging environment (requires simulating the alert trigger). Start with non-critical services or configure the automation to require manual approval initially. Refine the trigger conditions based on real-world experience to minimize false positives. Automated responses triggered by application monitoring are powerful but complex to implement reliably. Start cautiously, focusing on clear trigger conditions and robust safeguards, often targeting backend rollbacks as the primary action.
documents.s: Steps to Implement (Focus on Backend Rollback Example)

documents.t: Item: 106 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Monitoring | RELEASE | 5 | "When an issue has raised from infrastructure monitoring systems, there are actions that are automatically triggered that will not require manual intervention in order to fix it (for feasible services)." | (Infra) Implement autoscaling (e.g., HPA in Kubernetes) to automatically handle high CPU/memory load. | | (Note: This is an advanced DevOps/SRE practice focusing on the backend infrastructure supporting the mobile app.) This guide discusses implementing automated responses to specific infrastructure issues detected by monitoring systems, aiming for self-healing capabilities where feasible.
documents.s: Completing Item 106: Implement Automated Infrastructure Issue Response

documents.t: Fastest Possible Recovery (MTTR): Automated actions execute immediately upon detection, drastically reducing the time it takes to restore service compared to manual intervention. Reduced Toil: Frees up engineers from repetitive manual recovery tasks (like restarting services or scaling up). Consistency: Ensures corrective actions are performed consistently according to predefined logic. Improved Availability: Helps maintain service uptime and reliability, directly benefiting the mobile app's users.

Not all issues can be safely auto-remediated. Focus on predictable issues with well-defined, low-risk corrective actions: Autoscaling: Trigger: High CPU or Memory utilization across service instances (pods, VMs), or high request queue length. Action: Automatically provision and add more instances of the service (scale-out). Similarly, scale-in when load decreases. Implementation: Use platform features like Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA), AWS Auto Scaling Groups, GCP Managed Instance Groups. Unhealthy Instance Replacement: Trigger: Service instance failing health checks (e.g., liveness/readiness probes in Kubernetes). Action: Automatically terminate the unhealthy instance and start a new, healthy one to replace it. Implementation: Kubernetes handles this automatically for pods managed by Deployments/StatefulSets. Cloud provider instance groups often have similar autohealing features. Basic Service Restart (Use Cautiously): Trigger: Specific error patterns in logs or metrics indicating a potentially stuck process known to be resolved by a restart. Action: Automatically trigger a rolling restart of the service deployment. Implementation: Custom automation using monitoring tool webhooks (e.g., Datadog webhook triggering a Jenkins job or a serverless function that uses kubectl rollout restart). Requires careful design to avoid restart loops or masking underlying issues. Automated Rollback (Advanced): Trigger: Critical spike in error rates (e.g., 5xx errors) or latency immediately following a new deployment. Action: Automatically trigger the CI/CD pipeline to redeploy the previous known-good version. Implementation: Requires sophisticated CI/CD and monitoring integration (e.g., Canary Deployments with tools like Argo Rollouts, Flagger, or custom scripting comparing metrics before and after deployment).

Identify Candidate Issues for Automation: Analyze past incidents and monitoring alerts. Which issues occur frequently and have predictable manual resolution steps? Start with the simplest, highest-impact automation, usually autoscaling and relying on platform autohealing (like Kubernetes pod restarts). Implement Autoscaling: Configure HPA (or cloud provider equivalents) for stateless backend services supporting your mobile app. Base scaling on relevant metrics (CPU, Memory, custom metrics like requests per second). Define minimum and maximum instance counts. Test and tune the scaling thresholds and cooldown periods. Implement Health Checks: Ensure all backend services have appropriate liveness probes (is the service running?) and readiness probes (is the service ready to accept traffic?). Configure the orchestrator (Kubernetes) or load balancer to use these probes to automatically remove unhealthy instances from service and trigger replacements. Develop Custom Automation (Carefully): For actions like automated restarts or rollbacks: Define Precise Triggers: Use very specific alert conditions in your monitoring tool to avoid false positives. Build the Action Logic: Use webhooks, serverless functions (e.g., AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions), or automation platforms (e.g., Jenkins, Rundeck) to execute the corrective action (e.g., call Kubernetes API, trigger CI/CD pipeline). Implement Safeguards: Include cooldown periods, maximum retry limits, and clear notifications to prevent runaway automation or cascading failures. Test Thoroughly: Test the automation logic in a non-production environment under various failure scenarios. Configure Monitoring and Alerting for the Automation Itself: Monitor the autoscaler's activity. Alert if automated actions (restarts, rollbacks) are triggered frequently, as this might indicate a deeper underlying problem that needs investigation. Ensure clear notifications are sent to the team whenever an automated action is taken. Document the Automation: Document what automated actions are in place, what triggers them, and how they function. Include links to relevant configuration (HPA manifests, automation scripts). Explain how to manually override or disable the automation in emergencies. Automated infrastructure response represents a high level of DevOps maturity, significantly improving resilience but requiring careful design and implementation to avoid unintended consequences. Start with platform-native features like autoscaling and health checks.

Item: 108 | Architecture Execution | Continuous Monitoring | RELEASE | 5 | "The business monitoring tools are measuring key indicators (conversion rate, number of sold items, average response time, etc). If there is an issue with
any of those key indicators the team will get notified." | (Business) Set up alerts on the business dashboard (e.g., "Signups dropped 50% in 1 hour") that notify the PO and tech leads. | | This guide explains how to set up automated alerts based on significant changes or threshold breaches in your key business metrics (KPIs), ensuring relevant team members (especially Product Owners and Leads) are notified promptly.
documents.s: Completing Item 108: Configure Business Monitoring KPI Alerts

documents.t: Early Problem Detection: Sudden drops in KPIs (e.g., signups, conversion rate, active users) can be the first sign of a critical technical issue (e.g., broken login, payment failure), a usability problem, or even external factors (marketing campaign ended, competitor launch). Quantify Impact: Helps understand the business impact of technical incidents or feature releases.
