Feature flags (also known as feature toggles or feature switches) are a software development technique that allows you to enable or disable features in your application without deploying new code. This powerful pattern provides safer deployments, gradual rollouts, and the ability to quickly disable problematic features.

Feature flags are conditional statements in your code that determine whether specific features should be enabled or disabled for different users, environments, or conditions. They act as runtime switches that control the behavior of your application.

Safe Deployments: Deploy code with features disabled, then enable them gradually A/B Testing: Test different versions of features with different user groups Gradual Rollouts: Release features to a percentage of users incrementally Quick Rollbacks: Instantly disable problematic features without redeployment Environment Control: Enable features in staging but keep them disabled in production User Segmentation: Show features to specific user groups or roles
Purpose: Control the release of new features Lifecycle: Temporary (removed after full rollout) Example: New checkout flow in an e-commerce app
Purpose: A/B testing and experimentation Lifecycle: Temporary (removed after experiment concludes) Example: Different button colors to test conversion rates
Purpose: Operational control (circuit breakers) Lifecycle: Long-lived Example: Disable expensive features during high traffic
Purpose: Control access to features based on user roles Lifecycle: Long-lived Example: Admin-only features

// src/feature-flags/entities/feature-flag.entity.ts import { Entity, PrimaryGeneratedColumn, Column, CreateDateColumn, UpdateDateColumn } from 'typeorm'; export enum FeatureFlagType { BOOLEAN = 'boolean', PERCENTAGE = 'percentage', USER_SEGMENT = 'user_segment', MULTIVARIATE = 'multivariate', } @Entity('feature_flags') export class FeatureFlag { @PrimaryGeneratedColumn() id: number; @Column({ unique: true }) key: string; @Column() name: string; @Column({ type: 'text', nullable: true }) description: string; @Column({ type: 'enum', enum: FeatureFlagType, default: FeatureFlagType.BOOLEAN, }) type: FeatureFlagType; @Column({ default: false }) enabled: boolean; @Column({ type: 'json', nullable: true }) config: any; @Column({ type: 'json', nullable: true }) targeting: any; @Column({ default: 'development' }) environment: string; @CreateDateColumn() createdAt: Date; @UpdateDateColumn() updatedAt: Date; }

// src/feature-flags/feature-flags.service.ts import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common'; import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm'; import { Repository } from 'typeorm'; import { Redis } from 'ioredis'; import { FeatureFlag, FeatureFlagType } from './entities/feature-flag.entity'; export interface UserContext { userId: string; email?: string; role?: string; country?: string; segment?: string; customAttributes?: Record<string, any>; } export interface FeatureFlagResult { enabled: boolean; value?: any; variant?: string; reason?: string; } @Injectable() export class FeatureFlagsService { private readonly logger = new Logger(FeatureFlagsService.name); private readonly cachePrefix = 'ff:'; private readonly cacheTTL = 300; // 5 minutes constructor( @InjectRepository(FeatureFlag) private readonly featureFlagRepository: Repository<FeatureFlag>, private readonly redis: Redis, ) {} async isEnabled(flagKey: string, userContext: UserContext, environment = 'production'): Promise<FeatureFlagResult> { try { const flag = await this.getFeatureFlag(flagKey, environment); if (!flag) { return { enabled: false, reason: 'flag_not_found' }; } if (!flag.enabled) { return { enabled: false, reason: 'flag_disabled' }; } return this.evaluateFlag(flag, userContext); } catch (error) { this.logger.error(`Error evaluating flag ${flagKey}:`, error); return { enabled: false, reason: 'evaluation_error' }; } } private async getFeatureFlag(key: string, environment: string): Promise<FeatureFlag | null> { const cacheKey = `${this.cachePrefix}${environment}:${key}`; // Try cache first const cached = await this.redis.get(cacheKey); if (cached) { return JSON.parse(cached); } // Fetch from database const flag = await this.featureFlagRepository.findOne({ where: { key, environment }, }); if (flag) { await this.redis.setex(cacheKey, this.cacheTTL, JSON.stringify(flag)); } return flag; } private async evaluateFlag(flag: FeatureFlag, userContext: UserContext): Promise<FeatureFlagResult> { switch (flag.type) { case FeatureFlagType.BOOLEAN: return { enabled: true, reason: 'boolean_flag' }; case FeatureFlagType.PERCENTAGE: return this.evaluatePercentageFlag(flag, userContext); case FeatureFlagType.USER_SEGMENT: return this.evaluateUserSegmentFlag(flag, userContext); case FeatureFlagType.MULTIVARIATE: return this.evaluateMultivariateFlag(flag, userContext); default: return { enabled: false, reason: 'unknown_flag_type' }; } } private evaluatePercentageFlag(flag: FeatureFlag, userContext: UserContext): FeatureFlagResult { const percentage = flag.config?.percentage || 0; const hash = this.hashUserId(userContext.userId); const userPercentage = hash % 100; return { enabled: userPercentage < percentage, reason: 'percentage_rollout', value: userPercentage < percentage, }; } private evaluateUserSegmentFlag(flag: FeatureFlag, userContext: UserContext): FeatureFlagResult { const targeting = flag.targeting || {}; // Check user IDs if (targeting.userIds?.includes(userContext.userId)) { return { enabled: true, reason: 'user_id_match' }; } // Check user roles if (targeting.roles?.includes(userContext.role)) { return { enabled: true, reason: 'role_match' }; } // Check user segments if (targeting.segments?.includes(userContext.segment)) { return { enabled: true, reason: 'segment_match' }; } // Check country if (targeting.countries?.includes(userContext.country)) { return { enabled: true, reason: 'country_match' }; } return { enabled: false, reason: 'no_segment_match' }; } private evaluateMultivariateFlag(flag: FeatureFlag, userContext: UserContext): FeatureFlagResult { const variants = flag.config?.variants || []; if (variants.length === 0) { return { enabled: false, reason: 'no_variants' }; } const hash = this.hashUserId(userContext.userId); const totalWeight = variants.reduce((sum, v) => sum + (v.weight || 0), 0); if (totalWeight === 0) { return { enabled: false, reason: 'zero_weight' }; } const userWeight = hash % totalWeight; let currentWeight = 0; for (const variant of variants) { currentWeight += variant.weight || 0; if (userWeight < currentWeight) { return { enabled: true, variant: variant.key, value: variant.value, reason: 'variant_match', }; } } return { enabled: false, reason: 'no_variant_match' }; } private hashUserId(userId: string): number { let hash = 0; for (let i = 0; i < userId.length; i++) { const char = userId.charCodeAt(i); hash = (hash << 5) - hash + char; hash = hash & hash; // Convert to 32bit integer } return Math.abs(hash); } async createFeatureFlag(flagData: Partial<FeatureFlag>): Promise<FeatureFlag> { const flag = this.featureFlagRepository.create(flagData); const saved = await this.featureFlagRepository.save(flag); // Invalidate cache await this.invalidateCache(saved.key, saved.environment); return saved; } async updateFeatureFlag(id: number, updateData: Partial<FeatureFlag>): Promise<FeatureFlag> { const flag = await this.featureFlagRepository.findOne({ where: { id } }); if (!flag) { throw new Error('Feature flag not found'); } Object.assign(flag, updateData); const updated = await this.featureFlagRepository.save(flag); // Invalidate cache await this.invalidateCache(updated.key, updated.environment); return updated; } private async invalidateCache(key: string, environment: string): Promise<void> { const cacheKey = `${this.cachePrefix}${environment}:${key}`; await this.redis.del(cacheKey); } }

// src/feature-flags/feature-flags.controller.ts import { Controller, Get, Post, Put, Body, Param, Query, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common'; import { FeatureFlagsService, UserContext } from './feature-flags.service'; import { FeatureFlag } from './entities/feature-flag.entity'; import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../auth/jwt-auth.guard'; import { User } from '../auth/user.decorator'; @Controller('feature-flags') @UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard) export class FeatureFlagsController { constructor(private readonly featureFlagsService: FeatureFlagsService) {} @Get(':key/evaluate') async evaluateFlag(@Param('key') key: string, @Query('environment') environment = 'production', @User() user: any) { const userContext: UserContext = { userId: user.id, email: user.email, role: user.role, country: user.country, segment: user.segment, }; return this.featureFlagsService.isEnabled(key, userContext, environment); } @Post() async createFeatureFlag(@Body() flagData: Partial<FeatureFlag>) { return this.featureFlagsService.createFeatureFlag(flagData); } @Put(':id') async updateFeatureFlag(@Param('id') id: number, @Body() updateData: Partial<FeatureFlag>) { return this.featureFlagsService.updateFeatureFlag(id, updateData); } }

// hooks/useFeatureFlag.ts import { useState, useEffect, useCallback } from 'react'; import { useUser } from '../contexts/UserContext'; interface FeatureFlagResult { enabled: boolean; value?: any; variant?: string; reason?: string; loading: boolean; error?: string; } interface FeatureFlagCache { [key: string]: { result: FeatureFlagResult; timestamp: number; ttl: number; }; } const flagCache: FeatureFlagCache = {}; const CACHE_TTL = 5 * 60 * 1000; // 5 minutes export function useFeatureFlag(flagKey: string): FeatureFlagResult { const { user } = useUser(); const [result, setResult] = useState<FeatureFlagResult>({ enabled: false, loading: true, }); const evaluateFlag = useCallback(async () => { if (!user) { setResult({ enabled: false, loading: false, reason: 'no_user' }); return; } // Check cache first const cached = flagCache[flagKey]; if (cached && Date.now() - cached.timestamp < cached.ttl) { setResult({ ...cached.result, loading: false }); return; } try { const response = await fetch(`/api/feature-flags/${flagKey}/evaluate`, { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${user.token}`, 'Content-Type': 'application/json', }, }); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`); } const flagResult = await response.json(); // Cache the result flagCache[flagKey] = { result: flagResult, timestamp: Date.now(), ttl: CACHE_TTL, }; setResult({ ...flagResult, loading: false }); } catch (error) { console.error(`Error evaluating flag ${flagKey}:`, error); setResult({ enabled: false, loading: false, error: error.message, reason: 'fetch_error', }); } }, [flagKey, user]); useEffect(() => { evaluateFlag(); }, [evaluateFlag]); return result; }

While building your own feature flag system provides complete control, using a managed service like LaunchDarkly can significantly reduce implementation complexity. Here's how to integrate LaunchDarkly with your NestJS and Next.js applications.

# Install LaunchDarkly SDK npm install launchdarkly-node-server-sdk npm install @types/launchdarkly-node-server-sdk --save-dev // src/launchdarkly/launchdarkly.service.ts import { Injectable, OnModuleInit, OnModuleDestroy, Logger } from '@nestjs/common'; import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config'; import * as LaunchDarkly from 'launchdarkly-node-server-sdk'; export interface LaunchDarklyUser { key: string; email?: string; name?: string; country?: string; custom?: Record<string, any>; } @Injectable() export class LaunchDarklyService implements OnModuleInit, OnModuleDestroy { private readonly logger = new Logger(LaunchDarklyService.name); private client: LaunchDarkly.LDClient; constructor(private readonly configService: ConfigService) {} async onModuleInit() { const sdkKey = this.configService.get<string>('LAUNCHDARKLY_SDK_KEY'); if (!sdkKey) { this.logger.warn('LaunchDarkly SDK key not provided. Feature flags will be disabled.'); return; } // Initialize LaunchDarkly client this.client = LaunchDarkly.init(sdkKey, { timeout: 10, capacity: 1000, flushInterval: 5000, // Enable offline mode for testing offline: this.configService.get('NODE_ENV') === 'test', }); try { await this.client.waitForInitialization(); this.logger.log('LaunchDarkly client initialized successfully'); } catch (error) { this.logger.error('Failed to initialize LaunchDarkly client:', error); } } async onModuleDestroy() { if (this.client) { await this.client.flush(); this.client.close(); } } async getBooleanFlag(flagKey: string, user: LaunchDarklyUser, defaultValue = false): Promise<boolean> { if (!this.client) { this.logger.warn(`LaunchDarkly client not initialized. Returning default value for flag: ${flagKey}`); return defaultValue; } try { return await this.client.variation(flagKey, user, defaultValue); } catch (error) { this.logger.error(`Error evaluating flag ${flagKey}:`, error); return defaultValue; } } async getStringFlag(flagKey: string, user: LaunchDarklyUser, defaultValue = ''): Promise<string> { if (!this.client) { return defaultValue; } try { return await this.client.variation(flagKey, user, defaultValue); } catch (error) { this.logger.error(`Error evaluating flag ${flagKey}:`, error); return defaultValue; } } async getNumberFlag(flagKey: string, user: LaunchDarklyUser, defaultValue = 0): Promise<number> { if (!this.client) { return defaultValue; } try { return await this.client.variation(flagKey, user, defaultValue); } catch (error) { this.logger.error(`Error evaluating flag ${flagKey}:`, error); return defaultValue; } } async getJsonFlag(flagKey: string, user: LaunchDarklyUser, defaultValue: any = {}): Promise<any> { if (!this.client) { return defaultValue; } try { return await this.client.variation(flagKey, user, defaultValue); } catch (error) { this.logger.error(`Error evaluating flag ${flagKey}:`, error); return defaultValue; } } async getAllFlags(user: LaunchDarklyUser): Promise<LaunchDarkly.LDFlagSet> { if (!this.client) { return {}; } try { return await this.client.allFlagsState(user); } catch (error) { this.logger.error('Error getting all flags:', error); return {}; } } // Track custom events for analytics async track(eventKey: string, user: LaunchDarklyUser, data?: any): Promise<void> { if (!this.client) { return; } try { this.client.track(eventKey, user, data); } catch (error) { this.logger.error(`Error tracking event ${eventKey}:`, error); } } }

// src/launchdarkly/launchdarkly.controller.ts import { Controller, Get, Post, Body, Param, UseGuards, Req } from '@nestjs/common'; import { LaunchDarklyService, LaunchDarklyUser } from './launchdarkly.service'; import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../auth/jwt-auth.guard'; @Controller('feature-flags') @UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard) export class LaunchDarklyController { constructor(private readonly launchDarklyService: LaunchDarklyService) {} @Get(':flagKey') async getFlag(@Param('flagKey') flagKey: string, @Req() request: any) { const user = this.buildLaunchDarklyUser(request.user); // Try to determine flag type and return appropriate value const booleanValue = await this.launchDarklyService.getBooleanFlag(flagKey, user); const stringValue = await this.launchDarklyService.getStringFlag(flagKey, user); const numberValue = await this.launchDarklyService.getNumberFlag(flagKey, user); return { flagKey, value: booleanValue !== false ? booleanValue : stringValue || numberValue, user: user.key, }; } @Get() async getAllFlags(@Req() request: any) { const user = this.buildLaunchDarklyUser(request.user); const allFlags = await this.launchDarklyService.getAllFlags(user); return { flags: allFlags, user: user.key, }; } @Post('track/:eventKey') async trackEvent(@Param('eventKey') eventKey: string, @Body() eventData: any, @Req() request: any) { const user = this.buildLaunchDarklyUser(request.user); await this.launchDarklyService.track(eventKey, user, eventData); return { success: true, eventKey, user: user.key }; } private buildLaunchDarklyUser(user: any): LaunchDarklyUser { return { key: user.id, email: user.email, name: user.name, country: user.country, custom: { role: user.role, plan: user.plan, signupDate: user.createdAt, // Add any other custom attributes }, }; } }

# Install LaunchDarkly React SDK npm install launchdarkly-react-client-sdk // contexts/LaunchDarklyProvider.tsx import React, { createContext, useContext } from 'react'; import { withLDProvider, useLDClient, useFlags } from 'launchdarkly-react-client-sdk'; import { useUser } from './UserContext'; interface LaunchDarklyContextType { isEnabled: (flag: string) => boolean; getFlag: (flag: string, defaultValue?: any) => any; track: (eventKey: string, data?: any) => void; } const LaunchDarklyContext = createContext<LaunchDarklyContextType | undefined>(undefined); export function useLaunchDarkly() { const context = useContext(LaunchDarklyContext); if (!context) { throw new Error('useLaunchDarkly must be used within a LaunchDarklyProvider'); } return context; } function LaunchDarklyProviderInner({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) { const ldClient = useLDClient(); const flags = useFlags(); const isEnabled = (flag: string): boolean => { return flags[flag] === true; }; const getFlag = (flag: string, defaultValue: any = false): any => { return flags[flag] !== undefined ? flags[flag] : defaultValue; }; const track = (eventKey: string, data?: any): void => { if (ldClient) { ldClient.track(eventKey, data); } }; return <LaunchDarklyContext.Provider value={{ isEnabled, getFlag, track }}>{children}</LaunchDarklyContext.Provider>; } // HOC that wraps the app with LaunchDarkly provider export function LaunchDarklyProvider({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) { const { user } = useUser(); if (!user) { // Return children without LaunchDarkly if no user return <>{children}</>; } const ldUser = { key: user.id, email: user.email, name: user.name, country: user.country, custom: { role: user.role, plan: user.plan, }, }; const LaunchDarklyApp = withLDProvider({ clientSideID: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_LAUNCHDARKLY_CLIENT_ID!, user: ldUser, options: { streaming: true, useReport: false, }, })(LaunchDarklyProviderInner); return <LaunchDarklyApp>{children}</LaunchDarklyApp>; }

// hooks/useLaunchDarklyFlag.ts import { useFlags, useLDClient } from 'launchdarkly-react-client-sdk'; import { useEffect, useState } from 'react'; export function useLaunchDarklyFlag(flagKey: string, defaultValue: any = false) { const flags = useFlags(); const ldClient = useLDClient(); const [value, setValue] = useState(defaultValue); useEffect(() => { const flagValue = flags[flagKey]; setValue(flagValue !== undefined ? flagValue : defaultValue); }, [flags, flagKey, defaultValue]); const track = (eventKey: string, data?: any) => { if (ldClient) { ldClient.track(eventKey, data); } }; return { value, isEnabled: value === true, track, }; } // Multi-variate flag hook export function useMultiVariateFlag(flagKey: string, defaultValue: string = 'control') { const { value, track } = useLaunchDarklyFlag(flagKey, defaultValue); return { variant: value, isControl: value === 'control', isVariant: (variantName: string) => value === variantName, track, }; }

// components/LaunchDarklyFeatureFlag.tsx import React from 'react'; import { useLaunchDarklyFlag } from '../hooks/useLaunchDarklyFlag'; interface LaunchDarklyFeatureFlagProps { flag: string; children: React.ReactNode; fallback?: React.ReactNode; onFlagEvaluated?: (enabled: boolean) => void; } export const LaunchDarklyFeatureFlag: React.FC<LaunchDarklyFeatureFlagProps> = ({ flag, children, fallback = null, onFlagEvaluated, }) => { const { isEnabled, track } = useLaunchDarklyFlag(flag); React.useEffect(() => { if (onFlagEvaluated) { onFlagEvaluated(isEnabled); } // Track flag evaluation track('flag-evaluated', { flagKey: flag, enabled: isEnabled }); }, [isEnabled, flag, onFlagEvaluated, track]); return isEnabled ? <>{children}</> : <>{fallback}</>; }; // Multi-variate component export const LaunchDarklyVariant: React.FC<{ flag: string; variant: string; children: React.ReactNode; fallback?: React.ReactNode; }> = ({ flag, variant, children, fallback = null }) => { const { isVariant, track } = useMultiVariateFlag(flag); React.useEffect(() => { track('variant-evaluated', { flagKey: flag, variant }); }, [flag, variant, track]); return isVariant(variant) ? <>{children}</> : <>{fallback}</>; };

// pages/_app.tsx (Next.js) import { LaunchDarklyProvider } from '../contexts/LaunchDarklyProvider'; import { UserProvider } from '../contexts/UserContext'; function MyApp({ Component, pageProps }) { return ( <UserProvider> <LaunchDarklyProvider> <Component {...pageProps} /> </LaunchDarklyProvider> </UserProvider> ); } export default MyApp;

// utils/featureFlags.ts export const FeatureFlags = { NEW_CHECKOUT: 'new-checkout-flow', PREMIUM_FEATURES: 'premium-features', EXPERIMENTAL_UI: 'experimental-ui', MAINTENANCE_MODE: 'maintenance-mode', } as const; // Type-safe flag usage export type FeatureFlagKey = (typeof FeatureFlags)[keyof typeof FeatureFlags]; // Centralized flag evaluation with fallbacks export class FeatureFlagService { static async isNewCheckoutEnabled(user: any): Promise<boolean> { try { return await launchDarklyService.getBooleanFlag( FeatureFlags.NEW_CHECKOUT, user, false, // Safe default ); } catch (error) { console.error('Error evaluating new checkout flag:', error); return false; // Fail safely } } } This LaunchDarkly integration provides enterprise-grade feature flag management with minimal implementation overhead, while maintaining the flexibility to switch back to a custom solution if needed.
LD Relay is LaunchDarkly's edge proxy that acts as an intermediary between your applications and LaunchDarkly's servers. Whether you need it depends on your specific requirements and architecture.

LD Relay is a lightweight, high-performance proxy service that: Caches flag configurations locally Reduces latency for flag evaluations Provides network isolation and security Enables offline operation Scales flag delivery for high-traffic applications

For most applications, you don't need LD Relay if you have: // Simple direct integration works fine for: // - Small to medium applications (\< 10,000 requests/minute) // - Applications with normal latency requirements // - Cloud-hosted applications with good internet connectivity // - Development and testing environments // Direct LaunchDarkly integration const ldClient = LaunchDarkly.init(sdkKey, { timeout: 10, capacity: 1000, flushInterval: 5000, }); Scenarios where direct integration is sufficient: Small Teams: Less than 50 developers Low Traffic: Under 10,000 flag evaluations per minute Cloud Applications: Running on AWS, GCP, Azure with reliable internet Simple Architecture: Monolithic or simple microservices Standard Latency: Can tolerate 50-100ms for flag updates

documents.t: Consider LD Relay for these scenarios: 1. High-Traffic Applications​ # docker-compose.yml for high-traffic setup version: '3.8' services: ld-relay: image: launchdarkly/ld-relay:latest ports: - '8030:8030' environment: - LD_ENV_PRODUCTION=${LD_PRODUCTION_SDK_KEY} - LD_ENV_STAGING=${LD_STAGING_SDK_KEY} - USE_REDIS=true - REDIS_HOST=redis - REDIS_PORT=6379 depends_on: - redis redis: image: redis:7-alpine ports: - '6379:6379' app: build: . environment: - LAUNCHDARKLY_BASE_URI=http://ld-relay:8030 - LAUNCHDARKLY_STREAM_URI=http://ld-relay:8030 depends_on: - ld-relay 2. Network-Restricted Environments​ // src/launchdarkly/relay.service.ts import * as LaunchDarkly from 'launchdarkly-node-server-sdk'; @Injectable() export class LaunchDarklyRelayService { private client: LaunchDarkly.LDClient; async onModuleInit() { // Configure SDK to use LD Relay instead of LaunchDarkly directly this.client = LaunchDarkly.init(sdkKey, { baseUri: 'http://ld-relay:8030', // HTTP endpoint streamUri: 'http://ld-relay:8030', // Streaming endpoint eventsUri: 'http://ld-relay:8030', // Events endpoint timeout: 5, // Reduced timeout due to local relay capacity: 10000, // Higher capacity for relay flushInterval: 2000, // More frequent flushing }); await this.client.waitForInitialization(); } } 3. Kubernetes/Container Orchestration​ # kubernetes/ld-relay-deployment.yaml apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: ld-relay spec: replicas: 3 selector: matchLabels: app: ld-relay template: metadata: labels: app: ld-relay spec: containers: - name: ld-relay image: launchdarkly/ld-relay:latest ports: - containerPort: 8030 env: - name: LD_ENV_PRODUCTION valueFrom: secretKeyRef: name: launchdarkly-secrets key: production-sdk-key - name: USE_REDIS value: 'true' - name: REDIS_HOST value: 'redis-service' resources: requests: memory: '256Mi' cpu: '250m' limits: memory: '512Mi' cpu: '500m' --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: ld-relay-service spec: selector: app: ld-relay ports: - port: 8030 targetPort: 8030 type: ClusterIP 4. GCP Cloud Run with LD Relay​ # terraform/ld-relay-cloud-run.tf resource "google_cloud_run_service" "ld_relay" { name = "ld-relay" location = var.region template { spec { containers { image = "launchdarkly/ld-relay:latest" ports { container_port = 8030 } env { name = "LD_ENV_PRODUCTION" value = var.launchdarkly_sdk_key } env { name = "USE_REDIS" value = "true" } env { name = "REDIS_HOST" value = google_redis_instance.ld_cache.host } resources { limits = { cpu = "1000m" memory = "512Mi" } } } } metadata { annotations = { "autoscaling.knative.dev/minScale" = "2" "autoscaling.knative.dev/maxScale" = "10" "run.googleapis.com/cloudsql-instances" = "" "run.googleapis.com/vpc-access-connector" = google_vpc_access_connector.connector.name } } } traffic { percent = 100 latest_revision = true } } # Configure your app to use the relay resource "google_cloud_run_service" "app" { name = "feature-flags-app" location = var.region template { spec { containers { image = "gcr.io/${var.project_id}/app:latest" env { name = "LAUNCHDARKLY_BASE_URI" value = "${google_cloud_run_service.ld_relay.status[0].url}" } env { name = "LAUNCHDARKLY_STREAM_URI" value = "${google_cloud_run_service.ld_relay.status[0].url}" } } } } }

documents.t: Basic Configuration​ # ld-relay.conf [Main] port = 8030 baseUri = https://app.launchdarkly.com streamUri = https://stream.launchdarkly.com eventsUri = https://events.launchdarkly.com [Environment "production"] sdkKey = your-production-sdk-key [Environment "staging"] sdkKey = your-staging-sdk-key [Redis] host = localhost port = 6379 Advanced Configuration with Multiple Environments​ # docker-compose.production.yml version: '3.8' services: ld-relay: image: launchdarkly/ld-relay:latest ports: - '8030:8030' volumes: - ./ld-relay.conf:/etc/ld-relay.conf environment: - LD_REDIS_HOST=redis - LD_REDIS_PORT=6379 - LD_LOG_LEVEL=info - LD_OFFLINE_MODE=false depends_on: - redis restart: unless-stopped deploy: replicas: 2 resources: limits: cpus: '0.5' memory: 512M redis: image: redis:7-alpine command: redis-server --appendonly yes volumes: - redis_data:/data restart: unless-stopped volumes: redis_data:

Latency Comparison​ // Without LD Relay (direct to LaunchDarkly) // Typical latency: 50-200ms for flag evaluation // Network hops: App -> Internet -> LaunchDarkly -> Response // With LD Relay // Typical latency: 1-5ms for flag evaluation // Network hops: App -> LD Relay (local) -> Response // Benchmark example const performanceTest = async () => { const iterations = 1000; // Test direct LaunchDarkly const directStart = Date.now(); for (let i = 0; i < iterations; i++) { await directLDClient.variation('test-flag', user, false); } const directTime = Date.now() - directStart; // Test via LD Relay const relayStart = Date.now(); for (let i = 0; i < iterations; i++) { await relayLDClient.variation('test-flag', user, false); } const relayTime = Date.now() - relayStart; console.log(`Direct: ${directTime}ms, Relay: ${relayTime}ms`); // Typical results: Direct: 50000ms, Relay: 5000ms (10x faster) };

1. Corporate Firewalls​ # If your network blocks outbound connections to LaunchDarkly # LD Relay can be deployed in a DMZ with controlled access curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $LD_SDK_KEY" \ https://app.launchdarkly.com/sdk/latest-all # ❌ Blocked by firewall # But internal relay works curl http://internal-ld-relay:8030/sdk/latest-all # ✅ Works through internal network 2. Air-Gapped Environments​ // For completely offline environments const client = LaunchDarkly.init(sdkKey, { offline: true, // Start in offline mode baseUri: 'http://local-ld-relay:8030', // Relay sync with LaunchDarkly separately }); 3. High-Frequency Flag Evaluations​ // Applications doing \> 100,000 flag evaluations per minute // Direct LaunchDarkly has rate limits // LD Relay removes these constraints class HighVolumeFeatureService { async evaluateForBatch(users: User[]): Promise<Map<string, boolean>> { // With relay, this can handle thousands of users efficiently const results = new Map(); for (const user of users) { // Each evaluation: ~1ms with relay vs ~50ms direct const enabled = await this.ldClient.variation('feature', user, false); results.set(user.id, enabled); } return results; } }

If you decide you need LD Relay later: // 1. Start without relay const client = LaunchDarkly.init(sdkKey); // 2. Deploy relay alongside existing setup const relayClient = LaunchDarkly.init(sdkKey, { baseUri: 'http://ld-relay:8030', streamUri: 'http://ld-relay:8030', }); // 3. A/B test the relay const useRelay = await this.featureFlags.getBooleanFlag('use-ld-relay', user, false); const activeClient = useRelay ? relayClient : client; // 4. Gradually migrate traffic // 5. Remove direct client once relay is proven

NO - for most applications: Standard web applications Mobile backends Small to medium microservices Cloud-hosted services with good connectivity Development/staging environments YES - when you have: High traffic (>10k evaluations/minute) Strict latency requirements (<10ms) Network restrictions or firewalls Air-gapped environments Many microservices sharing flags Corporate compliance requirements Need for local caching and offline operation Start simple with direct LaunchDarkly integration and add LD Relay only when you encounter specific performance or network constraints that require it.

documents.t: // backend/src/feature-flags/analytics.service.ts import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common'; import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm'; import { Repository } from 'typeorm'; @Entity('feature_flag_events') export class FeatureFlagEvent { @PrimaryGeneratedColumn() id: number; @Column() flagKey: string; @Column() userId: string; @Column() enabled: boolean; @Column({ nullable: true }) variant: string; @Column() environment: string; @CreateDateColumn() timestamp: Date; } @Injectable() export class FeatureFlagAnalyticsService { constructor( @InjectRepository(FeatureFlagEvent) private readonly eventRepository: Repository<FeatureFlagEvent>, ) {} async trackFlagEvaluation( flagKey: string, userId: string, enabled: boolean, variant?: string, environment = 'production', ): Promise<void> { const event = this.eventRepository.create({ flagKey, userId, enabled, variant, environment, }); await this.eventRepository.save(event); } async getFlagStatistics(flagKey: string, environment: string, days = 7) { const since = new Date(); since.setDate(since.getDate() - days); const stats = await this.eventRepository .createQueryBuilder('event') .select([ 'COUNT(*) as total_evaluations', 'SUM(CASE WHEN enabled = true THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) as enabled_count', 'COUNT(DISTINCT userId) as unique_users', ]) .where('event.flagKey = :flagKey', { flagKey }) .andWhere('event.environment = :environment', { environment }) .andWhere('event.timestamp >= :since', { since }) .getRawOne(); return { ...stats, enablement_rate: stats.total_evaluations > 0 ? (stats.enabled_count / stats.total_evaluations) * 100 : 0, }; } }

// tests/feature-flags.e2e-spec.ts describe('Feature Flags E2E', () => { test('should respect percentage rollouts', async () => { // Create test users const users = Array.from({ length: 100 }, (_, i) => ({ id: `user${i}` })); // Set flag to 25% rollout await createFlag('test-flag', { type: 'percentage', config: { percentage: 25 } }); const results = await Promise.all(users.map((user) => evaluateFlag('test-flag', user))); const enabledCount = results.filter((r) => r.enabled).length; expect(enabledCount).toBeCloseTo(25, 5); // Within 5% tolerance }); test('should handle flag toggles immediately', async () => { const user = { id: 'test-user' }; // Enable flag await updateFlag('instant-flag', { enabled: true }); let result = await evaluateFlag('instant-flag', user); expect(result.enabled).toBe(true); // Disable flag await updateFlag('instant-flag', { enabled: false }); result = await evaluateFlag('instant-flag', user); expect(result.enabled).toBe(false); }); });

Raft is a consensus algorithm designed to be easy to understand and implement. It's equivalent to Paxos in fault-tolerance and performance but is decomposed into relatively independent subproblems, making it more accessible for practical systems development.

Consensus is a fundamental problem in fault-tolerant distributed systems where multiple servers need to agree on values. Key characteristics: Fault Tolerance: The system continues to operate even when some servers fail Majority Rule: A cluster can continue operating as long as a majority of servers are available Consistency: Once a decision is made on a value, that decision is final Safety: The system never returns incorrect results, even during failures

Consensus typically arises in the context of replicated state machines: State Machine: The component we want to make fault-tolerant (e.g., a hash table) Log: Contains commands that modify the state machine Consensus Algorithm: Ensures all servers agree on the commands in their logs
Raft decomposes the consensus problem into three relatively independent subproblems:

Purpose: Select a single server to manage the replicated log Process: Servers start as followers If no leader communication is received, a follower becomes a candidate Candidates request votes from other servers The candidate with majority votes becomes the leader

Purpose: Leader accepts log entries from clients and replicates them across the cluster Process: Leader receives commands from clients Leader appends entries to its log Leader sends entries to followers Leader commits entries once majority of servers have stored them

Purpose: Ensure that if any state machine applies a command as the nth entry, no other state machine will apply a different nth command Guarantees: Election Safety: At most one leader per term Leader Append-Only: Leaders never overwrite or delete entries Log Matching: If two logs contain an entry with same index and term, they're identical up to that index Leader Completeness: If an entry is committed in a given term, it will be present in leaders of higher terms State Machine Safety: If a server applies an entry at a given index, no other server will apply a different entry at that index
Each server in a Raft cluster can be in one of three states:
Default state for all servers Passive: Only responds to requests from leaders and candidates Timeout: If no communication from leader, transitions to candidate
Intermediate state during leader election Active: Requests votes from other servers Transitions: Becomes leader (majority votes) or reverts to follower
Active state: Handles all client requests Responsibilities: Accept client commands Replicate log entries Decide when entries are committed Heartbeats: Sends periodic heartbeats to maintain authority

Raft divides time into terms of arbitrary length: Sequential numbering: Terms are numbered with consecutive integers Leader per term: Each term begins with an election; at most one leader per term Term detection: Servers exchange current term numbers in communications Term updates: If a server's term is stale, it updates to the newer term
The Raft log consists of entries containing: Index: Position in the log (sequential) Term: Term number when the entry was created by the leader Command: State machine command
Monotonic: Logs only grow (never shrink or change existing entries) Ordered: Entries are applied to state machine in log order Durable: Once committed, entries are never lost
Followers wait for heartbeats from the leader If timeout expires without communication, follower becomes candidate
Increment current term Vote for self Reset election timer Send RequestVote RPCs to all other servers
Each server votes for at most one candidate per term Candidate must have log at least as up-to-date as voter's log First-come, first-served within a term
Win: Candidate receives majority votes, becomes leader Lose: Another candidate wins and sends heartbeat Tie: No candidate gets majority, new election begins

Client sends command to leader Leader appends entry to local log Leader sends AppendEntries RPCs to followers Leader waits for majority to store entry Leader commits entry and applies to state machine Leader returns result to client Leader notifies followers of commitment in subsequent RPCs
Contains: Previous log index/term: For consistency checking Entries to store: May be empty (heartbeat) Leader commit index: Tells followers what entries are committed
Follower checks if its log matches leader's log at the previous index If mismatch found, follower rejects the request Leader decrements next index and retries Eventually finds point where logs match
Candidate can only win election if its log contains all committed entries Voting server denies vote if candidate's log is not at least as up-to-date
Entry is committed when stored on majority of servers All preceding entries are also committed (implicit commitment) Leader never commits entries from previous terms directly
If two entries in different logs have same index and term: They store the same command The logs are identical in all preceding entries
Raft supports dynamic configuration changes while maintaining safety:
Joint Consensus: Old and new configurations overlap New Configuration: Transition to new configuration only
No point where both old and new majorities can make independent decisions Configuration changes are logged and replicated like normal entries

Batching: Send multiple entries in single AppendEntries RPC Pipelining: Send AppendEntries before previous ones are acknowledged Async Application: Apply committed entries to state machine asynchronously
Election Timeout: 150-300ms typical Heartbeat Interval: 50ms typical (much less than election timeout) RPC Timeout: Configurable based on network characteristics
Network Partitions: Minority partition cannot commit new entries Server Crashes: Restarted servers catch up via log replication Disk Failures: May require operator intervention for data recovery

Persistent State (stable storage): Current term Voted for candidate in current term Log entries Volatile State (all servers): Commit index Last applied index Volatile State (leaders only): Next index for each follower Match index for each follower

RequestVote RPC​ Arguments: - term: candidate's term - candidateId: candidate requesting vote - lastLogIndex: index of candidate's last log entry - lastLogTerm: term of candidate's last log entry Results: - term: current term for candidate to update itself - voteGranted: true if candidate received vote AppendEntries RPC​ Arguments: - term: leader's term - leaderId: for followers to redirect clients - prevLogIndex: index of log entry immediately preceding new ones - prevLogTerm: term of prevLogIndex entry - entries[]: log entries to store (empty for heartbeat) - leaderCommit: leader's commit index Results: - term: current term for leader to update itself - success: true if follower contained entry matching prevLogIndex and prevLogTerm
Consensus on transaction commits Leader election for primary replicas Configuration management
Metadata consensus Replication coordination Cluster membership management
Service discovery consensus Configuration distribution Leader election for singleton services

Understandability: Raft is designed to be easier to understand Decomposition: Raft separates leader election, log replication, and safety Strong Leadership: Raft uses a stronger form of leadership than Paxos

Fault Model: Raft assumes crash failures, PBFT handles Byzantine failures Performance: Raft generally performs better in crash-failure scenarios Complexity: Raft is simpler to implement and understand
RaftScope: Interactive Raft visualization The Secret Lives of Data: Guided visualization of Raft Raft Paper: "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm"
Popular Raft implementations across different languages: Go: HashiCorp Raft, etcd/raft Rust: TiKV, async-raft Java: Apache Ratis, SOFAJRaft C++: LogCabin, braft Python: PySyncObj, raftos
Odd number of servers: Ensures clear majorities (3, 5, 7 nodes) Geographic distribution: Spread across availability zones/regions Resource allocation: Ensure adequate CPU, memory, and storage
Term changes: Monitor for frequent leader elections Commit latency: Track time from client request to commitment Log growth: Monitor log size and compaction needs
Rolling upgrades: Upgrade followers first, then leader Backup strategies: Backup committed log entries and state machine snapshots Capacity planning: Plan for peak load and failure scenarios

The Raft consensus algorithm provides a practical, understandable solution for achieving consensus in distributed systems. Its clear separation of concerns and strong leadership model make it an excellent choice for building fault-tolerant distributed applications. The algorithm's emphasis on understandability has led to widespread adoption and numerous high-quality implementations across different programming languages and platforms.

Spotify is a prime example of a large-scale music streaming platform that handles millions of users and billions of songs. This document explores the system design principles, architecture patterns, and scalability considerations involved in building a platform like Spotify.

Artist Management: Artists can upload their songs to the platform Content Discovery: Users can search and browse songs, artists, and playlists Audio Playback: Users can stream and play songs with adaptive quality Playlist Management: Users can create, modify, and manage personal playlists User Profiles: Support for user accounts, preferences, and social features Monitoring: Basic observability with health checks, error tracking, and performance metrics

Users: ~500,000 active users Content: ~30 million songs in the catalog Daily Usage: Each user streams 10-15 songs daily Average Listen Time: 3.5 minutes per song Audio Quality: Multiple bitrates (64kbps, 128kbps, 320kbps for premium)

File Formats: Ogg and AAC with adaptive streaming support Quality Tiers: 64kbps: Mobile data saving mode 128kbps: Standard quality 320kbps: Premium/high-fidelity audio File Size: ~3MB per song at standard quality

Audio Storage: Raw audio: 3MB × 30M songs ≈ 90TB With replicas and regional distribution: 2-3x = ~270TB Multiple quality versions add additional overhead Metadata Storage: Song metadata: ~100 bytes × 30M songs ≈ 3GB User profiles and playlists: ~1KB × 500K users ≈ 0.5GB Total metadata: Negligible compared to audio storage Bandwidth Considerations: Average stream: 3-4MB per song (128-160kbps) Daily streams per user: 10-15 songs Peak traffic during commute hours and evening listening sessions Significant CDN and egress costs for audio delivery Key Insight: Audio content dominates both storage costs and bandwidth requirements, making efficient content delivery critical.

The Spotify system architecture follows a distributed, scalable design with clear separation of concerns: Client Layer: Mobile and web applications handle user interfaces and local caching Load Balancing: Distributes incoming requests across multiple API servers API Layer: Stateless application servers handle business logic and authentication Data Storage: SQL database with read replicas for metadata management Audio Storage: Blob storage (S3) for large audio files with CDN caching Supporting Services: Analytics, monitoring, and search capabilities Key Design Principles: Horizontal Scalability: Each layer can scale independently Fault Tolerance: Multiple replicas and fallback mechanisms Performance Optimization: CDN caching and direct audio streaming Cost Efficiency: Signed URLs reduce API server load for audio delivery

1. Mobile/Web Client​ Responsibilities: User interface and playback controls Local caching of recently played songs REST API communication for metadata Direct audio streaming from CDN/blob storage Graceful handling of network interruptions Key Features: Retry logic for API calls Adaptive bitrate streaming Local playback state management Offline mode support 2. Load Balancer​ Algorithm Options: Round-robin or least-connections Health Monitoring: 30-second health checks High Availability: Automatic removal of unhealthy instances Traffic Management: Handles traffic spikes during album releases Zero-Downtime Deployments: Enables rolling updates 3. API Layer (Web/Application Servers)​ Architecture: Stateless servers for horizontal scalability Authentication: JWT token validation Business Logic: Song metadata retrieval Signed URL generation for audio access User action tracking and analytics Reliability Patterns: Circuit breakers for database connections Connection pooling for resource management Fallback responses for non-critical features 4. Blob Storage (Object Storage)​ Technology: AWS S3 or similar object storage Organization: Hierarchical structure (/artist/album/song.ogg) Security: Time-limited signed URLs (few hours expiration) Benefits: Virtually unlimited scalability Built-in durability and regional replication Cost-effective for large files Trade-offs: Higher latency compared to local storage Potential egress cost implications

paths can be optimized with materialized views Archive Strategy: Old play history can be moved to cold storage

Why SQL Database?: Complex relationships requiring JOINs Referential integrity to prevent orphaned records ACID properties for consistent data operations Strong consistency requirements for metadata Performance Optimizations: Indexes for Common Queries: -- Fast search capabilities with fuzzy matching CREATE INDEX idx_songs_title_trigram ON Songs USING gin(title gin_trgm_ops); CREATE INDEX idx_artists_name_trigram ON Artists USING gin(name gin_trgm_ops); -- Playlist performance optimization CREATE INDEX idx_playlist_items_playlist_id ON PlaylistItems(playlist_id); CREATE INDEX idx_playlist_items_song_id ON PlaylistItems(song_id); -- User queries optimization CREATE INDEX idx_playlists_user_id ON Playlists(user_id); CREATE INDEX idx_songs_play_count ON Songs(play_count DESC); Trigram Indexes: Enable fast text search with typo tolerance and partial matching capabilities that users expect in search functionality.

Phase 1: User Interaction & Authentication (Steps 1-4)​ User Action: User taps the play button on a song UI Request: Mobile app sends authenticated request to API Load Balancing: Request routed to healthy API server Authentication: JWT token validated for user permissions Phase 2: Metadata Retrieval (Steps 5-8)​ Database Query: API fetches song metadata (title, artist, duration) URL Generation: Signed URL created for secure audio access (2-hour expiration) Response Formation: JSON response with metadata and streaming URL UI Update: Song information displayed to user Phase 3: Audio Streaming Setup (Steps 9-13)​ Progressive Loading: Audio streaming begins while UI updates CDN Request: First audio chunk requested from global CDN Cache Strategy: CDN serves from cache or fetches from S3 Content Delivery: Audio chunks delivered to mobile app Playback Start: Music begins playing immediately Phase 4: Continuous Streaming & Analytics (Steps 14-17)​ Buffer Management: App continuously requests next audio segments Analytics Tracking: Play progress sent every 30 seconds Play Count Updates: Database updated for recommendation engine Quality Adaptation: Bitrate adjusted based on network conditions

Latency Reduction​ CDN Edge Caching: Popular songs served from nearest edge location Parallel Processing: Metadata and audio streaming happen concurrently Progressive Loading: Song starts playing while buffering upcoming content Signed URLs: Direct CDN access bypasses API servers for audio delivery User Experience Enhancements​ Immediate Feedback: UI updates instantly on play button press Adaptive Quality: Automatic bitrate switching prevents buffering Offline Preparation: Recent songs cached locally for instant replay Error Recovery: Graceful handling of network interruptions Cost Optimization​ CDN Efficiency: Reduces origin server bandwidth costs Smart Caching: Popular content cached at multiple edge locations Connection Pooling: Efficient database connection management Analytics Batching: Play tracking data sent in optimized intervals

Target Response Times: Time to First Byte: < 200ms for audio streaming API Response Time: < 100ms for metadata requests CDN Cache Hit Ratio: > 85% for popular content Playback Start Time: < 500ms from play button to audio Scalability Indicators: Concurrent Streams: System handles 100,000+ simultaneous users Global Reach: CDN serves from 150+ edge locations worldwide Database Performance: < 50ms average query response time Storage Efficiency: 99.99% uptime for audio content delivery

Network Issues: Automatic retry with exponential backoff Quality degradation to maintain playback Local cache fallback for recently played songs Server Failures: Load balancer routes to healthy instances Database replica failover for read operations CDN automatically fetches from origin on cache miss Authentication Problems: Token refresh mechanisms Graceful degradation to guest mode Clear error messaging for user action This complete user journey demonstrates how Spotify's architecture prioritizes user experience through optimized data flow, intelligent caching, and robust error handling while maintaining scalability and cost efficiency.

Benefits: Global Distribution: Popular songs cached at edge locations worldwide Reduced Latency: European users served from European edge servers Cost Optimization: Reduced origin server load and bandwidth costs Improved User Experience: Faster load times and reduced buffering Cache Management: Eviction Policy: Least Recently Used (LRU) for automatic cache management Cache Miss Handling: Automatic fetch from origin storage Security: CDN uses signed URLs for secure content access Geographic Example: Song cached in Germany serves European users much faster than fetching from US origin storage.

Leader-Follower Replication​ Architecture: Leader: Handles all write operations (uploads, playlist changes) Followers: Handle read traffic (searches, metadata lookups) Read Bias: Music streaming is heavily read-dominant Benefits: Horizontal read scaling by adding followers Automatic failover capabilities Cost-effective scaling for read-heavy workloads Challenges: Replication Lag: Followers may be slightly behind leader Consistency Issues: Users might not immediately see their writes Operational Complexity: Managing multiple database instances Sharding Strategies​ When to Consider: Catalog growth beyond single database capacity Hot partitions causing performance bottlenecks Need for geographic data locality Sharding Options: Geographic Sharding: US users → US shard EU users → EU shard Benefits: Regulatory compliance, reduced latency Challenge: Global artists popular everywhere Artist ID Range Sharding: Artists 1-1000 → Shard 1 Artists 1001-2000 → Shard 2 Benefits: Even distribution, predictable routing Challenge: Popular artists creating hot shards Trade-offs: Pros: Horizontal scalability, improved performance Cons: Cross-shard queries expensive, loss of foreign keys, complex rebalancing

Stateless Server Design: No session state stored locally JWT tokens for authentication Database connections via connection pooling Auto-Scaling Benefits: Traffic Adaptability: Handle morning commutes and evening listening spikes Cost Efficiency: Scale up during peak hours, down during off-peak Fault Tolerance: Server failures don't impact overall availability Rolling Deployments: Zero-downtime updates Scaling Triggers: CPU utilization thresholds Request rate limits Response time degradation Queue depth monitoring

Phase 1: Single database, simple blob storage, basic CDN Phase 2: Add read replicas, implement caching Phase 3: Introduce sharding, global CDN, auto-scaling Phase 4: Microservices, advanced analytics, ML recommendations

Storage Architecture: Signed URLs vs Proxy Streaming: Signed URLs reduce API server load but provide less access control SQL vs NoSQL: SQL chosen for complex relationships and consistency requirements Blob Storage vs Distributed File System: Blob storage preferred for managed service benefits Scalability Trade-offs: Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling: Horizontal preferred for elasticity and fault tolerance Consistency vs Availability: Eventual consistency acceptable for non-critical features Cost vs Performance: CDN costs justified by user experience improvements

Audio Dominates Resources: Storage and bandwidth costs primarily driven by audio content, not metadata Read-Heavy Architecture: Music streaming is predominantly read-intensive, informing scaling strategies Geographic Considerations: Global content distribution requires regional CDN and data locality Gradual Complexity: Start with simple architecture and add complexity as scale demands Fault Tolerance Essential: Multiple fallback mechanisms required for reliable audio streaming Cost Optimization: CDN and efficient encoding critical for managing bandwidth costs

This document covers the comprehensive testing strategy used in the Next.js for Production project, including unit tests, integration tests, end-to-end tests, and performance testing.

Our testing approach follows the testing pyramid: Unit Tests (70%): Fast, isolated tests for individual components and functions Integration Tests (20%): Tests for component interactions and API endpoints End-to-End Tests (10%): Full user journey tests across the entire application
Vitest: Modern testing framework with TypeScript support Testing Library: Component testing utilities MSW: API mocking for isolated tests jsdom: Browser environment simulation
Playwright: Cross-browser E2E testing Custom Helpers: Reusable test utilities Visual Regression: Screenshot comparison testing
Artillery: Load and performance testing Lighthouse CI: Performance metrics automation

Arrange: Set up test data and conditions Act: Execute the code being tested Assert: Verify the expected outcome
Use descriptive test names that explain the scenario Follow the pattern: "should [expected behavior] when [condition]"
Each test should be independent and not rely on other tests Use proper setup and teardown for test isolation
Mock API calls, database operations, and third-party services Use MSW for API mocking in tests
Use factories or fixtures for test data generation Keep test data minimal and focused on the test scenario
Use specific assertions rather than generic ones Test behavior, not implementation details

This document outlines the threat model for the e-commerce application based on the provided C4 model and architecture diagrams. The model uses the STRIDE methodology (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege) to identify and mitigate threats at each layer of the system.
Before analyzing threats, let's identify what we're protecting (assets) and where the system's trust levels change (boundaries).

Data: Customer PII: Names, addresses, contact info (from UserService). Authentication Data: Password hashes, refresh tokens, user IDs (from AuthService, PostgreSQL, Redis). Payment Data: Payment method tokens/references (from PaymentService). Business Data: Order history, product details, sales analytics (from OrderService, ProductService). Infrastructure & Code: API Keys: Secrets for Auth0, Stripe, SendGrid, and Cloud Storage. CI/CD Pipeline: The ability to build and deploy code (GitHub Actions, ArgoCD). System Availability: The ability of the platform to remain online and process orders.

Internet ↔ Cloud Armor/LB: The primary external boundary. Untrusted users (Customers, Admins) interact with the system. Web App ↔ API Gateway: The boundary between the client-side browser and the server-side backend. API Gateway ↔ Microservices: An internal boundary. The gateway is the single entry point, but services must trust (or verify) that requests from it are legitimate. Microservices ↔ Data Layer: The boundary between the application logic and its state (databases, caches, queues). Microservices ↔ External APIs: The boundary where your system calls out to third-party services (Auth0, Stripe, SendGrid). DevOps Pipeline ↔ GKE Cluster: A critical administrative boundary. The CI/CD system has privileged access to deploy applications.
Here is a breakdown of potential threats (STRIDE) for each major component and boundary, along with planned and recommended mitigations.

This layer is the first line of defense against all external traffic. [S] Spoofing: An attacker impersonates a user via session hijacking. Mitigation (Planned): Use of JWTs. Mitigation (Recommended): Store tokens in Secure, HttpOnly cookies to prevent access from client-side scripts (XSS). Implement strict CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) protection. [T] Tampering: An attacker intercepts and modifies traffic (Man-in-the-Middle). Mitigation (Planned): Global HTTP(S) Load Balancer. Mitigation (Recommended): Enforce HTTPS-only traffic with HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) headers. [I] Information Disclosure: Client-side code in the Next.js app or Microfrontends leaks sensitive information (e.g., internal API paths, non-public keys). Mitigation (Recommended): Use Next.js environment variables correctly (prefixing with NEXT_PUBLIC_ only for non-sensitive, public-facing keys). All other keys must be server-side only. [D] Denial of Service: An attacker floods the application with traffic (L3/L4 or L7 DDoS). Mitigation (Planned): Cloud Armor (WAF & DDoS Protection) and Rate Limiter (in API Gateway). Mitigation (Recommended): Configure Cloud Armor rules to block known-bad IPs and geographic locations. Implement CDN caching via Cloud Storage for all static assets to reduce origin load. [E] Elevation of Privilege: An attacker injects a malicious script via Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) to steal a user's or admin's session cookie/token. Mitigation (Planned): React automatically escapes content, providing a baseline defense. Mitigation (Recommended): Implement a strict Content Security Policy (CSP) header to control which scripts, styles, and media can be loaded. Sanitize all user-generated content (e.g., product reviews, user profiles) before rendering.
documents.s: Component 1: Public-Facing & Edge (Web App, LB, Cloud Armor)

documents.t: This is the central chokepoint for all backend logic. [S] Spoofing: An attacker forges a JWT or replays a stolen one. Mitigation (Planned): JWT Middleware validates the token's signature, expiration (exp), and issuer (iss). Mitigation (Recommended): Use short-lived access tokens (e.g., 15 minutes) and longer-lived refresh tokens. Store refresh tokens in Redis (as hinted by your diagram) to allow for instant revocation (logout) or to detect token reuse. [T] Tampering: An attacker modifies a request payload after it passes the firewall (e.g., changing quantity to a negative number). Mitigation (Recommended): Implement rigorous DTO (Data Transfer Object) validation in NestJS (using class-validator) on all incoming requests at the controller level. [R] Repudiation: An admin or user denies performing a critical action (e.g., "I never deleted that product"). Mitigation (Planned): Request Logger (Audit & Monitoring). Mitigation (Recommended): Ensure logs capture the authenticated userId, source IP, timestamp, and the full request body for all state-changing operations (POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH). [D] Denial of Service: An attacker bypasses Cloud Armor with requests that are valid but resource-intensive (e.g., a complex search query). Mitigation (Planned): Rate Limiter (Request Throttling). Mitigation (Recommended): Implement rate limiting based on IP, user ID, and API key. Add pagination and complexity limits to all list/search endpoints (e.g., ProductController). [E] Elevation of Privilege: A regular user attempts to access an admin-only endpoint (e.g., /api/products/delete/123). Mitigation (Planned): Auth Guard (checks for authentication) and Role Guard (checks for authorization/RBAC). This is the correct approach. Mitigation (Recommended): Ensure the RoleGuard is applied to all sensitive endpoints and that roles are derived from the validated JWT, not from a parameter in the request body.

These components trust requests from the API Gateway. [S] Spoofing: A compromised microservice (e.g., NotificationService) calls another microservice directly (e.g., OrderService), bypassing the API Gateway's authorization. Mitigation (Recommended): Do not allow direct inter-service communication by default. If required, implement service-to-service authentication (e.g., mutual TLS (mTLS) within the GKE cluster or signed internal-use-only JWTs). [T] Tampering: An attacker finds a way to inject malicious data into the Message Queue (Kafka), (e.g., a fake "payment_success" event). Mitigation (Recommended): Secure Kafka topics with ACLs. Only the PaymentService pod's service account should have write access to payment topics. All consuming services (OrderService, NotificationService) must validate the schema of incoming messages before processing. [I] Information Disclosure: A microservice leaks internal data in an error message (e.g., ProductService returns a full database stack trace). Mitigation (Planned): NestJS framework conventions. Mitigation (Recommended): Implement global exception filters in each microservice to catch all unhandled errors and return a standardized, generic error message. Log the full details internally for debugging. [E] Elevation of Privilege: An attacker exploits an Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR). For example, an authenticated user A calls /api/orders/123 (their own order) but then changes the request to /api/orders/124 (user B's order). Mitigation (Recommended): This is a critical business logic flaw. The OrderService (and UserService, etc.) must not trust the ID from the URL alone. It must perform a check like: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 124 AND user_id = {authenticated_user_id_from_jwt}.

This is where your most valuable assets are stored. [T] Tampering: An attacker gains database access and modifies data directly (e.g., changes an order status to "Shipped"). Mitigation (Planned): Cloud SQL is in a separate data namespace. Mitigation (Recommended): Network: Use private IP for Cloud SQL and configure firewall rules so it only accepts connections from your GKE pod network. Auth: Do not use static database passwords. Use GCP Workload Identity to map GKE service accounts (e.g., order-service-sa) to GCP service accounts that have IAM permissions to access Cloud SQL. ORM: The use of TypeORM is a good defense against SQL Injection. [I] Information Disclosure: A database backup or Cloud Storage bucket is made public. Redis cache is exposed, leaking session tokens. Mitigation (Recommended): Storage: Enforce "Encryption at Rest" (default on GCP, but verify). Make all Cloud Storage buckets private by default. Use signed URLs for temporary access to media if needed. Redis: Deploy Redis within the GKE private network. Enable Redis authentication (AUTH command) with a strong password stored in a secret manager. [D] Denial of Service: A malicious query to Elasticsearch overloads the search cluster. Mitigation (Planned): Elasticsearch is used by ProductService. Mitigation (Recommended): The ProductService must sanitize, validate, and place limits on all search parameters (e.g., max query length, no leading wildcards) before passing them to Elasticsearch.

Your system is vulnerable to threats originating from or targeting these external partners. [S] Spoofing: An attacker sends a fake webhook to your PaymentService, spoofing a successful payment from Stripe. Mitigation (Recommended): Validate all webhook signatures. Stripe (and most other providers) includes a signature in the request headers. Your service must verify this signature using your shared secret before trusting the payload. [I] Information Disclosure: Your secret API keys for Stripe, Auth0, or SendGrid are leaked (e.g., committed to Git). Mitigation (Planned): Use of SonarQube (SAST) can help detect this. Mitigation (Recommended): Store all secrets in GCP Secret Manager. Use Workload Identity to grant GKE pods access to read specific secrets at runtime. Never store secrets in config files, environment variables in your Git repo, or Docker images. [R] Repudiation: Auth0 claims they never authenticated a user, or Stripe claims a payment was never made. Mitigation (Recommended): Log all outgoing API requests and the core details of the incoming responses (e.g., stripe_charge_id, auth0_user_id). This provides an audit trail for dispute resolution.

A compromised pipeline means a compromised application. [T] Tampering: An attacker with access to your GitHub repo injects malicious code into a branch, which is then automatically built and deployed by ArgoCD. Mitigation (Planned): GitHub Actions CI/CD, ArgoCD (GitOps), SonarQube (SAST), OWASP ZAP (DAST). Mitigation (Recommended): GitHub: Enforce branch protection rules on main. Require PRs, mandatory code reviews from at least one other developer, and successful SonarQube and ZAP scans before merging. Image Security: Scan Docker images for known vulnerabilities (e.g., with GCR's built-in scanner or a tool like Trivy) before they are deployed. [E] Elevation of Privilege: An attacker compromises a GitHub Actions runner or ArgoCD and uses its credentials to take over the GKE cluster. Mitigation (Recommended): Apply the principle of least privilege. The service account used by ArgoCD should only have permission to deploy to the Frontend and Backend namespaces, not kube-system or default. The GitHub Actions service account should only have permissions to push images to GCR and trigger ArgoCD syncs.

Your architecture has many strong, modern controls. The highest-priority risks to address are in business logic and configuration. Implement IDOR Protection: Ensure every microservice validates that the authenticated user (sub from JWT) is authorized to access or modify the specific resource they are requesting (e.g., their own order, their own profile). Validate All Webhooks: This is non-negotiable. Use signature validation for Stripe and any other webhook provider. Secure All Secrets: Use GCP Secret Manager + Workload Identity. Remove all static keys and passwords from code, configs, and environment variables. Enforce Strict CI/CD Security: Use GitHub branch protection rules. A PR and a successful security scan (SAST/DAST) must be mandatory to merge to main. Implement Service-to-Service Auth: If microservices need to call each other directly, secure that internal traffic with mTLS or internal JWTs. Apply a Strict CSP: This is your best defense against XSS, which is a primary vector for session/token theft.

You have just learned the basics of Docusaurus and made some changes to the initial template. Docusaurus has much more to offer! Have 5 more minutes? Take a look at versioning and i18n. Anything unclear or buggy in this tutorial? Please report it!

Read the official documentation Modify your site configuration with docusaurus.config.js Add navbar and footer items with themeConfig Add a custom Design and Layout Add a search bar Find inspirations in the Docusaurus showcase Get involved in the Docusaurus Community
Docusaurus creates a page for each blog post, but also a blog index page, a tag system, an RSS feed...

Create a file at blog/2021-02-28-greetings.md: blog/2021-02-28-greetings.md --- slug: greetings title: Greetings! authors: - name: Joel Marcey title: Co-creator of Docusaurus 1 url: https://github.com/JoelMarcey image_url: https://github.com/JoelMarcey.png - name: Sébastien Lorber title: Docusaurus maintainer url: https://sebastienlorber.com image_url: https://github.com/slorber.png tags: [greetings] --- Congratulations, you have made your first post! Feel free to play around and edit this post as much as you like. A new blog post is now available at http://localhost:3000/blog/greetings.
Documents are groups of pages connected through: a sidebar previous/next navigation versioning
Create a Markdown file at docs/hello.md: docs/hello.md # Hello This is my **first Docusaurus document**! A new document is now available at http://localhost:3000/docs/hello.

Docusaurus automatically creates a sidebar from the docs folder. Add metadata to customize the sidebar label and position: docs/hello.md --- sidebar_label: 'Hi!' sidebar_position: 3 --- # Hello This is my **first Docusaurus document**! It is also possible to create your sidebar explicitly in sidebars.js: sidebars.js export default { tutorialSidebar: [ 'intro', 'hello', { type: 'category', label: 'Tutorial', items: ['tutorial-basics/create-a-document'], }, ], };
Add Markdown or React files to src/pages to create a standalone page: src/pages/index.js → localhost:3000/ src/pages/foo.md → localhost:3000/foo src/pages/foo/bar.js → localhost:3000/foo/bar

Create a file at src/pages/my-react-page.js: src/pages/my-react-page.js import React from 'react'; import Layout from '@theme/Layout'; export default function MyReactPage() { return (

My React page

This is a React page

 ); } A new page is now available at http://localhost:3000/my-react-page.
Create a file at src/pages/my-markdown-page.md: src/pages/my-markdown-page.md # My Markdown page This is a Markdown page A new page is now available at http://localhost:3000/my-markdown-page.
Docusaurus is a static-site-generator (also called Jamstack). It builds your site as simple static HTML, JavaScript and CSS files.
Build your site for production: npm run build The static files are generated in the build folder.

Test your production build locally: npm run serve The build folder is now served at http://localhost:3000/. You can now deploy the build folder almost anywhere easily, for free or very small cost (read the Deployment Guide).
Docusaurus supports Markdown and a few additional features.

Markdown documents have metadata at the top called Front Matter: my-doc.md --- id: my-doc-id title: My document title description: My document description slug: /my-custom-url --- ## Markdown heading Markdown text with [links](./hello.md)

Regular Markdown links are supported, using url paths or relative file paths. Let's see how to [Create a page](/create-a-page). Let's see how to [Create a page](./create-a-page.md). Result: Let's see how to Create a page.

Regular Markdown images are supported. You can use absolute paths to reference images in the static directory (static/img/docusaurus.png): ![Docusaurus logo](/img/docusaurus.png) You can reference images relative to the current file as well. This is particularly useful to colocate images close to the Markdown files using them: ![Docusaurus logo](./img/docusaurus.png)

Markdown code blocks are supported with Syntax highlighting. ```jsx title="src/components/HelloDocusaurus.js" function HelloDocusaurus() { return

Hello, Docusaurus!

; } ``` src/components/HelloDocusaurus.js function HelloDocusaurus() { return

Hello, Docusaurus!

; }

Docusaurus has a special syntax to create admonitions and callouts: :::tip[My tip] Use this awesome feature option ::: :::danger[Take care] This action is dangerous ::: My tip Use this awesome feature option Take care This action is dangerous

MDX can make your documentation more interactive and allows using any React components inside Markdown: export const Highlight = ({children, color}) => ( { alert(`You clicked the color ${color} with label ${children}`) }}> {children} ); This is Docusaurus green ! This is Facebook blue ! This is Docusaurus green ! This is Facebook blue !
Docusaurus can manage multiple versions of your docs.

Release a version 1.0 of your project: npm run docusaurus docs:version 1.0 The docs folder is copied into versioned_docs/version-1.0 and versions.json is created. Your docs now have 2 versions: 1.0 at http://localhost:3000/docs/ for the version 1.0 docs current at http://localhost:3000/docs/next/ for the upcoming, unreleased docs

To navigate seamlessly across versions, add a version dropdown. Modify the docusaurus.config.js file: docusaurus.config.js export default { themeConfig: { navbar: { items: [ { type: 'docsVersionDropdown', }, ], }, }, }; The docs version dropdown appears in your navbar:

It is possible to edit versioned docs in their respective folder: versioned_docs/version-1.0/hello.md updates http://localhost:3000/docs/hello docs/hello.md updates http://localhost:3000/docs/next/hello
Modify docusaurus.config.js to add support for the fr locale: docusaurus.config.js export default { i18n: { defaultLocale: 'en', locales: ['en', 'fr'], }, };

Copy the docs/intro.md file to the i18n/fr folder: mkdir -p i18n/fr/docusaurus-plugin-content-docs/current/ cp docs/intro.md i18n/fr/docusaurus-plugin-content-docs/current/intro.md Translate i18n/fr/docusaurus-plugin-content-docs/current/intro.md in French.

Start your site on the French locale: npm run start -- --locale fr Your localized site is accessible at http://localhost:3000/fr/ and the Getting Started page is translated. caution In development, you can only use one locale at a time.

To navigate seamlessly across languages, add a locale dropdown. Modify the docusaurus.config.js file: docusaurus.config.js export default { themeConfig: { navbar: { items: [ { type: 'localeDropdown', }, ], }, }, }; The locale dropdown now appears in your navbar:
Build your site for a specific locale: npm run build -- --locale fr Or build your site to include all the locales at once: npm run build
